The intracellular chloride difference increases during stimulation, whilst the weaker apical electrochemical driving force in the knockout reduces chloride export and fluid secretion. The analysis also identifies the alkalinity requirement of sustained Ae4 transport and quantifies the additional NKCC1 and Ae2 transport needed to compensate for its loss. These results support intracellular chloride availability as a mechanism linking Ae4 loss to reduced salivary secretion.
affiliations: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology Graduate University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Xrp1 integrates cellular stress through different control modes in Drosophila
papers.abstract: Cells and tissues have the ability to respond to different stresses and maintain their homeostasis. The b-Zip transcription factor Xrp1 was found to play a pivotal role in this context in Drosophila. Xrp1 is required for the response to irradiation, in genetic conditions of ribosomal protein (Rp) deficiency leading to cell competition, and more generally in mediating the Integrated Stress Response (ISR). However, how these diverse stresses converge to and activate Xrp1 is still unclear. Our results demonstrate the existence of three separate mechanisms of Xrp1 induction. In response to Rp stress, a short isoform of Xrp1 is produced and requires the function of the ribosomal protein RpS12. In response to irradiation, a specific mRNA isoform is transcriptionally induced, which encodes the Xrp1-short protein isoform, in a p53-dependent manner. In response to the ISR, the long isoform of Xrp1 is translated by the derepression of a uORF present on the Xrp1 5'UTR, a mechanism that requires eIF2 phosphorylation, RpS12, and a transcriptional induction by ATF4. Therefore, our work provides a comprehensive understanding of the role of Xrp1 in different situations of cellular stress, illustrating the complex level of integration of the mechanisms controlling this central gene.
affiliations: CRBM, Univ Montpellier, CNRS (corresponding author)

papers.title: Intrinsically disordered regions influence protein motif usage in Drosophila Ubx and AbdA Hox proteins
papers.abstract: Hox proteins are evolutionary conserved transcription factors guiding morphogenesis in all bilaterian animals. Conservation mainly concerns the homeodomain (HD), a helix-turn-helix DNA binding motif and flanking sequences close by. Besides, sequences are poorly conserved and disordered. Here we investigate how poorly conserved Intrinsically Disordered Regions (IDRs) influence Hox protein activity, focusing on a closely related Drosophila Hox pair and using a wide range of in vivo function. Studying Drosophila Ultrabithorax (Ubx) and AbdominalA (AbdA) proteins, we find that conserved protein motifs close to the HD are differently used in Ubx and AbdA. Coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations identify a large set of intra-molecular interactions, notably involving poorly conserved disordered regions upstream and downstream the HD. Swapping these regions in Ubx and AbdA alters protein functions and switches motif dependency in some biological situations. This suggests that IDRs, predicted to mediate large and dynamic sets of intramolecular interactions, influence protein motif usage in a context dependent manner.
affiliations: Aix-Marseille Univ, CNRS, Developmental Biology Institute of Marseille (IBDM), IBDM-UMR 7288, Case 907, Parc Scientifique de Luminy, Marseille Cedex 09 13288, F (corresponding author)

papers.title: KDM6A Haploinsufficiency Is Insufficient to Disrupt Cochlear Structure and Auditory Function in Mouse Models of Kabuki Syndrome Type 2
papers.abstract: Objective: Kabuki syndrome type 2 (KS2) is a rare X-linked disorder caused by pathogenic variants in KDM6A and is frequently associated with hearing impairment. Because auditory phenotypes include sensorineural, conductive, and mixed hearing loss, we examined whether Kdm6a deficiency directly impairs cochlear morphology or auditory function in mice. Methods: We generated Nestin-Cre; Kdm6a conditional mutants and a germline-derived global Kdm6a deletion model using Sox2-Cre-mediated germline recombination. Auditory function and cochlear morphology were assessed by auditory brainstem responses (ABRs), distortion product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAEs), and histological analyses. Results: Whole-body hemizygous or homozygous Kdm6a deletion resulted in embryonic lethality. Analyses therefore focused on Nestin-Cre; Kdm6aflox/Y males and females carrying a germline-derived heterozygous Kdm6a deletion. In Nestin-Cre mutants, ABR thresholds, wave I amplitudes and latencies, and DPOAE measures at 8, 16, and 32 kHz were comparable with littermate controls at 4 and 8 weeks. In heterozygous deletion females, ABR thresholds, wave I amplitudes and latencies at 4-64 kHz and DPOAE measures at 8, 16, and 32 kHz were comparable with male and female wild-type controls. No overt cochlear pathology was observed in either model. Conclusion: Kdm6a deficiency in the viable mouse models examined did not produce overt cochlear pathology or baseline auditory dysfunction. These findings suggest that partial Kdm6a loss alone is insufficient to produce a robust primary cochlear phenotype in young mice and highlight the potential contributions of non-cochlear, developmental, central, and later-onset mechanisms to hearing impairment in KS2. Clinically, these findings support careful evaluation for potentially treatable middle-ear disease.
affiliations: University of Florida (corresponding author)

papers.title: A comprehensive genetic study of the vaginal microbiota composition of Holstein cows
papers.abstract: The vaginal microbiota is a potentially important component of the bovine reproductive tract and has been associated with fertility, health, and production-related traits in cattle. However, the impact of host genetics on the bovine vaginal microbiota and its genetic correlations with animal performance remain largely unexplored. To investigate this, we performed a comprehensive genetic study of the vaginal microbiota in Holstein cows. Vaginal swabs from 681 lactating cows across 18 herds in Northern France were collected, along with records of fertility, milk production, and health traits. The microbiota samples were sequenced for the 16S rRNA gene, generating count tables of amplicon sequence variants (ASV). We estimated genetic parameters for vaginal microbiota -diversity (Chao1, Shannon, and Simpson indices) and {beta}-diversity (Bray-Curtis dissimilarity matrix), as well as the centered log-ratio (CLR)-transformed abundances of taxa present in more than 50% of samples. Across the 173 analyzed taxa, heritability estimates ranged from low to moderate (h2 = 0.09 to 0.38) for five genera, three families, eight orders, three classes, and one phylum. Notably, the order Flavobacteriales exhibited the highest heritability estimate. The study also highlighted genetic correlations between heritable microbiota traits and host phenotypes related to fertility, production, and health. Sequence-based genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identified biologically relevant signals, including a quantitative trait locus (QTL) for the genus Alloprevotella on chromosome 6, with lead variants located within the NAF1 gene. Additionally, two signals on chromosome 17 for the Bacteroidales order and the Bacteroida class co-localized with IL15. Our findings show that host genetics contributes to variation in specific components of the bovine vaginal microbiota and suggest that microbiome-related traits may warrant further investigation as potential indicators in dairy cattle breeding and management research.
affiliations: Université Paris-Saclay, INRAE, AgroParisTech, GABI, Jouy-en-Josas, 78350, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: From variants to networks: resolving low SNP overlap in dairy cattle meta-analysis through multi-level functional mapping
papers.abstract: The objective of this study was to perform a systematic review and multi-level meta-analysis of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) for functional traits in dairy cattle, focusing on calving performance and udder health. We hypothesized that despite the limited replication of individual SNPs across independent studies, functionally related variants would converge on common genes, biological pathways, and genomic regions. Following a systematic literature search and a two-stage filtering process, we extracted data from 20 independent articles covering seven traits: direct and maternal calving ease, direct and maternal stillbirth, clinical mastitis, somatic cell count, and somatic cell score. We first conducted a conventional SNP-level meta-analysis, which demonstrated minimal variant overlap across studies, preventing the detection of significant pooled effects. To resolve this low overlap, we mapped the associated variants to higher organizational levels, including genes, proteins, KEGG and Reactome pathways, and quantitative trait loci (QTL), and combined the statistical evidence using Fishers method. This multi-level functional mapping revealed significant biological convergence. At the gene level, we identified shared genes such as CCDC170 linking maternal calving ease and maternal stillbirth, while DCK, TMPRSS11F, and SLC4A4 were significant for udder health traits. Pathway-level meta-analysis highlighted major functional networks, demonstrating that mastitis-related traits were strongly associated with immune response, signal transduction, and cellular stress pathways, whereas maternal calving traits were dominated by endocrine and calcium signaling. Furthermore, our cross-trait overlap analysis identified 35 shared pathways and 30 shared QTL, reflecting a common biological architecture connecting calving difficulties and mastitis susceptibility. Notably, the innate immune system and signal transduction pathways consistently overlapped across multiple functional traits. In conclusion, conventional SNP-level meta-analysis has limited utility for integrating dairy cattle GWAS due to insufficient cross-study marker overlap. Moving from individual variants toward higher-order functional units effectively reveals reproducible genetic signals and functional convergence. The identified genes, biological pathways, and genomic regions offer valuable insights that can be leveraged as biological priors to improve genomic prediction models for dairy cattle health and reproduction.
affiliations: Wroclaw University of Enviromental and Life Sciences (corresponding author)

papers.title: ALS-associated mutations reveal a conserved C-terminal self-assembly module in the TDP-43 low-complexity domain
papers.abstract: TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) is an RNA-binding protein whose low-complexity domain (LCD) mediates self-assembly, liquid-liquid phase separation, and pathological aggregation associated with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). Previous studies have established the central ultraconserved region (UCR) of the LCD as a major determinant of TDP-43 self-association. However, the contribution of the evolutionarily conserved C-terminal region remains poorly understood. To identify LCD residues required for self-assembly, we systematically analyzed 47 ALS-associated substitutions distributed throughout the TDP-43 LCD using hydrogel-binding and thioflavin T (ThT) assays. Several ALS-associated substitutions within the C-terminal conserved region (CCR) markedly reduced hydrogel incorporation and impaired fibrillization. Similar assembly defects were observed for methionine-to-serine substitutions at two conserved CCR residues, M405 and M414. Furthermore, CCR-containing C-terminal fragments encompassing residues 360-414 or 379-414 formed ThT-positive fibrillar assemblies in vitro. The assembly kinetics exhibited a characteristic lag phase followed by rapid fluorescence growth, consistent with the formation of cross-{beta}-rich assemblies. These findings identify the CCR as an additional conserved self-assembly module within the TDP-43 LCD and expand the prevailing UCR-centered model of TDP-43 assembly. The observation that multiple ALS-associated substitutions reduce rather than enhance self-association further raises the possibility that disruption of normal TDP-43 assembly contributes to disease pathogenesis.
affiliations: University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Strategies for Overcoming the Purification Challenges of Meis1 and HoxA9 and Their Functional Characterization
papers.abstract: Transcription factors are critical regulators of homeostasis, and disruption of their function is a common underlying mechanism in cancer. The homeobox Myeloid ecotropic integration site-1 (Meis1) and its binding partner Homeobox A9 (HoxA9) are among the most highly dysregulated transcription factors in cancer, particularly in Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML). Upregulation of HoxA9 is observed in more than 50% of AML cases and is a predictor of poor prognosis. Meis1 forms a cooperative DNA complex with HoxA9 and is required for HoxA9-mediated leukemogenesis. However, the mechanism by which HoxA9 and Meis1 interact and form a complex with DNA is unknown. To study the molecular mechanisms behind the HoxA9-Meis1-DNA complex and support future development of inhibitors, we describe optimized procedures for the recombinant expression and purification of full-length Meis1 and HoxA9. The constructs with an N-terminal His-tag showed degradation, but the addition of a small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO)-fusion tag improved solubility and stability for both proteins. Conditions were optimized for SUMO cleavage to obtain tag-free Meis1 and HoxA9 with high purity. We showed that both purified proteins bound to DNA with nanomolar affinities using a fluorescence polarization (FP) binding assay. The SUMO-fusion HoxA9 showed a distinct binding profile compared to the tag-free HoxA9 and formed a cooperative complex with Meis1. The tag-free HoxA9 appeared to oligomerize under the assay conditions. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report to visualize the HoxA9-Meis1 cooperative interaction in a high-throughput assay. Our work establishes a foundation for future studies to decipher the protein-protein interaction of Meis1-HoxA9 and the development of inhibitors.
affiliations: West Virginia University (corresponding author)

papers.title: The role of a G-quadruplex structure in mediating the interactions of miR-1249-3p with the 3-UTR of the HNRNPK mRNA
papers.abstract: Heterogenous nuclear riboprotein K (hnRNP K) is an important regulator of multiple signaling pathways involved in DNA repair and function whose expression has been found to be mis-regulated in many cancers and neurological diseases. The expression regulation of hnRNP K is not fully understood however it has been shown that the microRNA miR-1249-3p targets its mRNA 3-untranslated region (UTR), regulating its translation. In this study we identified a guanosine-rich sequence in the HNRNPK 3-UTR within the miR-1249-3p binding site that has the potential to form a G-quadruplex (GQ) structure. By using various biophysical methods, we show that this sequence forms a parallel GQ structure which modulates the binding of miR-1249-3p to HNRNPK 3-UTR in vitro. Additionally, using luciferase reporter assays, we determined that this GQ structure affects the hnRNP K protein expression, suggesting modulation of the binding interaction of miR-1249-3p to the 3-UTR of HNRNPK. This HNRNPK mRNA GQ-miR binding axis is an unexplored mechanism of regulation, offering a novel therapeutic target for diseases caused by abnormal hnRNP K expression.
affiliations: Duquesne University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Triacylglycerol fatty acid composition modulates ATGL regioselectivity and diacylglycerol output
papers.abstract: Adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL) catalyses the first and rate-limiting step of intracellular triacylglycerol (TAG) hydrolysis, yielding diacylglycerol (DAG) and a free fatty acid (FA). The site of TAG cleavage determines the regioisomeric identity of the DAG product, with distinct consequences for downstream signalling and lipid metabolism. Here, we show that ATGL prefers specific fatty acyl chain lengths and that this preference contributes to its regioselectivity on heterogeneous TAG substrates. Structural modelling identified a substrate-binding pocket comprising a hydrophilic anchor and a hydrophobic tunnel whose dimensions favour long-chain FAs. Mass spectrometry-based analysis of DAG products generated by ATGL from defined TAG substrates revealed an intrinsic preference for terminal (sn-1/sn-3) ester bond cleavage. Acyl-chain compatibility modulated this preference, with poorly accommodated terminal chains increasing the relative contribution of sn-2 cleavage. Consequently, ATGL generated predominantly sn-2-retaining DAG species from heterogeneous TAG substrates containing long-chain fatty acyl chains, including substantial amounts of the sn-1,2-DAG regioisomer, which has not previously been associated with ATGL activity. These findings link the fatty acyl chain composition of TAGs to the DAG regioisomer profile generated by ATGL-mediated lipolysis and provide substrate-dependent parameters for more species-resolved models of lipid metabolism.
affiliations: University of Graz (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Tandem Fluorescent Rh1::eGFP mCherry Reporter Reveals Rhodopsin 1 Trafficking and Turnover In Vivo in Drosophila Photoreceptors
papers.abstract: Rhodopsin 1 (Rh1), the major visual pigment of Drosophila photoreceptors, requires a vitamin A-derived chromophore for proper folding, maturation and transport to the rhabdomere. While the endocytic trafficking of mature, light-activated Rh1 to endolysosomal compartments is well characterized, the fate of immature Rh1 during defective ER maturation remains unclear. Here, we developed a Rh1::eGFP-mCherry tandem reporter to monitor Rh1 localization and compartment acidification in vivo. Exploiting the acid stability of mCherry, this reporter enables visualization of Rh1 after delivery to acidic environments and complements conventional antibody-based approaches. Under physiological conditions, pH-dependent quenching of eGFP fluorescence distinguished rhabdomeric Rh1 from Rh1 in acidic endolysosomal compartments. In vitamin A-deficient flies, immature apo-Rh1 accumulated within Calnexin-positive ER membranes, where we identified discrete acidified subdomains characterized by loss of eGFP fluorescence while mCherry fluorescence persisted. These structures remained continuous with the ER but were distinct from conventional endolysosomal compartments, revealing previously unrecognized acidified ER domains associated with immature Rh1. Together, our findings identify acidified ER subdomains as a previously unrecognized stage in Rh1 quality control and establish Rh1::eGFP-mCherry as a robust in vivo reporter for investigating rhodopsin trafficking, maturation and turnover under physiological and disease-relevant conditions.
affiliations: Uni Hohenheim (corresponding author)

papers.title: Inter-unit variability and rapid depletion of 2,3-diphosphoglycerate in stored red blood cells: implications for transfusion practice in neurocritical care
papers.abstract: Red blood cell (RBC) transfusion aims to restore tissue oxygen delivery, yet a stored unit's capacity to unload oxygen depends on 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG), the principal allosteric modulator of hemoglobin-oxygen affinity. Randomized trials comparing fresher with older units have been consistently null, and all have used storage duration as the exposure variable. We asked whether storage age reflects the metabolic state of individual units. Twenty-four leukodepleted packed RBC units were sampled serially from day 3 to day 42 of standard cold storage. 2,3-DPG was quanti-fied by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) with isotopically labelled internal standards, pH was measured in parallel, and trajectories were modelled by linear mixed effects with unit-level random intercepts. At day 3, 2,3-DPG spanned a twenty-fold range across units of identical age (0.8-14.7 mol/g Hb; median 4.8): some were already near-depleted at the earliest sampled timepoint, while others retained near-physiological concentrations. This heterogeneity collapsed rapidly - median val-ues fell to 27% of day-3 levels by day 7 and by more than 90% by day 14 ({beta} = -0.298 mol/g Hb per day, p < 0.001) - and were below the limit of detection in most units af-ter day 17. pH declined monotonically to 6.40 {+/-} 0.04 by day 42 ({beta} = -0.0163 units per day, p < 0.001). Units of identical storage age therefore differ markedly in the metabo-lite that governs oxygen unloading, and virtually all are depleted long before the 42-day expiry, indicating that storage-age dichotomies misclassify the exposure they are intended to represent.
affiliations: Vall d'Hebron Institut de Recerca (VHIR) (corresponding author)

papers.title: FLEX-DBS: a flexible wireless platform for bilateral constant-current deep brain stimulation in freely moving rodents
papers.abstract: Background: Preclinical deep brain stimulation (DBS) in rodents is central to understanding how DBS works, but most rodent DBS is delivered through a tether, which constrains behavior, home-cage experiments and uninterrupted stimulation. Most long-runtime wireless mouse stimulators achieve their runtimes by setting stimulation parameters before or around implantation and operating from supplies of about 3 V. New method: FLEX-DBS (Flexible Deep Brain Stimulation) is a head-mounted, battery-powered stimulator that delivers bilateral constant-current stimulation from improved Howland current pumps on +/-5 V rails. Amplitude, pulse width and frequency are programmable in continuous and burst modes from an iOS application over Bluetooth Low Energy, and stimulation continues autonomously after the phone disconnects. The device measures 19.5 x 22.5 x 8.72 mm, weighs 3.71 g in operation and runs on two size-13 zinc-air cells, which are exchanged by briefly detaching the device, pausing stimulation only for the exchange. Results: Into a 1 k{Omega} bench load, delivered current increased approximately linearly with the amplitude setting and was repeatable from pulse to pulse, with an asymmetric biphasic waveform whose recovery phase ran at about one fifth of the stimulating amplitude. Battery current was 1.47-1.89 mA in standby and 3.15-3.42 mA during stimulation at amplitude settings of 60-400 A, giving a projected three days of continuous stimulation per pair of cells. Firmware v0.5 left a net charge of 26-35 % of the stimulating-phase charge per pulse into 1 k{Omega}. Into 47 k{Omega}, within the in vivo load range, stimulating current was compliance-limited at 93 A. Pulse-derived estimates of the effective load presented by five implanted platinum electrodes in three mice had weekly means of 43-54 k{Omega} over eight weeks (32-80 k{Omega} across individual sessions), placing the maximum regulated current near 90 A (81-101 A at the weekly means). Analysis of the current-pump network bounds load-dependent current error at 3-8% for these loads. In vivo, we delivered cingulate FLEX-DBS at high amplitude settings intended to evoke a robust stimulation-associated behavioral phenotype in six mice. Time spent immobile in an open field rose from 46.5% at baseline to 75.7% during stimulation (a 62.7% increase in the group mean) and remained elevated after stimulation ended; without a sham control, this increase cannot be separated from within-session habituation. Comparison with existing methods: Among the published wireless rodent stimulators compared here, several offer some of these capabilities, but none combines bilateral constant current output, real-time wireless control that continues as autonomous stimulation after disconnect, and both continuous and burst modes; FLEX-DBS does so at the cost of runtime measured in days rather than weeks. Conclusions: FLEX-DBS is designed for untethered DBS experiments in which parameters must be set, changed and verified at the cage. Its measured power consumption permits a projected three days of continuous operation per cell pair; firmware v0.5 requires improved charge balancing before prolonged in vivo stimulation. The electrode load, rather than the programmable range, sets the usable stimulation amplitude in vivo. In vivo, stimulation at high amplitude settings was associated with increased immobility, consistent with effective stimulation through implanted electrodes; electrode impedance and delivered current were not measured in these mice.
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis (corresponding author)

papers.title: Surfactant-Enhanced Hybridization Capture for Direct Sequence-Specific RNA Extraction from Plasma and Whole Blood
papers.abstract: Direct recovery of low-abundance RNA from complex biological samples remains a major challenge for ultrasensitive detection. Sequence-specific hybridization capture enables selective enrichment, but recovery from crude samples is compromised by RNA degradation, protein interference, RNA secondary structure, and target sequence variation. Here, we address these limitations with a sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS)-based formulation that not only lyses virions and protects RNA, but also directly accelerates hybridization kinetics, substantially reducing the need for thermal denaturation. This enabled direct RNA capture from crude plasma or whole blood with near-quantitative recovery, outperforming a widely used silica-based kit at low input. Without centrifugation or plasma separation, we detected HIV RNA by RT-qPCR at 25 copies/mL directly from whole blood. We further developed a free energy ({Delta}G)-guided algorithm for mutation-robust probe design, achieving >85% mean recovery across HIV-1 subtypes with a single probe. This work opens low-abundance RNA biomarkers in crude biofluids to ultrasensitive detection, addressing a major barrier to early diagnosis.
affiliations: University of Washington (corresponding author)

papers.title: STARgrid: an open-source pipeline from Visium HD sequencing reads to count matrices
papers.abstract: In Visium HD, transcript positions are computed from sequenced barcodes, which are matched to a list of coordinate barcodes that map to a grid of capture locations. Quantifying reads and assigning their positions have relied on Space Ranger, whose end-user licence prohibits modification and whose published source cannot be redistributed. We present STARgrid, the first open-source pipeline that takes Visium HD FASTQ files from Flex or RNA-seq based quantitation to count matrices at 2, 8 and 16 um; it is part of STAR Suite. On three human slides its output agrees closely with Space Ranger's (correlations of gene totals are at least 0.9989), and STARgrid takes 20-35% less wall time under the tested configurations. STARgrid assigns each read barcode to the coordinate barcode with the most similar sequence, as assessed by edit distance. In an examination of Space Ranger's per-read output on one further slide, Space Ranger does the same for most reads, with two differences. First, where two coordinate barcodes overlap, the shorter being the longer without its first base, Space Ranger records the shorter barcode, although the longer one matches with fewer edits; in all, Space Ranger's location is not among the closest for 0.5980% of the reads that our decoder can place. Second, Space Ranger settles each read on its own, recording one location or none, and leaves 0.2916% of these reads without a location; STARgrid keeps every matching location and chooses among them for each molecule, using all its reads. Our molecule totals are 1.9-7.6% above Space Ranger's. The larger source of this difference is probably that we resolve location for each molecule and not for each read; STAR Suite's own gene assignment and molecule counting may also contribute. The counts that STARgrid adds behave like signal. On H&E images of the same sections they fall in cells at nearly the rate of the counts that both pipelines report. Against an adjacent Xenium section of one slide, our counts are closer to Xenium than Space Ranger's for 15 of the 20 genes of a cancer gene panel that Xenium measures most abundantly (P = 0.0414). The added counts therefore appear to improve the measurement of cancer-associated expression. These results are preliminary, but the method is now open, and every comparison reported here can be repeated, extended and improved upon.
affiliations: University of Washington Tacoma (corresponding author)

papers.title: Beyond Ramachandran distributions: quantifying secondary structure effects on amino acids and their pairs in the full torsional space
papers.abstract: The Ramachandran diagram has long served for understanding protein secondary structure elements (SSEs), despite the multitude of factors contributing to their occurrence. Starting from recentlyintroduced circula-based multivariate torsion-angle distribution (CBMD) mixture models -- accommodating covariance structure in the full torsion-angle space of amino acids, we define continuous densities for the 20 amino acids and 400 amino-acid pairs in dimension up to 14, conditioned by SSE labels. Projecting these higher-dimensional distributions onto the classical Ramachandran diagram reveals how secondary structures in the protein universe emerge from amino-acid-dependent conformational preferences reflecting influences beyond backbone dihedrals alone. Our analysis links the traditional geometric description of local protein structure to modern statistical models of the full conformational space of amino acids and amino-acidpairs, while providing a framework for generating protein conformations consistent with any given secondary structure environment -- a feature that remains difficult to enforce explicitly in current AI-based generative models.
affiliations: Inria (corresponding author)

papers.title: Probabilistic Modelling of Base Editing Efficiency and Bystander Outcome Composition
papers.abstract: Abstract. Base editors install single nucleotide substitutions without a double strand break or donor template, but editing at multiple susceptible positions can generate bystander alleles. Predicting the frequency of an intended outcome therefore requires both editing efficiency and the composition of edited products. Here we present crispAIBE, a probabilistic framework that uses separately trained transformer convolutional networks to predict Dirichlet distributions for editing efficiency and conditional allele composition. Split-conformal density-level regions are calibrated on data reserved from model selection, with composition thresholds fitted by outcome-set size. On held-out data, crispAIBE achieves Pearson correlations of 0.669 for efficiency and 0.896 for composition on measured allele sets, with empirical coverages of 0.902 and 0.906 at a nominal level of 0.90. On the published CRISPRon-BE benchmark, with test protospacers excluded from training, crispAIBE ranks first in seven of eight comparisons under the two-column Pearson statistic and first or second in seven of eight under the rank statistic. Within predicted-efficiency quintiles, the largest- and smallest-region deciles differ 1.9-fold in mean absolute error on average, compared with 1.7-fold for a boundary-distance ranking. When evaluated on U2OS, which was excluded from training, larger predictive regions were associated with larger absolute prediction errors. Local calibration with 100 U2OS protospacers yields median empirical coverage of 0.918 at the nominal 0.90 level. The crispAIBE repository is https://github.com/furkanozdenn/crispAIBE.
affiliations: University of Oxford (corresponding author)

papers.title: Multivalent ubiquitin recognition regulates multiple stages of Tau self-assembly
papers.abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) has emerged as an important intermediate in the pathological self-assembly of Tau, yet the molecular mechanisms that regulate this process remain incompletely understood. Although ubiquitin is a prominent component of pathological inclusions in tauopathies and other neurodegenerative diseases, its presence has largely been linked to targeting aberrant proteins for proteasomal or autophagic clearance. Here, we identify Tau as a ubiquitin-binding protein and demonstrate that multivalent, non-covalent ubiquitin recognition regulates multiple stages of Tau self-assembly. Biochemical, biophysical, structural, and computational analyses identified four ubiquitin-binding elements within the Tau microtubule-binding repeat region that engage the canonical hydrophobic patch of ubiquitin, providing a structural basis for multivalent recognition of mono- and poly-ubiquitin species. Functionally, mono- and poly-ubiquitin suppress Tau condensate formation while enhancing the liquid-like properties of condensates that persist. In contrast, mono-ubiquitin selectively enhances aggregation of the disease-linked Tau-P301L variant under conditions without detectable LLPS, demonstrating that ubiquitin exerts distinct effects depending on the molecular context and stage of Tau self-assembly. Together, these findings establish non-covalent ubiquitin recognition as a previously unrecognized mechanism regulating Tau phase behavior and aggregation. More broadly, they expand the role of ubiquitin beyond protein quality control, with ubiquitin architecture providing an additional layer of regulation over Tau condensate formation, dynamics, maturation, and aggregation.
affiliations: KU Leuven (corresponding author)

papers.title: Scalable Decoupling Contact and Configuration Spaces in a Quantum-Enabled Protein Folding Workflow
papers.abstract: Near-term quantum devices remain constrained by limited qubit counts, noise, and shallow circuit depth, restricting their direct application to peptide folding. This work addresses this limitation through a hybrid quantum-classical framework that separates global contact-space exploration from local configuration-space refinement. The pipeline was evaluated on the p53 transactivation peptide. The peptide was encoded using discrete torsional states and Miyazawa-Jernigan contact potentials. Global conformational search was performed using simulated annealing, followed by fragment-level CVaR-based variational quantum eigensolver refinement. Overlapping fragments were stitched and reconstructed into three-dimensional backbone coordinates for structural comparison. Three independent simulated annealing restarts produced negative-energy conformers. The workflow identified a best global conformer at E = -3.70 MJ using simulated annealing. Fragment-level CVaR-VQE refinement generated 30 candidate conformers across three overlapping fragments, the best assembled conformer reaching E = -2.58 MJ after DP stitching and post-stitch refinement. In this trial, the classical SA solution outperformed the VQE-assembled structure and was selected as the final output. The final 65-atom model was successfully reconstructed, but full-backbone alignment against 1YCR yielded an RMSD of 4.65 angstrom, improving to 2.90 angstrom after trimmed alignment. Our work demonstrates a practical quantum-enabled peptide folding workflow for short, flexible peptides, but the present structural accuracy is insufficient for claims of native fold recovery. Its main value is as an auditable framework for testing NISQ-compatible folding strategies.
affiliations: R V College of Engineering (corresponding author)

papers.title: Nanoscale identification of organic pigments in biogenic calcite by atom probe tomography
papers.abstract: Spatially-resolved mass spectrometry could contribute to the understanding of biological processes. Atom probe tomography (APT) is a technique which could, in principle, fill an analytical gap for nanoscale mass spectrometry. Yet, because of a limited understanding of the process of fragmentation of biomolecules, biological or biochemical interpretation of the obtained data has so far not been successful. Here, we report on analyses of synthetic and biogenic pigmented calcite minerals. The purple coloration of Sphaerechinus granularis sea urchin spines is due to the occlusion of polyhydroxylated naphthoquinone (PHNQ) molecules, mainly spinochrome A, within the calcite phase. Peaks relating to these pigments as well as to other intra-crystalline macromolecules were identified by APT analysis of the purple spine region with comparison to measurements of synthetic calcite single crystals, calcite crystals doped with PHNQ, and the uncoloured (white) region of sea urchin spines. To facilitate the molecular identification of peaks appearing solely in purple-coloured spines, which are possible fragments from PHNQ, we introduce novel APT data filtering techniques based on spatial and temporal correlations in the detection of ions of targeted mass-to-charge state ratios. This allows us to discuss the fragmentation of organic molecules under field conditions and improve the identification of peaks in the mass spectrum, while also determining nanoscale spatial distribution of fragments related to specifically targeted biomolecules in 3D and elucidate the relationship these organic pigment molecules have to the calcite lattice and inorganic elements such as magnesium. The study aims to improve identification of complex molecular structures by APT, including organic molecules, with the potential ability to provide structural information at a near-atomic scale for a range of materials.
affiliations: CNRS (corresponding author)

papers.title: Low CAR affinity enhances T-cell synapse dynamics and activation
papers.abstract: Low affinity chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) can clinically outperform high-affinity variants, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying affinity-dependent activity remain unclear. Here, we show that low CAR affinity enables faster CAR cluster motion, which is central to T-cell activation. We compared low-affinity CAT and high-affinity FMC63 CARs signaling at different stages of activation on supported lipid bilayers functionalized with defined CD19 densities. At low CAR expression on dense CD19 bilayers, low-affinity CAT CARs formed more mature and dynamic synapses, recruited ZAP70 more efficiently, and showed faster microcluster motion. These proximal signaling changes were accompanied by stronger calcium flux and increased NFAT nuclear translocation. Our data support a model in which weaker, lower-affinity CAR-antigen interactions promote receptor turnover, microcluster mobility, and signaling-adaptor recruitment, thereby enhancing downstream signal propagation. Our work provides a mechanistic basis for the superior functional performance reported for affinity-tuned CD19 CAR-T cells.
affiliations: AMOLF (corresponding author)

papers.title: Trastuzumab deruxtecan kills skin and uveal melanoma in vivo by HER2-independent payload release
papers.abstract: Background: HER2-directed CAR-T cells can eradicate melanoma despite low HER2 expression. We therefore asked whether melanoma would also respond to trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd), an antibody-drug conjugate targeting HER2. Patients and methods: T-DXd was evaluated in several patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models and as a compassionate use in one patient with metastatic uveal melanoma. We compared T-DXd with another ADC, trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1), and examined ADC sensitivity and trastuzumab uptake in vitro, and expression of HER2 and cathepsin L (CTSL) in xenografts. Results: T-DXd inhibited all subcutaneous PDXs, while liver models were less sensitive. T-DM1 had limited activity. Unexpectedly, parental and ERBB2-knockout melanoma xenografts showed similar initial responses to T-DXd, although knockout tumors regrew earlier. Tumor-derived CTSL was detected outside melanoma cells in the xenografts. Melanoma cells were largely resistant to both ADCs in vitro and showed little trastuzumab uptake compared to HER2-amplified breast cancer cells. Conclusions: T-DXd has a substantial HER2-independent component of activity in the tested melanoma xenografts. Presence of extracellular CTSL, an enzyme known to cleave T-Dxd, provide a possibility that linker cleavage and payload release can occur outside of the tumor cells.
affiliations: University of Gothenburg (corresponding author)

papers.title: High-throughput variant libraries and machine learning enable robust target-site selection for toehold-switch design in Detectrons
papers.abstract: Programmable RNA sensors enable sequence-specific detection of RNA inputs for diagnostics, genetic circuit control, and multiplexed molecular readouts. Although readily programmable, their performance varies substantially with the target site selected within a transcript, making target-site selection a major challenge. Here, we report DeSTAR (Detectron Sensor TARget-site ranker), a machine-learning-assisted target-site ranking model for programmable RNA sensors. To train this model, we generated transcript-wide, single-nucleotide-resolution tiling sensor libraries across six diverse RNA targets, enabling generalization to be tested across transcripts rather than within a single RNA. In leave-one-transcript-out evaluation, DeSTAR's top-ranked sites were enriched for high-performing sensors in held-out transcripts, driven predominantly by interpretable sequence grammar in the sensor stem rather than transcript-specific patterns. Prospectively, on an unseen SARS-CoV-2 transcript, the model's top-ranked sites yielded working sensors roughly five-fold more often than random selection. These results support DeSTAR as a generalizable strategy for target-site selection in RNA sensors across transcripts.
affiliations: Gladstone Institutes and UCSF (corresponding author)

papers.title: Modular Cell-Free Extract Mixing Enables Soluble, Active Biomanufacturing of Difficult-to-Express and Aggregation-Prone Proteins
papers.abstract: Cell-free protein synthesis (CFPS) is a powerful platform for rapid protein prototyping and biomanufacturing, but expression of complex proteins remains limited by labor-intensive extract preparation as well as the inability of conventional Escherichia coli extracts to efficiently support disulfide bond formation and prevent protein aggregation. We previously developed a Cell-Free Autoinduction (CFAI) workflow that simplifies extract preparation, however, CFAI-derived extracts retain the folding limitations of standard E. coli systems for producing traditionally difficult proteins. Here, we address these challenges by utilizing extracts enriched with molecular chaperones or Erv1p-based oxidative folding catalysts and combining them through a modular extract mixing strategy to enable independent tuning of the cell-free folding environment. This workflow supplies folding factors through enriched extracts, avoiding recurring purchases of purified supplements and enabling a modeled reagent-cost advantage. To evaluate real-world applications and utility of lysate mixing for protein production, we demonstrate a 10-fold increase in solubility of the aggregation-prone bacterial toxin Colicin M, achieving >95% soluble protein while retaining antimicrobial activity. We further used a Design of Experiments (DoE) framework to optimize combinations of chaperone-enriched and Erv1p-based oxidative folding extracts containing either protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) or DsbC. The optimized compositions produced >95% soluble truncated human tissue plasminogen activator (vtPA), comprising the kringle 2 and protease domains, while preserving enzymatic activity. Together, these results demonstrate that CFAI-derived modular extract mixing provides a tunable, high-throughput strategy with low modeled materials costs for tailoring cell-free biochemical environments for difficult-to-express proteins, expanding CFPS utility for protein engineering and biomanufacturing.
affiliations: California Polytechnic State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: The Human Gut Cell Atlas v1.0: A Unified, Community-BuiltReference of Cellular Diversity Across the Gut
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies have transformed our understanding of cellular diversity in the human intestine, but differences in anatomical sampling, experimental processing and cell-type nomenclature limit comparison across datasets. Here, we present the Human Gut Cell Atlas (HGCA) V1, a community-curated reference of 944,390 healthy and disease-adjacent intestinal cells from 502 samples, 265 donors and 24 landmark studies, linked to detailed anatomical, clinical, and technical metadata. As this metadata is of critical importance to human biology, we developed MetaManager, an open source data management framework for standardized metadata collection and tracking. A five-level consensus taxonomy resolves 94 homeostatic cell identities and enables transferrable, high-resolution annotation of new gut datasets. By assembling cell identity, sampling metadata, and independent spatial validation, intestinal segment and radial tissue depth were revealed to systematically shape cellular composition and transcriptional state, enabling inference of the presence of sampling-dependent tissue niches, including lymphoid follicles. Reference mapping accurately and rapidly recovered cohort-level Crohn's disease and treatment signatures without de novo annotation, while mapping human intestinal organoids quantified cell-type-specific identity, regional specification, maturation, and transcriptional fidelity to native tissue. The HGCA V1 provides a standardized cellular, anatomical coordinate, and metadata system for reproducible, high-quality analysis of intestinal biology across healthy tissue, disease-associated remodelling, and experimental models, providing a continuously evolving community reference for cumulative discovery in human intestinal biology.
affiliations: Division of Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition, Boston Children's Hospital, Boston, MA, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Decision-relevant measurement for precision microbiome interventions
papers.abstract: Human gut microbiome studies often rely on stool, despite increasing evidence that it incompletely represents the spatially heterogeneous intestinal ecosystem. Whether this loss of spatial detail matters for downstream intervention decisions is largely unresolved. We treat compositional reconstruction and decision preservation as separate objectives. Using 16 matched recovery events from 11 participants, each containing stool and four intended regional capsule measurements, we aggregated amplicon sequence variants into 11 prespecified taxonomic and functional proxy guilds. We evaluated models that reconstruct stool from regional measurements by nested leave one participant out validation under complementary compositional geometries. We then assessed decision preservation through three spatial proxy states and measurement induced decision loss (MIDL) across normalized binary intervention thresholds. Multi region CLR ridge and Aitchison models combining regional measurements with a population reference had the lowest point estimate Aitchison errors, but evidence that either outperformed the population Aitchison center was not retained after multiplicity correction. Rankings changed under total variation and after guild amalgamation; at the coarser resolution, the primary ordering showed a small, uncertain reversal that was sensitive to zero handling. The model with the lowest compositional error did not have the lowest MIDL curve calibration error. Population centers closely reproduced the nearly uninformative MIDL curves of observed stool while retaining little individualized regional information. These findings show that reconstruction, decision preservation, and calibration to observed stool decision loss answer different questions. Evaluation of microbiome measurement strategies should therefore treat compositional geometry, biological representation, and the downstream decision task as parts of the estimand.
affiliations: University of California Berkeley (corresponding author)

papers.title: Fast receptor-antigen dissociation kinetics promote CAR-T cell tumor infiltration, functional fitness, and antitumor efficacy in solid tumors
papers.abstract: Background: CAR-T cells have shown limited efficacy against solid tumors, where they face two major challenges: restricted tumor infiltration and sustained intensive engagement that drive them to exhaustion. Conventional CAR design has largely emphasized high-affinity interactions with slow dissociation, further limiting tumor infiltration and exacerbating exhaustion and dysfunction. We hypothesize that most current CARs are kinetically over-stabilized for solid tumors and that a fast-on/fast-off, cheek-kiss mode of engagement permits transient CAR-antigen disengagement, thereby facilitating tumor infiltration and preserving CAR-T cell fitness in tumor mass. Methods: We identified two monoclonal antibodies targeting the same epitope of epidermal growth factor receptor with comparable kon but distinct koff rates: cetuximab (Cet) and its humanized derivative H1. CAR-T cells incorporating these binders were evaluated in vitro and in vivo. Large, established human tumor xenografts were treated with low-dose CAR-T cells in NSG mice to model conditions of limited T cell availability and sustained tumor antigen exposure. Results: Cet and H1 exhibited comparable kon but markedly different koff rates, with H1 displaying fast-off kinetics with approximately 18-fold shorter binding dwell time. As CARs, H1 showed reduced antigen occupancy and less stable tumor-T cell engagement than Cet. Despite comparable in vitro cytotoxicity, H1 CAR-T cells accumulated more efficiently following tumor stimulation. At high doses, both CAR-T cell products eradicated established tumors. Under low-dose conditions, however, H1 CAR-T cells exhibited superior expansion, persistence, tumor infiltration, and antitumor efficacy, whereas Cet CAR-T cells showed limited expansion and only transient tumor control. Cet CAR-T cells progressively downregulated surface CAR expression, increased PD-1 expression, and exhibited reduced tumor infiltration and impaired functional recovery. In contrast, H1 CAR-T cells preserved surface CAR expression, exhibited greater tumor infiltration, maintained a less exhausted, more central memory-like phenotype, and retained effector function. Conclusion: Fast-on/fast-off binding kinetics enhance CAR-T tumor infiltration, expansion, persistence, and functional fitness, resulting in improved control of established solid tumors. The data provides a rationale for shifting CAR design from affinity optimization toward kinetic optimization to improve the efficacy and safety of CAR-T therapy for solid tumors.
affiliations: Augusta University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Tissue-resident memory T cells are diminished in the Kaposi sarcoma tumor microenvironment of people living with HIV
papers.abstract: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a rare neoplasm and an AIDS-defining diagnosis in people living with HIV (PLWH). Although and chronic infection with Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) contributes to KS progression, the local immune mechanisms that are lost during tumor progression remain incompletely understood. Here, we systematically characterized global patterns in the KS tumor microenvironment (TME) in both PLWH and HIV-negative individuals. Spatial transcriptomics revealed distinct niches comprising of tumor cells, immune cells, and surrounding skin cells. Tumor regions expressed a characteristic endothelial-fibroblastic signature attributable to KS tumor cells (CD34, LYVE1, SCN9A), TME regions expressed marker genes for T cells, B cells and cancer-associated fibroblasts. Analysis of putative cell-cell interactions demonstrated that tumor cells preferentially interact with cells of the TME, including T cells, indicating an important role as hub of cellular communication in KS. Immunofluorescence imaging confirmed increased numbers of T cells, specifically tissue-resident memory T cells (TRM), in KS samples compared to healthy skin, accompanied by a pronounced upregulation of PD-1 expression that was predominantly localized to the TME. Notably, we identified HIV-associated alterations in the KS immune microenvironment: PLWH exhibited loss of CXCR3+ and IFN-gamma producing CD8+ TRM cells in the KS TME compared to HIV-negative patients, a finding consistent with impaired antitumor immunity. Together, our findings reveal HIV-associated disruption of functional anti-tumor immunity in the KS TME of PLWH. Increased PD-1 expression within T cells of the TME highlights potential therapeutic use of immune checkpoint inhibitors in KS.
affiliations: Department of Dermatology, Medical University of Vienna (corresponding author)

papers.title: Unsupervised decomposition of massively parallel TraDIS-Xpress fitness data from Escherichia coli identifies distinct functional and expression modules of antimicrobial resistance determinants
papers.abstract: Linking genotype to phenotype is a central goal in biology, one way to do this is using transposon insertion sequencing (TIS) where the fitness impacts of mutations across a genome are assessed in different conditions. Traditional analyses use comparison of each gene response independently in control versus test conditions, so a compendium of hundreds of test conditions returns hundreds of separate ranked gene lists. To unlock the potential information hidden within large data sets, we applied independent component (ICA) analysis to 754 Escherichia coli BW25113 TraDIS-Xpress samples. These samples included a series of antibiotic and other stress condition exposures. ICA is designed to identify hidden structure within complex data and to extract meaningfully linked components. In this analysis each annotated gene was resolved into a gene body and 198 bp 5' and 3' features so that expression effects driven by the transposon's outwards facing promoter enter the matrix separately from gene disruption effects. The decomposition returned 99 components, which we term fxModules, which were defined as containing elements with similar responses across the whole compendium rather than per any individual experiment. Of the 754 stress samples, the antibiotic arm included 110 samples derived from exposure to 14 separate agents at multiple concentrations. Many of these have been highly studied allowing us to explore the accuracy of predicted responsive fxModules. This analysis showed excellent predictive power of the approach and the fxModules responsive to individual drugs typically reproduced known mechanisms at a resolution superior to analysis of single gene sets. For example, exposure to fosfomycin identified responsive fxModules containing genes which are known to be involved in uptake of the drug, cAMP-CRP control and exposure to gentamicin identified oxidative phosphorylation split across three fxModules responding with different magnitudes and directions at different concentrations. This recapitulates recent work studying the landscape of E. coli genes sensitive to this drug with high precision without any prior knowledge of functional annotation. Similarly precise predictions were made for other drugs. Responsive modules also identified novel groups of genes and linkages beyond the boundaries of defined pathways as being responsive to various stresses demonstrating the ability to predict new genotype-phenotype links. Inclusion of the regulatory regions also resolved fxModules which were entirely contributed by promoter regions, for example for chloramphenicol genes responsible for efflux were identified by signals in intergenic control regions, and unidirectional insertions in gene bodies, a signal that a gene level matrix would not be able to predict with accuracy. These data show that ICA decomposition provides an efficient and accurate annotation independent approach to identifying sets of genes with related functional impacts in any given condition in the compendium. The functional modular association of genes also help in predicting gene functions of unknown genes based on the group function. This approach allows rapid identification of novel genotype-phenotype links and unlocks the power of multiple comparisons of transposon mutagenesis data.
affiliations: Quadram Institute Bioscience (corresponding author)

papers.title: Pulling water from a stone: subaerial biofilm water dynamics on porous solid materials
papers.abstract: Subaerial biofilms (SABs) are microbial communities that colonize air exposed surfaces in both natural and engineered environments, forming an interface between the atmosphere and the substrate. Often water availability is crucial for their metabolic activity and survival. While precipitation may contribute to SAB hydration, the dynamic processes of evaporation and condensation - closely linked to fluctuating temperature and humidity conditions - can be key determinants of water availability and they constitute the main focus of this study. We present a model connecting the water-related dynamics in an SAB, its surrounding ambient air and underlying stone/masonry. A central feature of the model is the increased water affinity of the SAB in comparison to the stone pore network. Based on thermodynamic principles, the model captures changes in liquid water content and availability by accounting for the evaporation and condensation at liquid-gas interfaces through gradients in water chemical potential. It accounts for the SAB's capacity to delay water loss by drawing water from substrate material pores to compensate for atmospheric evaporation. The proposed model is compared to prior experimental observations of water transport in limestone samples with and without SAB. Additional numerical simulations under variable environmental conditions demonstrate how permeability of the substrate layer may influence SAB water activity, and how the presence or absence of an SAB might affect water content within stone/masonry.
affiliations: University of Naples Federico II, (corresponding author)

papers.title: Ethnic differences in gut microbiota composition and functional capacity persist over six years in the HELIUS multi-ethnic longitudinal cohort
papers.abstract: Background: Ethnic minority groups in Western Europe carry a disproportionate cardiometabolic disease burden not fully explained by conventional risk factors, and their gut microbiomes differ markedly from those of European-origin populations. Whether these differences persist over time has not been examined prospectively. Results: We followed 1,903 participants from six ethnic groups in the HELIUS cohort over 6 years, using faecal 16S rRNA sequencing across all groups and shotgun metagenomics in a matched Dutch and South-Asian Surinamese subset (N = 238 per group). The extent of microbiota compositional change over time differed between ethnic groups: Moroccan participants showed the largest change, while the Dutch and South-Asian Surinamese participants were most stable. Diabetes mellitus and medication use at baseline were associated with greater compositional drift. However, ethnic differences in composition were largely preserved across all six groups (16S: ethnicity R2 0.044 to 0.037; all 15 pairwise contrasts significant at follow-up) and in the shotgun subset (R2 0.047 to 0.037). At the species level, 61 of 78 ethnicity-associated species remained differentially abundant at follow-up. Alistipes putredinis, the species converging most strongly, was absent at baseline in 43% of South-Asian Surinamese participants, and the convergence was consistent with acquisition of this species by this group. At strain level, within-person strain sharing declined with follow-up duration but was similar between ethnic groups. Within hosts, 90% of A. putredinis populations were retained as the same or a closely related lineage, and within the retained subset, microdiversity increased in both groups. Ethnic differences in functional profiles persisted to a similar extent as those in composition, with limited convergence in fibre-degrading enzyme families (GH5_37, GH26). The total antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) burden in the gut microbiome declined similarly in both groups over time. Dutch participants showed higher baseline ARG diversity that converged toward South-Asian Surinamese levels, while class-level differences were predominantly stable. Conclusions: Six years of follow-up in a shared urban environment narrowed ethnic differences in the gut microbiome only modestly; assuming exponential decline, the observed change corresponds to a half-life of roughly two decades.
affiliations: Amsterdam UMC (corresponding author)

papers.title: Distribution and dynamics of Vibrio spp. and pathogen sequences among microhabitats and monsoon seasons in Singapore's coastal waters
papers.abstract: Marine infections are rising in temperate regions due in part to a warming climate. However, comparatively little is known about drivers of marine pathogen dynamics in the tropics where temperatures are high year-round. Vibrio bacteria are ubiquitous in both temperate and tropical marine environments, and many are important pathogens of marine organisms and humans. Here, we sampled an equatorial monsoonal site, the Singapore Strait, over 18 months and applied amplicon sequencing (16s rRNA V6-8 region) to three particle size fractions, qPCR quantitation of Vibrio spp., and generalized linear modelling with environmental variables to understand the factors that structure the Vibrio assemblage. We found that Vibrios represented the highest proportion of pathogen-related DNA sequences, with an assemblage composition influenced by microhabitats (size fractions) and monsoon seasons. Vibrio sequences were dominated by ASVs with highest identity to V. xuii, V. rotiferianus and V. caribbeanicus, and including ASVs matching agents of human disease in Singapore - V. parahaemolyticus, V. alginolyticus, and V. furnissii. Vibrio qPCR abundance was lowest in the largest size fraction (10-150 m), following planktonic DNA trends, even though pathogen-related sequences, including Vibrio, were enriched in this fraction. Temperature was a significant predictor of overall Vibrio abundance, but its effect was no longer significant after adjustment for monsoons, suggesting that the temperature association may reflect broader seasonal dynamics. Instead, effects of chlorophyll, ammonia, nitrate and suspended solids were more consistent within seasons. Furthermore, free-living and particle-associated Vibrios responded differently to environmental changes, suggesting that partitioning into microspatial habitats may lead to differences in their environmental sensitivity.
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Circadian phase alignment promotes survival under predictive oxidative stress
papers.abstract: Circadian clocks are endogenous time-keeping mechanisms that continue to oscillate with a period that approximates 24 h in the absence of cyclic environmental cues. This free-running period (FRP) varies from species to species and can vary within species across latitudinal clines. Because natural environments provide daily cues that reset circadian clocks to exactly 24 h, the importance of the FRP length is unclear. Using the cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus we show that the FRP length alters the alignment of a biological process with an environmental reference, known as phase angle of entrainment, across seasonal photoperiods, thereby repositioning stress response programs relative to the external environment. This phase relationship affects the overall fitness of the organism: strains that position stress-response programs to peak at the time at which the stressor peaks outcompete their early- or late-peaking counterparts. Our results suggest that the FRP length is selected for its ability to adjust the phase angle of entrainment across seasonal photoperiods: the wild-type FRP length was uniquely plastic in its ability to adjust stress-response programs to coincide with the stressor in all photoperiod conditions.
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (corresponding author)

papers.title: Isoindole-benzohydrazide derivative potentiates colistin activity to overcome resistance conferred by MCR-1 variants in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Polymyxin antibiotic resistance mediated by the mobilized colistin resistance (MCR) enzyme threatens the last-resort treatment of deadly multidrug-resistant pathogens, including Acinetobacter baumannii, and calls for urgent mitigation efforts. We used a multifaceted approach involving computational and wet-lab techniques to identify an isoindole-benzohydrazide derivative, JNAL-042, which potentiates colistin activity in an Escherichia coli MCR-resistance phenotype screening model. JNAL-042 lacked intrinsic antibiotic activity but potentiated that of polymyxin antibiotics at 12-24 mug/ml, as demonstrated by bacterial growth susceptibility screens. Cell viability counts and time-kill assays corroborated these findings, demonstrating complete abolition of MCR-mediated resistance by the antibiotic-adjuvant combination at concentrations mirroring those of empty vector controls. Post-induction treatment with this combination similarly prevented the propagation of the resistance phenotype, albeit at a higher antibiotic dose. This landmark study presents JNAL-042 as a promising antibiotic adjuvant to combat MCR-mediated resistance and offers a viable solution to preserve last-resort polymyxin antibiotics.
affiliations: Miami University (corresponding author)

papers.title: From dynamic transcripts to stable proteins: multi-omics revealed regulatory buffering of Candidatus Accumulibacter under cyclic conditions
papers.abstract: Enhanced biological phosphorus removal (EBPR) relies on polyphosphate-accumulating organisms that experience dynamic fluctuations in redox conditions and substrate availability. How these organisms regulate metabolism across molecular layers under cyclic operation remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated molecular regulation in a long-term, stable aerobic granular sludge system dominated by Candidatus Accumulibacter. We combined metagenomics, time-resolved metatranscriptomics, and matched metaproteomics across three consecutive operational cycles. Genome-resolved metagenomics revealed an Accumulibacter-dominated community encoding canonical EBPR functions. Time-resolved metatranscriptomics revealed extensive and reproducible transcriptional dynamics affecting hundreds of genes. These dynamics did not align with discrete EBPR phases or instantaneous environmental transitions, but instead unfolded gradually over the cycle. Despite pronounced transcript-level heterogeneity, aggregation at the functional level revealed strong consolidation, with only a limited number of KEGG orthologs exhibiting coherent temporal regulation. Quantitative metaproteomics revealed a stable proteome across EBPR cycles, with no individual proteins or functional categories showing significant differential abundance despite direct transcript-protein mapping and time-matched sampling. This indicated that transcriptional dynamics did not translate into measurable changes in protein pool size on the time scale of individual cycles, consistent with slow, growth-coupled proteome turnover relative to cycle duration. Together, these results support a hierarchical model of regulation in Candidatus Accumulibacter, in which dynamic transcriptional responses are buffered at both the functional and protein levels. This organization provides a plausible basis for stable EBPR performance under predictable cyclic operation and demonstrates how time-resolved multi-omics can be used to resolve regulatory dynamics across molecular layers in engineered microbial ecosystems.
affiliations: Laboratory for Environmental Biotechnology, Ecole Polytechnique Federale de Lausanne (EPFL) (corresponding author)

papers.title: High temperature ligation enables in vitro assembly of eukaryotic genes
papers.abstract: Our ability to efficiently construct synthetic DNA products is essential to studying and engineering biology. There is an abundance of widely adopted DNA assembly technologies suitable for generating synthetic constructs from diverse DNA inputs, but these techniques suffer from low specificity of connection during assembly, which decreases the accuracy, efficiency, and throughput of construction. Here we propose a broadly applicable paradigm for DNA assembly, High Temperature (HighT) assembly, that lowers misconnection rates by ligating complementary single strand DNA overhangs at reaction temperatures significantly higher than their predicted melting temperatures. By expanding the concept of melting temperature to demarcate smaller association fractions of DNA duplexes, we characterize HighT and demonstrate 40 percentage points increase in accuracy, and 4 orders of magnitude increase in yield of transformants when applying the technique to conventional assembly technologies. HighT is then applied to develop cloning pipelines for the development of efficient assembly-to-integration protocols, the construction of specific low-abundance isoforms of medically relevant proteins from human gDNA and oligos, and the de novo construction of a 10 kb, GC rich genomic region from the functionally extinct Northern White Rhinoceros created entirely in vitro.
affiliations: California Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Release of BEC-1 from CED-9 stimulates lysosome tubulation in C. elegans by engaging Class III PI3K complex I
papers.abstract: The anti-apoptotic protein CED-9 and the autophagy protein BEC-1 have been linked to autophagy regulation, but how their interaction modulates this process is not fully understood. Here, we find that the physical dissociation of BEC-1 from CED-9 influences lysosomal morphology in addition to autophagic activity in Caenorhabditis elegans. We present evidence that when autophagy is stimulated via dietary restriction, BEC-1 is released from CED-9 and assembles with VPS-34 and other members of the PI3K complex I to promote PI3P enrichment at lysosomal membranes and subsequent membrane tubulation. Mutation of two hydrophobic amino acids within a predicted BH-3 like motif of BEC-1 is sufficient to disrupt its interaction with CED-9, thereby constitutively inducing lysosomal tubulation and increasing autophagic cargo turnover. This phenotype is dependent on VPS-34 activity, linking the CED-9/BEC-1 dissociation to PI3K-dependent lysosomal remodeling. Collectively, our work identifies the CED-9/BEC-1 interaction as a molecular switch that governs apoptosis, autophagy, and lysosomal morphology.
affiliations: Louisiana State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Single-Cell Proteo-Transcriptomic Profiling Uncovers Post-Translational Regulatory Layers in Human Hematopoiesis
papers.abstract: Background: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) have the unique ability to produce all mature cell types in the blood and understanding the mechanisms governing their differentiation and renewal is a driving question in stem cell biology. While single-cell RNA sequencing has transformed our view of human hematopoiesis, mRNA abundance represents an incomplete proxy for functional cell states. Here, we apply single-cell multimodal profiling to simultaneously measure 280 surface and intracellular protein targets alongside whole transcriptomes within individual adult human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. Results: By directly coupling modalities within single cells, we show that protein-RNA correlations peak dynamically in transitioning intermediate progenitors across lineages, consistent with pervasive post-transcriptional mechanics underlying lineage choice. Furthermore, key transcription factor proteins maintain multilineage co-expression longer into commitment than their transcripts, demarcating a possible window of fate decision reversibility. Moreover, low and flat CTNNB1 mRNA levels mask late-erythroid {beta}-catenin protein enrichment, apparently pairing with E-cadherin expression and suggesting post-translational stabilization at the cell membrane. Conclusions: This dataset enables the observation of translational dynamics and RNA-protein relationships throughout the differentiation landscape at an unprecedented level of granularity. Together, our findings demonstrate that transcriptomics alone misses fundamental regulatory programs, establishing single-cell proteo-transcriptomics as a powerful tool for decoding human stem cell fate.
affiliations: University of Cambridge (corresponding author)

papers.title: Spatial proteomics identifies altered thick ascending limb cells as drivers of kidney disease through uromodulin retention
papers.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is increasingly prevalent and is a leading cause of mortality. Recent transcriptomic studies have identified the persistence of injury-induced renal tubular epithelial cell states, yet the cell populations that drive CKD remain unresolved. Uromodulin (UMOD) is the most abundant urinary secreted protein expressed exclusively in thick ascending limb (TAL) epithelial cells in the kidney. UMOD is strongly associated with CKD risk in genome-wide association studies, suggesting a broader, yet unexplored role of UMOD and TAL cells in CKD pathogenesis. Here, using spatial proteomics, we identified an injury-induced TAL cell state marked by intracellular UMOD accumulation. Spatially resolved multimodal integration revealed that UMOD accumulation occurred without transcriptional upregulation. Impaired urinary UMOD secretion further supported pathological intracellular retention. These altered TAL cells with UMOD retention exhibited inflammatory signaling, formed profibrotic niches enriched with M2-like macrophages across renal compartments, and were associated with CKD progression in multiple experimental models. Reducing the burden of UMOD retention diminished altered TAL cells and their profibrotic microenvironments, and attenuated CKD development. A similar altered TAL state was identified in human kidney disease and was associated with worse kidney function. Together, we identify pathological UMOD retention and altered TAL cells as key drivers of CKD development and potential therapeutic targets. This study also highlights that protein-level alterations can redefine disease-associated cell states beyond transcript profiling.
affiliations: Indiana University School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Developmental rewiring of EHMT1 function during human cortical neurogenesis
papers.abstract: Ubiquitously expressed chromatin regulators orchestrate cell-type-specific gene expression programs, yet how they acquire distinct regulatory functions during development remains fundamentally unresolved. Using temporally controlled protein depletion during human cortical neurogenesis in vitro, we show that the autism-associated histone methyltransferase EHMT1 is developmentally repurposed from epiblast to cortical neurons. Broadly expressed zinc finger proteins recruit EHMT1 to distinct cis-regulatory elements within changing chromatin landscapes associated with lineage-specific transcription factor activity, with extensive remodeling of EHMT1 enhancer occupancy during neural induction dependent on ZNF462. This genomic rewiring is accompanied by a fundamental shift from restraining premature developmental gene expression in pluripotent cells to supporting neuronal programs, with distinct transcriptional consequences of EHMT1 loss across neural progenitors and excitatory and inhibitory neuronal subtypes. Timed depletion and recovery experiments identify the neural progenitor stage as the onset of a developmental period during which EHMT1 is required for faithful neuronal maturation. Remarkably, EHMT1 can re-engage stage-specific targets after prolonged deficiency, allowing extensive transcriptional recovery with only limited molecular scarring. These findings reveal how ubiquitous epigenetic machinery acquires developmental specificity while demonstrating the resilience of developmental gene regulatory programs to prolonged disruption, with implications for neurodevelopmental disorders.
affiliations: Weill Cornell Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Alignment-Aware Genomic Coordinate Encoding for Long-Range DNA Modeling
papers.abstract: Existing genomic foundation models (GFMs) are adept at capturing local, sequential dependencies in DNA. However, their architectures often struggle to efficiently model gene regulation features, such as sparse motifs and distal regulatory elements that operate beyond linear proximity. Moreover, standard positional encodings fail to fully exploit the reference genome coordinate system. Therefore, we present USM-AA, an alignment-aware genomic foundation model that incorporates reference genome coordinates through a non-contiguous positional encoding, Alignment-Aware Rotary Position Embedding, and an alignment embedding module encoding chromosome, strand, and Compact Idiosyncratic Gapped Alignment Report (CIGAR) information. To improve long-range sequence modeling, USM-AA leverages a reverse-complement masked learning strategy. Pretrained on alignment-aware genomic sequences spanning cross-species evolution and human population variation, USM-AA consistently outperforms existing models across multiple downstream tasks, highlighting the importance of alignment-aware representations for genomic sequence modeling.
affiliations: AI for Life Sciences Lab, Tencent (corresponding author)

papers.title: Directed evolution of laccase from Thermus thermophilus HB27 reveals a variant with enhanced high temperature catalytic activity and electrochemical properties
papers.abstract: Laccases belong to the multicopper oxidase family (MCO). Compared with fungal laccases, bacterial laccases have high stability and activity under extreme pH and temperature conditions. Because of these characteristics, bacterial laccases have become highly impactful in industrial processes. In the present work, we engineered the Thermus thermophilus HB27 laccase (Tth-Lac) by directed evolution. The library had a size of 1.2 x105 colonies, and we screened mutants by malachite green decolorization on solid medium. The results showed that Q36H mutant exhibited higher catalytic activity than Tth-laccase (WT) at 90 degrees Celsius. Both enzymes showed similar pH profiles, but the activity at 90 degrees Celsius of Q36H mutant was X-fold higher than that of the wild-type enzyme. In contrast, the kinetic constants were similar for both enzymes. In the voltammetric responses, at 61.5 degrees Celsius, the Q36H mutant showed increased current, and the T1 copper potential shifted by 100 mV relative to the tth-Lac. These results suggest that the Q36H mutation has high potential for industrial applications because replacing a glutamine (Q) with a histidine (H) at position 36 enhances the enzyme's structural stability, allowing it to function efficiently under extreme temperature conditions.
affiliations: Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico (corresponding author)

papers.title: Pre-catalytic activation pathway of the Smc5/6 complex
