Enrichment analyses revealed a shared transcriptional signature in both interactions characterized by downregulation of xenobiotic- and central carbon-metabolism pathways, suggesting an early reduction in xenobiotic detoxification capacity rather than induction of detoxification programs. These findings suggest that phylogenetic proximity does not necessarily predict conserved early transcriptional responses, although comparisons of single isolates cannot separate species-level from isolate-level effects.
affiliations: Mediterranean Institute for Agriculture, Environment and Development & Global Change and Sustainability Institute, Institute for Advanced Studies and Research, (corresponding author)

papers.title: Glyphosate exposure minimally alters the Corbicula fluminea microbiome while associated bacteria exhibit high tolerance and degradation potentia
papers.abstract: Glyphosate (GLY), the active ingredient in Roundup, is a broad-spectrum herbicide widely used in commercial agriculture and residential landscaping. Due to its extensive application and high water solubility, GLY is frequently introduced into freshwater ecosystems where it has been shown to negatively impact aquatic life and beneficial microorganisms. The freshwater clam Corbicula fluminea, a nonnative bivalve species widely distributed throughout the United States, is highly tolerant of many environmental stressors and may serve as a reservoir for microbial taxa capable of tolerating or degrading environmental pollutants. As efficient filter-feeders, these clams are continuously exposed to waterborne contaminants, potentially facilitating interactions between pollutants and host-associated microbial communities. In this study, we investigated how glyphosate impacts the structure and diversity of Corbicula fluminea microbiomes and characterized GLY tolerance and degradation potential in individual microbiome members. We found that microbiome taxonomic composition and abundance-based diversity metrics were minimally impacted by glyphosate, while presence/absence-based phylogenetic diversity shifted depending on treatment concentration. Furthermore, high GLY concentrations were linked to reduced Faith''s PD alpha diversity, while other alpha diversity metrics were not impacted. Additionally, we isolated and characterized glyphosate-tolerant bacterial strains from clam tissues and assessed their presence within the microbiome. Several isolates exhibited tolerance to very high GLY levels (up to 1600 mg/L), and several also utilized GLY as a sole phosphorus source and possessed the phnJ gene, suggesting potential degradation capabilities. While isolated bacteria were minority members of the microbiome, more abundant uncultured taxa were phylogenetically related to known glyphosate degraders. Collectively, these findings suggest that freshwater bivalves may harbor diverse microbial taxa capable of tolerating or degrading herbicides, which may contribute to host resilience in contaminated freshwater environments and potentially represent unexplored avenues for bioremediation research.
affiliations: University of Memphis (corresponding author)

papers.title: Single-cell-resolved natural giant virus infections reveal conserved protist immunity
papers.abstract: Single-cell eukaryotes (protists) are key players in microbial ecosystems. Yet, our understanding of how they interact with viruses in nature and how antiviral defenses shape these relationships remains limited. Using a single-cell multi-omics approach, we mapped associations between giant viruses and their hosts and identified active giant-virus infections in an alpine lake protist community. In naturally infected dinoflagellates, infection was accompanied by the selective induction of viperin, an ancient antiviral enzyme conserved from bacteria to humans. We also observed virus-encoded homologs of immunity-related genes whose expression correlated with viperin expression, raising the possibility of a role in viral counter-defense. These findings reveal an ecological dimension of protist immunity and provide a framework for tracing the host-virus arms race across divergent cellular lineages.
affiliations: Weizmann Institute of Science (corresponding author)

papers.title: Assessment of antimicrobial potential of cell-free supernatant from Lacticaseibacillus paracasei SRG isolated from the vaginal microbiota of healthy women against uropathogens
papers.abstract: Among women, urinary tract infection (UTI) represents a major health concern. Approximately 50% of the adult female population experienced an episode of UTI at least once. UTI and recurrent UTIs caused by resistant bacteria are very common in clinical settings. The treatment and management of UTI is becoming more challenging because of the rise in antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Lactobacillus spp are the dominant bacterial genus in urinary and vaginal microbiota, which are also used as probiotics. In this study, Lacticaseibacillus paracasei SRG isolated from the vagina of healthy women were evaluated for its probiotic-associated properties and cell-free supernatant (CFS)-mediated antibacterial activity against eight uropathogens. The antibacterial activity of CFS was concentration- and pH-dependent, which was significantly evident at CFS/2 and CFS/4 concentrations and acidic pH values of 4 and 5. The antibacterial activity in CFS remains unaltered even after heat and proteinase K treatment, which suggests the role of heat- and protease-resistant metabolites beside the contributions from acidic conditions. L. paracasei SRG showed strong autoaggregation (85.32%) and cell-surface hydrophobicity (55.60%). In addition, it also exhibits co-aggregation with all indicator strains, suggesting substantial interaction with diverse pathogenic bacteria. These observations highlighted the L. paracasei SRG as a potential probiotic candidate developed from indigenous vaginal microbiota.
affiliations: Department of Zoology, Mahila Mahavidyalaya, Banaras Hindu University, Varanasi, India (corresponding author)

papers.title: A simple platform for in situ DNA-PAINT optimization enables improved multiplexed super-resolution imaging in Gram-negative bacteria
papers.abstract: DNA-PAINT enables super-resolution imaging with high multiplexing capacity, yet it is rarely used in nanoscale bacteriology. A likely reason is the lack of straightforward protocols and of systematic characterization of imager-docking strand pairs inside intact bacterial cells, whose envelope and dense cytoplasm differ markedly from both the DNA origami in vitro systems used to develop them, and eukaryotic cells. In this work, we establish a screening platform based on RNA-FISH, in which we extend the 16S rRNA-directed EUB338 probe with docking sequences of choice. This allows imager-docking pairs to be benchmarked directly inside Escherichia coli cells and characterized for parameters such as specificity, binding kinetics, and localization precision. We screened 12 different DNA-PAINT sequences and used an optimized set to perform four-target 3D Exchange-PAINT in single E. coli cells. We further applied our strategy to image three effector mRNAs in the Gram-negative pathogen Yersinia enterocolitica and quantified RNA clusters and their 3D distribution. Our work provides a framework and practical guidelines for high-quality 3D DNA-PAINT imaging in Gram-negative bacteria and should facilitate its broader adoption in nanoscale bacteriology.
affiliations: Rudolf Virchow Center, University of Wuerzburg (corresponding author)

papers.title: TFA-defluorinating microbial consortium achieved with analogue enrichment
papers.abstract: Trifluoroacetate (TFA) is an ultra-short chain perfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) and a pollutant of global significance; it is persistent and ubiquitous in the environment across compartments, including food, drinking water, animals, and humans. Concentrations in the environment are rising, concerns over the toxicity of the compound are increasing, and there are currently no efficient ways to remediate TFA pollution, as conventional methods are ineffective at scale under environmental conditions. Microorganisms possessing dehalogenating enzymes targeting the structurally analogous compound monofluoroacetate (MFA) present a potential solution to degrade TFA microbiologically. Due to previously demonstrated dehalogenation of difluoroacetate (DFA) by dehalogenases, the promiscuity of such enzymes was hypothesized to be extendable to TFA as well. In this study cultures obtained from an environmental sample of PFAS contaminated wastewater sludge were incubated in M9 minimal media supplied with 33 mM acetate and either 33 mM TFA, DFA, or MFA in an iterative manner, followed by testing in a 30-day experiment. Free fluoride (F-) was measured at 5 timepoints using a fluoride ion specific electrode (ISE). One culture designated MFA1C significantly degraded MFA, DFA, and TFA (two-way ANOVA mixed model, p < 0.05). MFA1C released 11.2 {+/-} 0.7 M F- which constitutes approximately 0.01% of the potential fluoride release from the total 33 mM TFA applied and with the greatest defluorination activity in the first 9 days of incubation. Fluoride release from TFA and formation of DFA and MFA was confirmed with 19F-NMR. Genetic sequencing and protein-ligand modelling identified two candidate dehalogenase enzymes from Achromobacter denitrificans and Stenotrophomonas sp., respectively, with potential capacity to degrade TFA. The findings of this study are a crucial first step towards future potential bioremediation of TFA, and are, to the best of our knowledge, the first to identify a TFA-degrading consortium of microorganisms.
affiliations: Department of Plant and Environmental Sciences, University of Copenhagen, Thorvaldsensvej 40, 1871 Frederiksberg C, Denmark (corresponding author)

papers.title: Exploring recurrent urinary tract infection: paired microbiota and culture-based profiling reveals stable dysbiosis and multidrug-resistant, virulence-enriched uropathogens
papers.abstract: **Objectives:** Recurrent urinary tract infection (rUTI) is increasingly complicated by antimicrobial resistance (AMR), yet urinary microbiome dysbiosis and isolate-level resistance-virulence are rarely examined together across different treatment states. In this study, we characterized both within the same sample in rUTI and in healthy controls. **Methods:** In this cross-sectional cohort, mid-stream urine was collected from women with untreated, treated and prophylaxis rUTI and age-matched healthy controls at four centres in South India. Of 80 samples collected, 75 were analysed (26 controls, 20 untreated, 20 treated, 9 prophylaxis) by 16S rRNA V3-V4 sequencing. In addition, 105 culturable isolates from the same samples were identified and tested for antimicrobial susceptibility (VITEK 2) and phenotypic virulence. **Results:** rUTI groups showed approximately half the alpha diversity of controls (median Shannon 1.07-1.18 vs 2.17; Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.041). Community structure differed from controls in every rUTI subgroup (PERMANOVA R-squared = 0.091, p = 0.004; pairwise FDR = 0.008) but not among subgroups. Mean Lactobacillus relative abundance fell from 29.2% in controls to <=13.2% in rUTI groups, while Escherichia-Shigella rose from 7.2% to 25.0-43.0%. Control-referenced dysbiosis z-scores were elevated in all rUTI groups (community distance: FDR <= 0.003; uropathogen: Lactobacillus index: FDR < 0.001 for treated and prophylaxis groups). Among isolates, Escherichia coli predominated (35/105; 16/35, 45.7% multidrug-resistant), followed by Klebsiella spp. (32% multidrug-resistant); carbapenem susceptibility was largely retained, and multidrug-resistant E. coli co-carried more virulence traits. **Conclusions:** rUTI is associated with a stable dysbiotic state that treatment does not restore, combining Lactobacillus loss and uropathogen dominance with a multidrug-resistant culturable reservoir that co-accumulates virulence traits. Reading the community and its isolates together may support microbiome-sparing, resistance-aware management of rUTI.
affiliations: Department of Food Science and Technology, Pondicherry University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Context-dependent regulation of RpoS-dependent and RpoS-independent gene transcription by Crl during exponential growth in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: RpoS, an alternative sigma factor, directly regulates approximately 10% of gene transcription in E. coli. The small protein Crl functions as a partner that assists RpoS in exerting its regulatory role, particularly during the stationary phase. However, the coordinating role of Crl during the exponential phase remains unclear. In addition, whether Crl can regulate gene transcription independently of RpoS is still unknown. Therefore, in this study, we used the RpoS-dependent operon hdeAB and the RpoS-independent operon proVWX as model systems to investigate the transcriptional regulatory function of Crl using RT-qPCR and 3C-qPCR. Since the expression of both Crl and RpoS is modulated by environmental signals, we further examined the transcription of these operons under different pH and osmotic conditions. The results showed that Crl can regulate transcription independently of RpoS and exhibits environment-specific bidirectional regulation. Overall, this study improves our understanding of the regulatory mechanisms of Crl and highlights the complexity of transcriptional regulation.
affiliations: Leiden University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Red and blue light cues drive contrasting remodeling of lipophilic metabolites and photophysiology in natural benthic diatom biofilms
papers.abstract: Intertidal mudflats are low hydrodynamic energy environments hosting microphytobenthic communities that experience strong spatiotemporal variability in light regimes, including changes in spectral quality and light intensity that can lead to cellular photooxidative stress. To cope with these fluctuations, autotrophs exhibit diverse and highly plastic adaptations that are often species-dependent and shaped by their ecological niches. This study investigates photophysiological responses and metabolic remodeling in a diatom assemblage originating from a natural winter microphytobenthic biofilm under contrasting red and blue light intensities. To this end, photosynthetic parameters were monitored alongside changes in lipophilic metabolites, including untargeted lipids and lipophilic pigments. While few metabolites showed temporal remodeling, rapid and contrasting changes were observed within 30 minutes in response to both spectral quality and light intensity. Red light treatments induced broader remodeling of lipophilic metabolites than blue light, whereas blue light appeared to have a greater impact on photosynthetic parameters. Moreover, red light induced xanthophyll-cycle responses comparable to those observed under blue light at equivalent incident intensity. We discuss these metabolic responses in relation to diatom photoadaptive strategies, placing these findings within the intertidal environmental framework. This work further underlines the importance of understanding rapid metabolic plasticity in coping with light fluctuations, providing new insights into the photoregulatory strategies of natural microphytobenthic communities.
affiliations: Museum National d'Histoire Naturelle (corresponding author)

papers.title: Role of small non-coding RNAs in DSB repair in Arabidopsis thaliana
papers.abstract: DNA double-strand breaks (DSB) are highly toxic lesions that must be repaired to avoid major losses of genetic materials or genome rearrangements. A number of highly conserved molecular pathways are involved in DSB repair, each resulting in different repair outcomes for a given DSB. Over the past decade, accumulating evidence has revealed the emergence of an unexpected new actor in DSB repair: RNA. Notably, small RNAs have been observed at DSB-flanking sequences and hypothesized to be involved in their repair. However, these DSB-induced small RNAs (diRNAs) were so far observed in studies using reporter systems, and their natural occurrence as well as their role in DNA repair remains debated. To address this question, we investigated diRNA biogenesis in Arabidopsis thaliana using CRISPR/Cas12a to induce targeted DSBs at three actively transcribed loci and one untranscribed locus. We found that 21-nt diRNAs are generated at transcribed loci, in a Dicer-like 4 (DCL4) dependent manner, but not at the untranscribed locus, indicating that active transcription is required for diRNA production. Remarkably, long-read DNA sequencing analysis shows that these diRNAs do not detectably influence DSB repair via either end-joining or microhomology-mediated end-joining. Furthermore, endogenous diRNAs have a modest effect on homologous recombination-associated repair, as impairment of the diRNA pathway in ago2 mutants resulted in only a slight reduction in RAD51 focus formation following Cas12a-induced DSBs. Together, these findings indicate that diRNAs are not essential for DSB repair itself but may function in the post-transcriptional silencing of damaged genes, likely to prevent aberrant transcription until proper repair is completed.
affiliations: Institute of Genetics, Reproduction and development (iGReD), Universite Clermont Auvergne, CNRS-UMR6293, INSERM-U1103, Clermont-Ferrand, France. (corresponding author)

papers.title: High-performance xenograft read-sorting for DNA methylation analysis
papers.abstract: Xenograft sorting tools separate sequenced DNA reads by species. We have enhanced the computational method and tool Xengsort to enable efficient epigenetic profiling of patient-derived xenograft models; it now supports cytosine-converted whole genome or reduced-representation data. Benchmarking Xengsort against several established methods (ICRG, bamcmp, XenofilteR) revealed consistently high accuracy across tools, but Xengsort outperformed the other tools in computational efficiency due to its alignment-free design.
affiliations: Saarland University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structure-Based Drug Design of Novel Inhibitors Targeting the Thiamine Biosynthesis Pathway in Bacteria
papers.abstract: Current generation antibiotics are limited by poor target selectivity and are often mismanaged, leading to widespread antimicrobial resistance. The bacterial thiamine biosynthesis pathway offers compelling alternative since it is highly essential for bacterial survival and yet absent in humans. Genetic perturbations within pathway lead to documented auxotrophy and virulence defects, indicating low mutational tolerance within this pathway. Thiamine phosphate synthase is a key bottleneck enzyme performing the crucial role of coupling thiazole and pyrimidine moieties to form thiamine monophosphate. To develop a suitable inhibitor against it, a structure-based drug design pipeline was implemented. High-throughput virtual screening of nearly 1.5 million molecules provided sufficient exploration of chemical space. Further, R-group substitution was utilized for lead optimization. Structure-Activity Relationship analysis upon molecular mutants reveals patterns among R-group interactions to catalytic residues across various scaffolds. Additionally, ADMET screening and validation using molecular dynamics simulations resulted in a potent orally bioavailable broad-spectrum bactericidal molecule.
affiliations: SASTRA Deemed University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structural basis for phosphorylation-induced inactivation of the rice ammonium transporter AMT1;1
papers.abstract: Ammonium (NH4+) uptake and transport in plants are mediated by ammonium transporters (AMTs), which are tightly regulated by phosphorylation to prevent excess ammonium influx and toxic accumulation. However, the mechanism of phosphorylation-mediated inactivation is unique and remains unclear. Here, we report cryo-EM structures of the rice (Oryza sativa) ammonium transporter OsAMT1;1 in its wild-type and phosphomimetic variant T452D states. OsAMT1;1 forms a stable homotrimer, with conserved motifs affirming a shared transport mechanism within the AMT/MEP/Rh superfamily. Our structural analysis reveals that T452D phosphomimetic stabilizes an intracellular salt-bridge network and maintains the channel in a closed state, in which the ICL5 loop positions the hydrophobic plug residue Leu360 near the cytoplasmic exit to occlude the channel exit and abolish complementation capacity. Our findings elucidate phosphorylation-induced inactivation mechanism for the plant AMT1 subfamily, providing a structural paradigm for the post-translational regulation of nutrient uptake.
affiliations: CAS Center for Excellence in Molecular Plant Sciences (corresponding author)

papers.title: Human Metalloenzymes Are Disproportionately Linked to Disease: The HEAM Structural Annotation Resource
papers.abstract: Catalytic metal-binding sites are established drug targets for many human diseases, yet systematic study of how metal function relates to disease is limited by the lack of a resource combining structural localization of human metal-binding sites with catalytic annotation at scale. We introduce HEAM (the Human Enzymatic Annotation of Metalloproteins), a structurally annotated dataset of 1,933 human metalloenzymes and 1,171 non-catalytic metalloproteins. HEAM incorporates annotated metals into protein structures at their corresponding binding sites and classifies each site as catalytic or non-catalytic using the machine learning classifier MAHOMES II. HEAM more than quadruples the human site-level coverage of the largest prior metalloenzyme database. Using HEAM, we show that human metalloproteins are significantly enriched in KEGG disease pathways relative to the human proteome, and that metalloenzymes specifically are significantly enriched in ClinVar pathogenic variants -- a distinction obscured in prior, catalytically unresolved metalloprotein datasets. These pathogenic variants are concentrated in metabolic disorders, indicating that metabolic dysfunction is a substantial contributor to metalloenzyme-linked disease. By pairing 3D structural annotation with catalytic classification, HEAM provides both a foundation for structure-guided drug design against metal-binding sites and a resource for determining how catalytic and non-catalytic metal function contribute to human disease.
affiliations: University of Kansas (corresponding author)

papers.title: DTCAMD, a disease-associated truncated form of CRYAB in neovascular age-related macular degeneration: a potential driver of subretinal fibrosis
papers.abstract: Abstract Purpose: Subretinal fibrosis causes irreversible vision loss in neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) and remains poorly controlled by anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) therapy. We investigated the role of B-crystallin (CRYAB) in angiogenic and fibrotic pathology and evaluated disease-associated CRYAB truncation as a therapeutic target. Methods: Aqueous humor from patients with nAMD was analyzed by quantitative proteomics and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. CRYAB function was assessed using knockout and knockdown approaches in a choroidal neovascularization (CNV) mouse model. CRYAB truncation and associated proteins were examined by immunoblotting, co-immunoprecipitation, and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). C-terminal truncation was further examined in mouse retinal tissue using antibodies generated against full-length CRYAB and its C-terminal region. Primary human retinal pigment epithelial (hRPE)-THP-1 co-cultures were used to examine CRYAB truncation under fibrosis-associated conditions. Pharmacological effects were tested using ({+/-})-threo-3-methylglutamic acid (T3MG) and 4-(2-aminoethyl)benzenesulfonyl fluoride hydrochloride (AEBSF). Results: CRYAB was upregulated in the aqueous humor of patients with nAMD. Higher CRYAB levels were associated with persistent lesions after initial anti-VEGF treatment. CRYAB knockout or knockdown reduced CNV pathology and decreased VEGFA and -smooth muscle actin (SMA) expression, without a significant substrain effect between C57BL/6N and C57BL/6J mice. A Ser45-phosphorylated truncated CRYAB species was detected in mouse laser-induced CNV model. We termed this species disease-associated truncated CRYAB in AMD (DTCAMD). Peptide mapping showed reproducible loss of distal C-terminal peptide coverage in truncated CRYAB. Consistent with this finding, C-terminal antibody recognition was reduced in CNV lesions. In hRPE-THP-1 co-cultures, DTCAMD accumulated with increased SMA expression. Proteomic analysis identified Prss1 as a candidate CRYAB-associated serine protease linked to truncation under CNV conditions. T3MG and AEBSF reduced DTCAMD-associated signals and CNV pathology. Conclusions: CRYAB contributes to angiogenic and fibrotic pathology in CNV. Disease-associated CRYAB truncation, particularly Ser45-phosphorylated DTCAMD, represents a potential therapeutic target for fibrotic remodeling in nAMD.
affiliations: College of Pharmacy, Chungbuk National University (corresponding author)

papers.title: How Bacterial Growth-Phase Reshapes Synthetic Gene Circuit Function
papers.abstract: The development of biological engineering tools have improved the ability to embed novel functions into living organisms. Concurrently, our understanding of the interface between synthetic genetic circuits and their host has accelerated in the past decade, enabling the development of context-aware predictive models. However, long-term circuit function remains difficult to predict when designs operate in field-relevant conditions. Specifically, while synthetic genetic circuits are typically characterized during exponential growth, these must operate for extended periods of time in nutrient-limited conditions and where bacteria enter stationary growth phase. In this work, we construct a mathematical model that captures the dynamics of a genetic circuit as cells transition into stationary growth phase. To achieve this, we construct synthetic genetic circuits with fluorescent reporter output and measure plasmid DNA copy number, mRNA level, protein level, and live cell count over the course of one week in stationary growth phase. We find that transcription rates plummet shortly after entering stationary phase but settle at a basal value that depends on both the promoter and ribosome binding site. Translation rates also decline in stationary phase, but protein accumulation due to lack of cell division can increase protein levels well beyond exponential phase. Our model recapitulates these findings and is capable of predicting the output of new genetic circuits. This model can serve as a tool to determine how a genetic circuit design may change on longer time scales where cells enter stationary growth phase.
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: A tissue time machine to forward-predict single-timepoint data applied to tuberculosis granulomas
papers.abstract: Recent advances have improved understanding of infection; however many detailed datasets are based on single timepoints post-infection and cannot generate longitudinal insights needed to predict infection outcomes. For example, pulmonary infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) initiates a complex system of immune and bacterial interactions that leads to granuloma formation, yet single snapshots in time need elaboration long-term. We develop a new approach, the tissue time machine, applied to predict outcomes of non-human primate granulomas from initiation to endpoint using single timepoint tissue datasets including high-dimensional spatial features. This involves identifying granuloma digital partners, simulations most closely resembling real granulomas from a virtual library of over 50,000. By analyzing digital partners, we predict infection outcomes of 22/28 granulomas, and that Mtb-specific, IFN-{gamma}-producing T cell recruitment rates influence uncertainty for the 6/28. This method is applicable to any system that allows for mechanistic predictions over time using heterogeneous, incomplete, and high-dimensional datasets.
affiliations: Department of Microbiology and Immunology, University of Michigan-Michigan Medicine, Ann Arbor, MI, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: A monoallelic immunopeptidome atlas of 10 prevalent canine DLA-88 alleles
papers.abstract: Characterization of naturally processed MHC class I (MHC-I)-bound peptides is essential for defining allele-specific peptide-binding features and understanding the functional consequences of MHC-I polymorphism. However, immunopeptidome analyses of dog leukocyte antigen (DLA) class I (DLA-I) molecules remain limited and comprehensive monoallelic ligand datasets for prevalent DLA-88 alleles are still lacking. Here, we established canine melanoma-derived cell populations expressing individual functional DLA-88 alleles and generated a monoallelic immunopeptidome atlas of prevalent DLA-88 alleles. Using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, we identified 32,702 naturally processed peptides of 7 to15 amino acids across 10 DLA-88 alleles, substantially expanding the available DLA-88 immunopeptidome landscape. These 10 alleles exhibited canonical peptide length distributions and allele-specific binding motifs that reflected variation in binding-groove pseudo-sequences defined from human MHC-I peptide-contact residues. Ligand sharing between DLA-88 alleles was associated with binding site distance. Incorporation of the comprehensively characterized DLA-88 ligand datasets in this study increased by more than fourfold the number of published canine DLA-I alleles with ligand-characterized reference alleles predicted to have similar peptide-binding features. We also found that antigen-processing signatures were highly conserved with those reported in humans. As a proof-of-concept application, we selected 54 DLA-88-bound peptides identified in our immunopeptidome analysis as candidate peptides for canine cancer immunotherapy by evaluating the normal tissue expression profiles of their source proteins. This DLA-88 immunopeptidome atlas provides insights into allele-dependent differences in antigen presentation and represents a valuable resource for developing accurate DLA-88-binding peptide prediction tools and supporting peptide-based immunological studies in dogs.
affiliations: Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Okayama University of Science, 1-3 Ikoino-oka, Imabari, Ehime 794-8555, Japan (corresponding author)

papers.title: T cell engagers convert acute tumor killing into endogenous vaccination
papers.abstract: T cell engagers (TCEs) redirect T cells to kill tumors by cross-linking CD3{varepsilon} to a tumor antigen, independently of T cell receptor specificity. Some patients achieve remissions that persist long after drug clearance, but whether TCEs can couple acute cytotoxicity to the generation of lasting adaptive immunity remains unknown. Here, using an immunocompetent mouse model for clinical-grade human TCEs, we show that TCE-mediated killing initiates an endogenous vaccination cascade. Intravital two-photon imaging reveals a perforin-dependent cytotoxic wave that peaks within 24 hours, then subsides despite massive T cell accumulation. Single-cell transcriptomics and adoptive transfers demonstrate that memory CD8 T cells, the principal effector reservoir in mouse and human, transit through a progenitor-like state before differentiating into cytotoxic effectors with recall competence. Crucially, tumor lysis fuels cross-priming of tumor-specific CD8 T cells by XCR1 type 1 conventional dendritic cells, a cDC1-dependent step essential for durable tumor control and protective memory upon rechallenge.
affiliations: Institut Pasteur (corresponding author)

papers.title: Spatiotemporal profiling of T cell repertoires in Lynch syndrome reveals convergent immune responses through neoplastic progression
papers.abstract: Surveillance of individuals with Lynch syndrome (LS), who are carriers of heterozygous inactivating mismatch repair (MMR) gene mutations that predispose to colorectal cancer, enables the study of tumour-immune coevolution during tumour initiation. Somatic loss of MMR activity in the LS colon leads to the accrual of cancer driver mutations, and also of neoantigens likely to generate an adaptive immune response. However, the spatial and temporal immune dynamics in colon and peripheral blood are uncharacterised. Here we show that the neoplastic evolution of mismatch repair deficient (MMRd) clones leads to large-scale and sustained reorganisation of the T-cell repertoire in colon and peripheral blood. We performed dense spatiotemporal profiling of T cell receptor (TCR) repertoires from 109 colonic biopsies (11 tumour samples, 98 normal bowel) from seven individuals, with eight matched blood repertoires. We additionally analysed 13 colorectal polyp repertoires from eight participants, 286 cross sectional blood repertoires from 242 participants (198 LS and 44 non-LS) and 52 longitudinal peripheral blood samples from 26 individuals with LS. We detected tumour-associated T cell clones, some of which were widely present in normal bowel tissue and also detectable in peripheral blood. Sequence similarity analysis revealed conserved TCR architectures across tissue compartments and recurrent clustering patterns between patients, that were not present in non-Lynch controls, consistent with convergent MMRd-associated antigen-driven immune selection. We identified systemic signatures associated with local tumour immune activity and revealed evidence of structured repertoire remodelling before overt malignancy. Longitudinal profiling revealed frequent turnover of low-abundance clonotypes, whereas highly abundant clonotypes persisted for several years. Collectively, our data defines the local and circulating TCR landscape associated with colonic neoplasia in LS, and provides a framework for LS blood-based immune monitoring, early interception and biomarker development.
affiliations: Institute of Cancer Research, London (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cannabinoid receptor 1 activity promotes microbial dysbiosis by stimulating the oxygen-dependent expansion of Enterobacteriaceae
papers.abstract: The endocannabinoid system is comprised of bioactive lipids that signal via cannabinoid receptors, which can modulate barrier and immune functions along the gastrointestinal tract. Clinical studies indicate that endocannabinoid activity is dysregulated in inflammatory bowel diseases. Here, we show that endocannabinoid activity promotes metabolic dysfunction within the colonic mucosa, resulting in microbial dysbiosis and exacerbated colitis. Stimulation of the cannabinoid receptor CB1 resulted in the expansion of Enterobacteriaceae within the gut microbiome, a common feature of inflammation-associated dysbiosis. Preceding this microbial change, CB1 activity induced transcriptional signatures of mitochondrial stress and immune activation within the colonic mucosa. This was followed by a reduction in mucosal ATP production and the induction of aerobic respiration genes in luminal Escherichia coli. Genetic inactivation of aerobic respiration in E. coli limited its proliferation, indicating that CB1 activity stimulates oxygen-dependent Enterobacteriaceae growth. In IBD susceptible mice, endocannabinoid activity promoted mucosal infection by an E. coli pathobiont, which corresponded with elevated pro-inflammatory markers. In inflammation resistant mice, acute CB1 stimulation was sufficient to accelerate the infection dynamics of an Enterobacteriaceae pathogen, resulting in exacerbated colitis. Taken together, our data support a model in which endocannabinoid signaling at the CB1 receptor disrupts respiratory metabolism in the colon, compromising the anoxic environment of the lumen that is critical for maintaining aerobically respiring pathogens at low abundance. More broadly, our findings highlight a proinflammatory effect of endocannabinoid activity that can contribute to intestinal disease development.
affiliations: University of South Carolina (corresponding author)

papers.title: LytM family endopeptidase LmdC is controlled by regulated auto processing and proteolytic destruction in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
papers.abstract: Enzymes that cleave the bacterial peptidoglycan sacculus, known collectively as autolysins, are critical for growth, division and morphogenesis, but their activities must be carefully controlled to avoid catastrophic lysis. Some autolysin control mechanisms have emerged, but we still know little about how most of them are regulated. Here, we report a novel control mechanism for the LytM/M23 family endopeptidase PA4404 in P. aeruginosa, which we have named LmdC. We have discovered that LmdC is auto catalytically cleaved into N- and C-terminal domains that are then degraded by the carboxyl-terminal processing proteases Prc and CtpA respectively. The effects of various mutations on LmdC-linked {beta}-lactam resistance suggested that full length LmdC is the functional enzyme, with its auto catalytic cleavage serving only to initiate its proteolytic destruction. The auto catalytic cleavage of LmdC was inhibited by overproducing a polymer-forming cytoskeletal protein bactofilin homolog encoded by PA0664, which we named Baf, and a protein of unknown function encoded by PA0663, which we named Api (auto processing inhibitor). We hypothesize that Baf and Api could promote a location specific role for LmdC. In this scenario, the dangerous potential for any free LmdC to cleave peptidoglycan at the wrong place would be prevented by its immediate auto processing and degradation. The widespread co-occurrence and linkage of lmdC and baf homologs, coupled with conserved features of those LmdC homologs, makes it likely that regulated LmdC auto processing is a widely conserved control mechanism.
affiliations: New York University Grossman School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Andes virus from the MV Hondius outbreak is highly pathogenic in hamsters and airborne shed
papers.abstract: In May 2026, an outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) caused by Andes virus (ANDV) was detected aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, sparking public health measures in multiple countries. ANDV infections in humans are mostly sporadic, most often linked to exposure to infected rodents in South America, although small clusters of human cases, like the 2026 outbreak on the MV Hondius occur as well. It is not known whether virological factors may contribute to this distinct epidemiology, and no phenotypic characterisation of the newly emerged ANDV (ANDV2026) has been carried out to date. Here, using an ANDV isolate from a presymptomatic patient from the MV Hondius, we studied pathogenesis, identified sites of viral replication, characterized innate and adaptive immune responses, and quantified shedding in golden Syrian hamsters. ANDV2026 proved to be highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe pulmonary disease reminiscent of HPS. ANDV2026 triggered a delayed type-I IFN response and inflammatory response in the lungs consistent with the key pathological features of HPS, and we detected viral replication in both respiratory and extra-respiratory tissues, including the brain. Infected animals mounted neutralising antibodies and T cell responses, the latter directed predominantly against the L and N proteins. Importantly, ANDV2026-infected animals shed virus through multiple routes, and we detected infectious virus in air samplers connected to cages housing ANDV2026-infected hamsters. In contrast, control hamsters infected with a rodent-derived ANDV isolate (ANDV9717869) shed little virus and air samples were consistently negative. These findings consolidate established features of ANDV pathogenesis, while revealing properties not previously described. Phenotypic characterisation of patient-derived ANDV isolates in animal models can strengthen outbreak preparedness, identify markers of disease severity, and support the development of medical countermeasures.
affiliations: Department of Viroscience, Erasmus University Medical Center, Rotterdam, the Netherlands (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Third-generation Lentiviral Vector System for Flow Virometry-based Analysis of HIV-1 Env and Other Viral Envelope Proteins
papers.abstract: Individual human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) particles can differ in their envelope protein (Env) despite being genetically identical. This non-genetic diversity can influence antibody recognition and has been implicated in the formation of persistent virus fractions that escape complete inhibition by broadly neutralizing antibodies. Investigating non-genetic diversity in HIV and other viruses requires approaches capable of characterizing antibody binding to individual viral particles. Flow virometry provides a promising tool for single-particle analysis, but a system combining high biosafety with specific particle labeling and versatility is lacking. Here, we developed a third-generation lentiviral vector system specifically designed for flow virometry. Fluorescent proteins were incorporated into the HIV-1 Gag polyprotein between the matrix- and capsid-encoding regions, flanked by viral protease cleavage sites, creating the packaging constructs pLentiFlow-eGFP and pLentiFlow-mCherry. Lentiviral particles (LVPs) based on pLentiFlow vectors were fluorescent and retained infectivity comparable to LVPs generated with the parental vector system despite reduced particle production. We optimized LVP detection on a CytoFLEX nano and defined a linear p24-based concentration range for reliable single-particle analysis. Using complementary controls, we demonstrated that background from the assessed sources accounted for no more than approximately 3% of events within a broad eGFP+ gate and confirmed that the detected fluorescent particles were predominantly membrane-enclosed. As a proof of concept, LVPs were pseudotyped with vesicular stomatitis virus glycoprotein, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 spike, or HIV-1 Env. Envelope-specific antibody binding was detected using 8G5F11, CR3022 or PGT128, respectively, demonstrating that different viral surface proteins can be analyzed on a common particle backbone. Together, these results establish a third-generation lentiviral vector system for flow virometry that combines intrinsic particle labeling with high biosafety and flexible pseudotyping. The system provides a platform for investigating envelope protein-associated non-genetic diversity and its consequences for antibody recognition in HIV and other viruses.
affiliations: Institute for the Research on HIV and AIDS-associated Diseases, University Hospital Essen, University of Duisburg-Essen, Essen, Germany (corresponding author)

papers.title: Exploring the antibiotic-producing capabilities of Canadian High Arctic bacteria
papers.abstract: Microbial communities in harsh environments such as the Canadian high Arctic, remain a relatively unexplored source of antimicrobial natural products. In this study, we developed a pipeline for screening and evaluating bacterial isolates cultured from 23 Canadian high Arctic soil, sediment, and active-layer permafrost samples to discover antibacterial compounds. The pipeline incorporated an undergraduate studentsourcing program and produced created a collection of over 350 bacterial isolates with preliminary antibacterial activity. Following dereplication, whole genome sequencing and secondary screening by co-culture assays, five isolates were prioritized to test crude extracts for antibacterial activity. Among bioactive crude extracts from these isolates, the Pseudomonas isolate with the most potent activity against S. aureus was analyzed. Using liquid chromatography bioactivity guided fractionation, we identified a potential bioactive compound known as koreenceine A, a compound previously only isolated from a Pseudomonas from temperate soil and involved in gene expression of other their microbial community. Here we expanded the known antibiotic activity of koreenceine A and confirmed that a {triangleup}kecBCD genetic knockout of the putative biosynthetic gene cluster significantly abrogated the antibacterial activity.
affiliations: McGill University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Murine cytomegalovirus m119-118 encodes a new viral Fc receptor antagonizing host Fc receptor activation
papers.abstract: Cytomegaloviruses (CMVs) encode numerous immunomodulatory proteins to counteract innate and adaptive immunity. One class of immune evasion proteins is viral Fc receptors (vFcRs), which bind to the Fc region of IgG antibodies and interfere with antibody-mediated effector functions crucial for antiviral defense. Despite the established role of vFcRs in modulating antibody-mediated immunity, their contribution to viral pathogenesis in vivo remains incompletely understood. Although human CMV (HCMV) encodes four vFcRs, only a single vFcR, fcr-1 encoded by gene m138, has been identified in murine CMV (MCMV). By comparing and cloning the genomes of MCMV strains v70, K181+, and K181Perth, we identified a frameshift mutation affecting the spliced m119-118 transcript in K181Perth. This finding prompted us to investigate the function of the m119-118 gene. We show that it encodes a second MCMV vFcR, which we named fcr-2. It is structurally similar to its positional homolog in HCMV, UL119-118/gp68, and binds specifically to the Fc part of murine IgG. Deletion of both vFcRs genes from the MCMV genome resulted in substantially reduced Fc-binding to the surface of infected cells, indicating a complementary function of the vFcRs. Functional assays with viral deletion mutants further demonstrated that both proteins inhibit host Fc receptor activation in a cooperative fashion. Although an m119-118-deficient MCMV was only marginally attenuated in infected BALB/c mice, an m119-118 and m138 double mutant attained significantly lower organ titers than the m138-deficient mutant. These data suggest an important cooperative function of the two MCMV vFcRs for viral dissemination and pathogenesis in vivo.
affiliations: Leibniz Institute of Virology (LIV) (corresponding author)

papers.title: Gain-of-function mutations in the RodZ juxtamembrane domain promote Rod system activity in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: The peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall protects bacteria from osmotic lysis and determines their shape. In rod-shaped bacteria, the lateral wall is elongated by the Rod system (elongasome). This synthetic machine is built around the RodA-PBP2 PG synthase complex, the actin-like protein MreB, and the accessory proteins MreC, MreD, and RodZ. Notably, RodZ shares a similar domain organization with FtsN, an essential division protein that triggers PG synthesis by the division apparatus (divisome). Both are single pass transmembrane proteins that bind actin-like proteins in the cytoplasm and have largely unstructured periplasmic regions capped by small, folded C-terminal domains. We therefore investigated whether RodZ might function like FtsN in activating the Rod system. To this end, gain-of-function variants of Escherichia coli RodZ were isolated that restored growth and shape to cells producing a hypomorphic mreC mutant. Production of these RodZ variants in wild-type cells increased resistance to the MreB antagonist A22 and enhanced sensitivity to the beta-lactam mecillinam. These phenotypes have all previously been associated with Rod system hyperactivation, and we found that they were caused by substitutions in the cytoplasmic juxtamembrane (JM) domain of RodZ. This domain is analogous to the N-terminus of FtsN known to promote divisome activation via its interaction with filaments of the actin-like FtsA protein. Structural modeling indicates that the JM domain of RodZ is similarly likely to associate with MreB filaments. Our results therefore support a model in which RodZ activates PG synthesis by the Rod system via a mechanism analogous to divisome activation by FtsN.
affiliations: Harvard Medical School (corresponding author)

papers.title: Five decades of human H1N1 evolution reveal conserved glycan receptor specificity
papers.abstract: H1N1 influenza viruses have circulated continuously among human populations for five decades. During evolution, the hemagglutinin has accumulated amino acid substitutions in and around the receptor-binding site (RBS), mainly due to antigenic pressure, potentially altering receptor recognition and binding profiles. Here, we investigated the glycan-binding properties of H1N1 strains collected from 1977 through 2024 using ELISA, flow cytometry, and tissue histochemistry to characterize changes in receptor-binding specificity over time. Across the strains examined, we observe a recurring preference for binding 2,6-sialylated di-LacNAc N-glycans. Binding to 2,3-sialylated glycans was generally undetectable, although A/Hongkong/117/1977 and A/New Caledonia/20/1999 bind chicken tracheal tissues. Interestingly, post-pandemic H1N1 viruses fluctuate in their relative binding avidities. The responsible amino acids, in turn, have different effects in pre-pandemic HA proteins. We also report a classical egg-adapted H1N1 mutant that shows null binding across platforms. These findings highlight the contribution of RBS mutations during initial adaptation and evolution of human H1N1 influenza viruses to glycan-binding properties, which, in contrast to H3N2 viruses, never fail to bind glycans that correlate with avian erythrocyte hemagglutination.
affiliations: Utrecht Institute for Pharmaceutical Sciences, Utrecht University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Evolutionary expansion of the bacterial ompW gene family enables functional diversification during host adaptation
papers.abstract: The outer membrane protein W (OmpW) family comprises minor porins essential for environmental adaptation and host interactions in Gram-negative bacteria. However, ompW is conventionally treated as a ubiquitous single-copy gene, masking its true evolutionary complexity. Through comprehensive phylogenetic analysis across thousands of reference genomes, we reveal that ompW is present in nearly half of Gram-negative lineages, exhibiting a patchy distribution governed by a birth-and-death model of evolution with recurrent duplications and horizontal transfer. Notably, copy number expansions concentrate in lineages associated with eukaryotic hosts, linking paralog accumulation to niche adaptation. Experimental validation in Acinetobacter baumannii reveals four distinct loci that maintain high structural conservation despite sequence divergence, yet undergo profound functional specialization spanning from baseline physiological maintenance to modulating host colonization and persistence in vitro and in vivo. These findings dismantle the single-copy paradigm, demonstrating that widespread gene family expansion and paralog diversification drive the phenotypic plasticity required for bacteria to colonize hostile host environments.
affiliations: University Pablo de Olavide (corresponding author)

papers.title: Dietary omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids interact with select gut microbes to produce bioactive metabolites found in infant gut metabolomes
papers.abstract: Gut microbes metabolize nutrients in infant diets, producing compounds that play roles in host health. Long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LCPUFAs) are an important component of infant diets, supporting neurological development and immune regulation. Emerging evidence demonstrates that gut microbes, alongside the host, participate in the metabolism of dietary lipids, highlighting an underexplored avenue for LCPUFA biology. In this work, alkyne-tagged eicosapentaenoic acid (EPAALK) was used to investigate interactions between LCPUFAs and the gut microbiota. Flow cytometry and comparative metabolomics identified gut microbial EPA interactors in the ileum of mice. Further comparative metabolomics analysis identified the conversion of EPA to N-acyl amino acids, including attachment to phenylalanine (EP-Phe) and leucine (EP-Leu). Targeted analysis of ex vivo stool cultures determined that EP-Phe and EP-Leu are produced by gut bacteria. A survey of lipid-relevant infant gut bacteria determined various flow cytometry-confirmed EPA-microbe interactions and identified Enterococcus faecalis, Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron, and Clostridium bifermentans as competent producers of EP-Phe or EP-Leu. Thus, both novel metabolites from diet-derived inputs and microbial producers of these metabolites were identified. Together, this highlights important microbiome-centric and mechanistic consequences of LCPUFA consumption and emphasizes that the gut microbiome may be an important consideration in targeted supplementation strategies.
affiliations: Cornell University (corresponding author)

papers.title: In Vitro Assessment of Chemically Modified Probiotic Bacteria as Receptor-Mimic Decoys for Cholera Toxin B Subunit
papers.abstract: Gastrointestinal infections remain a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Conventional antibiotic treatment can be ineffective or inappropriate in some settings, particularly in the context of increasing antimicrobi-al resistance. In many enteric infections, an early step in pathogenesis involves binding of pathogens or their toxins to oligosaccharide receptors on host-cell surfaces, making these interactions attractive targets for antimicrobial strategies that do not rely on conventional antibiotics. Here, we developed a non-recombinant, microbiome-based chemical engineering approach in which cholesteryl-peptides serve as flexible chemical scaffolds for displaying GM1 receptor mimics on probiotic bacteria. The GM1-cholesteryl-peptides generated surface-accessible GM1 on both the Gram-positive probiotic Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 and the Gram-negative probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle 1917. The resulting GM1-decorated bacteria showed concentration-dependent binding and sequestration of cholera toxin B subunit (CTB) in vitro and reduced CTB binding to Vero cells. These findings establish an in vitro proof-of-concept for a modular, non-recombinant bacterial decoy platform and may provide a basis for the future development of receptor-mimic strategies against toxin-mediated gastrointestinal infections.
affiliations: Technical University of Denmark (DTU) (corresponding author)

papers.title: CLARA: Compound Library Active Learning with Reasoning Agents
papers.abstract: Batch active learning for ligand discovery requires a recurring decision about whether to exploit high predicted affinity, reduce model uncertainty, or broaden chemical coverage. We test whether a language model can make this strategy-level decision while candidate ranking and label revelation remain controlled by a deterministic Gaussian-process environment. Across four protein targets, ten paired seeds, and a 360-compound assay budget, a GPT-5.6 Sol agent outperformed random sampling in all 40 matched campaigns. Its final top-2\% recall was 0.412 on D2R, 0.374 on Mpro, 0.448 on TYK2, and 0.683 on USP7. It was statistically tied with the strongest fixed policy on Mpro and USP7 but underperformed target-specific leaders on D2R and TYK2. The agent shifted from exploration-oriented early batches toward exploitation and produced 686 testable threshold claims with an 86.3\% atomic success rate, although 19.8\% of forecasts were not numerically scorable. In 200 prespecified information-ablation campaigns, removing uncertainty, diversity, or memory caused only small endpoint changes, while shuffling explanatory evidence reproduced the full allocation path in 39 of 40 paired campaigns. A deterministic 80\% availability constraint reduced recall on every target but preserved the target-dependent pattern of wins and losses. These results support language-model strategy control as a feasible and auditable layer.
affiliations: Shiv Nadar University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Urea is a dynamic and functional component of mammalian breast milk
papers.abstract: Urea is a constituent of human milk, yet its regulation and interactions with the infant gut microbiome have not been established. Combining three human cohorts, a mouse model, and microbiome analyses, we show that milk urea increases across lactation, is conserved across mammals, and is not explained by maternal serum urea or diet. Instead, we identify lactation-dependent remodeling of mammary urea metabolism and transport, including dynamic epithelial AQP3 localization consistent with regulated urea transfer into milk. Alongside urea, maternal milk and stool provide reservoirs of urea-metabolizing bacteria that help establish the infant "ureabiome", with encoded urea-utilization capacity. This maternal-infant axis is context-dependent: infant formulas provide higher urea levels than human milk, while functional assays show that urea supports both commensal and opportunistic bacteria in a concentration-dependent manner. Together, these findings define a maternal nitrogen axis linking milk urea to infant gut microbiome assembly and function.
affiliations: Center for Advanced Biotechnology and Medicine, Rutgers University, Piscataway, NJ, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Differential mRNA localization of karyopherin-β2 homologs in C. elegans and humans
papers.abstract: In Caenorhabditis elegans embryos, the nuclear transport receptor IMB-2 (Importin Beta Family-2, a karyopherin {beta}2) preferentially localizes to the nuclear envelope along with its encoding mRNA. This suggests that imb-2 mRNA is locally translated at the nuclear envelope. To test whether imb-2's two putative human orthologs, Transportin 1 (TNPO1) and Transportin 2 (TNPO2), exhibited similar mRNA localization, we performed smiFISH and microscopy in U2OS, HeLa, and human pluripotent stem cells. Neither human TNPO1 nor TNPO2 mRNA localized to the nuclear envelope in any tested human cell type. However, the human TNPO1 protein and the C. elegans IMB-2 protein both localized to the nucleus and its periphery. This suggests that despite their shared functional roles these karyopherins have different routes to expression.
affiliations: Department of Biochemistry & Molecular Biology, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO 80523, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: scGSCA: gene-set differential co-expression analysis for single-cell RNA sequencing data
papers.abstract: Understanding disease-associated pathway coordination requires distinguishing phenotype-related co-expression changes from differences across cellular contexts while accounting for cells sampled from the same subject. Bulk gene-set co-expression methods do not directly address the sparse counts, single-cell distributional noise, subject-level dependence, and cell-type heterogeneity of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. We developed single-cell gene-set co-expression analysis (scGSCA), a framework for pathway-level differential co-expression analysis in scRNA-seq data. scGSCA fits gene-wise zero-inflated negative binomial mixed models with subject-level random effects and computes gene-set co-expression statistics from quantile residual correlations. It provides an overall differential gene-set co-expression analysis and an interaction test to assess whether the co-expression pattern between two cell types varies by sample phenotype. We applied scGSCA to tumor-normal gastric, breast-subtype, and lung-skin comparisons with matched bulk and scRNA-seq data. The overall test identified signals not captured in bulk analysis, including Axon guidance in gastric cancer and estrogen-response, IL6-JAK-STAT3, and TNF/NF-{kappa}B pathways in breast cancer. The interaction test further identified co-expression contrasts across cell types. scGSCA extends gene-set co-expression analysis to single-cell data while retaining subject-level structure and cell-type-specific context. scGSCA is freely available as an open-source R package.
affiliations: University of Miami (corresponding author)

papers.title: CXCL-CXCR2 signaling drives cancer-endothelium interactions in SCLC metastatic seeding
papers.abstract: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a highly metastatic malignancy with tropism to the liver, yet the signals that enable organ-specific metastatic colonization remain largely undefined. During metastasis, disseminated cancer cells first encounter endothelial cells (ECs) at the vascular-tissue interface, positioning cancer-endothelium crosstalk as a key determinant of metastatic success. Defining the signaling pathways underlying this reciprocal communication may uncover actionable vulnerabilities for preventing and treating this lethal disease. Here, we uncover an EC-derived CXCL chemokine program that activates cancer-intrinsic CXCR2-RAC1 signaling as a critical mediator of SCLC liver metastasis. By integrating in vitro and in vivo models, we show that SCLC cells induce robust CXCL chemokine expression from liver ECs, which in turn enhances SCLC migration and reinforces cancer cell-EC interactions. We applied highly quantitative metastatic colony barcode sequencing coupled with individual gene inactivation to demonstrate that CXCR2 is essential for SCLC migration and liver metastatic seeding. Mechanistically, CXCL-CXCR2 signaling activates RAC1-dependent F-actin assembling to drive SCLC motility during CXCL-induced metastatic seeding. Pharmacologic inhibition of CXCR2 or RAC1 suppresses SCLC migration and prevents SCLC liver metastasis. Together, our research defined a chemokine-driven signaling circuit that governs cancer-endothelium communication during the metastatic cascade and nominate the CXCL-CXCR2-RAC1 axis as a promising therapeutic vulnerability for preventing and treating metastatic SCLC.
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis (corresponding author)

papers.title: TLR7-Dependent Autoimmunity Remodels Intestinal Immune Cell Dissemination
papers.abstract: Intestinal immune cell dissemination has emerged as a fundamental mechanism of tissue-to-tissue immune communication that shapes systemic immunity, yet how this physiological process changes across different stages of systemic autoimmunity remains poorly understood. Here, using photoconversion, inducible and spontaneous models of TLR7-dependent autoimmunity, and microbiota perturbation, we define how autoimmunity reshapes intestinal immune dissemination. TLR7-dependent autoimmunity progressively suppresses dissemination in a tissue-dependent manner across gut-associated and systemic tissues while selectively reconfiguring the intestinal emigrant pool, characterized by reduced lymphocyte dissemination and increased representation of myeloid populations, particularly dendritic cells. This divergence is already evident in young TLR7-transgenic mice before detectable splenomegaly. Moreover, microbial regulation of intestinal dissemination depends on timing and inflammatory context, with antibiotic treatment during ongoing autoimmunity producing broader changes in intestinal immune dissemination. Together, our findings establish remodeling of physiological intestinal immune dissemination as an early feature of TLR7-dependent autoimmunity and reveal how chronic inflammation reshapes tissue-to-tissue immune communication.
affiliations: University of Virginia School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Diacylglycerol Kinases Balance DAG Signaling to Control B Cell Maturation, Germinal Center Homeostasis, and Humoral Immunity
papers.abstract: Diacylglycerol (DAG) is a critical second messenger downstream of the B-cell receptor (BCR), but how DAG signaling is regulated during B-cell development and humoral responses remains incompletely understood. Here, complementary gain- and loss-of-function approaches revealed stage-specific requirements for diacylglycerol kinase (DGK)-regulated signaling in B cells. Expression of the gain-of-function DGK{zeta} mutant DGK{zeta}{Delta}NLS had limited effects on early BM B-cell development but progressively impaired transitional and mature B-cell populations. DGK{zeta}{Delta}NLS attenuated BCR-induced ERK1/2 and mTOR signaling, activation, and proliferation and, when expressed in AID-expressing B cells, reduced GC B-cell survival and T-dependent IgG responses without detectably impairing GC B-cell proliferation in vivo. Conversely, combined DGK/{zeta} deficiency resulted in marked spontaneous GC B-cell expansion associated with enhanced ERK1/2, Akt, and S6 signaling and increased glucose uptake. Despite this steady-state GC expansion, DGK/{zeta}-deficient mice developed spontaneous autoreactivity and mounted impaired antigen-specific antibody responses. Thus, B-cell developmental stages exhibit differential sensitivity to altered DGK activity, and opposing perturbations of DGK-regulated signaling produce reciprocal effects on GC B-cell accumulation while both compromise productive humoral immunity. These findings identify DGKs as critical regulators that tune lipid signaling for B-cell maturation, GC homeostasis, and effective antibody responses.
affiliations: Duke University School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Surrogate variables and the risk of overfitting in neuropsychiatric gene expression analyses
papers.abstract: The reproducibility crisis in biomedical research calls for re-evaluation of how common analytic approaches affect results. One such approach, surrogate variable analysis (SVA), is widely used to adjust for unmeasured drivers of variation in transcriptomic differential expression analyses. We systematically quantified the impact of SVA using synthetic data with known ground truth and fourteen brain RNA-seq and microarray datasets spanning Alzheimer's disease, autism spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and Parkinson's disease. In synthetic data, SVA usage frequently led to high false positive rates. This issue was not revealed by standard diagnostics nor resolved by strategies such as maximizing cross-dataset signal correlation. In real data, using SVA reduced cross-cohort reproducibility of differential expression signatures regardless of the number of surrogate variables included. These findings show that SVA risks inducing overfitting at realistic signal levels, advocating for a cautious, case-by-case application, with a preference for modeling known covariates.
affiliations: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai (corresponding author)

papers.title: Efficient approximate Bayesian inference for large, heterogeneous biological datasets
papers.abstract: Simulation-based inference (SBI) offers a route to connect biological data with mechanistic models. At the frontier of biology, datasets continue to grow in scale and richness, and increasingly record heterogeneity between individual observations that a mechanistic model can take into account. Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) remains a popular approach to SBI due to its ease of use, but incorporating this heterogeneity often requires a separate simulation of each observation, which is prohibitively expensive at scale. A previously proposed technique, minibatch Sequential Monte Carlo ABC (SMC ABC), reduces this cost by simulating a fixed-size random subset of observations for each proposal, at the price of sampling noise that limits precision. Here, we present an adaptive minibatch approach that uses small batches during early exploration and increases the batch size as the posterior is refined. The adaptive batch size is set by the target precision and does not grow with the size of the dataset, so the savings over full-data SMC ABC increase for larger datasets. We demonstrate the method on synthetic biological models and on real single-cell gene-expression data that vary in scale and type of heterogeneity, including cell geometry and initial condition. In each case, the adaptive scheme obtains posteriors close to those of full-data SMC ABC at a fraction of the cost. Altogether, adaptive minibatching improves the tradeoff between speed and precision in SMC ABC and opens the door to mechanistic inference on large, heterogeneous biological datasets.
affiliations: University of Utah (corresponding author)

papers.title: Optimizing copy number profiles for tumor cell phylogeny inference from low-coverage single-cell sequencing data
papers.abstract: Motivation: Accurate reconstruction of tumor cell phylogenies is crucial for understanding cancer evolutionary dynamics, inferring intra-tumor heterogeneity, and designing effective and personalized cancer treatment strategies. One of the most promising and cost-effective approaches for reconstructing tumor phylogenies for large numbers of cells is to use copy number alteration (CNA) data obtained from low-coverage single-cell DNA sequencing of sampled tumor cells. However, error and uncertainty in inferred copy number profiles (CNPs), resulting from low sequence coverage, can have a drastic negative effect on the reconstruction accuracy of tumor cell phylogenies. Results: In this work, we show that careful selection of bin size, a critical tuning parameter for inferring CNPs, is necessary to maximize the accuracy of tumor cell phylogeny inference. Specifically, we (i) use three previously published low-coverage single-cell DNA sequencing datasets from real tumors to demonstrate that even small changes in bin size can have a drastic impact on downstream tumor phylogeny reconstruction, (ii) show that this effect persists even when using simulated low-coverage datasets generated under idealized conditions with minimal noise, and (iii) propose a simple computational approach to select bin sizes that maximize tumor phylogeny accuracy. Our experiments span a wide range of bin sizes and account for the impact of various factors including coverage-level, phylogeny reconstruction method, and CNP inference method, and explicitly account for phylogenetic reconstruction uncertainty. Our evaluation of the proposed computational approach for bin size selection shows that it can significantly improve tumor cell phylogeny reconstruction accuracy compared to baseline methods. Availability: Freely available from https://github.com/Tanveer14/BinSelector.
affiliations: University of Connecticut (corresponding author)

papers.title: A matrikine organizes the dendritic cell- T cell triads that build tertiary lymphoid structures
papers.abstract: Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) predict checkpoint-inhibition response, and conventional dendritic cells (cDC) are required to build and maintain them. What renders a tumor niche permissive is unknown: chemokines recruit constituent cells but do not specify essential tricellular units. Here we show that the organizing signal is a matrix fragment. Proteoglycan versican (VCAN) proteolysis releases the matrikine versikine, constitutively in germinal center light zones and inducibly in tumor stroma. Versikine activates CD11b+ cDC and expands cDC1 to assemble TLS-archetypal triads, apposed DC:CD4+T:CD8+T units. Versikine-conditioned DC engage progenitor-exhausted CD8+ T cells (Tpex) and Tpex-sustaining, Th1-polarized follicular helper CD4+ T cells. Excess unproteolyzed VCAN inverts this toward DC-Treg crosstalk and Tpex loss. In a prospective PD-1 blockade trial in metastatic colorectal cancer, all VCAN-proteolysis-predominant patients were alive at 4.1-year median follow-up. Versikine (mRNA or recombinant protein) sensitizes proteolysis-weak experimental tumors to PD-L1 blockade. Matrikines organize chemokine-recruited cells into functional intratumoral immune niches.
affiliations: Rush University Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Inhomogeneity of negative enthalpy enables excellent mechanical properties in nanosized single crystals of multi-principal element alloys
papers.abstract: Many nanosized metals with limited dislocation nucleation and multiplication usually exhibit poor plasticity. Previous studies have demonstrated that multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) can achieve a combination of strength and plasticity. However, whether these mechanical properties extend to their nanosized counterparts and how nanosized MPEAs accommodate plastic deformation remains unknown. Using a homemade in-situ device, we captured the atomic-scale tensile process and measured the stress-strain curve of Fe 48 Mn 32 Co 10 Cr 10 nanosized single crystals (NSCs). We find that NSCs achieve a strength of ~3 GPa and a uniform elongation of ~20%. We show that this combination arises from the inhomogeneous distribution of enthalpy, which produces a broad spectrum of energy barriers for the nucleation of full dislocations, partial dislocations, and nanotwins. Consequently, dislocations and nanotwins are randomly generated throughout MPEA NSCs, effectively suppressing local stress concentration and leading to both high strength and large uniform elongation.

papers.title: GlycoStamp-seq: Single-cell nascent sialoglycometabolomics captures sialylation dynamics in immune cells of an oxaliplatin-treated bladder cancer mouse model

Keep medical doctors in academia — without them, health-care research will suffer

What does a PhD pay? Data reveal huge gaps across Europe
Hidden signals in sleep can predict future health

Does the decline of book reading mark the end of rational thinking?
Private, offline and yours: how to search the literature with local AI systems
Targeting MDA5 induces immunogenic cell death and promotes anti-tumor immunity
Plant invasions are associated with lower community stability at multiple spatial scales
A health-system-scale, episode-resolved multimodal atlas of cancer cachexia
papers.abstract: Using longitudinal data from 52,236 patients with cancer, this study created a multimodal atlas of cancer cachexia, demonstrating that weight loss episodes are linked to systemic serologic signatures and specific tumor genotypes and can be predicted using integrated clinical and molecular data, enabling earlier identification.

papers.title: Zbtb44-mediated transcriptional repression critically regulates colonic inflammation
papers.abstract: Poojary and colleagues show that the transcription factor Zbtb44 suppresses colonic inflammation and epithelial cell damage by deregulated T cells.

papers.title: An RNA mark for pluripotency
papers.abstract: A chemical modification of 7SK RNA links RNA modification to chromatin remodeling during human cell reprogramming. PUS7 installs this modification, enabling reprogramming without exogenous OCT4 and providing an alternative route to induced pluripotency.

papers.title: PUS7 pseudouridylation of 7SK orchestrates human somatic cell reprogramming into iPS cells
papers.abstract: Reprogramming human somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS cells) provides huge potential for regenerative medicine but its molecular regulation remains incompletely understood. In this study, we identify PUS7 as an RNA modification checkpoint that promotes acquisition of pluripotency. PUS7 loss markedly impairs reprogramming, whereas its overexpression accelerates reprogramming efficiency and kinetics. Mechanistically, PUS7 pseudouridylates U250 of the chromatin-associated noncoding RNA 7SK, enhancing its interaction with the BRG/BRM-associated factor (BAF) complex. Loss of this modification disrupts 7SK–BAF association, reduces BAF chromatin occupancy and decreases global chromatin accessibility. We further establish PSKM (PUS7, SOX2, KLF4, MYC) reprogramming, which generates iPS cells with faithful imprinting, robust lineage potential and improved developmental fidelity. PSKM-iPS cells differentiate efficiently toward neural and hematopoietic lineages and undergo gastrulation-like morphogenesis. These findings link 7SK pseudouridylation to chromatin remodeling and establish PSKM as a framework for generating high-quality human iPS cells for modeling and regenerative medicine.

papers.title: Skin-resident CXCR6+ memory CD4+ T cells and dendritic cells form dermal perivascular hubs that drive relapse in allergic dermatitis
papers.abstract: Tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells are heterogeneous, but how pathogenic subsets drive relapse in allergic dermatitis remains unclear. Asahina et al. identify a pathogenic CXCR6+ CD4+ TRM subset sustained through CXCL16-dependent clustering with CD301b+ cDC2s, revealing the TRM-DC niche as a potential therapeutic target for allergic dermatitis.

papers.title: Microbial cues for a stem-like lymphoid niche
Hitting KRAS G12D without the gut punch: Can immunotherapy make it last?
Toward the next generation of CAR T cell therapies for cancer
papers.abstract: CAR T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of blood cancers but faces persistent challenges in solid tumors. In this review, Usta and Mackall synthesize clinical lessons, next-generation engineering strategies, and emerging in vivo manufacturing approaches to define opportunities for broader, safer, and more effective CAR T cell therapies.

papers.title: A CK2-β-TrCP kinase-E3 ubiquitin ligase cascade is a metabolic sensor regulating tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase stability
papers.abstract: How metabolic enzyme levels are regulated is poorly understood. Studying the tryptophan (Trp)-metabolizing enzyme TDO2, Thielen et al. discover a CK2 kinase-β-TrCP E3 ligase pathway that regulates stability in response to substrate availability. Trp occupation of an exosite restricts degron accessibility, whereas low Trp releases the degron for phosphorylation-ubiquitylation-mediated degradation.

papers.title: PHYHD1-mediated translational control regulates renal cell carcinoma progression
papers.abstract: Liang et al. identify phytanoyl-CoA dioxygenase domain containing 1 (PHYHD1) as a tumor suppressor that regulates protein production in kidney cancer. Loss of PHYHD1 promotes disease progression by increasing ceramide transporter 1 (CERT1) production, uncovering a regulatory pathway that may help predict patient outcomes and provide a therapeutic opportunity for PHYHD1-deficient tumors.

papers.title: Rotational settings quantize nucleosome movement by chromatin regulators
papers.abstract: Chromatin regulators are thought to override intrinsic DNA sequence preferences. La et al. show regulators move nucleosomes in quantized 10 bp steps to take advantage of the shallow energy potential created by DNA sequence, preserving rotational setting and the DNA face contacting histones.

papers.title: Meningeal inflammation and arachnoid barrier breakdown in a mouse model of neonatal bacterial meningitis
papers.abstract: Kim et al. show the neonatal arachnoid barrier is compromised after GBS infection, causing increased permeability and proinflammatory signaling in most meningeal cell types including meningeal fibroblasts. A systemic injection of TNF-α alone is sufficient to break down the arachnoid barrier, suggesting its potential contribution in in vivo meningitis model.

papers.title: Aberrant recursive splicing in a human disease locus
papers.abstract: Boone et al. delete a recursive exon in CADM2 to understand the role of recursive splicing (RS) and explain these deletions’ association with ADHD. RS loss alters intronic RNA abundance, impacts transcript usage, decreases CADM2 expression, reduces exon usage downstream of the missing recursive exon, and perturbs neuronal gene programs.
