papers.title: Disease-causing helix-8 mutations reprogram parathyroid hormone receptor-1 effector selectivity
papers.abstract: Höppner et al. show that disease-associated substitutions in PTH1R helix-8 selectively rewire receptor coupling to G proteins and βarrestin. Distinct mutations bias PTH1R engagement toward either Gαq or βarrestin pathways and impair Gαs activation. These findings reveal mutation-driven shifts in effector selectivity as a previously unrecognized mechanism in PTH1R-associated disease.

papers.title: Orally delivered metabolically reprogrammed probiotics for cascade-activated antitumor immunity in colorectal cancer
papers.abstract: Wang et al. develop an oral metabolically engineered bacterial platform (EcN-HlpA-CGL [EHC]) for colorectal cancer immunotherapy, which triggers ferroptosis in colorectal cancer cells to boost immunogenicity, while the bacterial adjuvanticity reshapes the immunosuppressive microenvironment. This approach activates both systemic and gut mucosal immunity, effectively suppressing orthotopic tumor growth and metastasis.

papers.title: Gene regulation at the early human maternal–fetal interface
papers.abstract: Human placentation establishes a dynamic maternal–fetal interface in which fetal trophoblast cells coordinate tissue remodelling, immune adaptation and resource exchange to support pregnancy. In this Review, the authors discuss how single-cell, spatial and functional omics are uncovering gene regulatory mechanisms underlying trophoblast differentiation and maternal interactions and how these insights are advancing understanding of healthy placentation and pregnancy disorders.

papers.title: Filling the massive AI drug discovery data gap
Human-specific CCG-repeat insertion in the RBFOX1 promoter implicated in autism and speech enhances EGR1-responsive activity
papers.abstract: Human-specific promoter innovations have been predicted to shape human-specific traits. Here, we investigated the RBFOX1 splice regulator gene, which is specifically upregulated in human and songbird speech/song brain areas. We found that the human RBFOX1 promoter associated with autism and language impairment harbors a human-specific CCG trinucleotide insertion creating a functional CCG-repeat motif. Comparative single-nucleus transcriptome analyses of primate brains indicate that the human promoter drives differential expression in cortical excitatory neurons. Reporter assays show that the human CCG-repeat motif, relative to the chimpanzee allele, increases promoter activity with the EGR1 transcription factor. Genome-wide, the CCG-repeat motif marks core promoters of 104 genes, related to postsynaptic function and autism. In PTCHD1, a clinical duplication in autism patients creates another CCG-repeat motif that similarly increases EGR1-responsive promoter activity. Our findings suggest that small CCG-repeat variants in regulatory regions can exert large effects on gene regulation and apparent associated traits.
affiliations: The Rockefeller University (corresponding author)

papers.title: A StayGold-based calcium ion indicator
papers.abstract: Genetically encoded calcium ion (Ca2+) indicators (GECIs) enable visualization of Ca2+ dynamics in living systems but often suffer from limited photostability during prolonged imaging. The recent discovery of StayGold, a green fluorescent protein (FP) with exceptional brightness and photostability, opened the possibility of addressing this longstanding challenge. Here, we sought to establish whether a monomeric variant of StayGold (mStayGold) could be converted into a single FP-based GECI. Through extensive protein engineering, we generated a functional mStayGold-based GECI, HiCaRI (Highly intensiometric Ca2+ Responsive Indicator) by fusing Calmodulin (CaM) and the ckkap binding peptide from K-GECO1 into mStayGold(J). HiCaRI exhibits a large Ca2+-dependent inverse fluorescence response ({triangleup}F/Fmin = -15) while retaining high brightness and improved photostability relative to previously reported GFP-based GECIs. Although the current variant represents a first-generation prototype with shortcomings in terms of Ca2+ affinity and photostability (relative to StayGold and mStayGold(J)), this work demonstrates the feasibility of constructing single FP-based GECIs from a highly photostable fluorescent protein.
affiliations: The University of Tokyo (corresponding author)

papers.title: The essential role of connective-tissue cells during axolotl limb regeneration
papers.abstract: Axolotls (Ambystoma mexicanum) are known for their remarkable limb-regeneration abilities, which involve the formation of the blastema, a specialized structure consisting of progenitor cells contributed by all major tissues of the limb. Lateral plate mesoderm (LPM)-derived connective tissue (CT) cells dedifferentiate and play a critical role in blastema formation and subsequent limb regeneration. However, the complexity of the blastema cellular composition and the extent of CT participation and necessity have not been rigorously explored. To address this gap, we conducted spatial transcriptomics using a select array of probes, revealing that CT cells constitute up to 75% of the blastema cells. Genetic ablation of CT cells significantly delays or truncates limb regeneration, underscoring their necessity during this process. Analysis of the molecular profile during blastema formation identifies a temporally ordered gene expression pattern reflecting sequential phases of CT cell dedifferentiation, proliferation, and redifferentiation. Finally, a cell-cell communication inference identifies a CT-cell-autonomous FGFR1/AKT1 signaling axis as a cell-intrinsic molecular requirement for limb regeneration. Together, our work reaffirms the central role of CT cells in axolotl limb regeneration and lays the foundation for identifying molecular mechanisms that govern blastema formation during the initial phases of limb regeneration.
affiliations: Mount Desert Island Biological Laboratory (corresponding author)

papers.title: AmyloCore-ML: AI/Machine Learning Enabled Identification of Amyloid Fibril Core Regions Using Protein Language Models
papers.abstract: Identification of amyloid forming regions in proteins remains central to understanding of their aggregation behaviour, which are central to various neurodegenerative and systemic disorders. Many predictors have been designed to identify amyloid forming regions, however they may not necessarily identify total residues found in actual disease associated fibril structures. To address this, we formed a sequence-based based predictor-AmyloCore-ML to ascertain structural amyloid-core propensity. The predictor was developed using experimentally determined fibril structures obtained from Amyloid Atlas. Ordered residues in the experimental structures were designated as core, and unresolved sampled from the same proteins as matched controls as non-core. Core and non-core regions were encoded using various physicochemical descriptors and protein language model (PLM) embeddings (ESM-2, ANKH, ProtT5) and evaluated using protein-grouped cross-validation. PLMs consistently outperformed physicochemical descriptors, with the best models reaching AUROC values of ~0.88 and AUPRC values of ~0.85. Locked full-length protein scans further localized experimental cores, with ESM-2/ExtraTrees achieving AUROC 0.833, AUPRC 0.751, and a mean peak distance of 12.4 residues. In comparative benchmarking, our predictor showed better performance metrics than CrossBeta and AggrescanAI. The framework therefore provides residue-resolved prediction of structurally incorporated amyloid-core regions directly from sequence.
affiliations: University of Denver (corresponding author)

papers.title: Non-canonical cleavage expands prime editing in 5' direction
papers.abstract: Cleavage-dependent CRISPR-Cas gene editing relies on RNA-guided DNA cleavage that drives cellular machinery to incorporate intended edits. Beyond canonical cleavage, CRISPR nucleases can also execute non-canonical cleavage on the displaced DNA strand. Here, we report a modified design principle for prime editing that leverages the non-canonical cleavage activity, enabling editing in the 5' direction of a classic nick site. We elucidate the non-canonical-cleavage-driven reverse transcription pathway that initiates upstream of the classic nick site. We identify competition between the canonical and non-canonical routes, which can be modulated by rationally designing RNA templates carrying the intended edits. We demonstrate that cellular physiology enhances editing efficiency from individual reverse-transcription product yet exerts limited influence on pathway competitions. Our findings revise the design principle of prime editing and establish a new dimension for engineering CRISPR-Cas systems by harnessing its intrinsic, non-host-specific, non-canonical cleavage activity.
affiliations: Shandong University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Quantification of grapevine yield losses as a function downy mildew severity on foliage and cluster
papers.abstract: To quantify the relationship between grapevine disease severity and crop losses at the plant scale, we conducted a three-year field experiment at two sites near Bordeaux (France), monitoring mildews and rots on both foliage and clusters. Preliminary analyses revealed that only downy mildew (DM) significantly impacted yield under our experimental conditions. We capitalized on this single-disease dominance to isolate the effect of DM severity (assessed via standardized AUDPC), on both foliage and clusters, on yield loss at the individual vine scale. At a cluster AUDPC of 5%, yield consistently declined by 24% across all years and sites. Conversely, yield loss at a 5% foliar AUDPC ranged from 9% to 60% depending on the site and year, reflecting a tenfold variation in the damage coefficient. This variability strongly correlated with a moisture risk index computed between the phenological stages of visible inflorescences and pre-ripening berries. Specifically, at 5% foliar AUDPC, the expected yield loss escalated from 9% in a dry season (10th percentile of the index) to 15% in an intermediate season (median), reaching 39% in a wet season (90th percentile). Future research should aim to validate these statistical models across broader climatic, geographic, and agronomic contexts, including the characterization of cultivar-specific responses.
affiliations: INRAE (corresponding author)

papers.title: Identifiability of metabolic resilience from sparse longitudinal metabolomics
papers.abstract: Sparse and irregular longitudinal metabolomic measurements can make dynamical quantities numerically estimable without making them scientifically identifiable. We formulate effective-landscape inference as an observation-timescale inverse problem and evaluate its operating characteristics using stochastic systems with known ground truth and longitudinal stool metabolomics from the Integrative Human Microbiome Project. Across simulation ensembles, recovery of a known double-well topology declined sharply as observations became sparse, whereas the tested monostable controls did not generate spurious secondary minima. Findings establish an identifiability hierarchy: global topology requires sufficient within-subject state-space coverage, whereas local return descriptors remain vulnerable to bias from the observation process. The framework therefore shifts the emphasis from assigning stability labels to determining what a sampling design can support. It provides a basis for designing denser longitudinal experiments and for validating clinical and machine-learning studies in which sparse observations might otherwise be overinterpreted as evidence about underlying dynamics.
affiliations: UC Berkeley (corresponding author)

papers.title: Chromid transforms opportunistic pathogen into beneficial symbiont to raise coral's thermal tipping point
papers.abstract: Resilient turbid coral reefs, found 1{degrees} north of the equator, experience fewer and less intense bleaching events despite being situated within the world's busiest shipping port in highly urbanised Singapore. We hypothesised that bacteria within the coral holobiont play a role in maintaining coral health by conferring traits that enhance thermal tolerance. Eleven Pseudovibrio isolates were obtained from the scleractinian coral Pachyseris speciosa, and their genomes differed by only four single nucleotide polymorphisms. A ~490 kbp chromid, pCJH, was present in 7 of the 11 isolates. A Pseudovibrio isolate without pCJH is an opportunistic pathogen of P. speciosa, accelerating bleaching disease. In contrast, the chromid reduces Pseudovibrio's fecundity, enhances its host colonisation and consequently increases P. speciosa's thermal tolerance by 1 {degrees}C. Interaction analyses in experimentally heat-stressed corals revealed a negative interaction between Pseudovibrio and Vibrio ASVs. The Pseudovibrio genomes and chromid encode several diffusible antibiotic biosynthetic gene clusters and two type six secretion systems (T6SS) for contact-dependent inhibition, with both types of inhibitory activity shown against opportunistic coral pathogens from local (i.e. isolated from the same coral host) and type-strain Vibrio spp. Together, these findings support the Coral Probiotic Hypothesis that bacteria enhance coral resilience, and identify a chromid responsible for Pseudovibrio's climatically driven Jekyll-and-Hyde lifestyle from opportunistic pathogen to beneficial symbiont.
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (corresponding author)

papers.title: Spatiotemporal distribution of Delta-like protein 1 during mouse pituitary ontogeny and its relationship with differentiating endocrine cell populations
papers.abstract: Delta-like protein 1 (DLK1) is a transmembrane protein involved in the regulation of cellular differentiation and stem cell maintenance in several tissues, including the pituitary gland. Although DLK1 expression has been reported in the adult pituitary, its spatiotemporal distribution during mouse pituitary development remains incompletely characterized. The aim of this study was to analyse the distribution of DLK1 during embryonic and postnatal development of the mouse pituitary gland and to characterize its relationship with hormone-producing cell populations. Immunohistochemistry was performed in Swiss albino mice from embryonic day 9.5 (e9.5) to postnatal day 15 (p15). Double immunofluorescence was used at e18.5 and p15 to examine the association of DLK1 immunoreactivity with ACTH-, TSH-, GH-, FSH- and PRL-producing cells. DLK1 immunoreactivity was detected from the earliest stages of pituitary development in Rathke`s pouch and the ventral diencephalon. During embryonic development, DLK1-ir cells were widely distributed throughout adenohypophyseal and neurohypophyseal primordia. As development progressed, DLK1 immunoreactivity became progressively regionalized within the anterior, intermediate and tuberal lobes, as well as in the median eminence of the hypothalamus and the posterior pituitary lobe. Colocalization of DLK1 with each of the hormone-producing cell populations analysed was observed at e18.5 and p15. Semiquantitative analysis at p15 indicated that approximately 32% of adenohypophyseal cells were DLK1-immunoreactive. These findings provide a detailed description of the spatiotemporal distribution of DLK1 during mouse pituitary ontogeny and suggest that DLK1 immunoreactivity is associated with differentiating endocrine cell populations throughout pituitary development.
affiliations: Universidad de La Laguna (corresponding author)

papers.title: Coordinated Enhancement of Molecular and Spatial Fidelity for Biological Inference in Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Understanding tissue organization requires accurate molecular quantification and faithful spatial localization. Spatial omics, particularly spatial transcriptomics (ST), face measurement trade-offs that limit simultaneous achievement of molecular and spatial fidelity across spatial resolution, detection sensitivity, molecular-tissue alignment and cell-level fidelity. Existing computational methods typically target individual aspects and optimize them in isolation, despite their interdependence. Here we present FOCUS, a multimodal generative foundation model for coordinated ST enhancement. FOCUS integrates native ST with histology images, cell masks, scRNA-seq references and spatial co-expression priors through task-specific modules, with cross-task coordination enabling joint correction of co-occurring limitations. FOCUS improved the performance of individual enhancement tasks and provided additional gains with coordinated mitigation of coupled limitations. Across immunology, tissue development and oncology, FOCUS recovered biologically consistent patterns obscured in native ST or isolated enhancement, enabling clearer inference of neutrophil-tumor interactions, spatial osteocyte differentiation and primary-metastatic HNSCC programs. Together, FOCUS establishes coordinated enhancement of molecular and spatial fidelity as a strategy for downstream biological inference from ST.
affiliations: Department of Clinical Neurosciences, University of Cambridge, UK (corresponding author)

papers.title: Inherent limitations of zero-shot mutation prediction in protein engineering
papers.abstract: Predicting mutation effects is critical for protein engineering. A commonly pursued strategy is zero-shot prediction with deep-learning models, whose performance is typically evaluated using aggregate benchmark scores that obscure multidimensional biological tradeoffs. Here, we evaluate sequence, structure, and hybrid foundation models across curated datasets to expose the practical limitations of zero-shot predictions. We demonstrate that model performance is highly variable and heavily influenced by experimental noise and competing phenotypic goals. Notably, predictions from competing models often correlate more strongly with one another than with experimental outcomes. While current models effectively filter deleterious mutations and enrich high-scoring variants for natural functions, they struggle to identify precise optimal mutations and consistently fail to predict mutations that drive new-to-nature functions. These models learn from evolutionary constraints that tend to oppose the extreme biophysical optimizations required in targeted engineering. Consequently, zero-shot scoring serves as a valuable initial filter but cannot substitute for task-specific prediction.
affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin (corresponding author)

papers.title: A critical evaluation of Gene Ontology priors in biologically-informed neural networks
papers.abstract: Biologically-informed neural networks (BINNs) embed prior knowledge such as the Gene Ontology (GO) into their architecture to produce interpretable representations, yet whether and how this prior improves performance or interpretation remains unclear. We introduce GONNECT, a BINN incorporating GO into an autoencoder. We evaluate GO constraints in the encoder, decoder, or both on RNA-seq tumour samples from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), comparing against published BINNs (OntoVAE, VEGA), an unconstrained baseline, randomized priors, and untrained networks. Across various performance metrics, GO structure adds little to reconstruction or latent-space organization, frequently matched by randomized or unconstrained models. Node activations agree with a gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA)-derived reference, but this agreement largely arises from the architectural constraint: it is lost when GO connections are randomized, present even before training in the encoder, and learned in the decoder. Regularized soft links outside GO (GONNECT-SL) are unstable across runs and concentrate where the ontology is sparse, compensating for the prior's constraints rather than revealing new biology. Within this setting, we find no evidence that node activations capture biological information beyond that encoded by the predefined gene sets, suggesting that their apparent interpretability largely reflects the prior imposed by the architecture.
affiliations: Delft University of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Histology-aware Inference of Cell-cell Communication in Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Cell-cell communication (CCC) is fundamental to tissue organization and function, yet inferring communication from spatial transcriptomics (ST) remains challenging because molecular and spatial information does not fully capture the anatomical context of signaling. Paired hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained images provide complementary insights into tissue architecture and cellular morphology, which remain underutilized as the explicit contextual constraint of CCC inference. Here we present HARMONIC, a histology-aware graph learning framework for anatomically contextualized CCC inference from ST and H&E images. HARMONIC uses conditional mutual information to model dependencies among tissue architecture, ligand-receptor-mediated signaling, gene expression and morphology, and integrates these representations through self-supervised graph learning. Across synthetic and biological datasets spanning platforms, species and tissues, HARMONIC suppresses less anatomically plausible interactions while recovering context-supported signaling across tumor-immune interfaces, necrotic transitions, anatomical compartments and microvascular structures. These findings establish tissue architecture as the explicit contextual constraint of spatial CCC inference.
affiliations: Department of Clinical Neurosciences, University of Cambridge, UK (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cell Painting and machine learning for mechanistic profiling of hepatotoxic botanicals and their constituents
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Botanicals are widely consumed as herbal remedies and plant-derived products, but their complex and variable chemical composition presents major challenges for safety assessment. Although hepatotoxicity has been reported for several botanicals, the constituent compounds responsible and the underlying mechanisms often remain poorly characterised. OBJECTIVES We aimed to determine whether Cell Painting could identify candidate constituent drivers of botanical bioactivity and generate hypotheses about potential mechanisms of action in primary human hepatocytes. METHODS We profiled 13 botanical extracts and 85 known constituents across multiple concentrations using Cell Painting alongside assays of metabolic activity and membrane integrity. To interpret morphological phenotypes, we trained machine-learning models using a Cell Painting reference atlas of >1,000 chemicals linked to ToxCast/Tox21 molecular and cellular bioactivity annotations. RESULTS Cell Painting detected bioactivity in 11/13 botanical extracts and 46/85 constituents, compared with 9/13 extracts and 40/85 constituents in the cell-health assays, and generally detected activity at lower concentrations. For 9/13 extracts, at least one constituent was active at a lower concentration than the corresponding botanical extract, supporting the contribution of a subset of potent constituents to mixture-level responses. Aristolochia and goldenseal were the most potent extracts across Cell Painting and cell-health assays and contained highly active constituents. Reference-atlas models generated specific mechanistic hypotheses, including cytotoxicity-, endocrine-, and genotoxicity-associated responses for several botanicals and constituents. CONCLUSION These results support Cell Painting combined with machine learning as a sensitive approach for characterising cellular responses to botanicals, prioritising candidate constituent drivers of hepatotoxicity-associated phenotypes, and generating testable hypotheses about potential mechanisms of action.
affiliations: European Bioinformatics Institute, European Molecular Biology Laboratory, Hinxton, UK (corresponding author)

papers.title: Targeting Lysosomal MCOLN1/TRPML1 Ion Channels to Alleviate Diabetes Mellitus via a Ca2+- CaMKKβ-AMPK pathway
papers.abstract: Type 2 Diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a metabolic syndrome characterized by hyperglycemia and various complications. Current drugs are limited by side effects and resistance, necessitating novel targets and therapies. Previous studies have shown that MK-83, a synthetic agonist of transient receptor potential mucolipin 1 (TRPML1/ MCOLN1), a lysosomal Ca2+ channel, activates adenosine 5'-monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a key therapeutic target in diabetes. However, whether targeting TRPML1 can treat T2DM remains unclear. In this study, we found that transgenic overexpression or pharmacological activation of TRPML1 regulates AMPK phosphorylation via a Ca2+-CaMKK{beta}-dependent mechanism. This activation promotes glucose transporter 4 (GLUT4) translocation and increases intracellular glucose uptake. Conversely, genetic inactivation or pharmacologically inhibition of TRPML1 blocks both AMPK activation and glucose uptake. More importantly, pharmacological activation of TRPML1 in vivo alleviates hyperglycemia in db/db mice (a T2DM model), as evidenced by random blood glucose levels, fasting blood glucose levels and HbA1c levels. Furthermore, other hallmark features of db/db mice- including impaired oral glucose tolerance, reduced insulin tolerance, and elevated ALT and AST levels- were all ameliorated upon TRPML1 activation. Hence, targeting lysosomal TRPML1 channel represents a promising therapeutic strategy for T2DM, with highly specific TRPML1 agonists as potential anti-diabetic agents.
affiliations: Zhejiang University of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Mesodermal-niche interactions direct specification and differentiation of pancreatic endocrine cells in human multilineage organoids
authors: Martinez Garcia de la Torre, R. A.
papers.abstract: Tissues develop and function within complex microenvironments, where diverse cell types interact through tightly regulated spatial and temporal cues. These interactions shape cell identity, differentiation, and spatial organisation, ultimately establishing functional tissue architecture. Understanding and modelling these processes in humans therefore require multicellular systems that capture the cellular diversity and interactions of developing tissues. Here, we combine spatial transcriptomics of the human foetal pancreas with an induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-based multilineage model that recapitulates key features of human endocrine pancreatic development and incorporates a mesoderm-derived cellular niche. We comprehensively characterise the multilineage organoid transcriptomes across differentiation stages and benchmark their fidelity against single-cell and spatial transcriptomic profiles of human foetal pancreas. We demonstrate that iPSC-derived pancreatic mesenchymal cells promote endocrine commitment by restricting off-target cell fates and enhancing {beta}-cell differentiation. Together, these findings establish a framework for investigating the cellular mechanisms underlying human endocrine development and disease.
affiliations: King's College London (corresponding author)

papers.title: simSOMA: a cell-lineage based simulator of the somatic VAF spectrum in plants
papers.abstract: Plants accumulate somatic mutations during growth, some of which spread into branches, organs, or reproductive tissues. These variants are of growing interest because they underlie bud-sport traits in perennial crops, contribute to within-organism selection, and are a source of heritable genetic variation. Recent genomic sequencing of bulk or layer-enriched plant tissues has revealed complex variant allele-frequency (VAF) spectra. Interpreting these spectra requires modelling how somatic mutations are filtered or amplified by shoot growth, branching, and organ formation, a problem that is difficult to derive analytically. Here, we present simSOMA, a modular simulator linking plant topologies to shoot apical meristem cell-lineage dynamics. simSOMA models mutation accumulation during stem-cell self-renewal, clonal expansion to the meristem periphery, branch founding, and organ formation. We demonstrate how simSOMA isolates developmental processes that shape organ-level VAF spectra and among-organ variant sharing, and transforms spectra for bulk or layer-enriched sampling, phased or unphased readouts, and read-level sequencing noise. SAM layers can be simulated as independent cell lineages and combined into bulk tissue samples. simSOMA can be used to explore developmental hypotheses about the origin of somatic variation, and to design somatic sequencing experiments and variant-detection strategies. simSOMA is available at https://github.com/jlab-code/simSOMA.
affiliations: Technical University of Munich (corresponding author)

papers.title: Microbial Invasion and Immunosuppression Drives Adenoma Progression in Early Colorectal Cancer Development
papers.abstract: Several inherited predispositions to colorectal cancer exist, most notably familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), which typically involves a germline loss-of-function mutation in one APC allele. A second hit in APC or related loci leads to aberrant Wnt signalling, triggering adenoma formation with near-complete penetrance. Yet, substantial variability in disease onset and severity, even among siblings with identical APC germline mutations, implicates environmental modifiers. Emerging evidence points to the gut microbiome as a critical regulator of adenoma initiation and progression, particularly in early-onset CRC. Here, we show that bacterial invasion is associated with neutrophil immunosuppression, T-cell exclusion and adenoma progression in a porcine model of FAP. Longitudinal mapping of progressing and regressing polyps using single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics and integrated microbiome profiling resolved the cellular and microbial architecture underlying these divergent lesion states. Single-cell RNA-seq identified 35 cell subpopulations and showed that regressing polyps are enriched for central-memory CD4+ T cells, cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and inflammatory neutrophils, whereas progressing polyps contain immunosuppressive/PD-L1-associated neutrophils, regulatory and dysfunctional T cells. Spatial transcriptomics with a custom host panel and targeted bacterial probes linked bacterial-high adenomatous regions to immunosuppressive neutrophil niches and T cell exclusion, while regressing lesions showed predominantly lumen-adjacent bacterial localization and spatially organized immune surveillance. These results provide a spatially resolved map of cellular and microbial organisation in early colorectal polyp progression and regression and reveal a microbiome-driven, neutrophil-mediated mechanism of early tumour progression with implications for CRC interception.
affiliations: Technical University of Munich (corresponding author)

papers.title: Phosphorylation of β-arrestins impacts recruitment to Parathyroid Hormone Receptor 1 (PTH1R) at the cell surface and endosomes
papers.abstract: {beta}-arrestins 1 and 2 are intracellular adaptor proteins that regulate the subcellular localisation and signalling of GPCRs including Parathyroid Hormone Receptor 1 (PTH1R), which produces {beta}-arrestin-dependent signalling that may selectively stimulate bone anabolism. {beta}-arrestins can themselves be regulated by post-translational modifications including phosphorylation, which dictates the translocation and signalling of the few GPCRs studied in this context to date. We aimed to investigate whether phosphorylation of {beta}-arrestins modulates their subcellular translocation in response to PTH1R activation. Translocation of {beta}-arrestins to the plasma membrane and early endosomes was quantified using BRET biosensors and immunocytochemistry with high content analysis. Phosphoknockout or phosphomimetic mutations were introduced to previously demonstrated phosphorylation sites in {beta}-arrestins 1 and 2, initially in bulk to assess overall effects. Plasma membrane translocation was altered only subtly, whereas early endosome translocation was markedly reduced for both mutations but to a greater degree for the phosphomimetic. Contributions of individual or paired sites were assessed by restoration to wildtype from the bulk phosphomimetic mutants. Dual restoration of S13 and T275 in {beta}-arrestin 1, or the analogous sites in {beta}-arrestin 2, restored the greatest degrees of early endosomal translocation, with complete restoration for {beta}-arrestin 1 and partial for {beta}-arrestin 2. Restoration of other sites had minimal or no effect. Dephosphorylation therefore appears to be required for PTH1R-stimulated {beta}-arrestin early endosomal translocation, with different phosphorylation sites implicated than some other GPCRs. These findings raise the possibility of differential {beta}-arrestin regulation by distinct stimuli which may have implications in therapeutic targeting of {beta}-arrestin-dependent pathways.
affiliations: University of Auckland (corresponding author)

papers.title: Spatial isotope tracing maps compartmentalized nutrient use across the adult fruit fly
papers.abstract: Drosophila melanogaster is a powerful model for studying systemic metabolism. Although metabolism is compartmentalized across tissues, prior work in adult Drosophila has mostly measured it in dissected tissues rather than in situ, limiting the spatial information that can be gained. Here, we combine whole-fly mass-spectrometry imaging with stable-isotope tracing and flux modeling to quantify metabolic activities across the adult fruit fly in a spatially resolved manner. Across 68 tracer-fed Oregon-R female flies and 187,709 pixels, we map 81 metabolites onto eight annotated regions, including muscle, fat body, gut, and nervous system. Glucose labeling and fitted relative fluxes indicate higher glycolytic and tricarboxylic acid cycle turnover in thoracic muscle than in abdominal fat body; proline labels the nervous system and eye; glutamine the abdominal reproductive system and gut. Alanine carries glucose-derived carbon through the hemolymph and transfers nitrogen into glutamate. In flies bearing yorkie-driven gut tumors, alanine contribution to malate rises in gut and abdomen, and reducing gut alanine uptake lowers tumor burden. Together, this work establishes a framework for quantitative spatial metabolic analysis, showing compartmentalized nutrient use across the adult fruit fly.
affiliations: Harvard Medical School (corresponding author)

papers.title: Beyond the Final Layer: Evaluating Single-Cell Foundation Model Representations for Molecular Prediction
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models (scFMs) are commonly benchmarked using final-layer embeddings, although useful depth may depend on the task. We evaluate Geneformer, scBERT, scGPT, and scFoundation as frozen feature extractors for cell-type and perturbation-response prediction using layer-wise probes, leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) selection, readout controls, representation diagnostics, centered kernel alignment (CKA), and retrieval/collapse analyses. Intermediate layers significantly improve cell-type accuracy for scGPT and scBERT in several settings, while Geneformer and scFoundation generally show performance comparable to their final layers. For perturbation prediction, LODO identifies layer 1 as an earliest-on-par candidate across all four models, without establishing universal superiority. Paired scGPT CLS and mean-pooling analyses show that readout affects preferred depth. CKA and representation metrics reveal model- and task-dependent geometric changes, while retrieval and collapse checks support the robustness of perturbation findings. We recommend reporting extraction depth, readout, selection protocol, and task-specific diagnostics. A validated non-final layer may also reduce computation, although efficiency was not directly benchmarked.
affiliations: Department of Computational Medicine and Bioinformatics, University of Michigan (corresponding author)

papers.title: SP2 impedes the pluripotent-to-totipotent state transition in an RA-dependent manner
papers.abstract: The pluripotency-to-totipotency transition represents a transient developmental reversal that remains not fully understood. Although chemical approaches can induce a 2-cell (2C)-like state in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs), how cells choose between totipotency acquisition and alternative developmental fates remains unclear. Here, we established a chemical induction system that efficiently drives mESCs toward the 2C-like state. We found that mESCs under induction treatment followed distinct trajectories, with a subset activating developmental programs rather than acquiring 2C-like features. SP2 was preferentially expressed along this developmental trajectory and progressively reduced during successful 2C-like induction. Loss of SP2 enhanced 2C-like cell formation, whereas SP2 overexpression impaired the transition. Transcriptomic analysis of SP2-deficient cells showed reduced expression of developmental genes, including Hox family genes, accompanied by increased expression of 2C-associated genes. Consistent with this finding, SP2 occupied the promoters of Hox family genes in the reprogrammed cells. Notably, the effect of SP2 loss was particularly evident upon activation of retinoic acid (RA) signaling, linking SP2-dependent developmental gene activation to the RA-responsive branch of the transition. Altogether, our findings identify SP2 function as a barrier that limits acquisition of the 2C-like state by promoting a competing developmental program, highlighting the importance of coordinated extracellular signaling and transcriptional regulation in directing cell fate transitions.
affiliations: Guangzhou National Laboratory, Guangzhou, China (corresponding author)

papers.title: ETSAM: effectively segmenting cell membranes in cryo-electron tomograms
Anticipatory regulation of stem cell-based technologies: a UK case study
papers.abstract: Biotechnological advances are prompting governments to fear falling behind and missing out on growth and investment. Yet science often moves faster and less predictably than legislation. Using the United Kingdom’s stem cell regulation as a case study, we examine anticipatory regulation, sandboxes, and other agile governance tools for managing both over-regulation and regulatory gaps.

papers.title: Autonomous AI agents discover reverse transcriptases with tandem repeat arrays
papers.abstract: Metagenomic databases hold vast quantities of unexplored genetic material that can seed tools for biotechnology and medicine, but discovery is limited by our ability to examine sequence data at scale. Here, we show that large language models (LLMs) in an autonomous harness can alleviate this bottleneck and surface novel molecular systems. We deployed Claude Code instances to survey reverse transcriptase (RT) loci across 1.9 billion protein clusters. Among the top candidates were array-associated RTs (ART), a novel family of jumbo-phage RTs coupled with an array of ~200-nucleotide units and a dedicated partner gene. Session transcripts show that Claude identified the ART family by directly examining its DNA sequences and recognizing the atypical repeats, a behavior attributable to specific Mythos 5 internal signals that respond to repeated DNA. ART arrays are highly expressed and appear as discrete units during Staphylococcus phage infection, suggesting an RT system directed by a repertoire of distinct RNAs. These findings indicate that LLMs can autonomously detect anomalies and drive analyses to initiate biological discoveries.
affiliations: Anthropic, PBC (corresponding author)

papers.title: kitAb: an automated framework for assay-specific antibody developability modeling and large-scale landscape analysis
papers.abstract: Antibody developability is determined by multiple physicochemical properties, and the relevance of individual properties varies among experimental assays. Existing computational approaches, however, often provide fixed assessments or rely on computationally intensive descriptors. We present kitAb, an open-source framework for scalable physicochemical characterization of antibody Fv regions and assay-specific developability modeling. kitAb calculates 59 interpretable sequence- and structure-based descriptors and integrates them with automated feature selection and regression. We evaluated kitAb across ten public datasets comprising 46 experimental endpoints, using sequence-aware or predefined splits where feasible. Predictive performance was strongly assay-dependent. In nested evaluations with sequence-aware or predefined data splits, models using kitAb descriptors achieved predictive performance comparable on average to those using PROPERMAB descriptors, while outperforming models based on TAP or sequence-only features. In a single-structure CPU timing benchmark, kitAb descriptor calculation was approximately 11-fold faster than PROPERMAB. Predictive performance was similar across the three structure-generation backends, and broader AutoML searches did not substantially improve mean performance. We further applied the same descriptor representation to approximately 3.4 million paired natural antibodies and 706 Phase II or later therapeutic antibodies. Repertoire-scale analysis revealed systematic differences in surface charge, hydrophobic and aromatic organization, CDR length and germline-associated physicochemical profiles. The kitAb code and analysis workflows are openly available at https://github.com/katyachemistry/kitAb/.
affiliations: MSU Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Lomonosov Moscow State University, Moscow, Russia (corresponding author)

papers.title: DeSPA uncovers genes with cross-state spatial pattern remodeling and coordinated spatial programs across multi-slice spatial transcriptomics atlases
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics increasingly generates multi-slice atlases spanning developmental, regenerative, and disease-associated states. Identifying genes with spatial pattern remodeling across these states is essential for understanding tissue reorganization and the underlying gene programs, yet few existing methods systematically detect such changes while accounting for variation among replicate slices. Here we introduce DeSPA, a statistical framework that models gene-specific spatial variation within each slice using a linear mixed model, tests for cross-state remodeling by aggregating evidence across replicate slices, and organizes identified genes into interpretable spatial co-expression modules that reveal coordinated spatial programs. Simulations show that DeSPA achieves high power while controlling the false discovery rate under inter-slice heterogeneity. In mouse embryogenesis, it recovers programs linked to extracellular matrix organization, muscle formation, neural development, and erythrocyte development. In diabetic testis, it reveals disruption of a late-spermatid spatial program consistent with known spermatogenic dysfunction, while maintaining stable gene rankings under coordinate rotation. In axolotl brain, regeneration preserves a developmental-like biosynthetic backbone but reorganizes it into regeneration-specific modules. Across two mouse intracerebral hemorrhage models, DeSPA resolves a conserved spatial injury program alongside model-specific synaptic and tissue-response programs. Together, these findings establish DeSPA as a scalable and interpretable framework for detecting spatial pattern remodeling and resolving coordinated spatial programs across diverse biological states.
affiliations: Fudan University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Human Intestinal Absorption Revisited: The 1998 Descriptors Survive, and the Method Extends to Permeability
papers.abstract: In 1998 we predicted percent human intestinal absorption (HIA) for 86 drug and drug-like compounds from six molecular descriptors chosen by a genetic algorithm with a small neural network serving as the fitness function. That result rested on one division of the compounds into three sets: training, cross-validation and external prediction. Repeating the division shows it was a rather fortunate one. An extraction is one random draw from a wide distribution, so we repeat every experiment 250 times and report the result as a distribution. Across 250 stratified extractions, 14 match the published cross-validation error and only one matches the published external prediction error. Reconstructed this way, the published six descriptors give a mean extraction error roughly twice the external prediction value we reported in 1998 (Table 1). We then applied the same six descriptors to a larger set of 780 compounds from a public compilation. Under the 1998 network they give 22.50 %HIA units on training compounds against 25.77 on extracted compounds, whereas on the 86 they give 13.43 against 30.39. More compounds close the gap between fitting and prediction. Four datasets are modeled here: 780 small molecules with HIA measured in man, 3,771 small molecules and 1,281 cyclic peptides measured across Caco-2 cell monolayers, and 7,298 cyclic peptides measured across artificial membranes. Each is its own prediction problem, and one procedure is applied to all four. A genetic algorithm chooses which descriptors to use and how many, and a random forest grades each choice on compounds its own trees never saw. The descriptors chosen most often across the 250 extractions form one consensus set for each dataset. For absorption, 25 consensus descriptors under a random forest reach an extraction rms of 20.47 %HIA units at R 0.76. On the same compounds and the same extractions, the six 1998 descriptors under the 1998 network reach 25.77 at R 0.59. The four models are served at predicthia.ai, where a structure can be drawn or pasted, scored against its training set for similarity, and the training data with fitted models downloaded. Each model served is its fixed consensus set fitted on every compound in its dataset; the accuracy quoted beside a prediction comes from evaluating that same set across 250 extractions (Table 3). The fixed sets hold 25 descriptors for absorption, 55 for Caco-2 small-molecule permeability, 50 for Caco-2 peptide permeability and 25 for artificial-membrane permeability. Keywords: human intestinal absorption; QSPR; genetic algorithm; descriptor selection; cyclic peptides; membrane permeability; oral bioavailability; repeated extraction
affiliations: Eidogen-Sertanty, Inc. (corresponding author)

papers.title: Tissue retention of dendritic cells drives age-associated protective tolerogenic lymphoid structures
papers.abstract: Ectopic lymphoid structures are typically associated with chronic tissue inflammation in autoimmunity and cancer, where they can amplify local immune responses. Similar structures arise spontaneously with age, yet their origin and function remain unclear. Here we identify tissue retention of mature migratory conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) as a driver of age-associated lymphoid organization. Mature cDCs accumulated within lymphoid structures in aged human and mouse tissues. We demonstrate that impaired cDC egress or pharmacological cDC expansion induced de novo structures in mice across multiple otherwise homeostatic organs without associated pathology. Strikingly, senescence-associated tissue cues, which promoted a distinct cDC maturation state, were required for lymphoid niche initiation. Unlike inflammatory structures described in disease, these cDC-driven structures preferentially accumulated tissue-adapted regulatory T cells and protected against inflammatory injury, revealing a previously unrecognized regulatory dimension of age-associated lymphoid organization.
affiliations: Genentech Inc. (corresponding author)

papers.title: CD19 CAR Engineered T Regulatory Cells Promote Durable Immune Tolerance in Experimental Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
papers.abstract: While the immune reset induced by CD19 CAR T therapies has shown striking promise in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), the nature and duration of benefit mediated by B cell depletion remains unclear. Loss of tolerance in SLE is driven by extrafollicular and germinal center interactions between dendritic cells and self-reactive T and B cells. We hypothesized that CD19 CAR-engineered regulatory T cells (CAR19 EngTreg), capable of suppressing multiple autoimmune effector cell types, might promote long-term tolerance without producing high-levels of inflammatory mediators. To generate CAR19 EngTreg, we combined CD19 CAR delivery with homology directed repair at the FOXP3 locus to drive constitutive, stable FOXP3 expression in CD4 T cells. CAR19 EngTreg expressed canonical Treg markers; exhibited minimal inflammatory cytokine production; and blocked human B cell differentiation into antibody secreting plasma cells. In humanized mouse models, transfer of CAR19 EngTreg led to a reduction in B cell numbers with low inflammatory cytokine production relative to CD19 CAR Teff, and reduced tissue inflammation. In a short-term, in vivo imiquimod-induced inflammatory model, murine CAR19 EngTreg reduced skin pathology, spleen size, and inflammatory cytokines. Finally, in two distinct mouse models of lupus, CAR19 EngTreg persisted for >4 months leading to reduced autoimmune T and B effector populations, sustained reduction in multiple autoantibodies and improved renal function and histopathology. Thus, CAR19 EngTreg may offer a promising and durable therapeutic avenue for B cell-mediated autoimmune disorders capable of long-term regulation of both autoreactive B and T cells.
affiliations: University of Washington (corresponding author)

papers.title: Microglia transcriptomic response to doxorubicin-induced genotoxic stress
papers.abstract: Chemobrain, characterized by cognitive dysfunction, has emerged as a significant health concern following cancer treatment. Doxorubicin, an FDA-approved chemotherapeutic agent, is widely used to treat various cancers. However, its adverse effects raise concerns regarding toxicity in non-cancerous cell types. Microglia, the resident immune cells of the brain, play a central role in maintaining neural homeostasis. Despite this, the mechanisms by which microglia become dysfunctional following doxorubicin exposure remain poorly understood. Understanding the transcriptomic alterations induced by doxorubicin in microglia could provide critical insights into mechanisms underlying its neurotoxic effects. In this study, the transcriptomic response of human microglia to doxorubicin using mRNA sequencing combined with bioinformatic analysis was investigated. Exposure to doxorubicin significantly altered microglial morphology, promoting a shift toward a process-bearing phenotype in human HMC3 cells. This phenotypic change was accompanied by elevated levels of DNA damage and was associated with the induction of cellular senescence. At the gene regulation level, the Illumina-based transcriptomic analysis provided 25,834 gene expression profiling in which 5,669 were differentially expressed. The future analyses revealed that 3,431 (upregulated) and 2,238 (downregulated) were differentially expressed under the treatment of doxorubicin. Genes associated with the p53 signaling pathway and inflammatory responses were upregulated, whereas genes involved in translation, DNA replication, and cell-cycle progression were downregulated. This transcriptional dysregulation was accompanied by differential expression of key transcription factors. This study provides transcriptomic evidence elucidating the genotoxic response to doxorubicin in microglial cells, offering mechanistic insights into chemobrain and highlighting key molecular pathways as potential targets for therapeutic intervention.
affiliations: Mahidol University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Serine metabolism changes link sphingolipid and one-carbon metabolism to cardiovascular risk factors in a cross-sectional study of asymptomatic adults
papers.abstract: Background: Metabolic perturbations associated with cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factors prior to clinical disease manifestation may inform novel preventative measures. Here we characterize metabolome-wide associations with various cardiometabolic risk factors in an asymptomatic population to develop a mechanistic metabolic framework of preemergent metabolic shifts. Methods: Plasma was collected from a clinically healthy cross-sectional cohort (n = 361; Clinical Trials.gov ID: NCT02367287). Cohort mass spectrometry-based metabolomics (biocrates MxP(R) Quant 500 kits) were complemented with expanded lipidomic coverage for a sex/age-matched subset with LDLc difference > 60 mg/dL (n = 38). LDLc-focused partial least square regressions and discriminate analyses were performed, after false discovery rate corrections. Results: As LDLc levels increased, plasma sphingolipids and cholesteryl esters, and transulfuration products were higher, while ether-linked phosphatidylcholines serine, glycine, alanine, methionine were lower. The subset analysis further highlighted elevations in triglycerides and deoxyceramides with elevated LDLc. When adjusted for alanine concentrations, deoxyceramide concentrations increased as serine declined (p = 0.0012), and the deoxyceramide:ceramide ratios were higher in the high LDLc group (p = 0.039). Lower serine levels were also accompanied by parallel changes in glycine (p= 0.0004), and anti-parallel changes in transsulfuration pathway metabolites particularly when adjusted for ceramide levels. Notably, the alanine:serine ratio was more strongly associated with fasting triglycerides (r = 0.38; p <0.0001) than LDLc. Conclusions: Serine depletion by increased demands of sphingolipid, and possibly transsulfuration pathway, metabolism is associated with elevations in cytotoxic deoxyceramides and reductions in glycine and methionine availability for one-carbon metabolism. These changes were strongly associated with fasting triglycerides and insulin resistance, a key marker of residual CVD risk.
affiliations: USDA-ARS Western Human Nutrition Research Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: FastaLake selects compact metaproteomic databases from large sequence reservoirs by de novo peptide lookup
papers.abstract: Metaproteomics analyses require protein sequence databases, yet the microbial proteins present in complex communities are not known in advance. Searching reference catalogs containing hundreds of millions of candidate sequences reduces identification sensitivity, while generating sample-specific databases through metagenomic sequencing adds time and cost. We introduce FastaLake, a computational workflow that uses full-length de novo peptide predictions by AlphaNovo to retrieve complete proteins from broad sequence resources and selects compact databases for conventional searching. In a defined eight-member community, FastaLake approached reference-search peptide yields without knowing its members. Using public sequence catalogs, FastaLake identified about as many peptides as matched metagenomic databases in two stool cohorts and 20-35% more in intestinal fluid at the same nominal 1% peptide false discovery rate. The resulting proteomes reveal personal functional profiles that persist across intestinal regions despite differences in leading species between intestinal fluid and stool. DNA, RNA and protein profiles agreed on broad differences between patients but only weakly on individual functions. All 726 acquisition-specific databases were smaller than the human reference proteome. Compact databases allowed non-specific searches of all 347 CapScan acquisitions, revealing histidine enrichment at peptide C termini in intestinal fluid. FastaLake enables metaproteomics analysis without matched metagenomic sequencing by constructing search databases from sequence resources and de novo peptide sequencing.
affiliations: Proteomics and Signal Transduction, Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry, Martinsried, 82152, Germany (corresponding author)

papers.title: Capture-(Hi)C analysis with PostChicago: Integrative metaprofiling and quantitative comparison of chromatin interactions
papers.abstract: Functionally linking enhancers to gene promoters at high resolution often entails analysis of 3C datasets, including viewpoint-based methods such as Capture-(Hi)C. Quantitative comparison across samples and experiments, together with visualization and integration of promoter interactions with other datasets are of critical importance. While existing statistical tools identify significant interactions and quantify underlying signal, systematically comparing the shape and extent of this signal across large sets of intervals remains challenging. Moreover, experimental artefacts, such as inefficient crosslinking, can affect downstream interpretation, but are difficult to detect systematically. Here we introduce PostChicago, an R/Bioconductor package that fills this gap. Building upon the widely used interaction-calling package Chicago, PostChicago provides a complete workflow for quality control, visualization, integration and quantitative analysis of promoter interactions between multiple samples, including annotation and quantification of genomic regions based on external datasets. PostChicago extends visual quantitative comparisons beyond individual viewpoints by computing normalized metaprofiles around large sets of intervals that visualize the distribution of interaction signal, enabling comparison between narrow and broad interaction patterns. We further demonstrate how PostChicago can identify experimental crosslinking artefacts. Together, PostChicago enables integrative, shape-sensitive analysis and quality control of promoter Capture-(Hi)C datasets at a scale that would otherwise require extensive custom scripting.
affiliations: German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) (corresponding author)

papers.title: Robust V(D)J Recombination in the Absence of SA1/2-mediated Chromatin Loops
papers.abstract: The cohesin ring complex organizes and mediates functional activity of the genome through chromatin loop extrusion1,2. Cohesin comprises a core SMC1-SMC3-RAD21 ring associated with multiple regulatory proteins, including SA1 and SA2 paralogs that bind mutually-exclusively to a RAD21 site3,4. Functional studies of cohesin complexes in vivo often employ inactivation of particular components2,3. However, inactivation of SA1 or SA2 in mice is limited by mouse embryonic lethality5-7 and, for dual SA1/2-inactivation by cycling cell lethality8-10. For these reasons, it remains unknown whether the requirement for SA1/2 in loop extrusion in vitro11,12 applies in vivo1,2, and whether these factors have overlapping or distinct functions in regulating this process3. Here, we employ G0/G1-arrested v-Abl pro-B lines, which are viable in the absence of cohesin-complex factors13,14, to dissect SA1 and SA2 functions in V(D)J recombination, a strictly G0/G1-specific process that harnesses loop extrusion to effect distinct Igh and Ig{kappa} locus recombination mechanisms15,16. Robust long-range Igh or Ig{kappa} V(D)J recombination continued unabated in the absence of SA1 or SA2. However, inactivation of both abrogated most positioned chromatin loops genome-wide and also abolished long-range Igh V(D)J recombination with a phenotype similar to RAD21 (cohesin) inactivation13. Yet, robust Ig{kappa} V(D)J recombination continued upon dual SA1/2-inactivation, which along with Hi-C findings, demonstrates ongoing loop-extrusion in the absence of SA1/2. Correspondingly, replacement of weak Igh V(D)J recombination signal sequences (RSSs) that target V(D)J recombination activity, with strong Ig{kappa} counterparts15 restored long-range Igh V(D)J recombination in SA1/2 inactivated cells. We conclude that SA1/2 together maintain loop extrusion impediments and genome-wide architecture in G0/G1-arrested cells; and, in their absence, loop extrusion proceeds unimpeded. Remarkably, strong RSSs allow Ig{kappa} to function normally in the absence of internal positioned loop structure across the 3.1-mega-base Ig{kappa} locus. We discuss implications of our findings for long-range gene regulation in G0/G1-arrested cells more broadly.
affiliations: Boston Children's Hospital Harvard Medical School (corresponding author)

papers.title: Large-scale pooled selection enables mapping of modifiers of RNAi gene knockdown effects in C. elegans
papers.abstract: Genetic interactions contribute to phenotypic variation, yet most studies characterize them in a small number of reference backgrounds rather than across natural populations. Studying genetic interactions in Caenorhabditis elegans is facilitated by RNAi by feeding, which enables gene-specific knockdowns across many genetic backgrounds without the need to construct individual mutant lines. However, individually screening hundreds of isolates across many RNAi conditions is laborious. Here, we developed a pooled platform that uses whole-genome sequencing to quantify the fitness of hundreds of genetically distinct C. elegans strains competing in a single flask. We leveraged this platform to evaluate RNAi responses in a pooled population of RNAi-sensitive C. elegans strains and identified two classes of QTL that influence RNAi responses. The first class influences responses to knockdowns of specific genes and is exemplified by a QTL that is specific to knockdown of mig-6. The second class influences general RNAi-response across multiple knockdowns. One QTL in this class localized to the right arm of chromosome III and was detected by both GWA and xQTL mapping, which suggests that a common large-effect variant underlies this QTL. We identified a T96K missense change in the dsRNA receptor SID-2 as the underlying causal variant. The 96K allele resides in the extracellular domain of SID-2 and confers increased RNAi sensitivity relative to the 96T allele. We hypothesize that the 96K allele enables greater uptake of ingested lumenal dsRNA through higher-affinity binding to the dsRNA phosphate backbone. The platform we developed enables systematic mapping of genetic interactions across natural populations at a previously impractical scale.
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (corresponding author)

papers.title: PeTFlow: Flow-Matching Based All-Atom Peptide Design through Side-Chain State Tokenization
papers.abstract: Peptide offers a powerful modality for targeting protein-protein interfaces, yet their computational design remains challenging because sequence identity, backbone geometry and side-chain packing must be optimized simultaneously within a three-dimensional pocket constrained environment. Here we present PeTFlow, a pocket-conditioned all-atom peptide co-design framework that rationalizes this constrained design problem through discrete side-chain state tokenization. In PeTFlow, each residue is represented as a chemically compatible state token, enabling unified modeling of peptide sequence, conformation and all-atom interface geometry. PeTFlow achieved superior generation quality on peptide-design benchmarks and can further be applied to therapeutically relevant peptide drug design.
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Anti-Infective Drug Discovery and Development, Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Chiral Molecule and Drug Discovery, School of Phar (corresponding author)

papers.title: Lateral opening site of human oligopeptide transporter 2 plays a key role in the interaction with polymyxins
papers.abstract: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-negative bacteria pose a critical global health threat, while polymyxins remain a last-line therapy. However, their clinical use is limited by nephrotoxicity. Human oligopeptide transporter 2 (hPepT2) is a membrane transporter mediating the reabsorption of polymyxins in renal cells and contributes to their nephrotoxicity, but the molecular basis of their interaction remains unclear. Here, we investigated the structure-interaction relationship (SIR) of polymyxins with hPepT2 by integrating computational, chemical, and cell biology approaches. Bioinformatic modelling predicted an outward-facing hPepT2 structure and a potential transport pathway, with polymyxins interacting at the lateral opening, particularly E214, D215, D317, D342, and E622. Transporter mutagenesis and molecular analyses confirmed that D215 is critical for polymyxin binding, while other residues influence transporter turnover and/or expression. We subsequently synthesised polymyxin analogues with modifications at Dab1, Dab3, Dab5, and Dab9 of polymyxins, which reduced interactions with hPepT2. Notably, alanine substitution at Dab3 reduced nephrotoxicity in mice while retaining antibacterial activity. Overall, this proof-of-concept study demonstrates that the hPepT2-polymyxin SIR model provides a viable strategy for developing novel, safer lipopeptide antibiotics.
affiliations: The University of Sydney (corresponding author)

papers.title: WarpDemuX-custom - Multiplexed sequence-specific direct RNA sequencing
papers.abstract: Nanopore direct RNA sequencing has emerged as a powerful technology for studying RNA and modifications at single-molecule resolution. Although originally developed for polyadenylated RNAs, protocol adaptations have extended its application to non-polyadenylated RNA species, including tRNAs and rRNAs. However, the lack of open and flexible (de)multiplexing solutions remains a limitation for large-scale sequencing studies. Existing community-driven approaches enable multiplexing of polyadenylated RNAs and, more recently, tRNAs, but do not fully address the challenges of targeted sequence-specific Nanopore sequencing of non-polyadenylated RNAs. Here, we present an improved sequence-specific direct RNA sequencing protocol for ribosomal RNAs, achieving enhanced capture and longer read lengths as demonstrated for human 28S rRNA. We complement this protocol with an expanded WarpDemuX software toolbox for flexible sequence-specific (de)multiplexing. We validate the approach using human cell lines carrying knockouts of different C/D box snoRNAs involved in site-specific 2'-O-ribose methylation of 28S rRNA. Our results demonstrate efficient multiplexed detection of sequence-specific RNA molecules and associated modification changes. While established here using rRNA, we validate our approach on another panel of non-polyadenylated RNA species, providing an open and scalable framework for targeted direct RNA sequencing and RNA modification analysis
affiliations: Universitat Heidelberg (corresponding author)

papers.title: Chain of Structures: Connecting Reasoning and Generation for Protein Design
papers.abstract: Scientific design requires reasoning in scientific spaces that represent the objects being designed. Building on Scinetics' Chain of Science Tokens, we present chain-of-structures (COS) as a concrete protein-design case study that connects reasoning and generation through explicit structural states. In this technical report, we apply COS to enzyme design, where catalytic function requires precise local geometry within a compatible global fold, making it a demanding test of reasoning from chemical requirements to protein structure. Starting from a reaction specification and target length, COS couples a language reasoning expert with an all-atom generation expert across four rounds: catalytic core, active site, global backbone, and complete sequence and structure. Each reasoning state directly conditions generation, and the resulting structure becomes context for the next decision. Discrete residue constraints and continuous latents connect the two experts, enabling structural supervision of the reasoning interface. On the evaluated benchmark, COS leads the compared baselines on five of six metrics, achieving 57.0% EC3 agreement and a TM-score of 0.729.
affiliations: HKUST (corresponding author)

papers.title: IsoGraph resolves coordinated transcript choice and gene abundance in the aging human brain
papers.abstract: Relative transcript usage can change without a corresponding change in total gene expression, but resolving coordinated transcript choice across genes while separating it from abundance remains challenging. We present IsoGraph, a gene-centered framework that represents isoform usage and abundance as paired network channels, identifies gene modules, and quantifies their channel-specific contributions. In synthetic benchmarks, IsoGraph preferentially recovered network structure when coordinated transcript usage carried the planted signal, whereas abundance-based representations were more informative in abundance-dominated and RNA-degradation settings. Applied to BrainSEQ and GTEx adult brain transcriptomes, IsoGraph identified age-associated transcript-usage signals that persisted after conditioning on gene abundance and, in a region-dependent manner, after adjustment for estimated cellular composition. Modules were stable across donor subsets, and frozen module axes retained age associations across cohorts even when exact gene partitions differed. IsoGraph module context captured predictive information about held-out differential transcript usage beyond gene-wise evidence and conventional co-expression. Convergent evidence from structural annotation, short-read junction usage, independent long-read sequencing, and within-donor allelic analyses supported constituent transcript events. Disease colocalization further prioritized candidate isoform events at neurological and psychiatric disease loci, including an alternative terminal-exon event at *PRDM2* associated with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Together, these results establish coordinated transcript usage as a reproducible component of transcriptomic organization and provide a framework for resolving its contribution alongside gene abundance and for tracing network-level signals to candidate transcript events.
affiliations: Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: DNA methylation-based prediction of differentiation state at cell-type resolution reveals an age-associated epigenetic mesenchymal drift
papers.abstract: Quantifying the differentiation state of cells is an important task in regenerative medicine, cellular reprogramming and in elucidating how differentiation hierarchies are altered in aging and disease. For DNA methylation data (DNAm) there is however an accute shortage of methods for quantifying differentiation state. Here we use machine learning to build EpiDiff, a predictor of differentiation that yields a continuous absolute differentiation index (DI) when applied to a DNAm sample. We extensively validate EpiDiff in single-cells, sorted cells and bulk tissue, as well as in in-vitro differentiation, organoid, reprogramming and cellular rejuvenation experiments. In mixed samples, EpiDiff measures the extent of differentiation across all cellular lineages. In sorted cell populations, we find that DI increases with age and, underpinning this increase, we discover that many cell-types undergo a developmental epigenetic drift that is most prominent towards the mesenchymal lineage. When applied to normal-tissues, EpiDiff is predictive of carcinogenic exposure and cancer risk. In summary, EpiDiff is a unique, general and versatile tool that can accurately quantify the global differentiation state of a DNAm sample with broad applicability to many disciplines.
affiliations: Chinese Academy of Sciences (corresponding author)

papers.title: EvSpark: Lossless Speculative Decoding for Hybrid DNA Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Hybrid DNA foundation models combine convolutional, recurrent, and attention layers, making speculative decoding more difficult than truncating a KV cache. We present EvSpark, a speculative decoding system for Evo2 that verifies draft blocks in parallel and restores all three classes of inference state by selecting retained intermediate states, without replay. A compact, hidden-state-conditioned drafter proposes each block in one parallel forward pass. On Evo2 7B, a 48-prompt benchmark with three training seeds yields a 2.96-fold speedup on 43 real-sequence prompts and a 3.27-fold speedup including five synthetic controls. Acceleration persists at 262k-token context (1.84-2.43-fold speedup on two bacterial genomes) and over 32k generated tokens. Retraining the same drafter architecture for Evo2 20B and 40B yields 2.18-2.46-fold speedups on real sequences and 2.51-2.78-fold speedups on the full suite. Autoregressive drafter comparisons and batch measurements show why low draft latency, rather than acceptance alone, determines the gain. The method preserves the target distribution. Greedy checks find no non-tie divergences across 48 prompts and six checkpoints; complementary sampling diagnostics quantify decoding fidelity. A drafter trained on 30M supervised positions reaches a 2.82-fold speedup on real sequences, compared with a 2.96-fold speedup at 150M positions. In regulatory-DNA design, EvSpark achieves a median 1.57-fold complete-workflow speedup over a calibrated batched native baseline.
affiliations: CreatiPhage Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (corresponding author)

papers.title: CRISCross: Integration of Epigenetic Information for Deep-Learning-Based Prediction of CRISPR-Cas9 Off-Targets Across Cell Types
papers.abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 enables precise genome editing but remains limited by off-target effects, raising safety concerns and necessitating accurate prediction. Although epigenetic features influence Cas9 binding and cleavage, their predictive signals are often weak, highlyvariable, and context-dependent, limiting the effectiveness of existing machine learning approaches. Cross-cell-type settings are especially challenging: epigenetic landscapes differ substantially, and models trained on one cell type frequently fail to generalize. Here, we systematically investigate the role of epigenetic context in off-target prediction and demonstrate that its utility depends on modeling interactions with sequence features rather than treating it as an independent signal. Tabular and deep learning experiments demonstrate that epigenetic features provide a consistent but modestly complementary signal, and that late-stage fusion strategies are insufficient to effectively exploit this information. To address this, we introduce CRISCross, a cross-attention-based architecture that captures sequence-epigenetic interactions at the nucleotide level, alongside CRISPRAT, a synthetic pretraining strategy that learns transferable representations from genome-derived sgRNA-off-target pairs without relying on dataset-specific pretraining. CRISCross, incorporating AlphaGenome-derived chromatin accessibility signals, shows better predictive performance than sequence-only baselines across three independent test datasets spanning two cell types, demonstrating improved generalization across guide RNAs, datasets, and cellular contexts. This is particularly relevant for therapeutic applications involving cell types or patient-derived contexts that lack dedicated experimental datasets. In such settings, predicted chromatin accessibility may provide scalable contextual information when direct epigenomic profiling is unavailable or impractical. Together, these results show that accurate CRISPR off-target prediction benefits from interaction-aware integration of epigenetic context alongside generalizable pretraining strategies.
affiliations: Bioinformatics Group, Department of Computer Science, University of Freiburg (corresponding author)

papers.title: Latent-Space Residue-Pair Networks from Molecular Dynamics Distinguish Ligand-Activated and SAVI-Associated STING
papers.abstract: Stimulator of interferon genes (STING) provides an informative model system for developing methods to extract and compare residue-pair fluctuation patterns from molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories. We combined a one-dimensional convolutional autoencoder trained on apo STING with temporal mean pooling, Mahalanobis-distance clustering, and residue-pair similarity networks to compare apo, ligand-bound, and SAVI-associated multi-mutant datasets using 25-dimensional latent descriptors. Networks constructed from clusters capturing state-dependent fluctuation patterns showed lid-dominated organization in the ligand-bound dataset and a1b1-enriched, structurally distributed relationships involving residue 281 in the multi-mutant dataset. These findings identify contrasting residue-pair fluctuation signatures in the analyzed trajectories and provide an interpretable framework for generating hypotheses about ligand-associated and mutation-associated dynamic allostery.
affiliations: National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Linker stretching optimizes bonding entropy in sticker-spacer condensates
papers.abstract: Phase separating biopolymers are often described by the sticker-spacer model, which accounts for non-attractive linkers that connect discrete attractive moieties. "Associative polymer" theories describe these systems as two coexisting fluids of stickers and spacers, respectively. In such theories the stickers and spacers are decoupled in the sense that sticker binding does not affect spacer conformations or vice versa. Informed by coarse-grained simulations, we develop a phenomenological mean-field theory to determine the microscopic coupling between the sticker and spacer degrees of freedom. Accounting for linkers connecting adjacent spacers introduces free energy contributions due to conformational entropy of the spacer and the binding combinatorics of the stickers. These contributions have opposite dependencies on spacer length because longer spacers allow a greater volume to search for binding partners but incur a greater entropy cost upon bond formation. The length dependent terms from these contributions cancel leaving a length-independent elastic term arising from the fact that a small amount of spacer stretching lowers the free energy by increasing the number of possible binding partners. The cancellation of spacer length from the theory justifies the decoupling approximation and supports mean-field treatments of heterogeneous spacers.
affiliations: Kansas State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: TRF2 mediates force-resistant bridging of distal telomeric DNA repeats
papers.abstract: Shelterin binds telomeres, regulates telomere length, and protects chromosome ends from mis-repair, which is essential for genome stability. Telomere end-protection uniquely depends on the TRF2 subunit, which assembles telomeric DNA into a protective T-loop structure in vivo, yet the biochemical mechanism underlying this process remains unresolved. Using single-molecule optical tweezers and atomic force microscopy, we show that the human shelterin complex tethers distal telomeric DNA repeats, looping the intervening DNA. These bridges withstand tens of piconewtons of applied load, rupture at a force that scales with telomeric repeat number and re-form on relaxation.
