Structure-function analysis demonstrates that this force-resistant tethering is TRF2-dependent under our conditions and depends on multiple interfaces, with the TRFH domain making a major but non-exclusive contribution: introducing the TRF2 TRFH domain into TRF1 is sufficient to confer tethering, whereas its deletion from TRF2 reduces but does not abolish activity. We propose telomeric dsDNA tethering by TRF2 as a candidate first step in T-loop formation, preceding invasion of the telomeric 3' ssDNA overhang.
affiliations: Francis Crick Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: Intracellular complement Factor B couples inflammatory sensing to metabolism, chromatin regulation and maladaptive tissue repair
papers.abstract: Inflammatory signals are broadly conserved, yet how tissue context converts them into programs of recovery or maladaptive repair remains unclear. Using kidney injury as a model of inflammation-to-repair transitions, we identify an injury-induced proximal-tubule complement program in which cell-intrinsic complement proteins are repurposed across subcellular compartments to couple inflammation to metabolic and chromatin regulation and promote maladaptive fibrotic remodeling. Mechanistically, myeloid-derived IL-1b; signals through IL-1R1 on injured tubular cells to recruit NF-kB and AP-1 to C3 and Cfb, coordinately inducing complement component 3 (C3) and Factor B (FB). Cytoplasmic FB drives cleavage-activation of cell-intrinsic C3, which supports tubular cell mitochondrial metabolic adaptation to stress and accumulation of C3aR-expressing macrophages around injured tubules. Nuclear FB, on the other hand, binds chromatin through a previously unrecognized DNA-binding interface and mediates histone H3 proteolysis and the preferential remodeling of chromatin promotors enriched in transcriptional programs relevant to maladaptive repair. Key features of this injury-associated C3-FB response, including intranuclear FB, are conserved in human kidney disease, associate with kidney dysfunction, and distinguish diseased from healthy kidneys. Together, these findings suggest that extracellular complement-targeting therapies may miss disease-relevant intracellular functions and suggest nuclear FB as a distinct target whose chromatin interaction and processing capacity could selectively limit maladaptive tissue responses beyond conventional inhibition.
affiliations: National Institutes of Health (corresponding author)

papers.title: Gut bacterium of Leishmania donovani-non-transmitting sand fly induces IL-23~Th17 axis to protect hosts from drug-resistant visceral leishmaniasis
papers.abstract: Background: Visceral leishmaniasis (VL) is caused by Leishmania donovani and differentiates under the influence of biotope-specific gut bacteria in the Leishmania donovani-transmitting sand fly vector, Phlebotomus argentipes, which coexists with the Leishmania donovani-non-transmitting Sergentomyia species in the Indian subcontinent. Hypothesis: Sergentomyia are primarily herpetophilic. Interestingly, we identified a specific population of anthropophilic Sergentomyia babu babu, a proven naturally non-competent vector for transmitting Leishmania donovani, with high abundance and human-bite incidences in VL-non-endemic regions, compared with VL-endemic regions of India. Thus, the possibility of egesting gut bacteria to humans from VL-non-transmitting Sergentomyia and inducing downstream immune cascades remains undeniable. Innovation: We characterized gut bacteria from anthropophilic Sergentomyia babu babu in both VL-endemic and VL-non-endemic regions of India and found that a heat-inactivated formulation of Heyndrickxia sporothermodurans [NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA): PRJNA1403236], isolated from anthropophilic Sergentomyia babu babu from a VL-non-endemic region, prevented and cured L. donovani infection by inducing IL-23~Th17. More importantly, it also prevented the initial parasite establishment by inducing phagocytosis, ROS, and TNF- in circulatory Ly6G-CD11b+Ly6Chi monocytes. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report confirming that the gut bacteria of VL-non-transmitting sand flies are critical and need to be investigated in depth for developing therapeutics and/or prophylactics against visceral leishmaniasis (VL), and suggests that possible bite-transfer of gut bacteria from disease-non-transmitting vectors to hosts may restrict disease pathogenicity. Further clinical trials are needed to warrant (Indian patent: 202511041013, April 28, 2025).
affiliations: West Bengal State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: CXCR3 on transferred T cells enables vaccine-boosted adoptive T-cell therapy in solid tumors
papers.abstract: Adoptive T-cell therapy (ACT) has demonstrated marked clinical benefit in hematological malignancies but has limited efficacy against solid tumors. Cancer vaccines can improve ACT, but the mechanisms underlying this combination are poorly understood. Here, we combined ACT with chimpanzee adenovirus ChAdOx1 (ChAd) and modified vaccinia Ankara (MVA) encoding tumor antigens. Whereas PD1 blockade failed to improve ACT, the combination with ChAd/MVA vaccination drove durable regression of established tumors, correlating with expansion of tumor-reactive T cells in lymphoid organs and increased tumor infiltration by T cells. Mechanistically, ChAd priming induced CXCR3 ligands (CXCL10 and CXCL9) in the vaccine-draining lymph node, thereby recruiting transferred T cells to this node independently of cognate antigen. CXCR3 expression on the transferred T cells, but not on host cells, was required for the anti-tumor effect of the combination therapy and favored T-cell accumulation in the vaccine-draining lymph node and the tumor. These findings identify CXCR3 on the transferred T cells as a determinant of ACT plus vaccination synergy and provide a rationale for combining viral-vector vaccines with TCR-T therapies, and for selecting or engineering T cells to retain CXCR3 expression.
affiliations: Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, Nuffield Department of Medicine, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genomic and proteomic insights into the virulence of a native Heterorhabditis indica-Photorhabdus akhurstii complex active against Spodoptera spp.
papers.abstract: A native entomopathogenic nematode isolate, Heterorhabditis indica Che4.1, was recovered from soils in Valencia (Spain), and its symbiotic bacterium, Photorhabdus akhurstii Che4.1, was isolated and characterized. Nematode identification was confirmed by ITS and 28S rDNA sequencing, while genome-based analyses supported the taxonomic assignment of the bacterial symbiont. The nematode-bacterium complex exhibited insecticidal activity against Spodoptera exigua and Spodoptera littoralis. H. indica Che4.1 showed an LC of 53.7 infective juveniles (IJs)/mL against S. exigua, comparable to that of the commercial reference Larvanem (54.3 IJs/mL). Against S. littoralis, Che4.1 exhibited an approximately twofold lower LC than Larvanem (77.3 versus 155.9 IJs/mL), with non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals. The complete genome of P. akhurstii Che4.1 consists of a single circular chromosome of 5.66 Mb encoding a diverse repertoire of putative virulence factors, including toxin complex (Tc) components, YenTc-like proteins, Mcf toxins, App-family proteins, Pra/Prb proteins, and chitinases, together with several predicted secondary metabolite biosynthetic gene clusters. LC-MS/MS analyses of bacterial culture supernatants and infected insect cadavers detected multiple predicted virulence-associated proteins, including Tc-related, YenTc-like, App-family, and Pra/Prb proteins. In addition, bacterial cell-free supernatants caused 68.8-81.3% mortality in S. exigua neonates under laboratory conditions. Together, these findings reveal a diverse repertoire of potential virulence determinants in P. akhurstii Che4.1 and demonstrate the insecticidal potential of its native nematodebacterium complex. The performance of H. indica Che4.1 relative to a commercial reference supports further evaluation of this isolate for biological control of Spodoptera spp., particularly under greenhouse and field conditions.
affiliations: Universidad de Valencia (corresponding author)

papers.title: Pervasive effect of bottom trawling on benthic biodiversity unravelled by metabarcoding across the Tree of Life
papers.abstract: Bottom trawling is the most widespread human disturbance on the seafloor, known to affect seabed structure and benthic biota. Yet, its impact on benthic communities remains documented mainly for taxa identifiable through morphology, leaving microscopic benthic communities largely overlooked. The Gulf of Lion continental shelf has been trawled for decades by French and Spanish fleets, to the point that encountering untrawled reference areas became elusive. Here, we examined prokaryote, protist and Animalia benthic communities at eight stations, using eDNA metabarcoding of core sediment samples, with five primer-pairs. Benthic communities were cross-referenced with contrasted trawling impacts, integrated across three periods: over one month, three years or ten years preceding the sampling. The community composition was primarily structured by ecological habitats, yet, trawling pressure showed association with prokaryotes and Animalia diversity. Diversity was higher at sites trawled more intensively in the preceding month, whereas long-term trawling was associated with a significant erosion of Animalia alpha diversity. Unexpectedly, communities did not display consistent vertical structure and the relative contributions of trawling and hydrodynamic reworking remain unresolved due to the absence of untrawled sites. Overall, our results show that trawling effects extend to prokaryotic compartments rarely considered in impact assessments, providing a proof of concept for eDNA-based assessment, and underline a pervasive long-term effect on Animalia communities. This study also highlights the importance of the timescale used to quantify fishing pressure and underscores the complexity of impact assessment when monitoring begins too late to establish a clear baseline, particularly when no reference site remains.
affiliations: University of Montpellier, Ifremer, CNRS, IRD, MARine Biodiversity Exploitation and Conservation (MARBEC), Sete, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: Antiviral Sulfonated Polymersomes Inhibit Corona-, Influenza-, and Alphavirus
papers.abstract: A broad-spectrum antiviral is required to enable rapid intervention against current, newly emerging and mutating viruses. Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), influenza A virus (IAV), Sindbis virus (SINV) and chikungunya virus (CHIKV) all engage negatively charged moieties on host cells, such as heparan sulfate (HS) and sialic acid, to facilitate attachment for entry and infection. We designed HS-mimetic nanoparticles in the form of polymer vesicles (polymersomes) by blending membrane-forming and sulfonated copolymers. These biocompatible polymersomes successfully inhibited host cell infection of HS-dependent SARS-CoV-2 and HS-independent IAV in vitro with sub-nanomolar potency. Multivalent interaction of several virus ligands with a single polymersome as quantified by fluorescence correlation spectroscopy likely contributes to their potency. The sulfonated polymersomes also functioned in vivo as demonstrated by a reduction in the spread of SINV, an alphavirus model for CHIKV, in zebrafish embryos, which led to a significantly increased survival. Hence, our polymersomes could form the basis for an urgently required multifunctional broad-spectrum antiviral nanomedicine.
affiliations: Imperial College London (corresponding author)

papers.title: Benchmarking interface confidence as a selection criterion for computational nanobody design against survivin's BIR-domain groove
papers.abstract: Designed binders are routinely filtered on predicted interface confidence, which reports how self-consistently a model places an interface, not where it lies. We designed 200 nanobody loops against the survivin BIR-domain groove, co-folded 196, and checked epitope contact in every predicted complex. Confidence showed no detectable association with epitope engagement ({rho} = +0.100, 95% CI -0.04 to +0.24, n = 196); its highest and lowest quartiles failed alike (odds ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.41 to 2.26). It tracked instead the run's other confidence estimates ({rho} = +0.61). Twelve-seed replication separated two candidates the criteria had not: one reached the complete epitope in 10 of 12 runs, the other never. Across 155 predictions the top-ranked model was no better than one drawn at random from its five (P = 0.610), though only 3 of 31 failed on every model. Nothing was assayed; nb_cand_057 is an in silico candidate only.
affiliations: Department of Anesthesiology and Surgical Intensive Care Unit, Xinhua Hospital, School of Medicine and School of Biomedical Engineering, Shanghai Jiao Tong Univ (corresponding author)

papers.title: AI-guided discovery for low-resource peptide engineering using evolutionary scale modeling
papers.abstract: Data scarcity is a major bottleneck in artificial intelligence (AI)-guided peptide engineering, where experimental training sets often contain only tens to a few hundred sequences, and it is difficult to judge in advance whether a protein language model (PLM) will effectively guide iterative discovery before committing to wet-lab work. Here we present SCARSE, a machine learning framework that couples ESM2 protein language model embeddings with Gaussian process regression. Benchmarked across 24 diverse peptide and small-protein datasets spanning substitution and indel variants, antimicrobial peptides, and hemolytic peptides, SCARSE significantly outperformed hand-engineered descriptor baselines on substitution and indel tasks in low-data regimes (20-500 training samples) and performed comparably on short non-mutant peptides. In active learning simulations it consistently prioritized high-performing candidates, discovering up to 7-fold more top-tier peptides than random sampling. Cross-validation (CV) R2 correlated strongly with final active learning performance (Pearson r = 0.80-0.84), and evaluating on as few as 50 labeled peptides reduced CV R2 variance enough for it to serve as a practical, data-efficient criterion for assessing model suitability before iterative screening. SCARSE thus provides an early diagnostic indicator for active learning success and is freely available as an open-source Python package (pip) and through an interactive Hugging Face Spaces web interface.
affiliations: Division of Molecular Bioscience, Department of Life Sciences, Chalmers University of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: CHORUS: A proteome-scale atlas of membrane interaction interfaces constructed using cross-protein language model embeddings from sequences alone
papers.abstract: Membrane proteins drive vital cellular signaling and bioenergetics yet resolving their physical interaction interfaces remains hindered by the paucity of experimental complexes and the breakdown of sequence alignments across hydrophobic bilayers. Here, we present CHORUS, a sequence-only deep-learning framework that decodes interaction sites across membrane proteins without requiring 3D structures, multiple sequence alignments (MSAs), or predefined partner identities. By systematically synthesizing complementary latent representations across diverse protein language model (pLM) families and functional layer depths, CHORUS outperforms 18 established sequence- and structure-based methods across 4,655 homology-isolated test contexts (average precision: 0.643), demonstrating amplified predictive capacity within the lipid-embedded core (0.746). We show that CHORUS delineates quaternary contact boundaries across megadalton respiratory supercomplexes directly from sequences alone (0.984). We deliver the CHORUS Atlas (https://chorus.atlas.sunnylab.org), providing precomputed, residue-resolved interaction landscapes for 80,619 reviewed transmembrane proteins spanning 4,918 species and 33.7 million residues to empower interactome-scale discovery and allosteric therapeutic design.
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) (corresponding author)

papers.title: TopFor: Automated Preparation of AMBER-Compatible Parameters for Noncanonical Amino Acids in Peptides
papers.abstract: Peptides containing noncanonical amino acids (ncAAs) are becoming increasingly important in drug discovery, but their molecular dynamics (MD) simulation remains limited by labor-intensive residue parameterization and topology preparation. Here, we present TopFor (Topology and Residue Force-Field Parameter Preparation), an open-source, peptide-oriented workflow that automates the generation of ncAA residue templates and force-field parameter files for MD simulations with AMBER using established charge-derivation methods. TopFor supports single-residue, whole-peptide, and batch parameterization workflows. The workflow was validated using the MDM2-p53 complex by comparing native AMBER residue definitions with residues processed by TopFor using three charge-derivation methods, each evaluated in three independent 100 ns MD simulations. TopFor-generated residue definitions showed structural and conformational behavior comparable to the native AMBER representation. Applicability to more complex peptide architectures was demonstrated using the head-to-tail cyclic peptide cyclosporin A and the cyclic depsipeptide cyclohexylgriselimycin. At library scale, 1,138 of 1,214 cyclohexylgriselimycin derivatives (93.7%) successfully completed TopFor parameterization and the subsequent initial AMBER-based computational workflow across two derivatization campaigns. TopFor was further integrated into a structure-based peptide discovery workflow based on the DnaN-griselimycin complex. Six GM-derived peptides were computationally prioritized and experimentally evaluated, of which four produced SPR responses against Mycobacterium smegmatis (M. smegmatis) DnaN and three showed concentration-dependent responses. TopFor reduces the manual effort required to prepare ncAA-containing peptides for MD simulations and enables their integration into both library-scale computational screening and structure-based peptide discovery workflows. Keywords: noncanonical amino acids; peptide parameterization; molecular dynamics; AMBER; AmberTools; peptide design; high-throughput virtual screening
affiliations: Helmholtz Institute for Pharmaceutical Research Saarland (HIPS) (corresponding author)

papers.title: MetworkPy: A Python Package for Graph- and Information-theoretic Investigation of Metabolic Networks
papers.abstract: Background: Metabolism plays an important role in physiology and disease. In silico Genome-Scale Metabolic Models (GSMMs) are useful for informing analysis of metabolism and contextualizing high-throughput molecular profiling data. Flux balance analysis (FBA) based approaches can use GSMMs to predict metabolic reaction flux states and condition-specific alterations, but most FBA methods are limited by: 1) needing metabolic objective functions that are difficult to define experimentally, and 2) confining comparisons to extrema of reaction flux distributions. Results: We introduce MetworkPy, a Python package that implements a flexible toolbox for objective-free graph- and information-theoretic analyses of GSMMs and flux distributions. MetworkPy includes methods to construct graph representations of GSMMs, to deconstruct GSMMs into topologically-aware gene sets that inform downstream bioinformatic analyses, and to assess shifts in flux distributions for groups of reactions. To demonstrate utility, we used MetworkPy to identify metabolic features perturbed by the transcription factor ArgR, a known regulator of arginine biosynthesis in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. MetworkPy successfully linked reaction flux shifts in ArgR's transcriptome-constrained GSMM to arginine biosynthesis, which cannot be easily ascertained by FBA-based approaches. Conclusions: MetworkPy is a customization-friendly toolkit for topological- and flux sampling based- analyses of GSMMs. MetworkPy's tools provide multiple complementary metabolic contextualization approaches for microbial or eukaryotic genes of interest, and MetworkPy's architecture facilitates user-designed workflows.
affiliations: Seattle Childrens Research Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: Concurrent de novo inference of cell types and gene regulatory networks with NetMap
papers.abstract: Existing methods for GRN inference based on single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) data typically require prior cell type calling and then infer GRNs at cell type resolution. This risks propagation of errors from cell annotation to GRN inference. Moreover, it makes existing methods blind to regulatory programs that are shared between different cell types, as well as to subtle differences in regulatory activity between cells of the same type. To address these limitations, we present NetMap, a pipeline that jointly infers cell-level GRNs and clusters cells based on shared regulatory programs, combining state-of-the-art single-cell autoencoders and explainable artificial intelligence methods. NetMap outperforms existing methods on synthetic data with a known ground-truth GRN and is able to reliably detect biologically plausible regulons on real data. Moreover, requiring only a small set of user-provided marker genes, NetMap can be used for GRN structure-informed probabilistic cell type assignment. We demonstrate the utility of this approach using PBMC data, where we achieve near perfect clustering and cell type recovery performance compared with manually created cell type labels. Finally, we applied NetMap to a data set with naive, activated and exhausted T-cells, and were able to verify that NetMap retrieves relevant T-cell state signatures from the data, with two approaches. NetMap can be installed as a python package from https://github.com/bionetslab/netmap and is compatible with the scverse system. Scripts to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/bionetslab/netmap-evaluation.
affiliations: Friedrich-Alexander-Universitaet Erlangen-Nuernberg, (corresponding author)

papers.title: Understanding when and how knowledge graphs add value to EHR-based clinical prediction across Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, and chronic pain
papers.abstract: Biomedical knowledge graphs (KGs) have emerged as a promising approach for incorporating biological knowledge into machine-learning models trained on electronic health record (EHR) data. However, their large scale and heterogeneous structure impose substantial computational cost, and it remains unclear whether their benefits generalize across diseases or depend on how the graph is constructed. We systematically evaluated KG integration across three diseases spanning distinct biological and clinical characteristics: multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, and chronic pain. For each disease we compared five modelling strategies, spanning EHR-only features and graph diffusion over concept-level, cohort-derived, disease-anchored, and full SPOKE (Scalable Precision Medicine Open Knowledge Engine) subgraphs, asking whether graph construction affects predictive performance and computational cost, whether KG integration improves classification over EHR-only models, and what the graph does to model behavior. Cohort-derived subgraphs, comprising roughly 45% of SPOKE's nodes and one-fifth of its edges, matched or modestly exceeded the full graph's performance while substantially reducing computational cost in all three diseases. The predictive benefit of KG integration, however, was strongly disease-dependent: it improved classification in Parkinson's disease, had no measurable effect in multiple sclerosis, and reduced performance in chronic pain. These differences were not explained by the amount of biological information incorporated: the disease with the largest shift toward molecular features showed no improvement, the sole beneficiary showed only a modest shift, and the disease with no molecular shift was penalized. Mechanistically, graph diffusion redistributed each disease's existing signal across many correlated features rather than adding independent biological signal, so that any gain depended on whether it added information beyond the EHR. These findings show that cohort-derived subgraphs offer a computationally efficient alternative to full-scale knowledge graphs, and that KG integration functions less as a universal accuracy booster than as a data- and disease-dependent transformation of the patient representation.
affiliations: Rancho BioSciences (corresponding author)

papers.title: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Frontier and Local LLMs Querying a Biomedical Knowledge Graph
papers.abstract: We combine GeneNetwork's 1TB structured database with its metadata as an RDF graph and an associated literature corpus. We benchmark frontier and local LLMs querying it through four architectures: document, graph and agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and a combination of the three. We evaluate them on 40 domain specific expert-curated questions with a new metric: the satisfaction frequency psi (psi, i.e, the share of questions answered with precision and recall of at least 70% or an f1 of at least 60%). psi ranks systems the same way precision, recall and f1 -- a machine learning metric built from the harmonic mean of precision and recall -- but is easier to read and assess for humans. System architecture had a large effect: with full use of Claude Opus 4.8 the plain document RAG of our earlier GNQA system had a psi of 36% against 86% for our new combined tools. Delegating most of the work from Claude Opus 4.8 to a local model halved query costs while still reaching a psi of 59%.
affiliations: University of Tennessee Health Science Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Linking UV absorption of DNA with base pair sequences
papers.abstract: The absorption of ultraviolet (UV) radiation is the first step in a chain of events which can induce DNA damage associated with cancer and aging, yet the sequence dependence of UV absorption remains to be investigated. Here, we present a systematic study of UV absorption spectra of DNA based on all-electron Hartree-Fock calculations. We analyze all possible sequences up to four base pairs, as well as longer randomized sequences and genomic nullomers - motifs which are missing in a given genome. We observe a pronounced sequence dependence: cytosine- and guanine-rich motifs exhibit significantly enhanced absorption, whereas adenine-thymine-rich sequences absorb less in the mid-UV range. Most genomes are biased toward adenine-thymine-rich sequences which leads to decreased absorption of UV radiation by the sun. In addition, we introduce a computational framework enabling spectral calculations of large DNA and RNA fragments, opening the door to large-scale optical analyses.
affiliations: University of Kassel (corresponding author)

papers.title: A base-modifying enzyme extends the range of anti-phage defense provided by DNA glycosylases
papers.abstract: The most abundant prokaryotic mechanisms of defense against phage predation involve the recognition and destruction of the infecting DNA. One method of counter-defense is the incorporation of modified nucleobases into the phage genome to avoid interaction with enzymes that target the viral DNA. T-even coliphages replace cytosine with 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) that in some cases are further decorated with glucosyl groups. To explore the diversity of immunity genes that recognize 5hmC, we infected a library of metagenomic DNA inserts from uncultured, non-sequenced soil bacteria with a mutant T4 phage that harbored only non-glucosylated 5hmC on its genome. Bacteria that resisted infection carried a DNA glycosylase, Brig3, that specifically excises 5hmC nucleobases to generate abasic sites in the phage genome and prevent viral proliferation. The crystal structure of Brig3 bound to its substrate revealed a catalytic mechanism in which the 5hmC nucleobase is flipped out of the DNA into the active site and replaced by an asparagine residue that inserts into the double helix to contact the complementary guanosine. Brig3 is encoded within an operon that also encodes BapA, a hydrolase that removes glucosyl groups from glucosyl-5hmC present in the genome of otherwise Brig3-resistant T-even phages carrying this hypermodified base. Our results uncover a defense strategy in which base-modifying enzymes widen the immune response provided by DNA glycosylases.
affiliations: Rockefeller University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Proteomics reveal temperature-coupled cobalamin homeostasis and pathogenicity in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
papers.abstract: The opportunistic pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa is highly adaptable to different environmental conditions due to its versatile sensing and metabolic capabilities. Both external temperature and metal availability have a strong influence on the virulence and pathogenicity of P. aeruginosa, but the coupling between these two factors is not well understood. While iron is recognized as major player in nutritional immunity, the role of cobalt and the cobalt-containing vitamin B12 (cobalamin) during host infection remains unclear. Here, we investigate the environmental isolate P. aeruginosa PA254 using high-resolution global proteomics and cellular cobalamin measurements over a temperature gradient spanning environmental, host-associated, and heat-stress conditions (22-42 C). PA254 occupies a continuum between an ambient-temperature state characterized by secreted virulence factors, exopolysaccharide-rich biofilms, and planktonic swimmers and surface swarmers; and a host-associated state characterized by a distinct set of virulence factors, alginate-dominated biofilms, and a strong proportion of surface twitching motility. Pathway analyses indicate a shift toward carbon sparing, energy conservation, redox control, and metabolic maintenance during a host-adapted lifestyle, along with the increased production of alternative iron acquisition strategies relying on heme and siderophores. Proteins of the cobalamin biosynthetic pathway declined significantly above ambient temperatures, despite constant intracellular B12 concentrations and sustained abundance of B12-dependent enzymes across all conditions. This decoupling of biosynthesis from cellular pools implies temperature-dependent changes in prioritization, biosynthetic efficiency, or recycling within B12-dependent processes, while the lack of B12 production at human body temperatures creates avenues for therapeutics interfering with B12 supply. Altogether, this work highlights a gradual rather than stepwise reprogramming of the P. aeruginosa proteome in response to environmental cues, and highlights proteomics as a comprehensive tool to investigate system level mechanisms of challenging pathogens.
affiliations: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (corresponding author)

papers.title: A peptidomimetic inhibitor blocks Vibrio cholerae adhesin FrhA.
papers.abstract: Cholera is a diarrheal disease resulting from colonization of the small intestine by the Gram-negative bacterium Vibrio cholerae. The peptide-binding domain (PBD) of the adhesion protein FrhA is critical for V. cholerae intestinal colonization and biofilm formation. In a program aimed at blocking cholera infection, antagonists of the FrhA-PBD are described based on a tripeptide motif, such as H-Trp-Thr-Asp-OH. Notably, constraining the N-terminal tryptophan residue using 1,2,3,4-tetrahydro- {beta} - carboline-3-carboxylic acid (Tcc) and co-crystallization of H-(S)-Tcc-Thr-Asp-OH with a FrhA construct have provided structural information to guide inhibitor design. The diastereomer H-(R)-Tcc-Thr-Asp-OH exhibited nanomolar binding affinity Kd = 101 {+/-} 30.2 nM), blocked bacterial hemagglutination mediated by FrhA-PBD, and reduced biofilm formation in vitro. It also inhibited intestinal epithelial cell adhesion to an immobilized recombinant FrhA-PBD construct (IC50 = 24 M; 95% CI, 11 - 51 M). Its resistance to chymotrypsin proteolysis supports further investigation as an anti-adhesion peptidomimetic.
affiliations: McGill University (corresponding author)

papers.title: PhageHost-GNN: novelty-aware and locally adaptable strain-level Klebsiella-phage prediction
papers.abstract: Interest in bacteriophages as alternative treatments for bacterial infections has grown amid the ongoing crisis of multidrug resistance. However, their narrow host range makes it labor-intensive to identify matching phages for bacterial isolates using conventional experimental methods. Although existing computational models based on biomolecular features have shown promise for phage-host matching, the performance of alternative model settings, including data embeddings, across datasets with different degrees of novelty remains underexplored. This study introduces PhageHost-GNN, a novelty-aware framework using routed models to predict strain-level Klebsiella-phage interactions, evaluated under three clinical scenarios. Using multiple embedding models to encode sequence, structural, and genomic-context features, the framework achieved AUPRCs reaching 0.784, 0.731, and 0.642 in host-unseen, phage-unseen, and both-unseen in silico evaluations, respectively. Benchmarks on experimentally validated datasets showed the clearest advantage over fixed embeddings when both hosts and phages were new to the trained model. In addition to direct inference and de novo training, the framework further implements a fine-tuning pipeline to adapt existing models to local custom datasets while reducing model-training time. Overall, PhageHost-GNN provides a flexible framework for model selection, evaluation, and local adaptation in practical phage-therapy screening.
affiliations: Southern University of Science and Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Toxicity by Consortium Revisited: Structural Neighbors and Cross-Family Reach
papers.abstract: A compound's toxicity can be gauged from the toxicities of the compounds it resembles. We showed that in 2003 for rat oral LD50: the compounds in a reference set of 13,645 that most resemble the query form a consortium and vote on its toxicity. This work returns to that method twenty-three years later, on public data, because the reference set used in 2003 is no longer public. Rebuilt on 11,989 curated rat oral LD50 values, the method answers for 67.0% of the held-out compounds carrying an exact value, and 92.1% of those answers land within one log unit; in 2003 the figures were 94% within one log unit on 57.3% of compounds. We then ran it over 28 further endpoints, each recording whether a compound showed a particular toxicity, from cytochrome inhibition to mutagenicity to clinical toxicity: 149,224 measurements on 34,162 compounds. The method answers only when a compound has close enough neighbors, and on those it correctly identifies a median 72.9% of the compounds that showed the toxicity and 96.5% of those that did not. Separately we asked whether a reverse screen carries information about these endpoints beyond molecular size and lipophilicity. We search a compound against a published index of 27,910 ligands solved inside proteins and count the protein families those sites belong to. A compound whose matches reach no protein family inhibits CYP3A4 2.5% of the time; one whose matches span sixteen or more families inhibits 51.0% of the time. Added to heavy atom count, molecular weight and cLogP, the screen raises the mean area under the ROC curve from 0.72 to 0.76 across the 28 endpoints. The OpenADMET consortium has since measured CYP3A4 inhibition on 2,335 compounds, and the same pattern holds. Compounds that resemble known binders of sixteen or more protein families inhibit CYP3A4 24.60% of the time; compounds that resemble no known binder at all inhibit it 5.00% of the time. The more protein families a compound resembles binders of, the more likely it is to inhibit CYP3A4. This association is strong enough to act on before anything is made. Scoring a library on how far its compounds reach across protein families, together with their size and lipophilicity, and setting aside the riskiest fifth removes two thirds of the androgen receptor binders and about half of the CYP3A4 inhibitors. Scoring needs only a two-dimensional structure, with no docking and no conformer generation at query time. Interactive scoring, the data and the pool are at toxpred.ai. Keywords: toxicity prediction; structural similarity; nearest neighbors; reverse screening; target breadth; promiscuity; LD50; cytochrome P450; virtual library triage
affiliations: Eidogen-Sertanty, Inc. (corresponding author)

papers.title: The quantum environment in cryptochrome enhances light absorption of FAD
papers.abstract: Cryptochromes are blue-light photoreceptors that regulate circadian rhythms and, in some species, contribute to magnetic-field sensing through excitation of the flavin chromophore FAD. However, theoretical descriptions of cryptochrome photoexcitation usually treat only the chromophore quantum mechanically, neglecting quantum effects of the surrounding pro-tein because of the computational cost of electronic-structure calculations. Here we present a computational framework that extends the quantum-mechanical region from the chromophore alone to approximately 1,200 atoms, enabling explicit treatment of the surrounding amino acids and cofactors. The approach combines relaxed-accuracy real-time time-dependent Hartree-Fock simulations with a post-processing correction that compensates for systematic errors. The framework resolves the spatial origin, wavelength and oscillator strength of individual absorption processes throughout the quantum region. Our calculations reveal that the quantum-mechanical protein environment substantially enhances the light absorption of FAD, demonstrating that neighboring residues actively modulate the photophysical response of cryptochrome rather than merely providing a structural scaffold.
affiliations: University of Kassel (corresponding author)

papers.title: Reversion to the Meta Body Form of Life after Complete Cell Death in Pure Liquid Water
papers.abstract: The prevailing view holds that simpler animate beings predating the dawn of cellular life once existed, yet they have long since vanished from the present-day Earth. Our hypothesis posits that these animate beings persist to this day. To this end, we devised a long-term experiment spanning over a decade, keeping Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) within a sealed aqueous system of pure water. The findings illustrated that, upon the complete cell death (CCD) of the S. aureus, as cellular remnants progressively succumbed to dissolution, the aqueous solution underwent self-purification, bringing forth a class of lipid bilayer membrane microspheres containing RNA and proteins. These structures maintained long-term sustainable stability within the thermodynamic storm of water molecules and underwent dynamic size fluctuations over time - collectively exhibited phenomena indicative of being "alive". This study reveals that the cell, upon complete cell death, undergoes reversion to a living entity simpler than the cell itself - the Meta Body (MB). The discovery of MB opens an entire re-conceptualization of what death ultimately brings.
affiliations: Congqing Medical University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Sequence context decodes multi-state conformational heterogeneity from crystallographic B-factors
papers.abstract: Protein function is governed by conformational ensembles, yet the overwhelming majority of experimentally determined structures capture only static snapshots, leaving the multi-state heterogeneity that underlies biological activity largely inaccessible. X-ray crystallography, the dominant source of these structures, does carry one experimental proxy for motion, the atomic B-factor, but crystal packing and refinement artifacts frequently obscure its link to solution-state dynamics. Here we show that sequence context is sufficient to decode a protein's multi-state conformational heterogeneity from this seemingly noisy signal. We introduce the B-Factor Corrector (BFC), a fine-tuned protein language model that reframes B-factor analysis from a purely physical calculation into a sequence-context-aware translation task. By leveraging deep contextual embeddings to decouple intrinsic conformational heterogeneity from lattice constraints, BFC recovers the residue-wise heterogeneity ranking derived from crystallographic structural ensembles, reproducing the normalized profile at a Pearson correlation of 0.83 while correcting the distortions that analytical formulas leave in the raw signal. We further demonstrate the utility of this sequence-inferred signal across structural-biology applications: it provides an integrable prior for molecular docking that is statistically equivalent to experimental B-factors, unmasks cryptic conformational heterogeneity essential for chaperone function, and guides the energetic refinement of antibody interfaces to resolve steric conflicts. These results suggest that the static structures of the Protein Data Bank can be effectively repurposed to decode the conformational heterogeneity latent within them.
affiliations: Xinjiang University (corresponding author)

papers.title: RtmR is a membrane-embedded RRM-family RNA-binding protein
papers.abstract: The animal symbiont Vibrio fischeri has served as a model organism for molecular processes underlying bacterial group behaviors, including quorum sensing and biofilm development. Here, using a genetic approach to identify negative regulators of biofilm formation in V. fischeri, we identified a membrane-bound RNA-binding protein, RtmR (VF_2432), that acts as an inhibitor of the symbiosis polysaccharide (SYP) biofilm. Membrane localization of the protein seems to be required for protein stability or expression, as truncation of the transmembrane helices led to an inability to detect the protein. The conserved RNP1 and RNP2 motifs in RtmR's cytoplasmic RNA recognition motif (RRM) domain are required for function, and we demonstrate binding to RNA substrates. Identification of RtmR RNA ligands was conducted with a iiCLIP-seq approach that revealed a large interactome. One transcript identified was that of the biofilm regulatory histidine kinase RscS. We found that RtmR biofilm inhibition depends on RscS activity and that RtmR negatively regulates levels of RscS. Overall, this work characterizes a novel type of bacterial RNA-binding protein.
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cereblon on Steroids: Beyond the Canonical Ligand Space
papers.abstract: Cereblon (CRBN) is widely used in targeted protein degradation, but its ligand space has remained dominated by a narrow set of cyclic imide chemotypes. Here, we show that the accessible CRBN ligand space extends substantially beyond this canonical space. A high-throughput screen of > 40,000 compounds, followed by orthogonal biophysical validation, X-ray crystallography and SAR analyses, identified several chemically distinct ligand classes. These include linear acetyl-based motifs, a phthalide-derived scaffold, steroidal compounds, and a range of bicyclic ligands. They engage CRBN through distinct recognition modes, several of which deviate from the canonical hydrogen-bonding pattern. Steroidal scaffolds were particularly notable: cortisone binds the human CRBN thalidomide-binding domain with an affinity comparable to thalidomide, with its A-ring occupying the tri-tryptophan pocket in a glutarimide-like orientation despite lacking the canonical imide NH donor. SAR within this series showed substantial tolerance for chemical modification and scaffold simplification, raising the possibility that endogenous steroidal metabolites may contribute to the physiological ligand landscape of CRBN. Bicyclic lactams additionally provided synthetically accessible scaffolds with tunable affinity and promising sites for linker attachment. Across the identified ligand classes, none of the tested representatives induced detectable degradation of canonical CRBN neosubstrates, and several showed largely clean proteomic profiles. Together, these findings broaden the chemical, mechanistic and potential physiological landscape of CRBN recognition and provide diverse starting points for alternative, potentially neosubstrate-sparing CRBN recruiters.
affiliations: Max Planck Institute for Biology Tubingen (corresponding author)

papers.title: CodonBench: separating gene context, exon position, and variant-specific component in synonymous-variant classification
papers.abstract: Background. A synonymous variant leaves the protein unchanged, so a classifier that still separates pathogenic from benign examples must be reading something beyond the protein. Such variants test cleanly what a codon-level model adds to a protein-level one. Methods. We assembled SynPath, a benchmark of ClinVar synonymous variants, and scored frozen representations under two splitting protocols. Under gene-held-out folds whole genes are withheld, and each coding-sequence model is compared against a position-matched control. Results. The models were not trained for this task, so these numbers describe transfer, not designed performance. Random splitting flatters every representation. Once whole genes are held out, they fall into a narrow band near chance, the best at 0.58, and low-rank fine-tuning does not restore the random-split level. A feature that reads no sequence, only the distance from the variant to the nearest exon junction, reaches 0.84 under the same folds, above every neural representation tested. In a protein model the variant-specific component is zero by construction, because both alleles present the same input. In coding-sequence models only the response vector, the difference between the alternate and reference embeddings, keeps signal on unseen genes and beats its position-matched control. Conclusions. Synonymous-variant pathogenicity is predictable mainly from gene identity and from position. Only a small part reflects the variant itself, and only in models that read the coding sequence. Benchmarks judged on random splits will overstate what these models have learned.
affiliations: Intelligent Medicine Institute, Shanghai Medical College, Fudan University, Shanghai 200032, China (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structural basis of context-dependent RORγt target gene activation on chromatin
papers.abstract: ROR{gamma}t is a key transcriptional regulator that supports protective pathogen clearance but also drives autoimmune disorders. Genetic studies have identified ROR{gamma}t mutations that selectively protect from autoimmunity without compromising host defense. Herein, we describe the molecular principles governing how ROR{gamma}t selectively drives these context-dependent gene programs. Structural studies revealed the selectivity-determining mutations lie in an -helix, the C-terminal extension (CTE), which nucleates when ROR{gamma}t engages partially occluded DNA response elements at nucleosome entry/exit sites. In ex vivo Th17 cells, the CTE is required for full genomic occupancy and expression of inflammatory effector genes, while residual DNA binding supports partial occupancy that, alongside context-dependent transcription factors, induces lineage-stabilizing gene expression. These findings support a model where ROR{gamma}t uses distinct chromatin binding modes to engage an expansive chromatin landscape to activate target gene programs, explaining the complex phenotypes of CTE mutant mice.
affiliations: The Salk Institute for Biological Studies (corresponding author)

papers.title: Multi-Modal Mass Spectrometry Imaging Reveals Isomer-Specific PFOS Distribution and Spatial Lipid Disruption in Mouse Liver
papers.abstract: The linear and branched isomers of perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS), a legacy per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), show differential bioaccumulation and toxicological responses. However, their spatial distribution within tissues and their effects in spatial contexts remain insufficiently resolved. In this work, we present a multi-modal mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) strategy to resolve the on-tissue distribution of linear (n-) and branched (br-) PFOS isomers in mouse liver and PFOS-induced spatial lipid disruption. Liver samples from exposed mice were analyzed by multi-modal MSI, integrating matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization-trapped ion mobility spectrometry (MALDI-TIMS)-MSI and post-MALDI immunofluorescence of canonical zonation markers. We found that PFOS exhibited dose-dependent and zonation-specific distribution, with enrichment in pericentral regions compared to periportal. br-PFOS displayed a more homogeneous distribution compared to n-PFOS. Spatial lipidomics revealed concomitant zonal disruptions in hepatic lipid abundance and distribution, reflecting zonal lipid disruptions not accessible by bulk measurements. Together, this study establishes a multi-modal, spatial-resolved analytical workflow for mapping on-tissue PFOS isomer distribution and lipid disruptions. By demonstrating that PFOS isomeric structure governs tissue localization and is associated with zonal lipid disruptions, our findings provide new insights into the spatial dimension of toxicokinetics/ toxicodynamics and underscore the need for isomer-resolved, spatial-focusing approaches on environmental and toxicology research.
affiliations: 1.Department of Chemistry, 3.MSU PFAS Research Center, Michigan State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: A prioritized medium-throughput screen identifies fibroblast growth factors as protective for human stem cell derived insulin secreting beta cells
papers.abstract: Stem cell-derived {beta}-like cells (SC{beta} cells) are an alternative to cadaveric {beta} cells for replacement therapy in type 1 diabetes. However, SC{beta} cells face a multitude of stresses. Both {beta} cells and SC{beta} cells reside in complex microtissues and are modulated by hundreds of autocrine/paracrine signals. Here, we leveraged multi-omics data from late-stage SC{beta} cells and human islets to map ligand-receptor pairs and generate a prioritized list of ligands for high-content SC{beta} cell survival screening. Our medium-throughput screen tracked cell number, cell death, and INS production over several days using automated, high-content imaging. Members of the fibroblast growth factor (FGF) family significantly prevented cytokine-induced cell death, with the top validated hits being FGF4, FGF5, and FGF8F. With these results, there is the potential to improve SC{beta} cell survival in vitro via readily targetable pathways and to produce a more robust product for translation to the clinic.
affiliations: University of British Columbia (corresponding author)

papers.title: Asymmetric bloom lengthening drives high-latitude ocean chlorophyll accumulation imbalance
papers.abstract: This study shows that unequal changes in bloom duration between hemispheres contribute to contrasting high-latitude ocean chlorophyll trends, linking asymmetric phytoplankton phenology to marine ecosystem changes under climate warming.

papers.title: In situ reduction-driven formation of sub-nanometer alternating heterostructures
papers.abstract: Sub-nanometer heterostructures offer opportunities to tune interfacial reactivity, but their precise construction remains challenging. Here, the authors report alternating Ni/NiMoO₄ heterostructures that promote hydrogen evolution and sustain durable high-current electrolysis.

papers.title: A method quantifying soil melanin to understand fungal impacts on soil carbon stability
papers.abstract: Fungal necromass, particularly dead microbial cells rich in melanin, is an important contributor to long-term soil carbon stabilization. Progress in understanding the role of soil melanin is limited by the lack of validated analytical methods. DNA-based approaches estimate only the genetic potential for melanin production and therefore provide indirect evidence of melanin occurrence. To directly assess soil melanin, we evaluated spectroscopic and spectrophotometric assays; however, both approaches proved insufficiently specific due to interference from chemically related compounds. Here, we introduce a liquid chromatography method that enables quantification of major fungal melanin types in soils. By enabling direct quantification of fungal melanin in soil, this framework allows longstanding hypotheses regarding melanized fungal necromass and soil carbon stabilization to be tested mechanistically. Here, we show with the proposed method that soil melanin concentrations are strongly correlated with total soil carbon, supporting a central role for fungal melanin in long-term soil carbon stabilization.

papers.title: A supergene and genomic mosaicism are associated with phenotypic evolution in Galápagos tree finches
papers.abstract: Adaptive radiations provide powerful models to study the origins of phenotypic novelty and species diversity. Darwin’s finches constitute a classic example of adaptive radiation, in which beak morphology is a key trait related to fitness. Here, we focus on Camarhynchus tree finches by analyzing whole genomes in combination with morphological data to revisit long-standing questions regarding their origins raised before genetic evidence became available. Camarhynchus diversified over the last 100,000 years, yielding some striking morphological differences despite shallow genetic divergence. We identify several highly differentiated loci, including G03 , a supergene affecting beak and body size. We reveal a striking example of genomic mosaicism, in which autosomal differentiation between two sympatric species is restricted primarily to a single locus -( G03 )- that approaches fixation, shifting them from one phenotypic optimum to another. Contextualized in a broader phylogenetic framework, we also reveal an unexpected diversity of G03 haplotypes and show that the small and large G03 alleles diverged early in the radiation, suggesting a key genetic innovation enabling ecological expansion among species of Darwin’s finches. Our results further establish Camarhynchus as a model example of speciation with gene flow, underscoring the broader role of hybridization in generating biodiversity.

papers.title: HCV incidence and prevalence trends among people who use drugs in France 2004 to 2023
papers.abstract: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) remains a key public health challenge, particularly among people who use and inject drugs (PWUD, PWID). While direct-acting antivirals (DAA) have revolutionized HCV treatment, meeting the WHO’s 2030 elimination target requires accurate estimation of incidence and prevalence to guide prevention and care. We analyze cross-sectional surveys conducted in France in 2004, 2013, and 2023, recruiting PWUD at harm reduction services and collecting behavioral and biological data. We estimate age-and time-dependent prevalence of HCV antibodies and HCV RNA using multivariate regression models while incidence was estimated from two-state transmission models. The demographic profile of PWUD has aged over time (mean age 35 years in 2004 vs. 44 in 2023) while injection prevalence remained stable (61.7% in 2023). Between 2013 and 2023, HCV burden declined substantially: HCV RNA prevalence fell from 19.4% (95% CI 16.3–23.0) to 9.5% (7.2–12.3) among all PWUD, and from 29.6% to 14.5% among PWID. Incidence among PWID decreased from 6.5 (4.1–8.0) to 2.4 (1.4–4.2) per 100 person-years. These reductions likely reflect the combined impact of DAA scale-up and harm reduction policies, marking substantial progress toward elimination targets. However, ongoing transmission highlights persistent barriers requiring targeted public health actions.

papers.title: Time-lapse RESOLFT nanoscopy empowered by deep learning
papers.abstract: Capturing the dynamic interplay of proteins and organelles within cells requires microscopy methods with high spatial and temporal resolution. Reversible Saturable OpticaL Fluorescent Transition (RESOLFT) demonstrated great potential for live cell nanoscopy by using patterned light and reversibly switching fluorescent probes. Despite the latest improvement in both switching probes and optical schemes, the duration and frame rate of the time-lapse are still limited by photobleaching and spatial sampling steps. Here, we present two distinct strategies based on deep learning to restore low signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) or under-sampled images pushing the experimental boundaries of RESOLFT. We demonstrate the capability of Hierarchical DivNoising (HDN) to restore low-SNR RESOLFT data while maintaining full spatial resolution, both in supervised and unsupervised settings. This allows a 10-fold reduction of light dose per frame, and up to 5 times longer imaging. Then, we present Fast-MoNaLISA, a method that reduces the acquisition time of any point-scanning systems. This allows a 4-fold increase in frame rate, and a reduction of scanning artefacts. Overall, our methods open up possibilities for dynamic data acquisition at the sub-organelle level, such as vesicles budding in and out from intact mitochondria, or the actin meshwork formation and dissociation.

papers.title: Intensification of near-inertial currents in the Atlantic Ocean over the past two decades
papers.abstract: Ocean drifter observations reveal that Atlantic near-inertial currents intensified by almost 4% per decade during 2003–2022. This intensification is primarily driven by changes in wind forcing associated with mesoscale weather systems.

papers.title: An automated operon refactoring workflow for heterologous expression of non-ribosomal peptide biosynthetic gene clusters
papers.abstract: Existing approaches for biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) discovery are labor-intensive, depend on de novo DNA synthesis and are difficult to scale. Here we show that an automated platform for one-step assembly and refactoring of BGCs facilitates facile novel product discovery.

papers.title: Scalable methylome-transcriptome profiling resolves clonal organization in human hematopoiesis
papers.abstract: Understanding human tissue maintenance and remodeling requires linking clonal ancestry to molecular state, yet scalable joint measurement remains challenging. Here, we introduce Droplet-MT and an integrated computational workflow for joint transcriptome and methylome profiling at ~10,000 cells per library. Methylation epimutations enable mutation-independent clonal reconstruction from high-coverage methylomes, while reference-based label transfer assigns cells to established clones at ~0.2% CpG coverage, reducing sequencing cost. Clone-aggregated somatic variants provide genetic annotation without additional single-cell genotyping. Across ~21,000 paired profiles from healthy blood and longitudinal acute myeloid leukemia, we resolved small and expanded clones with heterogeneous lineage output. In leukemia, the framework distinguished changes in malignant clonal abundance, state remodeling within persistent clones, and recovery of healthy polyclonal hematopoiesis. Malignant monocytes remained transcriptionally and epigenetically distinct from healthy and recovery-associated cells despite treatment-associated remodeling. Droplet-MT enables scalable analysis of human tissues by linking clonal organization with molecular state and retrospective genetic annotation.
affiliations: Westlake University (corresponding author)

papers.title: An iPSC-based experimental framework for investigating phenotypic variation associated with Jomon ancestry in the present-day Japanese population
papers.abstract: Ancestry-related genomic variation may contribute to phenotypic diversity. However, its cellular consequences remain difficult to evaluate. To address this, we developed a human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-based framework for investigating such phenotypes. We used the Japanese population as a model of Jomon-related and continental East Asian ancestry admixture. Jomon ancestry, estimated using the Jomon allele score (JAS), was associated with clinical measures, including renal-related traits and serum triglycerides in 34,152 Tohoku Medical Megabank participants. Peripheral blood mononuclear cell transcriptomics of donors from the upper and lower extremes of the JAS distribution (n = 10) suggested group-level differences in immune-related gene expression. To test whether the serum triglyceride association coincided with hepatic cellular phenotypes, we differentiated hiPSCs from these donors into hepatocyte-like cells. Neither intracellular triglycerides nor lipid-related gene expression differed between groups. These findings highlight the value of a genetically characterized hiPSC-based framework for investigating ancestry-associated phenotypes across cellular contexts.
affiliations: Department of Biological Sciences, Graduate School of Science, The University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cromosomal genomes assemblies of twelve sheep breeds
papers.abstract: The sheep research community benefits from a genome assembly that has been refined over the last 15 years. However, the rich diversity of sheep breeds suggests that a single individual genome is not enough to represent the species full genomic content. Third-generation sequencing technologies have recently made it possible to generate high quality assemblies that should enable to elucidate unique and/or complex phenotype determinisms depending on genetic structural variations. In the SeqOccin project, twelve breeds were selected to represent (mostly French) sheep genetic diversity: Basco-Bearnaise, Black Belly, Blanche du Massif Central, Corse, Ile de France, Lacaune, Manech Tete Noire, Noire du Velay, Ouessant, Rambouillet, Vendeen, Soay. High-molecular-weight DNA was extracted from blood samples and subjected to long read whole-genome sequencing. The reads were used to generate de novo assemblies and were aligned onto the public reference to call structural variants. PacBio HiFi and parental Illumina reads were used to assemble phased haplotypes of the Lacaune breed. For the other breeds, PacBio raw (CLR) or ONT reads were generated. Our work demonstrates the feasibility of assembling genomes with a reasonable amount of data and appropriate software packages, delivering one high-quality assembly and 11 standard sheep assemblies that pave the way for pangenome construction and structural variant functional studies.
affiliations: INRAE, US 1426, GeT-PlaGe, Genotoul, France Genomique, Univ Toulouse, Castanet-Tolosan, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: The Genetic Landscape of Structural Variants in Aspergillus flavus using ONT and PacBio Sequencing
papers.abstract: Genetic rearrangement in the absence of selection is poorly understood. Long-read, high-depth sequencing has enabled analysis of the genetic landscape of spontaneous structural variants. We have applied PacBio Revio sequencing to identify the major classes of genetic alterations during long-term vegetative growth in Aspergillus flavus. These classes include a) precise deletions frequently associated with the flanking region of homology, b) clusters of short deletions that are heavily enriched within centromeric and subtelomeric regions that are typically 94% A+T, and c) deletions and expansions within a subset of homopolymer tracts. We find 70 homopolymer tracts longer than 44 bp, dispersed throughout the genome in noncoding regions and unassociated with transposable elements. A broader analysis of third-generation sequenced datasets from fungi found within the Phylum Ascomycota showed a high but variable prevalence of homopolymeric tracts across species. The adventitious identification of a putative flbA mutation, responsible for an altered conidial phenotype, by the Deep Variant AI system also demonstrates the power of this approach. These studies show that high-depth, long-read sequencing can probe SNPs, indels, homopolymeric tracts, and large-scale rearrangements in an unbiased fashion, and demonstrate that short deletions and homopolymer tract expansions arise spontaneously in A. flavus and other filamentous fungi.
affiliations: Tulane University (corresponding author)

papers.title: GenDiMug: a generic inclusive multigraph framework to analyze genomic organizations and -omics data at multiple scales
papers.abstract: After decades of investigation, analyses of genome organization remain challenging. This is because genome descriptions are very information-rich and usually rendered as a linear map of genomic features corresponding to an ordered list of position intervals on a nucleic acid macromolecular backbone. This formalism, while accurate, is not fully optimized to mathematically analyze all genome structural properties, in particular the relations between genomic features, nor to integrate large amounts of -omics data, such as transcriptomes, epigenomes, proteomes, meltomes or chromatin accessibility data, which are increasingly available. We therefore developed GenDiMug, a tool that uses a network representation of the genome as a backbone, providing a natural framework to integrate spatial and ontogenetic relationships between genomic features and multi-omics data. We illustrate how this generic approach can be applied to all sorts of genomes, both to visualize genomic topology at contig and chromosomal scales at base-pair resolution, and to analyze genome positional effects using various graph metrics. Using GenDiMug, we further reveal clumping of genes with similar expression levels in eukaryotic genomes and their possible circadian regulation in a photosynthetic alga.
affiliations: Sorbonne Universite, CNRS, IBPS, Department of Computational, Quantitative and Synthetic Biology (CQSB), UMR7238, 75005, Paris, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: Inferring ecDNA Evolution from Allele Frequency Spectra
papers.abstract: Extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) can arise early in the development of aggressive tumors or later upon progression, but the impact of chronology on patient outcome is not known. Currently, it is not possible to determine when an ecDNA arose in the course of tumor development and progression, based on genome sequencing data. Here, we develop an analytic method, ecEvol, to infer ecDNA emergence time, selection strength, mutation rate, and clonal dominance from allele frequency spectra in bulk whole-genome sequencing. EcEvol outperforms other methods and predicts parameters with high accuracy across a wide range of parameter values. Applying ecEvol to primary, treatment-naive tumors, we find that ecDNA typically emerges early and undergoes strong positive selection, albeit with substantial variation across cancer types. EcDNAs carrying known oncogenes emerge earlier and reach greater clonal dominance than ecDNAs lacking known oncogenes. In advanced and predominantly treated tumors, ecDNA emerges substantially later than in matched primary tumors, consistent with the generation and selection of new ecDNA during tumor progression and therapy. Longitudinal samples further support continued expansion of ecDNA-bearing lineages. Finally, earlier ecDNA emergence is associated with poorer overall survival. These results provide insight into the chronology of ecDNA formation from a single tumor biopsy taken at any point during the course of the disease, revealing that allele-frequency spectra encode the evolutionary history of ecDNA and provide a quantitative framework for reconstructing its emergence and expansion.

papers.title: In silico subtractive genomics and reverse vaccinology approach reveal outer membrane proteins OMP47 and LptD as dual-purpose drug and vaccine targets in Pasteurella multocida Pm70
papers.abstract: Drug targets and vaccines for bacterial diseases are challenging to develop. Computational subtractive genomics and reverse vaccinology offer a viable substitute for conventional drug and vaccine development approaches. In recent years, Pasteurella multocida, a Gram-negative pathogen responsible for severe infections in humans along with major diseases in livestock and poultry, has developed resistance to multiple drugs. As a result, there is an urgent demand for research into reliable, efficient, highly potent, and cost-effective strategies to combat the rise of Pasteurella multocida infections. To address this, the present study integrated an in silico subtractive genomics and reverse vaccinology workflow to pinpoint proteins with potential value as both drug and vaccine targets. From the complete Pasteurella multocida Pm70 proteome, we identified 446 proteins that had no similarities with human proteins, out of which 129 were found to be essential for the pathogens survival. These 129 proteins are therefore potential candidates for drug development. Further metabolic pathway analysis, virulence potential, subcellular localization, and structural analyses revealed two outer membrane proteins, namely, 47 kDa outer membrane protein and lipopolysaccharide-assembly protein LptD, as promising candidates for therapeutic development. Subsequent antigenicity analysis revealed both outer membrane proteins as potential vaccine targets, exhibiting highly favorable antigenicity scores. Candidate B- and T-cell epitopes were systematically mapped from these two targets based on antigenicity, immunogenicity, toxicity, and allergenicity potential and only high-confidence epitopes were assembled using adjuvants and class-specific linkers to construct the final multi-epitope vaccine (MEV). The designed MEV construct was demonstrated to be highly antigenic, non-toxic and non-allergenic to humans, while possessing favorable structural and physicochemical properties, and exhibited strong binding interactions with human toll-like receptors with minimal molecular deformability. Although further experimental validation is recommended to fully assess their efficacy, the present study establishes a solid foundation for the development of novel therapeutics and vaccine candidates against P. multocida, ultimately contributing to the reduction of its rising infections.

papers.title: Version-aware question answering over living oncology guidelines
papers.abstract: Living clinical guidelines revise recommendations as evidence emerges, so an AI answer can be faithful to a real guideline and still be out of date. Here we examine this failure using ASCOBench, 288 unique questions in 96 three-turn conversations grounded in versioned American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) breast and prostate cancer guidelines, with oncologist-reviewed reference answers. Oncologists corrected one in four version-sensitive answers drafted by a frontier model, against fewer than one in ten factual ones. Across the guideline corpus, 19 recommendations changed between versions, seven of them reversals, yet only 1 of 14 superseded documents states that it has been replaced. With a strong model, retrieval over several guideline versions made stale answers four times more frequent than answering without retrieval. SentryLine, a verification-first system, lowered incorrect answers to 4.2-5.2% from 9.7-22.9% for baselines across three models. Recognizing change before a guideline declares it remains an open problem.
affiliations: Arizona State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: AI-Driven Design of Next-Generation Immunoinformatics Multi-Epitope Subunit Vaccine Targeting the Most Virulent Mpox Proteome: A Structural and Kinetic Validation Framework
papers.abstract: The resurgence of the Mpox virus (MPXV) highlights the urgent need for scalable, mutation-resistant countermeasures. Slow development timelines hinder traditional empirical vaccine discovery, while conventional vaccinology often yields high false-positive rates because it relies on static, linear sequence-based screening. These classical informatics filters consistently fail to predict physical structural stability or the dynamic presentation of immune cells under physiological conditions, creating a distinct translational gap between computational design and in vitro efficacy. To address these limitations, here we engineered an advanced, AI-augmented vaccine discovery pipeline targeting the most virulent components of the MPXV proteome. We systematically screened eight critical viral targets essential for replication, membrane morphogenesis, and host-cell entry to map highly conserved T-cell and B-cell epitopes. Moving beyond standard heuristic filtering, we implemented a high-fidelity deep learning validation layer: ESM-2 protein language models (pLMs) were deployed to calculate pseudo-perplexity scores across chimeric linker junctions (EAAAK, GPGPG) to guarantee structural naturalness, MHCflurry ensemble models successfully verified active intracellular antigen presentation, and structure-informed graph neural networks (GNNs) simulated the physical node-attention dynamics of the immune synapse. Finally, recurrent neural networks (RNNs)-driven mRNA kinetic modeling optimized translation initiation rates and minimum free energy profiles during in silico cloning. This multi-layered pipeline successfully yielded three structurally refined, multi-epitope vaccine constructs optimized for maximum global population coverage. ESM-2 structural validation confirmed exceptionally low perplexity scores at structural junctions, indicating that the engineered chimaeras have native-like stability and a minimized risk of proteolysis. GNN-based immune synapse modeling demonstrated highly stable binding kinetics and robust binding free energies between the target epitopes and human HLA alleles. Furthermore, RNN kinetic optimizations established that the cDNA sequences are optimized for high-yield expression in heterologous expression hosts without risk of ribosomal stalling or translational bottlenecks. This study establishes a deep learning-augmented framework that bridges the gap between theoretical sequence optimization and biopharmaceutical scalability. By validating the structural naturalness, real-world immunogenicity, and manufacturing kinetics of our vaccine chimeras, this framework presents a robust, proactive paradigm for rapid vaccine architecture against emerging orthopoxvirus threats.
