papers.title: Mutation in Ralstonia pseudosolanacearum F1C1 cytochrome p450 homologue impairs virulence through root but not through shoot of tomato plants
papers.abstract: Ralstonia pseudosolanacearum causes a lethal bacterial wilt disease in many plants. The pathogen enters through roots and systemically colonizes the xylem tissue, resulting in wilting and eventual death of the host. Using transposon mutagenesis followed by screening in tomato seedlings, we identified a mutant exhibiting virulence deficiency by root inoculation, but not by leaf inoculation. The mutation was recreated in the wild-type genome via natural transformation to prove the linkage of virulence deficiency with the transposon insertion. Whole genome sequencing revealed that the transposon insertion was in a cyp450 homologue, encoding cytochrome P450 monooxygenase. Two independent targeted mutations were generated in the cyp450 gene, and both the mutants recapitulated the root-specific virulence deficiency. The mutants rarely cause disease in mature plants following soil drenching but remained fully virulent upon petiole pricking inoculation. Complementation with the full length cyp450 gene amplified from the wild-type strain F1C1 restored virulence in the mutant. Compared to the wild-type F1C1, the cyp450 mutants exhibited greater sensitivity to tomato root extracts. HR-LCMS of tomato root extracts revealed the occurrence of several antimicrobial compounds. Cytochrome P450 enzymes are known to mediate the degradation or biosynthesis of diverse metabolites in bacteria. Considering the virulence difference due to the mode of inoculation, our findings indicate that cyp450 contributes to tissue-specific adaptation of the pathogen during infection has opened an avenue for integrating tissue metabolomics with bacterial wilt susceptibility research.
affiliations: Department of Molecular Biology and Biotechnology, Tezpur University, 784028, Assam, India (corresponding author)

papers.title: Living representatives of the spiralian ancestral karyotype revealed by two Lima genomes
papers.abstract: Conserved synteny enables the reconstruction of ancestral chromosome organization across deeply diverged lineages, as demonstrated across metazoans. In Spiralia, comparative genomic analyses have suggested an ancestral karyotype comprising 20 chromosomes. We report high-quality genome assemblies for two Lima species (Lima caribaea and Lima lima) with 20 chromosomes and show that their chromosome organization matches this ancestral state, including four previously described fusion-with-mixing events. Interestingly, other Limidae genus did not retain the ancestral karyotype: they have undergone subsequent lineage-specific fusions. The conserved organization of Lima chromosomes provides a rare genomic anchor for reconstructing ancestral chromosome organization and lineage-specific chromosome evolution across Spiralia and, more broadly, Metazoa.
affiliations: Genoscope, CEA Institut de Genomique (corresponding author)

papers.title: Exploring protein duplication across Archaea genomes
papers.abstract: Gene duplication is a major driver of genomic innovation, but whether paralog accumulation scales uniformly with increasing genome size across the domain Archaea remains unclear. This study presents a domain-wide analysis of 1,829 archaeal genomes and their predicted proteomes to evaluate protein family expansions, their distribution, and lineage-specific patterns of gene duplication. Protein family expansions were classified as recent (90% sequence identity), intermediate (70%), or old (40%) duplications based on sequence-identity thresholds within each family. The findings show that gene duplication content is decoupled from overall proteome size at high sequence-identity levels, indicating that recent paralog retention does not correlate with proteome expansion. Archaeal lineages exhibit contrasting gene duplication profiles. All 1,829 genomes contained paralogs at the 40% sequence identity threshold, indicating the widespread presence of ancient or divergent duplication events. In contrast, paralogs detected at the 90% identity threshold, showed substantial variation across lineages. Their proportion reached up to 16.6% in groups such as Halobacteria, whereas only 74 genomes (4.04%) completely lacked paralogs at this threshold. Highly duplicated families are enriched for membrane transport systems (ABC/MFS), central metabolic enzymes (e.g., acetyl-CoA synthetase), a high proportion of uncharacterized functions, and mobile elements, predominantly transposases. Notably, we identified 314 transposase protein families in Archaea, distributed in 161 unique families in Archaea and 153 families shared with Bacteria, suggesting mechanisms of interdomain gene transfer. Overall, paralog accumulation in Archaea is a lineage-specific phenomenon shaped by targeted functional duplications and mobile element activity, rather than a simple consequence of proteome growth.
affiliations: Laboratorio de Genomica Ambiental, Departamento de Biologia Celular, Facultad de Ciencias, Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico, Avenida Universidad 3000, 04 (corresponding author)

papers.title: An improved Trypanosoma vivax genome assembly confirms the distinct organisation of its variant antigen repertoire
papers.abstract: Trypanosoma vivax is a unicellular parasite spread by biting flies and an important livestock pathogen across sub-Saharan Africa and South America. Alongside its better known relative, T. brucei, it causes animal trypanosomosis. An accurate genome sequence is essential to functional genetics as well as the design of novel diagnostics, drugs and vaccines. However, the existing T. vivax genome sequence is fragmentary, making it difficult to examine genomic features such as the Variant Surface Glycoprotein (VSG) genes that are the basis for antigenic variation, a key phenotype that underpins immune evasion by African trypanosomes. Our aim was to produce a T. vivax genome sequence with improved contiguity to properly characterise the VSG genes. We present a new core genome assembly in 23 scaffolds, forming approximately 10 chromosomes. Many scaffolds are articulated with extensive sub-telomeric domains that, like T. brucei, contain VSG gene arrays but in T. vivax these are near-perfect repeats of intact genes. Using transcriptomic and proteomic analysis of VSG expression during bloodstream infection we show that the active VSG is expressed from a sub-telomeric array while other arrays are silent. We find no evidence for a VSG expression site at the telomeres or elsewhere. Therefore, although monoallelic expression and antigenic switching occur in T. vivax, the familiar regulatory mechanism of T. brucei does not exist in T. vivax. This improved T. vivax genome assembly demonstrates that T. brucei is a poor guide for T. vivax genetics generally and for regulation of antigenic variation specifically.
affiliations: Institute of Infection, Veterinary and Ecological Sciences, University of Liverpool (corresponding author)

papers.title: Spatiotemporal AI modeling of gene regulation and variant effects in the developing human brain
papers.abstract: Understanding how genetic variation shapes gene regulation in the developing human brain remains a central challenge in neuroscience, particularly in transient cell types and developmental stages where data are limited. We present Seal, an interpretable AI transfer learning framework for genome-based modeling of gene expression and variant effects with spatiotemporal resolution across 26 brain regions, 30 cell types, and seven developmental stages. Seal predictions enable characterization of both germline and somatic brain variants, and provide mechanistic interpretation by linking sequence variants to transcriptional regulators in spatiotemporal context. Applying Seal to genome-wide association studies, we identify cell types and developmental windows relevant to neuropsychiatric disease risk, revealing shared and distinct regulatory architectures across six neuropsychiatric conditions that align with clinical trajectories. In the Simons Simplex Collection autism cohort whole genome data, Seal uncovers a significant burden of de novo regulatory variants in transient fetal excitatory neurons, revealing a cell-type and developmentally specific regulatory burden. By connecting genetic variation to spatiotemporal regulatory programs, Seal offers a general framework for uncovering mechanisms of human brain development and disease.
affiliations: Flatiron Institute, Simons Foundation; Princeton University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Contrasting gene gain and loss shape metabolic diversification in the Ralstonia solanacearum species complex
papers.abstract: Metabolic repertoires are continually remodeled by gene acquisition and loss, but how these contrasting processes jointly generate phenotypic diversity within bacterial species complexes remains poorly understood. Here, we elucidated the genetic and evolutionary basis of the classical biovar phenotypes of the Ralstonia solanacearum species complex (RSSC), which are defined by differential utilization of three hexitols (sorbitol, mannitol, and dulcitol) and three disaccharides (lactose, maltose, and cellobiose). Although this classification has been used for over half a century, the genetic determinants and evolutionary origins of these phenotypes have not been systematically resolved. Machine-learning analysis of genomic data from 250 RSSC strains with documented biovar phenotypes, combined with genome-wide association analysis and gene deletion, identified the smoEFGK gene cluster and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)-dependent glucose dehydrogenase (FADGDH) as the major determinants of hexitol and disaccharide utilization, respectively. Comparative phylogenomics revealed fundamentally different evolutionary histories of these loci. An ancestral smoEFGK system was lost early in RSSC evolution and subsequently reacquired by the ancestor of phylotype I through horizontal transfer from a Burkholderia-related lineage, whereas vertically inherited FADGDH underwent recurrent, independent losses across multiple RSSC lineages. Extending the analysis to 1,082 RSSC strains further showed that disaccharide-utilization capacity was significantly depleted among monocot-associated strains after accounting for phylogenetic relatedness and geographic origin. Together, these findings reveal how contrasting trajectories of gene gain and loss can reshape bacterial metabolic repertoires, generate lineage-associated phenotypic diversity, and potentially contribute to ecological differentiation.
affiliations: South China Agricultural University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cellular and molecular census of the pleiotropic disease locus Negr1 in zebrafish
papers.abstract: A major challenge in precision medicine is to understand the cellular origin of disease-causing genetic alterations. One prominent example is the Negr1 locus, where common non-coding variants are associated with an unusually broad range of human traits and conditions, including body mass index (BMI), major depression, schizophrenia, autism-spectrum conditions and anorexia. Yet, no coding loss-of-function allele has been established as causal. These observations suggest that distinct Negr1-expressing cell populations underlie distinct traits. However, this hypothesis is difficult to test in tractable experimental systems without first determining where this gene may act. To overcome this limitation, we generated a knock-in reporter at the zebrafish Negr1 locus and combined single-cell transcriptomics with whole-brain registration and single-neuron projection mapping. We found that Negr1 is expressed in a graded manner across neuronal classes of the brain and retina, radial glia and astrocyte-like cells, and most consistently in oligodendrocyte progenitor cells. Projection mapping suggests three conserved hubs formed by olfactory bulb projection neurons, tectal periventricular projection neurons and cerebellar eurydendroid cells. Our findings are consistent with the idea that Negr1 pleiotropy arises from dose perturbation of a rather broadly expressed gene. More generally, this integrative approach to produce granular multimodal datasets should enable high-resolution etiological studies in models of human disease.
affiliations: New York University Abu Dhabi, Abu Dhabi, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates (corresponding author)

papers.title: Goat genome assemblies, nine breeds for pangenome contribution
papers.abstract: The goat research community benefits from one of the most comprehensive livestock genome assemblies, ARS1. However, the rich diversity of goat breeds suggests that a single individual genome is not enough to represent the species full genomic content. Third-generation sequencing technologies have recently made it possible to generate very high quality assemblies that should enable to elucidate unique and/or complex phenotype determinisms depending on genetic structural variations. In the SeqOccin project, nine goat breeds were selected to represent French goat genetic diversity: Alpine, Boer, Creole, Fosses, Poitevine, Provencale, Pyreneenne, Rove and Saanen. High-molecular-weight DNA was extracted from blood samples and subjected to long read whole-genome sequencing. There reads were used to generate de novo assemblies and were aligned onto the public reference to call structural variants. PacBio HiFi and parental Illumina reads were used to assemble phased haplotypes of the Alpine breed. For the other breeds, PacBio raw (CLR) or ONT reads were generated. Our work demonstrates the feasibility of assembling genomes with a reasonable amount of data and appropriate software packages, delivering one high-quality assembly and 8 standard goat assemblies that pave the way for pangenome construction and structural variant functional studies.
affiliations: INRAE, US 1426, GeT-PlaGe, Genotoul, France Genomique, Univ Toulouse, Castanet-Tolosan, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genome sequence data of Ascogaster reticulata (Hymenoptera: Braconidae)
papers.abstract: Parasitoid wasps develop in or on other arthropods and have evolved a wide range of strategies for exploiting their hosts. Ascogaster reticulata is a solitary egg to larval endoparasitoid wasp belonging to the subfamily Cheloninae of Braconidae. We constructed a genome assembly using long-read sequence data. The assembled genome was 280.5 Mbp, consisting of 209 contigs. The N50 value and GC content ratio were 13.9 Mbp and 30.43%, respectively. The percentage of transposable elements and repetitive regions was 52.43%. The predicted number of genes is 27,261. Merqury revealed that the QV value and completeness of the genome were 61.79 and 99.3917%, respectively. BUSCO analysis detected approximately 99% of the core genes. These results suggest that the genome data were of sufficient quality for use as a reference genome. Therefore, these data can be utilized as a genomic resource for comparative studies within Braconidae and for future investigations into the biology and evolution of Cheloninae parasitoid wasps.
affiliations: Institute of Agrobiological Sciences, National Agriculture and Food Research Organization (corresponding author)

papers.title: From APTs to advanced persistent biological threats (APBTs): a taxonomy and large-scale metadata audit of genomic surveillance infrastructure
papers.abstract: Open genomic repositories have become critical infrastructure for pathogen surveillance, variant tracking, outbreak reconstruction, and public health decision making. However, many of these repositories were designed to support rapid scientific data sharing rather than adversarial verification, creating potential security gaps. This paper introduces Advanced Persistent Biological Threats (APBTs), as a framework for understanding how malicious cyber biological actors can gradually disrupt genomic surveillance without entering a laboratory or releasing a biological agent. Instead of altering biological material, an attacker targets the sequence data, metadata, reference datasets, and analytical models used by surveillance systems. We present, to our knowledge, the first integrated multilayer taxonomy of APBTs, structured around a four phase lifecycle, and investigate whether the metadata weaknesses identified by this framework are present in an operational genomic repository. To assess this, we audited 100,000 SARS-CoV-2 BioSample records obtained from the NCBI. A framework of 23 checks was applied across five metadata layers: temporal, geographic, host and specimen, provenance, and technical metadata. Every record triggered at least one APBT relevant metadata vulnerability indicator, with a mean of 7.34 indicators per record (SD = 1.34). Overall, 97.3% of records were classified in the High or Critical severity categories. Every record also contained at least one indicator in both the provenance and technical metadata layers. These results largely reflect the optional status of several fields in the current BioSample submission model rather than isolated errors by individual data contributors. Temporal and geographic information was comparatively complete, while fields needed for provenance reconstruction, chain of custody assessment, technical validation, and analytical interpretation were frequently missing. These findings do not indicate deliberate manipulation. However, the structural incompleteness of BioSample metadata creates vulnerabilities that an adversary can exploit to introduce poisoned, misleading, or weakly traceable metadata into genomic repositories. As a result, maliciously altered metadata can appear plausible, remain undetected, and influence downstream genomic analysis and surveillance. The findings therefore show that widely used pathogen genomic repositories already contain structural weaknesses that can support metadata poisoning as part of an APBT operation.
affiliations: School of Computing, University of Portsmouth, Portsmouth, UK (corresponding author)

papers.title: Ayahuasca plant genomes reveal retrotransposon-derived centromeres and contrasting routes to DMT and β-carbolines
papers.abstract: Ayahuasca, used religiously for centuries by Amazonian Indigenous peoples and increasingly studied for its therapeutic potential, owes its psychoactivity to two plants: Psychotria viridis supplies N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT), whereas Banisteriopsis caapi supplies beta-carbolines that render DMT orally active. Here we show that the two plants have distinct genome histories: P. viridis is hexaploid (2n = 6x = 66), consistent with autopolyploidy, and B. caapi is diploid (2n = 2x = 20). CENH3-bound regions of both species are nonetheless enriched in CRM-type Ty3/Gypsy retrotransposons, with additional LINE elements and CRM-derived satellites in B. caapi. In P. viridis, a single multifunctional methyltransferase catalyzes both N-methylations of tryptamine to DMT. In B. caapi, beta-carboline biosynthesis combines dedicated enzymes with an acetaldehyde-dependent Pictet-Spengler cyclization that can proceed non-enzymatically, followed by enantioselective oxidation to harmaline. These resources link the ethnobotanical history of ayahuasca to its molecular basis, providing genomes of both source plants, the genetic structure of traditionally recognized cultivated varieties, and the enzymes behind the alkaloids long combined in this decoction.
affiliations: Max Planck Institute for Plant Breeding Research, Cologne, Germany (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genome assemblies and annotations of the poneroid ants Platythyrea mocquerysi (Ponerinae) and Stigmatomma oregonense (Amblyoponinae)
papers.abstract: We present draft genome assemblies for two poneroid ant species with distinctive life history traits: Platythyrea mocquerysi Emery, 1899 (Ponerinae) and Stigmatomma oregonense Wheeler, 1915 (Amblyoponinae). Platythyrea mocquerysi is a Malagasy ant in which larvae produce secretions from a ventral tubercle that are consumed by adults, representing an unusual form of larva-to-adult trophallaxis. Stigmatomma oregonense, a North American "dracula ant," feeds non-lethally on larval haemolymph. Using PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing, we assembled the P. mocquerysi genome (187 Mb, 307 scaffolds, N50 = 5.26 Mb, BUSCO 99.2% complete) and the S. oregonense genome (262 Mb, 1,189 scaffolds, N50 = 0.84 Mb, BUSCO 98.3% complete). These genomes encode 10,860 and 12,354 protein-coding genes, respectively. Repeat content is higher in S. oregonense than in P. mocquerysi, 54.3% against a lower bound of 15.7%. Most of the difference is in unclassified repeats, which we show to be diverged transposable elements. Comparative analysis with two additional poneroid genomes from closely related species reveals that genome size variation across poneroid ants is largely explained by transposable element dynamics, with notable expansions in several gene families including carboxylesterases, serine proteases, and lipid metabolism genes in Amblyoponinae. These genomes provide essential resources for investigating the molecular basis of unconventional brood management strategies in ants.
affiliations: University of Cambridge (corresponding author)

papers.title: Gene functional-state covariance reveals modular structure in the Arabidopsis thaliana dispensable genome
papers.abstract: Classical multilocus theory predicts that selection acting on combinations of loci can maintain non-random associations among allelic states, causing selection to act on multilocus genotypes rather than individual alleles. Across eukaryotic species, pangenome studies have documented thousands of genes that vary in functional status between individuals, yet this variation is analyzed as if each gene evolves independently. Here we test for non-random association within the dispensable pangenome across 1,012 natural genotypes of Arabidopsis thaliana to better understand the structure and evolution of eukaryotic pangenomes. Genome-wide pairwise association testing of loss-of-function alleles across genotypes identified 150,033 significantly covarying gene pairs among 5,679 unique genes after controlling for kinship and population structure. Most associations were between genes on different chromosomes, and covarying gene pairs showed greater co-expression and functional similarity than expected by chance. Network analysis revealed a non-random higher-order architecture comprising stable functional communities with distinct biological functions and structured connectivity among communities. The enriched functions and connectivity of communities revealed a tight coupling of modules involving plant immunity, environmental response, and specialized metabolism, highlighting how these systems integrate and evolve in response to dynamic ecological pressures. Taken together, these results show that the dispensable genome has a complex higher-order structure driven by functionally interacting genes, and that variation in gene content provides a population-scale resource for investigating the organization and evolution of biological systems.
affiliations: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew (corresponding author)

papers.title: Disrupted chromatin architecture blocks B lymphopoiesis in Down syndrome
papers.abstract: Human fetal haematopoiesis requires developmental potential to be encoded before lineage identity becomes transcriptionally apparent, but whether three-dimensional genome architecture provides such information is unknown. Here we develop ChromE-seq, a scalable single-cell assay that jointly profiles chromatin conformation and transcription, and integrate it with chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation to generate a multimodal atlas of ~400,000 haematopoietic cells from disomic and trisomy 21 (T21) human fetal liver. Chromatin contacts frequently preceded lineage-specific transcription or persisted after transcription declined, revealing 3D chromatin priming and memory. Unexpectedly, B-lineage and erythroid differentiation followed opposing architectural trajectories, with progressive loss and gain of chromatin connectivity, respectively. T21 disproportionately disrupted B-lineage architecture, redistributed interactions towards shorter genomic distances and weakened an EBF1-centred regulatory circuit. Deletion of a T21-sensitive EBF1 loop anchor reproduced the CLP-to-B-progenitor bottleneck observed in T21. These findings establish 3D genome architecture as an organizing layer of human fetal haematopoiesis that links developmental potential with lineage-specific vulnerability to genomic perturbation.
affiliations: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai (corresponding author)

papers.title: BoNTax: a curated genome-based framework for taxonomic classification and characterization of Clostridium botulinum Group I and Clostridium sporogenes
papers.abstract: Clostridium botulinum Group I and Clostridium sporogenes are closely related genomic lineages for which historical toxin-based nomenclature can obscure species-level relationships. We developed BoNTax, a curated taxonomy-first framework that separates average nucleotide identity (ANI)-based species assignment from botulinum neurotoxin (BoNT) characterization while integrating assembly quality assessment, multilocus sequence typing (MLST), AMRFinderPlus-based detection of bont genes, other virulence-associated genes, and antimicrobial resistance genes into standardized outputs. Analysis of 966 genomes informed genome-size criteria and the selection of 46 representative references comprising 22 C. botulinum Group I and 24 C. sporogenes genomes. Pairwise ANI resolved these references into two distinct species clusters: within-species ANI values were >95%, whereas between-species values were <95%, supporting a 95% species-level assignment threshold. BoNTax was implemented in GalaxyTrakr as complementary FASTQ- and FASTA-input workflows that converge on a common downstream analysis. The workflow completed analysis of all 42 validation genomes. Among the 32 genomes with a reported taxonomic identity, 29 assignments were concordant and three prompted taxonomic re-evaluations. For the ten genomes reported as taxonomically unknown, BoNTax provided ANI-based assignments. Of the three discordances, BT-22100019 was assigned to C. sporogenes rather than the reported C. botulinum Group I, whereas R1125/03 and R1135/03 showed 99.96% ANI to C. caseinilyticum DSM 46279, supporting their identification as C. caseinilyticum. MLST assignments were concordant for genomes with established profiles except PNUSAB000061, for which ST183 was not assigned by the MLST database version used in this analysis. BoNT type and subtype detection was fully concordant across toxigenic genomes, including bivalent strains. Thirty-one genomes met the predefined assembly-size QC criterion, whereas 11 received QC warnings, including all eight datasets representing four known mixed cultures. BoNTax therefore provides a reproducible genomic framework for resolving closely related clostridial lineages, identifying taxonomic annotations requiring re-evaluation, and reporting clinically relevant toxin information without conflating toxin genotype with species identity.
affiliations: FDA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Massively scaled variant effect mapping across the MAPK pathway reveals the importance of molecular and cellular context
papers.abstract: Variation alters inherent protein properties like thermodynamic stability and catalytic activity, and these intrinsic effects are shaped by the complex cellular environment. Signaling cascades typify this complexity, with tens or hundreds of proteins acting in concert through regulated states and interactions to transduce signals. Here, we measure the effect of 186,676 variants across 17 proteins in the RAS-MAPK pathway on protein abundance and pathway activity in human cells under diverse conditions, for a total of 503,099 variant effect measurements. We discovered 14,412 dominant negative variants across 12 proteins, nearly all previously unknown, that disrupt specific domains or interaction interfaces while leaving other functions intact and that are depleted from the human population. Measuring the abundance of 106,642 variants across 10 proteins under HSP90 inhibition showed that HSP90 shapes the effect of 67% of missense variants across the pathway, buffering destabilizing variants in both strong and weak clients. Our variant effect data, collected in the context of an intact proteome, enabled us to assess the functional importance of 395 experimentally and computationally modeled MAPK protein interactions. Using additional mutational scans, we resolved how the promiscuous switch II helix binding surface of KRAS accommodates overlapping interactions with LZTR1 and SOS1, revealing distinct allosteric networks that support each interaction. Thus, we establish a framework for measuring variant effects at unprecedented scale in human cells, illuminating fundamental MAPK pathway signaling mechanisms and demonstrating that cellular context profoundly shapes the effect of most variants.
affiliations: Department of Genome Sciences, University of Washington; Brotman Baty Institute; Department of Bioengineering, University of Washington (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Plasmid-Derived Machinery Drives Chromosomal Replication Initiation in the Colorectal Cancer-Associated Bacterium Fusobacterium nucleatum and Its Close Relatives
papers.abstract: Chromosome replication initiation in bacterial genomes typically occurs at a single origin, called oriC, through the binding of the DnaA initiator protein to specific chromosomal repeats known as DnaA-boxes. Here, relying on comparative genomics, we show that the family Fusobacteriaceae, which belongs to the order Fusobacteriales alongside the family Leptotrichiaceae, deviates from this paradigm. Our analysis revealed a stark contrast between the two lineages: while dnaA flanks oriC in Leptotrichiaceae, it is notably missing from Fusobacteriaceae genomes. Adjacent to oriC in Fusobacteriaceae, we identified a gene encoding replication initiator protein A (RPA). We characterized RPA as a Rep-type initiator involved in plasmid replication that likely originated from an iteron-containing plasmid, iterons being the plasmid analogues of DnaA-boxes. Phylogenetic reconstruction indicates that the gene encoding RPA was acquired together with its associated iterons and subsequently domesticated by the Fusobacteriaceae ancestor, successfully displacing the ancestral chromosomal dnaA gene at the origin of replication. This shift to a plasmid-derived replication system may represent an adaptive trait of the Fusobacteriaceae, potentially offering new insights into the biology of Fusobacterium nucleatum, a member of this family known to be a major driver of colorectal cancer progression within the tumor microenvironment.
affiliations: MNHN (corresponding author)

papers.title: A unified framework for quantitative splicing and transcript prediction
papers.abstract: RNA splicing is frequently disrupted by genetic variation, contributing to a wide range of human diseases. Identifying the variants responsible for altered splicing is therefore crucial but has long been challenging. Deep learning models that predict splicing from genomic sequence have substantially advanced their detection, but accurately resolving their quantitative effects on splicing and the resulting transcripts remains an unmet need. Here we introduce SpliceAI2, a deep learning model trained end-to-end on splice site, splice junction, and transcript usage across multiple mammalian species. SpliceAI2 reconstructs complete transcripts directly from genomic sequence and considerably improves identification of splice-altering variants and quantification of their effects in diverse benchmarks spanning cryptic splicing, splicing quantitative trait loci, and massively parallel reporter assays. Human population datasets provide independent validation of these predicted functional effects through evidence of natural selection and associated changes in plasma protein abundance. Application to a rare disease cohort reveals that predicted splice-altering variants are highly enriched in disease-associated genes and account for 15% of the excess genetic burden, with approximately half residing in deep intronic regions likely missed by exome sequencing. Together, these findings establish SpliceAI2 as a major step forward in interpreting splice-altering variants across the human genome.

papers.title: Forecasting next-year change in antimicrobial resistance genes in Klebsiella pneumoniae and Acinetobacter baumannii from genomic surveillance data
papers.abstract: Background: Surveillance tells laboratories which antimicrobial resistance genes are circulating now, but not which will change next. We built a model that forecasts, for each resistance gene and year, whether the following year brings a previously unseen allele (sequence variant), called emergence, or a change in the most common allele, called turnover. We tested it separately in Klebsiella pneumoniae and Acinetobacter baumannii. Results: We used genomes annotated with AMRFinderPlus: 2,385 gene-years across 331 genes for K.pneumoniae and 1,059 across 216 for A. baumannii. To remove the effect of sequencing effort, each gene-year was sampled to 10 records and the analysis repeated 25 times. Models were trained on earlier years and tested on later ones, and on genes held out of training. On later years every model ranked genes by risk better than simple baselines in both organisms, and results for held-out genes were close. In K.pneumoniae, turnover was predicted better than emergence (best area under the ROC curve, AUROC, 0.909 versus 0.819). In A. baumannii the order reversed (emergence 0.789, turnover 0.722). The two events also relied on different features. Emergence depended mainly on how many alleles a gene had already accumulated, in both organisms. Turnover in K. pneumoniae depended mainly on how dominant the leading allele already was, and a stability index added a small gain. In A. baumannii it was spread across many weaker features. There, 56% of changes in the leading allele involved only alleles already seen, against 23% in K. pneumoniae, which may make them harder to predict. Conclusions: Changes in resistance genes can be forecast a year ahead from routine genomic surveillance data, including for genes the model has not seen. How well it works, and what it depends on, differs between organisms, so models should be built and validated for each organism, not assumed to transfer. Such models could help laboratories decide which resistance genes to monitor most closely. Keywords: antimicrobial resistance; genomic surveillance; forecasting; machine learning; allele dynamics; Klebsiella pneumoniae; Acinetobacter baumannii
affiliations: Morehouse School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structural variants from donor-specific assemblies affect recurrent chromatin contact divergence in humans
papers.abstract: Structural variants (SVs) are a major source of human genetic diversity, yet their contribution to three-dimensional (3D) genome organization remains difficult to resolve using a standard reference genome. Here, we integrate haplotype-resolved chromatin interaction maps across 354 human and 12 nonhuman ape haplotypes with matched genome assemblies and long-read transcriptomes to determine how inherited SVs influence chromatin organization. We observe significant improvements in contact mapping, with 13.2% of cis Hi-C contacts showing >25 kbp changes in inferred genomic separation and an additional 2.8% of valid contact pairs recovered when using donor-specific assemblies instead of standard references. We show that haplotype-specific chromatin differences are highly selective rather than pervasive, concentrating within 1,790 recurrent contact difference hotspots associated with a restricted subset of SVs. We identified 2,495 chromatin-structure-associated SVs that are enriched in regulatory genomic contexts and are linked to expression variation. Notably, more than 90% of these SVs are derived in the human lineage, consistent with recent remodeling of regulatory architecture at the population level. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating haplotype diversity from pangenomes into studies of chromatin organization and provide a framework for understanding how inherited genomic differences are linked to functional consequences across populations and evolution.
affiliations: Department of Genome Sciences, University of Washington School of Medicine, Seattle, WA, USA; Howard Hughes Medical Institute, University of Washington, Seattle (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Unified Comparison of 10X Genomics and Parse Biosciences scRNA-seq Technologies
papers.abstract: Droplet-based and split-pool barcoding are the two dominant high-throughput single-cell RNA-seq paradigms, yet their systematic biases remain incompletely characterized. We compared seven matched 10X Genomics Chromium and Parse Biosciences Evercode WT sample pairs from five studies spanning multiple tissues and species focusing on gene counts and compositional differences rather than cell-type resolution. By separating Parse reads by priming strategy, we distinguished biases arising from priming chemistry from platform-level effects. These effects were largely independent, with platform-level differences substantially larger. Priming strategy introduced a GC-content bias within Parse, whereas the two platforms showed a consistent compositional shift across priming strategies, supported by differential capture of nuclear- and cytoplasmic-enriched transcripts. We interpret this shift as a relative enrichment of nuclear RNA in Parse. Finally, using contamination measures that do not assume a droplet-specific model, we found background RNA contamination in Parse to be comparable in magnitude to that in 10X, contrary to claims of substantially lower contamination. Together, these results indicate that expression measurements and cell-type composition are not directly interchangeable between the two platforms.
affiliations: California Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Gene-environment interaction loci with signatures of mid- to late Holocene selection show evidence for diet-dependent genetic effects
papers.abstract: Environmental change is a major driver of adaptation, yet most evolutionary studies assume that genetic effects remain constant across environments. Recent biobank-scale studies have identified widespread gene-environment interactions (GxE), but their contribution to recent human evolution remains unclear. Here, we combined genome-wide GxE maps with allele-frequency trajectories spanning the last ~10,000 years to test whether environmentally responsive variants contributed to recent human adaptation. Among 45 independent loci, three showed significant signatures of directional selection. These loci, associated with urate, LDL-C and cholesterol levels, showed parallel frequency increases and overlapping acceleration points around 4,700-7,200 years ago. Selection-associated GxE loci were enriched for urate-related variants and for interactions involving meat and cheese consumption. Diet-associated variants showed a consistent interaction direction across loci. Notably, across candidate traits, GxE variants were enriched among significant GWAS loci with selection signatures. Furthermore, analyses across worldwide populations revealed broadly shared derived allele frequency increases and comparable temporal patterns. Taken together, our results suggest that gene-environment interactions present an important and previously underappreciated component of recent human evolution.
affiliations: Institute of Genomics, University of Tartu (corresponding author)

papers.title: A mathematical model of the HPA axis demonstrates bifurcations under varying stress and systemic conditions
papers.abstract: In this study, we develop a mathematical model of the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal (HPA) axis and systematically investigate the model complexity required to reproduce observed hormone dynamics. The model is fitted to ACTH and cortisol measurements from five healthy volunteers reported in the literature. We show that simultaneous reproduction of both hormone profiles requires a delay differential equation model with at least five state variables among the model architectures considered. Following fitting the volunteer data, we investigate the response of the model to sustained stress using bifurcation analysis. The coupled system exhibits bifurcations over a range of stress intensities. This analysis reveals bifurcations whose critical stress thresholds depend strongly on the modulatory state of the system. These results provide a mathematical framework for investigating transitions between physiological and dysregulated HPA axis dynamics, which may be related to states of health and disease.
affiliations: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Western Macedonia, 50131 Kozani, Greece (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cause-excluded Effect Evaluation: a framework for the faithful assessment of genetic perturbation target identification
papers.abstract: Identifying which gene drives a desired cell-state transition is a foundational inverse problem in target discovery and cell-state engineering, yet far less developed than forward prediction. We show that prevailing benchmarks inflate performance through two artefacts: training leakage, where test-perturbation cells are seen during fitting, and evaluation leakage, where the perturbed gene's own expression change exposes the answer. Here, we introduce Cause-excluded Effect Evaluation (CEE), a framework that separates train and test perturbation targets, removes target-gene self-effects from expression profiles and scores candidates in downstream response space. With CEE, we find that simple structure-based methods consistently outperform complex deep learning models across 16 single-cell perturbation datasets, revealing that the recoverable signal is governed by low-rank and additive structure in perturbation responses rather than by model complexity. Our work disentangles evaluation artefacts from genuine predictive capacity and offers a design principle for developing perturbation target identification methods.
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Stem Cell and Reproductive Biology, IOZ, CAS; ISCRM, CAS; BISCRM; SAIS, UCAS (corresponding author)

papers.title: Linking somatic variants to altered methylation profiles in nanopore-derived breast and pancreatic cancer genomes using unduliner
papers.abstract: Research shows that genetic variation directly influences DNA methylation, and this association has generally been explored on germline SNPs and at a population level. The presence of genomic variation and base modification on sequence reads generated from a technology like nanopore sequencing offers an opportunity to link disease-specific variants to methylation changes in individual genomes. Here, we present unduliner, a framework with an embedded pretrained convolutional neural network model, that predicts somatic variants, single-nucleotide (SNVs) and structural (SVs), associated with methylation pattern changes in cancer genomes. We trained the model (accuracy = 0.803 on validation; 0.897 on held-out test) using phased sequence reads, single-nucleotide germline variants, per-base methylation probability, and variant proximity or presence in haplotype-specific differentially methylated regions (DMRs). Unduliner was applied to subline-specific variants from MCF7 breast cancer cell lines as proof-of-concept, and we demonstrated its ability to identify variant-stratified methylation differences independent of haplotype-based methylation differences. In a pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) sample, we identified coding and non-coding SNVs and SVs associated with tumour-normal DMRs, allele-specific methylation, and intratumour DMRs. These observations demonstrate that integrating long-read methylation and variant information can provide additional interpretative context for both coding and non-coding genomic variation beyond the conventional variant impact prediction tools. The results from unduliner include variant information, size and direction of methylation change with respect to the variant (increase or decrease), and genomic location of methylation change. Unduliner is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/Chisomgold/unduliner.
affiliations: Mater Research Institute-University of Queensland (corresponding author)

papers.title: Filling the Missing Puzzle: Integrating Interaction and Evolutionary Information to Enhance Protein Fitness Prediction in Inverse Folding
papers.abstract: Protein inverse folding, which infers compatible amino acid sequences from a given backbone structure, is central to rational protein design. Current methods rely largely on sequence recovery rate as the evaluation metric, emphasizing structural compatibility but seldom addressing function. Yet functional activity depends on the proper network of non-covalent interactions-protein-ligand contacts being a prime example. We argue that function-oriented protein design is governed by three complementary constraints: structural, interaction, and evolutionary, none of which are handled in a unified manner by existing pretrained models. To bridge this gap, we introduce zPolaron, a graph neural network built on protein-ligand complexes for functional protein design. zPolaron represents residues and ligand atoms as a heterogeneous graph and jointly encodes structural, interaction, and evolutionary information by fusing physical-interaction-enhanced graph representations with ESM-2 embeddings. Across multiple fitness prediction benchmarks, zPolaron outperforms all baselines, with gains evident across structural, interaction, and evolutionary dimensions. Wet-lab experiments further confirm its utility in functional enzyme screening and design: the optimized CalA6-D205A-S160G mutant achieves a 17.84-fold improvement in activity, while the CalB-I121M mutant yields a 1.91-fold increase. Together, these results show that integrating interaction and evolutionary information fills the missing puzzle of inverse folding, enhancing protein fitness prediction beyond structural compatibility. zPolaron is available at https://github.com/zelixirSH/zPolaron.
affiliations: Shanghai Zelixir Biotech (corresponding author)

papers.title: Exploiting Low-Rank Structure in Genomic Relationship Matrices for Computationally Efficient Optimum Contribution Selection
papers.abstract: Motivation: Optimum contribution selection (OCS) maximizes genetic gain under a constraint on relatedness. Genomic relationship matrices are dense, so the quadratic term costs O(n^3) operations, and existing OCS software assumes pedigree sparsity. Results: We replace the relationship matrix by its leading eigenpairs, computed by randomized SVD, and solve OCS in factorized form. On Norway spruce population (n=5,525), ranks 10--30 kept the exact objective within 1% of the optimum at 110--330-fold speedups; on the QTL-MAS 2010 (n=3,226), ranks up to 100 were needed (24-211 fold). The required rank rises as the diversity constraint loosens. Gain alone is a misleading accuracy check, since coancestry exceeded the optimum by up to 28%, so we choose the rank on the exact objective, which can be checked without a dense solve. The speedup comes from computing only the leading eigenpairs. We extend the factorization to robust OCS (18-fold). Availability and implementation: Julia implementation, and examples are available at https://github.com/jonhar97/fastocs under the MIT license (archived at Zenodo, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23214804).
affiliations: Skogforsk Savar (corresponding author)

papers.title: Perturb-Seqr: Signature Search Engine Integrating Connectivity Mapping Resources
papers.abstract: High-throughput transcriptomics can be used to develop Connectivity Mapping resources for identifying potential reversers and mimickers of disease signatures for drug and target discovery. Recently, several new Connectivity Mapping datasets have emerged, but no efforts were made so far to evaluate and integrate them. Motivated by this opportunity, we have developed Perturb-Seqr, a comprehensive Connectivity Mapping search engine that integrates nine small molecule transcriptomics Connectivity Maps and seven single gene perturbation followed by expression Connectivity Maps. Specifically, Perturb-Seqr contains processed data from LINCS (L1000), Tahoe-100M, Novartis Institute for Biomedical Research (DRUG-seq), the original CMap (cDNA microarrays), Ginkgo Bioworks (DRUG-seq), SciPlex (scRNA-seq), DeepCover MoA (PISA proteomics), Perturb Atlas (RNA-seq), Replogle et al. (Perturb-seq), CREEDS (cDNA microarrays), CM4AI (Perturb-seq), and RummaGEO (RNA-seq). To serve these Connectivity Maps in one unifying search engine, we converted the expression signatures from these resources into 450,271 gene sets of up- and down-regulated genes measuring the effects of 9,856 unique drug and 17,643 unique gene perturbations, targeting 917 cell lines and cell types. We demonstrate how Perturb-Seqr, and the gene sets it serves, can be used to identify targets for drugs and drugs for targets, uncover new pathways, and identify potential side effects for preclinical compounds. Overall, Perturb-Seqr is a comprehensive up-to-date Connectivity Mapping search engine and database, enabling the discovery of new drugs and targets. Perturb-Seqr is accessible from: https://perturbseqr.maayanlab.cloud/.
affiliations: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai (corresponding author)

papers.title: Transcriptomic reconstruction of an interregional molecular connectome in schizophrenia
papers.abstract: Background: Schizophrenia is increasingly viewed as a disorder of multi-regional brain networks, but molecular and pathophysiological hypotheses are often studied at the level of single brain regions or neurotransmitter systems. A multi-regional, multi-neurotransmitter analysis is needed to clarify how molecular abnormalities relate to circuit-level hypotheses of the disorder. Methods: Transcriptomic data from 2,209 post-mortem brain samples spanning five brain regions in 1,037 individuals were integrated. Directed connectivity strengths between regions were estimated using co-expression between presynaptic and postsynaptic neurotransmission-related genes. These estimates constitute an "interregional molecular connectome". Macaque transcriptomic data were used to benchmark the estimation pipeline against reference macaque connectomes. Connectivity differences between healthy controls and patients with schizophrenia were calculated, and a directional consistency filter was applied to identify candidate dysregulations. An LLM-augmented literature screening framework was used to assess the level of literature support for our candidates. Results: Our estimation pipeline showed concordance with reference connectomes, outperformed whole-transcriptome and random-gene co-expression measures, and remained stable when applied to macaque data. A total of 10 connections were marked as candidate dysregulations in schizophrenia at a nominal permutation threshold. Three of the candidates align with established anatomical connectivity, and another three with anatomical connections through relay regions. These candidates were characterized by bidirectional abnormalities in the cortico-striatal circuitry. The remaining four candidates had no well-established monosynaptic connection between two regions. These candidates were interpreted as co-regulated co-expression coordination changes. Literature screening quantified the number of articles discussing each candidate and how many of the articles directly support or refute each candidate. Our candidates collectively highlight the role of the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia. Conclusions: Interregional co-expression of neurotransmission-related genes carries more anatomical information than whole-transcriptome co-expression. Applied to schizophrenia, our analysis recapitulates known hypotheses and also proposes hypothesis-generating data-driven findings for experimental follow-up. This approach complements conventional region-wise analyses. Our approach could support a unified, multi-regional, and multi-neurotransmitter perspective of schizophrenia and point to candidate molecular mechanisms for further studies.
affiliations: KAIST (corresponding author)

papers.title: SORT disentangles multilevel gene programs across heterogeneous spatial transcriptomic atlases
papers.abstract: Understanding how transcriptional programs are organized across biological contexts is essential for deciphering tissue development, disease progression, and species-specific adaptations. Spatial transcriptomic atlases spanning patients, developmental stages, and species provide an opportunity to resolve gene expression programs (GEPs) that are sample-specific, group-shared, or region-associated, yet strong sample-specific variation can obscure weaker shared programs. Here we introduce SORT, a matrix factorization framework that jointly recovers multilevel GEPs and their spatial activities, using orthogonality to reduce program redundancy and graph total variation to preserve spatial boundaries. In simulations with strong patient variation, SORT more accurately recovered patient-specific, subtype-shared, and region-associated programs than existing methods. Across 108 pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma sections, SORT resolved tumor and stromal programs with distinct and overlapping activities and linked these activities to survival across four external cohorts. In a cross-species cerebellar atlas, SORT distinguished conserved layer-associated programs from species-specific activity variation. Across eight stages of mouse organogenesis, SORT revealed GEPs with anatomical redeployment and graded spatial activity, as well as stage-dependent local co-deployment of distinct programs.
affiliations: Fudan University (corresponding author)

papers.title: GLARE: Genomic Language model for Automated Repetitive Element classification
papers.abstract: Reliable classification of transposable elements (TEs) is important for genome annotation and evolutionary analysis, yet remains challenging: TE families differ widely across taxa, reference databases label them inconsistently, and many TEs are represented only by degraded copies. We introduce GLARE (Genomic Language model for Automated Repetitive Element classification), a TE classifier built by fine-tuning a genomic language model on harmonized PanTEon and Repbase reference data to predict TE superfamily across 32 superfamilies in 11 orders. Among the genomic language models compared, Nucleotide Transformer v3 provided the strongest representation. Built on this backbone, GLARE exceeded all nine classifiers in the PanTEon benchmark, reaching 0.966 weighted superfamily F1 on its 30-superfamily task. GLARE also showed stronger generalization to clades absent from training, consistently exceeding state-of-the-art classifiers on holdouts spanning three taxonomic ranks: the order Poales, the phylum Arthropoda, and the kingdom Fungi. Training on both PanTEon and Repbase reduced the performance drop seen when a single-source model was applied to the other database. Under simulated sequence decay, GLARE was the most robust classifier tested, and it performed best on independently curated degraded libraries. These findings show that genomic language models fine-tuned on harmonized multi-source references can classify TEs robustly under the taxonomic, database, and sequence-quality shifts that matter in practice. GLARE is available at https://code.jgi.doe.gov/NHaas/glare.
affiliations: DOE Joint Genome Institute, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (corresponding author)

papers.title: KEDROS: A Comparative Genomics and High-Resolution Phylogenetic Profiling Workspace
papers.abstract: Phylogenetic profiling infers gene function from the presence and absence of genes across genomes, but it loses resolution in eukaryotes, where many protein families contain several functionally distinct paralogs. Existing resources address parts of this problem separately: web services build trees for one family at a time, orthology databases provide precomputed orthologous groups for predefined species sets, and tree-profiling tools require users to supply their own trees and groupings. Here, we present KEDROS, a web platform that builds gene trees for any protein family across UniProt reference proteomes, splits each tree into subfamilies at inferred gene duplications, and profiles each subfamily separately. The organisms, the families and the taxonomic depth at which trees are split are all chosen by the user, so the same workflow serves any question that can be posed as a contrast between two sets of organisms: a pathogen and its host, a pest and non-target species, or lineages with and without a trait. KEDROS answers such contrasts at two levels. Across families and subfamilies, it ranks those present in one set and absent from the other, pointing to lineage-specific genes and candidate targets. Within a subfamily shared by both sets, it identifies amino acid positions that differ consistently between them and may underlie functional divergence, and displays them on AlphaFold structures. All analyses run in a web browser, with no installation or programming. Each of these steps exists in some form elsewhere, but to our knowledge no other resource runs them end to end, at the scale of whole proteomes, on organism sets defined by the user. We illustrate KEDROS with two cases. In the trypanothione reductase family of trypanosomatids, it recovers parasite-specific subfamilies and the substrate-binding substitutions that separate the parasite enzyme from human glutathione reductase. In the bacterial phylum Bacillota, it recovers the sporulation machinery from phenotype labels alone across 1,218 proteomes, and ranks an uncharacterized family among the strongest markers of the trait. KEDROS thus offers a general, code-free route from a comparative question to testable hypotheses about genes and residues. KEDROS is freely available at https://kedros.cgenomicslab.org.
affiliations: Institute of Molecular Biology and Biotechnology (IMBB), Foundation for Research and Technology-Hellas, Heraklion, Crete, Greece (corresponding author)

papers.title: Transcriptional perturbation effects remain structured beyond the leading global trend
papers.abstract: Prior work has described a global transcriptional response to gene perturbation, with many perturbations moving cells along a common direction. We find that perturbations contribute differently to this leading global trend and that substantial organization remains beyond it, including transferable perturbation-specific effects across datasets and a common hierarchy of responsive genes across perturbations. These patterns make simple strategies surprisingly competitive even in predicting effects beyond the leading global component.
affiliations: Department of Statistics, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: A multi-tissue transcriptome strategy for genomic resource development in Pinus edulis
papers.abstract: Premise:: Conifers comprise one-sixth of global forests and landscape genomic studies are urgently needed to understand their biology, yet relatively few conifer species have reference genomes. Targeted exon-capture is a practical alternative to whole-genome sequencing, but selecting loci without a reference genome remains a barrier. We developed a multi-tissue reference transcriptome for pi non pine (Pinus edulis) to ask how multi-tissue sampling improves probe design, and what is lost under a conventional single-tissue approach. Methods: We assembled a reference transcriptome from four diploid tissues (needle, phloem, root, vegetative bud) and one haploid tissue (megagametophyte), using the latter as a pseudo-guide. We designed a target-capture probe-set by prioritizing highly expressed P. edulis transcripts and transcripts matching a conifer exon database. Results: We recovered 76% of conserved plant genes with few duplicated transcripts. Filtering yielded 15,664 transcripts totaling 31.4 Mb, ~0.1% of the genome. Tissue-specific expression was substantial: 27.4% of transcripts occurred exclusively in non-needle tissues. Functional annotation confirmed complementary contributions, including seed-desiccation and germination genes from megagametophytes, and defense- and stress-associated genes from roots and phloem. Discussion: We built a transcriptome and efficient probe set using a roadmap suitable for other non-model plants with large genomes; keys to success were prioritizing complementary tissues and using expression-based filtering.
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley (corresponding author)

papers.title: Intrinsically flexible inorganic piezoelectric subnanowire enables wireless wearable bioelectronics for non-invasive multimodal human-machine interfacing
H3K27M cooperates with ASCL1 to maintain progenitor states and drive gliomagenesis
papers.abstract: Histone 3 lysine 27-to-methionine substitutions (H3K27M) drive aggressive diffuse midline gliomas by blocking differentiation of radial glial progenitor cells committed to oligodendrogenesis. We establish prolonged differentiation as a powerful tool to uncover regulators of glioma cell states and demonstrate that the pioneer transcription factor (TF) ASCL1 is a key mediator of H3K27M-driven plasticity and tumorigenesis. H3K27M prevents Polycomb silencing of ASCL1 , co-opting this TF to maintain oligodendroglial progenitor states. Consistently, ASCL1 loss drastically impairs tumor formation in vivo. Mechanistically, ASCL1 synergizes with H3K27M to redistribute the chromatin remodeler BRG1 to regulatory elements co-enriched for ASCL1 and SOX motifs, promoting expression of stem and neural progenitor genes at the expense of mesenchymal genes in DMGs. ASCL1 loss acts as a “fire exit”, enabling alternative differentiation despite H3K27M, underscoring the therapeutic potential of targeting stalled differentiation and tumor plasticity in histone-mutant gliomas and cancers with a stem cell hierarchy.

papers.title: Fruit-eating adaptations in a Late Cretaceous oviraptorosaur (Theropoda)
papers.abstract: The diversification of herbivorous dinosaurs and the rise of angiosperms in the Late Cretaceous are each well established, but the link between them is debated. Broad-scale diversity patterns in the two groups appear not to closely align, and there is no direct evidence of dinosaur adaptation to angiosperm-based diets. Here we describe Infernogallus jamesi gen. et. sp. nov., a diminutive caenagnathid oviraptorosaur, and show that these theropods were specialised herbivores that originated alongside the rise of fleshy angiosperm fruits. The nearly complete, articulated skull of Infernogallus jamesi —the first for the clade—reveals drastic changes to the adductor musculature organisation, unique in non-avian theropods but converged upon by extant frugivorous parrots. These modifications enabled extensive oral processing of soft food using anteroposterior movement of the mandible and occlusion of ridges and grooves on opposed elements. Altogether, this attests to a highly specialised herbivorous diet in caenagnathids, which likely consisted in large part of fleshy angiosperm fruits, which increased in size and diversity in concert with the radiation of oviraptorosaurs. Caenagnathids thus provide one of the strongest candidates for angiosperm-based diet adaptations in dinosaurs, but their role in the Late Cretaceous proliferation of fruit—which shaped early Cenozoic flora—remains unclear.

papers.title: Large-scale identical-location electron microscopy enables quantifying nanoparticulate electrocatalyst degradation
papers.abstract: Fuel cells convert chemical energy into electricity, and their performance relies on electrocatalysts whose durability during operation remains poorly understood. Deep mechanistic insight into electrocatalyst stability is essential to design durable, resource-efficient fuel cells. Nanoparticulate electrocatalysts degrade via diverse nanoscale processes, yet particle-to-particle heterogeneity in structure, support interaction, and local microenvironment make true particle-level quantification and understanding impossible with classical approaches. Here we scale up identical-location scanning transmission electron microscopy, which repeatedly images the very same nanoparticles, to track the structural evolution of hundreds of carbon-supported platinum-cobalt nanoparticles, a prototypical oxygen reduction reaction electrocatalyst. We present a three-step image analysis workflow comprising segmentation, tracking, and degradation-event classification with progressive automation, including machine-learning-assisted detection of overlapping particles. By pairing nanoscale resolution and local history with population-level statistics, the pipeline enables unbiased identification and quantification of degradation pathways across statistically meaningful particle sets. We reveal particle size- and shape-dependent effects, showing that smaller and irregular nanoparticles are more prone to detachment, and provide a data-driven framework for probing electrocatalyst degradation at scale.

papers.title: Quantum-sensing-based super-resolution live cell microenvironment imaging
A dual-attribution framework reveals how foreign investment and trade redistribute cobalt availability
PRPF19 drives hepatic stellate cell activation and liver fibrosis via PKM2-mediated glycolytic reprogramming
Corpus Callosum Dysgenesis is concomitant with reduced metacognitive efficiency and sensitivity across multiple cohorts and modalities
A self-limiting mechanotransduction feedback loop ensures robust organ formation
Extensive genomic diversity in Desulfovibrio reveals species-specific functional traits associated with disease
papers.abstract: Desulfovibrio spp. are associated with inflammatory diseases and human health, yet limited representative genomes and isolates hinder our understanding of their role in disease. Here, we assembled a comprehensive database of 2658 Desulfovibrio genomes across 90 diseases and 32 countries, including 24 human isolates. Genomic analyses showed extensive species diversity and revealed disease-associated functional traits, including flagellin and adaptation-associated genes (i.e., ureases). Flagellin-mediated Toll-like receptor 5 activation was species-specific and D. desulfuricans flagellin downregulated TGF-beta signalling in murine small intestinal organoids, suggesting impaired immune tolerance. Additionally, we investigated genomic capacity for hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S) production, a main Desulfovibrio metabolite. While health- and disease-associated Desulfovibrio spp. mainly encoded dissimilatory sulfate reduction, tetrathionate metabolism-encoding bacteria were exclusively detected in inflammatory bowel diseases, including Proteus mirabilis and Morganella morganii . Overall, our study provides a comprehensive genomic Desulfovibrio resource and identifies new links associating strain variation, functional traits and H 2 S-production with inflammatory diseases.

papers.title: Disability related disparities in diagnosis and survival of digestive system cancers in Northern Italy
papers.abstract: Individuals with disabilities may experience disparities in cancer diagnosis, but population-based evidence remains limited. We conduct a population-based cohort study using linked cancer registry and administrative healthcare data for digestive system cancers diagnosed between 2018 and 2021 in Northern Italy, examining diagnostic routes and one-year survival according to pre-existing impairments. Individuals with impairments are more likely to be diagnosed following emergency presentation compared with those without impairments (51.8% compared with 37.9%; adjusted odds ratio 1.41, 95% confidence interval 1.23–1.61), particularly those with impairments of mental and neuromusculoskeletal functions. They also have higher one-year mortality (hazard ratio 1.36, 95% confidence interval 1.26–1.46), independent of socio-demographic and clinical factors. Here, we show that disability-related disparities in emergency cancer diagnosis and survival persist across multiple impairment categories, providing population-based evidence from a European setting on differences in diagnostic pathways across heterogeneous disability groups.

papers.title: Transposable element-mediated structural variations shape gene expression and agronomic trait diversity in Brassica napus
Long-term nitrous acid evolution modulates ozone and secondary aerosol variations in global megacities
Giant step-boundary-triggered nonlocal modulation of magnetization reversal in multi-stepped van der Waals ferromagnet Fe3GaTe2
Fluorescence-illuminated diffraction tomography using explicit neural fields
papers.abstract: Multimodal fluorescence and phase imaging provides complementary information about biological samples. However, existing simultaneous fluorescence-phase techniques primarily operate in transmission mode and are limited to thin specimens, restricting their use in thick tissues and in vivo applications. Although multiphoton microscopy enables deep-tissue fluorescence imaging, combining it with three-dimensional refractive-index (RI) imaging remains challenging because few methods can reconstruct the RI of bulky, label-free tissues in reflection mode at subcellular resolution. Here, we introduce fluorescence-illuminated diffraction tomography (FDT), which reconstructs the 3D RI of label-free and fluorescence-labeled objects from diffracted fluorescence images acquired in reflection mode under two-photon excitation. FDT uses the transport of intensity equation and a self-supervised neural network based on explicit neural fields. Compared with state-of-the-art implicit neural fields, this approach improves computational speed, reconstruction accuracy, and interpretability. We demonstrate FDT in two experimental regimes: reconstructing the 3D RI of label-free tissues up to 300 μ m thick placed on a fluorescent substrate, and reconstructing the 3D RI of fluorescence-labeled, 3D-cultured cells without transmission-side access using fluorescence emitted by the cells themselves. FDT establishes a foundation for accessible reflection-mode multimodal fluorescence-phase imaging in complex biological systems.

papers.title: Structural basis of ammonium transport and coordinated regulation of AMT1;1 in Arabidopsis thaliana
papers.abstract: Efficient ammonium uptake is essential for plant growth and nitrogen-use efficiency, yet the structural basis of ammonium transport and regulation in plant AMTs remains unclear. Here, we determined multiple cryo-electron microscopy structures of the Arabidopsis thaliana ammonium transporter AMT1;1 in apo, ammonium-bound, methylammonium-bound, low-pH and phosphomimetic states. These structures reveal a conserved ammonium conduction pathway comprising an aromatic recruitment vestibule, a Phe-gate/Twin-His-containing pore, and a polar intracellular exit region. We further identified a conserved extracellular N-terminal disulfide bond required for oligomer stability and transport activity, suggesting potential redox-dependent regulation. On the cytoplasmic side, phosphorylation modulates C-terminal interactions with intracellular loops, revealing an allosteric regulatory mechanism. Comparison with the bacterial ammonium-sensing protein Sd -Amt1 uncovers a conserved ammonium-recognition region in At AMT1;1 that contributes to transport activity but lacks the signaling module and ligand-dependent conformational switching observed in Sd -Amt1. Together, these findings provide structural insight into ammonium transport and coordinated regulation in plant AMT transporters.

papers.title: Somatosensory cortex shapes perceptual decision bias via the superior colliculus
papers.abstract: Sensory inputs reach cortical and subcortical areas in parallel, but how they coordinate to guide decisions remains unknown. We examined the roles of the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and the superior colliculus (SC) in mice performing whisker-mediated tactile detection. While inactivating S1 contralateral to the stimulus increased detection threshold, inactivating ipsilateral S1 decreased it. These opposing effects reflected shifts in choice bias rather than sensitivity. Unilateral SC inactivation produced similar directional effects, whereas bilateral inactivation of either S1 or SC neutralized bias. Furthermore, SC lesions impaired detection performance, and combined S1 inactivation caused no further impairment, indicating that S1-mediated shifts in bias were SC-dependent. S1 inactivation also decreased sensory-evoked neural activity in SC, and choice decoding revealed that behavioral impairment was more closely associated with changes in SC population activity than with loss of sensory encoding in S1. Thus, S1 shapes perceptual bias by modulating SC-dependent circuits that transform sensory evidence into perceptual decisions.

papers.title: Preserved higher-order mentalising during strategic interactions after medial prefrontal cortex damage
papers.abstract: Mentalising, the ability to infer the beliefs and intentions of others, is essential for successful social interaction. Previous studies have implicated the medial prefrontal cortex in mentalising, but whether this region is necessary for higher-order mentalising remains unclear. Here we show that people with focal damage to the medial prefrontal cortex retain the ability to engage in higher-order mentalising during a strategic social game. We compare their performance with patients with brain damage in other regions and lesion-free participants. Individuals with medial prefrontal cortex damage achieve similar rewards and use comparable mentalising strategies, but they are slower when making strategic decisions. Computational modelling indicates that this slowing reflects a greater tendency to require evidence before committing to a choice. Voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping identifies medial prefrontal regions linked to altered decision processes rather than mentalising. These findings suggest that the medial prefrontal cortex supports strategic decisions while higher-order mentalising remains intact.

papers.title: CREST functions as a molecular bridge between neuron-specific enhancers and epigenetic regulators in mature motor neurons
papers.abstract: Motor neuron development requires precise transcriptional regulation mediated in part by BAF (BRG1/BRM-associated factor) chromatin remodeling complexes. The neuron-specific BAF subunit CREST is critical for neuronal function and is mutated in some cases of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), yet its underlying genomic mechanisms remain unclear. Using mouse embryonic stem cell differentiation, we show that CREST is essential for motor neuron maturation by activating mature neuronal genes and repressing progenitor genes. Mechanistically, CREST interacts with the neuronal transcription factors ONECUT1 and NGN2, and the BRM ATPase to target pre-existing accessible enhancers of neuronal genes. CREST deletion selectively prevents CBP histone acetyltransferase recruitment, reducing histone H3K27 acetylation at these enhancers and downregulating target gene expression, without disrupting BRM binding, enhancer accessibility, or long-range chromatin architecture. Overall, our findings identify CREST as a crucial epigenetic mediator bridging lineage-specific transcription factors, BAF complexes, and CBP to activate enhancers and promote proper motor neuron development.

papers.title: Multilayer analysis reveals extensive hidden population complexity in a dairy starter microbiome comprising few species
papers.abstract: The genomic and epigenomic complexity of microbiomes with low species richness remains poorly characterized. Here, we integrated 111 non-redundant isolate genomes with deep long-read metagenomics to investigate an undefined mesophilic dairy starter. Closely related isolates harboured distinct combinations of features associated with fermentation traits and phage defence, including surface polysaccharide genotypes, plasmids, prophages, defence systems, and methylation profiles. Metagenomics revealed additional elements and inferred host associations. However, the limited overlap between approaches across core-genome lineages and accessory repertoires underscored complementary but incomplete recovery, to the extent that the dominant metagenomic cell wall polysaccharide genotype (29.6% abundance) was absent from isolates. Metagenomic methylation signatures supported 36 species-level plasmid-host assignments, corroborated by isolate genomes in nine of ten testable cases. Our findings revealed extensive combinatorial diversity hidden from either approach alone, providing a plausible molecular basis for phage resilience, while likely representing only a lower bound on population complexity.
affiliations: University of Copenhagen (corresponding author)

papers.title: A chimeric infection program and epigenetic conflict underpin endogenous giant virus latency
papers.abstract: Giant endogenous viral elements (GEVEs) are ubiquitous in eukaryotic genomes, but how the virus adapts to the host and is capable of reactivation despite host defense mechanisms remains unclear. Here we examined this process in the green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and its latent giant virus, punuivirus, which is integrated into the host genome. We reveal a chimeric genomic architecture in which punuivirus latency genes are enriched in spliceosomal introns and 6-methyladenine marks, mirroring host transcriptional regulation, while virulence genes are predominantly controlled by a conserved viral promoter. Using single-cell RNA-seq, we show that nearly 70% of cells express viral transcripts, but only a small subpopulation commits to viral production, expressing virulence genes with host transcriptional shutoff. Moreover, we find that the intact punuivirus GEVE remains refractory to host 5-methylcytosine (5mC) silencing, whereas a naturally occurring deletion variant is associated with widespread 5mC accumulation across the GEVE and elsewhere in the host genome. The deleted region encodes a highly expressed ten-eleven translocation dioxygenase (TET), and epigenetic profiling of intact and deletion strains implicates this GEVE gene in removing 5mC marks, thereby maintaining the virus in a transcriptionally permissive latent state. Our study provides novel insights into the molecular underpinnings of host-virus co-existence in a giant virus-alga interaction.
affiliations: Virginia Tech (corresponding author)

papers.title: Macrophage DYRK1A is broadly required for bacterial phagocytosis
papers.abstract: Listeria monocytogenes is an intracellular foodborne pathogen that causes the serious illness listeriosis. Macrophages are central to the outcome of L. monocytogenes infection, yet the host requirements that facilitate bacterial uptake remain incompletely understood.
