In a previous genome-wide screen for macrophage factors that influence L. monocytogenes infection, we identified the macrophage kinase DYRK1A, which has been studied largely in neurodevelopment and cancer models but has no described role in bacterial infection. Here we show that DYRK1A promotes efficient internalization of L. monocytogenes by macrophages. Using several complementary approaches, we find that DYRK1A acts early during infection, primarily by promoting bacterial attachment to the macrophage surface. Transcriptomics of DYRK1A-deficient macrophages revealed reduced abundance of transcripts encoding membrane-associated proteins and components of innate immune and phagocytic pathways, suggesting a transcriptional basis for the attachment defect. Consistent with the broad nature of these changes, the role of DYRK1A extended beyond uptake of L. monocytogenes to the Fc receptor pathway and to additional bacterial species spanning multiple genera, establishing a broad role in macrophage phagocytosis. Together, these findings define a previously undescribed role for the host factor DYRK1A in macrophage phagocytosis and expand the function of DYRK1A beyond its established roles to innate immune defense.
affiliations: University of Washington (corresponding author)

papers.title: Design and characterization of peptide-responsive biosensors
papers.abstract: Gram-positive bacteria use secreted peptides and peptide-responsive transcription factors for quorum sensing. Here, we demonstrate that intracellular expression of these peptide effectors with their cognate transcription factors leads to regulation of gene expression in both in vitro and in vivo systems. Because both effector and regulatory parts can be readily expressed, complex circuits, including auto-activation schemes, can be developed, with switch-like behaviors. Moreover, the peptide effectors can be fused to proteins, enabling a direct intracellular readout of translation and potentially allowing any protein to encode regulatory interactions in cells. Our results support a foundation for regulatory circuits that extend beyond canonical components such as LacI and TetR.
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Geometrical Class of Population Growth Models, across Scales and Population Structures
papers.abstract: We develop a general geometrical framework for growth processes in which the growth rate depends exponentially on the number of active growth-supporting components. The framework separates the fraction of active components from the size of the accessible component space, allowing qualitatively different growth laws to arise from the same underlying construction. Bacterial population growth provides an example of a fixed-size component space controlled primarily by activation and deactivation, whereas examples such as human population growth or speciation provide an expanding component space in which interactions between individuals promote further growth. This motivates a Replicative geometrical law, dX/dt= X exp({beta} X^{gamma}), whose exponent characterizes the scaling of the effective growth-supporting component space and is tested against historical human-population regimes and eukaryotic lineage-through-time data. For innovation indicators such as patents and arXiv manuscript submissions, where an existing item need not itself reproduce, the same construction motivates a Direct Geometrical production law without the prefactor X. The framework therefore provides a common description of fixed and expanding component spaces while distinguishing Replicative from Direct Geometrical growth.
affiliations: University of Exeter (corresponding author)

papers.title: UniMedSeg: Unified Multi-Modal Medical Image Segmentation via Uncertainty Guided Encoding and Frequency-Spatial Dual-Prompt Decoding
papers.abstract: Text-driven medical image segmentation demands unified models based on multi-modal learning, capable of processing diverse imaging modalities while providing spatially reliable prediction estimates for clinical practice. Nevertheless, existing vision-language model solutions suffer from poor domain generalization and exhibit limited capability for uncertainty estimation to model the cumulative unreliability of cross-modal alignment across network layers. In this paper, we propose UniMedSeg, a unified vision-language framework for multi-modal medical image segmentation built upon frozen pre-trained vision-language backbones. Our framework incorporates modality-aware adaptation, cross-layer uncertainty-guided encoding, and a frequency-spatial dual-prompt decoder, wherein the progressive uncertainty propagation mechanism of the encoder suppresses misleading cross-modal features, whereas the decoder disentangles anatomical structure and boundary details in the frequency domain under dual textual prompts. Auxiliary losses further sharpen boundary representations and calibrate pixel-wise uncertainty maps. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UniMedSeg preserves competitive in-domain segmentation performance, improves domain generalization, and yields clinically useful spatial risk estimation.
affiliations: City University of Macau (corresponding author)

papers.title: Establishing genetic tractability in Jeongeupia sacculi HS-3: disruption of rpoS hinders biofilm formation
papers.abstract: Jeongeupia sacculi (HS-3) is a novel {beta}-proteobacterium with a unique multicellular life cycle. The genetic tractability and mechanisms underlying differentiation are unknown. Here, we adapt a method of homologous recombination for genetic modification in HS-3 and generate a disruption mutant of rpoS, which encodes the alternative sigma factor{sigma} S commonly associated with general stress response or major behavioral switches. We then characterize phenotypes associated with rpoS disruption. Under low-nutrient conditions, rpoS disruption reduced Congo red binding, consistent with rpoS acting as a regulator of low-nutrient response by upregulating production of biofilm-associated materials. Surprisingly, rpoS disruption did not significantly alter survival in response to other stressors in general stress response assays tested. Our work establishes a method for genetic manipulation in HS-3 and enables future investigation into the life cycle of HS-3, including whether rpoS has a role in differentiation triggered by low-nutrient response.
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Commensal Bacteria in the Gut Microbiome Encode Previously Unrecognized Aromatic Hydrocarbon Catabolic Machinery
papers.abstract: Introduction. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) toxicology has been primarily defined by host metabolic bioactivation to reactive intermediates. Yet ingested PAHs and biliary-delivered metabolites also enter the intestinal lumen, where they encounter the gut microbiota, an additional but understudied metabolic compartment that may alter toxicant fate. Although PAH interactions are well characterized in environmental microbes, resulting in defined enzymatic pathways for their catabolism, whether gut commensal organisms express related machinery in vivo remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we used an oral murine-exposure model of naphthalene and integrated compartment-resolved 16S rRNA gene profiling, global metaproteomics, and chemoproteomics to resolve the PAH-processing repertoire of the gut microbiota and its spatial distribution. Results. Naphthalene, a common environmental toxicant and representative PAH, elicited a compartment-dependent functional response that was most pronounced in the large intestine. Distally, exposure was associated with 2,386 differential proteins and accounted for 48.4% of metaproteomic variation, compared with 7.9% of 16S rRNA gene compositional variation. The small intestine showed a reduced proteomic response, with 994 differentially abundant proteins. Hydrocarbon catabolic markers showed a 4.8-fold distal expansion (36 to 172 proteins), including the naphthalene-catabolic nahE, proteins associated with phenylacetate, {beta}-ketoadipate, catechol/TOL, and anaerobic CoA-linked redox machinery. The small-intestinal repertoire decreased from 19 to 14 proteins, though aromatic-catabolic markers doubled, indicating a selective expansion. Critically, these homologs concentrated in Lachnospiraceae, a gut family that is prevalent in humans, primarily known for anaerobic fermentation, with no priorly described PAH-processing capacity. An uncultured Acetatifactor showed the largest hydrocarbon hits (14 to 82 protein increase), with additional contributions from Kineothrix, Eisenbergiella, and Petralouisia. Chemoproteomics, using a naphthalene-based probe, revealed enrichment of an orthogonal proteome of proteins interacting with naphthalene, capturing 171 small-intestinal and 67 large-intestinal proteins that were undetected in the global metaproteomes. Conclusions. Gut commensals express homologs of aromatic-hydrocarbon catabolic enzymes characterized in environmental microorganisms, and naphthalene amplifies this repertoire most strongly in the large intestine. The decoupling of taxonomic structure, expressed-protein representation, and probe engagement identifies a functional dimension of PAH exposure that composition-based profiling does not resolve and positions microbiome variation as a candidate modifier of PAH metabolic fate.
affiliations: Baylor University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Comparison of intracellular and encapsidated viral RNA reveals selective constraints on reovirus recombination
papers.abstract: Recombination can generate genetic diversity among RNA viruses; yet, mechanisms governing recombination for segmented, double-stranded RNA viruses remain poorly understood. Reovirus genomes contain ten segments of double-stranded RNA. Previous analyses suggested low rates of reovirus RNA recombination and led to a proposed mechanism of recombination during minus-strand synthesis. These analyses focused on recombination events detected in genomic double-stranded RNA extracted from purified viral particles. In the current study, we looked deeper into the origins of the observed recombination events by assaying total cellular material, which comprises viral genomic material, as well as replication intermediates, mRNAs, and products of recombination that may not be eligible for packaging into virus particles. Intracellular viral RNA, which is almost exclusively plus-strand RNA, exhibited substantially higher recombination frequency than particle-associated double-stranded RNA. The diversity and frequency of identified junctions were more similar among samples of a given type (intracellular or virion-encapsidated) from distinct infections than between distinct sample types from the same infection. Although potential recombination sites are widely distributed across the genome, a more limited set was used in junctions in packaged viral RNA than in intracellular viral RNA. Together, these observations suggest recombination may occur more frequently than previously recognized during reovirus infection, and many such events likely occur during plus-strand synthesis. However, recombination products generated during viral transcription may be selectively incorporated into viral particles.
affiliations: Vanderbilt University Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Repurposing clofarabine against enteric pathogens via metabolic starvation
papers.abstract: Enteropathogenic and enterohaemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EPEC/EHEC) cause severe global diarrhoeal disease, exacerbated by rising antimicrobial resistance. Pathogenesis relies on "attaching and effacing" lesions, where bacteria generate actin pedestals to adhere, replicate, and destroy intestinal microvilli. To identify novel anti-virulence candidates targeting this process, we conducted a high-throughput phenotypic screen quantifying pedestal formation via high-content fluorescence microscopy. We identified the anticancer nucleotide analogue clofarabine as a potent inhibitor of EPEC growth and pathogenesis. Distinct from its oncology mechanism - inducing DNA chain termination and apoptosis - clofarabine competes with bacterial ATP-dependent processes to impede gene transcription, protein synthesis, and Type III Secretion System (T3SS) function. Remarkably, EPEC counteracts this inhibition by cleaving clofarabine, enabling restored protein synthesis and resumed growth. Furthermore, we report for the first time that clofarabine suppresses protein translation in human monocytes, suggesting an uncharacterised translational impact on mammalian cells. These findings reveal host and bacterial translation as interconnected vulnerabilities to purine antimetabolites, offering a novel strategy to disarm enteric pathogens while uncovering a bacterial enzymatic mechanism for neutralizing host-targeted therapeutics.
affiliations: University of Sheffield (corresponding author)

papers.title: The essential lipoprotein maturation enzyme Lgt is required for flagellar and membrane integrity in Helicobacter pylori
papers.abstract: Pre-prolipoprotein phosphatidylglycerol diacylglyceryl transferase (Lgt) catalyzes the first step in the lipoprotein modification pathway and is essential for growth and viability of Helicobacter pylori. We explored the fate of H. pylori cells under Lgt depletion conditions to obtain insight into Lgt function on morphology and physiology. Downregulation of lgt expression led to growth arrest and a heterogenous population of small rod-shaped cells and small round cells with spiky protrusions, a loose outer membrane and disintegrated flagella. H. pylori overcomes a defect in lipoprotein modification through alteration of its gene expression profile resulting in so-called revertants. Outer membrane protein synthesis, carbon metabolism and nutrient uptake was reduced, and protein translation and flagellar biogenesis increased. Lgt specific regulation was observed in phospholipid biosynthesis resulting in an initial increase in cardiolipin followed by an increase in lysophospholipids at the time of adaptation. Suppressors of {Delta}lgt that were selected on solid media under restrictive conditions either lacked chromosomal mutations or had mutations in the cagUT-tetR regulon controlling the expression of lgt. A suppressor without mutations had an altered expression profile that led to downregulation of a DNA methyltransferase and upregulation of HP_0014, a motility associated glycosyltransferase family protein. Transmission electron microscopy and single cell video microscopy showed that a subpopulation of cells is motile in the revertant while the suppressor regained full motility with higher average speed compared to the wild type strain. Overall, our data show that lipoprotein modification by Lgt is important for membrane and flagellar integrity and that the heterogenous character of H. pylori cultures allows individual cells to overcome this cell envelope stress and survive. Our findings are important for antibacterial development strategies targeting essential integral membrane enzymes involved in lipoprotein modification and stimulate exploration of synergetic activity between known antibiotics and novel antibacterial agents targeting novel cellular pathways.
affiliations: Institut Pasteur (corresponding author)

papers.title: Coronavirus nucleocapsid proteins differentially antagonize RIG-I-like receptor signaling to shape pathogenicity
papers.abstract: Coronaviruses cause human infections with divergent clinical outcomes. Viral proteins likely play important roles in the severity of human diseases but are poorly defined. In this study, we discovered that viral nucleocapsid (N) proteins from various human coronaviruses have distinct abilities to antagonize human innate immune responses. N proteins from more pathogenic coronaviruses, such as SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2, have more potent activities specifically against human RIG-I-like receptor (RLR) activation than less pathogenic coronaviruses including OC43 and HKU1. Mechanistically, the SARS-CoV-2 N protein interacts with RLR pathway viral RNA sensors MDA5 and RIG-I and inhibits their interaction with MAVS. The CTD of SARS-CoV-2 N protein is an important region for RLR antagonism. Consequently, N proteins from more pathogenic coronaviruses promote viral replication more effectively than N proteins from less pathogenic coronaviruses. Blocking N protein function may be a promising antiviral strategy.
affiliations: Zhejiang University (corresponding author)

papers.title: EF-P-resolved ribosome stalling and collision trigger Rae1-mediated mRNA decay
papers.abstract: Ribosome stalling compromises proteome integrity and cellular fitness, and requires efficient mechanisms to eliminate problematic mRNAs and rescue blocked ribosomes. We previously identified Rae1 as an endoribonuclease that cleaves mRNAs at the tail end of stalled ribosomes to promote mRNA degradation in Bacillus subtilis. Here, we show that Rae1 has a broader role in the quality control of mRNAs that encounter translation problems. Global 5-end sequencing identified 31 previously unknown Rae1 cleavage sites, many of them associated with ribosome pausing at polyproline motifs in the absence of elongation factor P (EF-P). We also demonstrate that Rae1 cleaves mRNAs with ribosomes stalled on truncated transcripts lacking a stop-codon (non-stop mRNAs), provided that the transcript is sufficiently long to accommodate multiple collided ribosomes. Rae1 cleavage depends on a cytosine-poor context at the cut site, showing that both ribosome collisions and RNA sequence at the cleavage site govern the ability of Rae1 to promote the removal of stalled ribosomes from mRNA.
affiliations: CNRS UNIVERSITE PARIS CITE (corresponding author)

papers.title: Matrix-Mechanical Genetic Susceptibility and Reduced Inflammatory and Immediate-Early Programs in Keratoconus
papers.abstract: Purpose. To determine which proposed keratoconus (KC) mechanisms carry its genetic susceptibility and how it relates to corneal structure, and which describe its corneal tissue. Methods. Six mechanism modules and two attribution sets (transforming growth factor-{beta} [TGF-{beta}] and canonical type-2 atopy) were tested for enrichment in three independent European KC genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and in GWAS of central corneal thickness (CCT) and corneal resistance factor (CRF), with colocalization at matrix loci. Tissue expression was pooled across nine arms from eight studies with control-source meta-regression; activator protein-1 (AP-1)/immediate-early regulatory activity was scored in 107 donors, spatial expression in 21, and serum responses in human and rabbit stromal cells. Results. Extracellular matrix (ECM) was the only module enriched in all three KC sources (P [≤] 5.46 x 10-) and for CCT, CRF, and thickness-independent CRF (P [≤] 2.07 x 10-). COL5A1 shared causal variants with CCT in all three sources (posterior probability 0.985-0.991), and FNDC3B and COL1A1 with CRF or its thickness-independent component (0.961-0.986). Pooled, KC corneas had lower general and corneal-local inflammatory and stress/immediate-early expression (log2 fold-change -0.97, -0.98, -0.82; P [≤] 0.049). In whole-cornea and stromal tissue, ECM expression reversed between postmortem-donor and pathological controls (log2 fold-change +0.36, -2.34), whereas inflammatory and TGF-{beta} programs were lower against both. AP-1/immediate-early regulatory activity was lower in four donor cohorts (Hedges' g -1.50) and stress/immediate-early expression in two spatial cohorts; serum raised immediate-early readouts in human and rabbit cells. Conclusions. KC combines matrix-mechanical genetic susceptibility with a low-inflammatory, low-immediate-early corneal state whose matrix expression direction depends on the control source. Because this susceptibility is genetically shared with corneal thickness and resistance, interventions on the inherited disease are judged by corneal structure and mechanics.
affiliations: Department of Ophthalmology, Peking Union Medical College Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College, Beijing 100730, China (corresponding author)

papers.title: Rational Design of 5' UTRs for Optimized mRNA Expression and Cost-Effective, Rapid Analysis of Capped mRNA
papers.abstract: In vitro-transcribed (IVT) messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics require rigorous quality control of 5' capping efficiency and 3' poly(A) tail length, both of which constitute critical quality attributes (CQAs). Current analytical workflows for these CQAs rely on hybridization with nucleic acid probes and biotin-based affinity purification, which constrain throughput and increase per-assay cost. Here, we report a rationally designed 5' untranslated region (5' UTR) that sustains high translational efficiency while enabling probe-free, one-step purification for rapid quantification of capping efficiency and poly(A) tail length distribution. This approach exploits a strategically engineered 5' UTR incorporating a purine-only RNase A-resistant fragment terminating at a single pyrimidine cleavage site, together with a translation-enhancing element comprising an N6-methyladenosine (m6A) deposition motif and an 18S rRNA complementarity sequence. This dual-function design accommodates GA-rich sequence segments without compromising mRNA translational output. Compared with conventional probe- and biotin-dependent workflows, the present method substantially reduces cost and processing time and is compatible with simultaneous detection of segmented AmGn poly(A) tail variants. This integrated platform provides a simplified, probe-free and construct-universal for high-throughput in-process control (IPC) of mRNA therapeutics.
affiliations: Shanghai University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Ab initio CryoEM maps minimizing preferred orientation problems in heterogeneous mixtures: ReconSIREN
papers.abstract: Cryo-Electron Microscopy (CryoEM) Single Particle Analysis (SPA) is pivotal for elucidating protein structures and their conformational dynamics. Several critical steps are required to obtain accurate maps. First, the \textit{ab initio} relative orientations and shifts between images must be determined. Second, the common issue of specimens presenting a preferred orientation should be adequately addressed. Third, all of the above must account for particle flexibility and sample heterogeneity. Additionally, these steps are interrelated, making the search for all these parameters a real challenge when considering convergence robustness. In this context, we present ReconSIREN, a novel deep learning framework that addresses the key steps outlined before in an \textit{ab initio} manner while greatly minimizing one of the most important practical burdens in SPA, namely the errors introduced in the CryoEM maps by the existence of preferred orientations; the latter is achieved by a change of the optimization approach that avoids the so-called ``attraction problem'', and by the introduction of a new type of geometrical priors. It does so fully \textit{ab initio}, using deep learning training/inference steps without resorting to more traditional optimization approaches, and generating highly accurate initial reconstructions. We present maps as both homogeneous (consensus) maps and a full conformational landscape for analyzing flexibility and heterogeneity. Thanks to its Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, ReconSIREN distributes the estimation workload across independent experts, improving optimization efficiency and simplifying the process.
affiliations: National Centre for Biotechnology (CSIC) (corresponding author)

papers.title: De Novo Design of Flavoproteins with Controlled Excited State Dynamics
papers.abstract: Designing photochemical properties in proteins is a frontier challenge in biomolecular design, which, when realised, will open new avenues in catalysis and biomolecular electronics. Here we demonstrate an integrated computational design framework, supported by ultrafast spectroscopy, combining protein design, quantum mechanical/molecular mechanics molecular dynamics (QM/MM MD) and electronic structure calculations, to control flavin excited states in de novo proteins. Iterative design yields FC-4D2, a flavocytochrome with covalently bound flavin and non-covalently bound heme B and Fl-4D2, where the heme-binding site is removed. Both proteins are highly thermostable, and access all physiologically relevant flavin redox and protonation states, while high-resolution X-ray crystallography confirms the near-[A]ngstrom-level accuracy in design. Incorporating QM/MM MD and linear-response time-dependent density functional theory (LR-TDDFT) into the design workflow enables engineering of a flavin-tryptophan charge-transfer variant, Fl-4D2CT, that modifies the flavin absorption spectrum, substantially alters its redox properties and suppresses fluorescence. Ultrafast studies reveal how protein design reshapes the excited state relaxation timescale and mechanism. Our study establishes a modular strategy for programming flavin photochemistry in designed proteins.
affiliations: University of Bristol (corresponding author)

papers.title: Autofocusing molecular simulations for integrative structural biology of broad conformational ensembles
papers.abstract: Integrative structural biology seeks molecular descriptions consistent with complementary experimental measurements. A particular challenge arises for molecules whose broad conformational ensembles resist description by a few representative structures, such as natively unfolded proteins and fluid-phase biomembrane lipids. Although molecular simulations can generate such ensembles, their simultaneous agreement with a large number of experimental constraints is commonly prevented by model inaccuracies. Here we introduce autofocusing as an approach that integrates experimental information by automated finetuning of the physical model generating the ensemble. We demonstrate it for a fluid bilayer of the phospholipid POPC, for which no existing force field has simultaneously reproduced the complete set of 82 NMR C-H bond order parameters. Autofocusing brings all the 82 within experimental uncertainty while preserving agreement with independent small-angle X-ray scattering measurements and retaining or improving agreement with untargeted NMR relaxation rates and effective correlation times, thus supporting its description of membrane structure and dynamics beyond the calibration targets. The resulting simulations challenge a long-standing two-state interpretation of phosphatidylcholine headgroup structure, instead supporting a broad conformational ensemble poorly represented by crystal-derived conformers. These results establish autofocusing as a practical approach to constructing experimentally grounded conformational ensembles while retaining the computational tractability of classical molecular dynamics.
affiliations: University of Bergen (corresponding author)

papers.title: Chain-Length-Dependent Interactions of Polyethylene Nanoplastics with Human Catalase reveals Size based Nanoplastic Toxicity
papers.abstract: Nanoplastic contamination is increasingly recognized as a biochemical stressor, yet the molecular determinants governing how polymer fragment size dictates protein-level interactions remain poorly understood. Here, we combine molecular docking and all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to characterize the interaction of polyethylene (PE) oligomers of increasing length (n = 3, 5, 7, and 14 repeat units) with human catalase, a tetrameric heme enzyme central to cellular antioxidant defense. Single-chain simulations reveal that short PE fragments (3-, 5-, and 7-mer) migrate from an initial domain-connector pose toward a heme-proximal, previously characterized inhibitor-binding site, whereas the 14-mer remains kinetically confined to a peripheral surface site, implicating short-chain PE as a potential catalase inhibitor. In multichain corona systems, backbone dynamics show a non-monotonic, chain-length-dependent destabilization, with the 3- and 5-mer inducing the greatest structural perturbation and the 14-mer best preserving native-like dynamics despite forming an extensive, percolating surface network across all four subunits. MM-PBSA free energy decomposition identifies van der Waals interactions as the dominant thermodynamic driver of binding, while electrostatic surface mapping indicates that cationic surface patches instead govern long-range spatial targeting of PE chains. These findings establish a framework linking nanoplastic fragment size to protein-level toxicity, with direct implications for assessing the biochemical risk of environmentally weathered polyethylene.
affiliations: National Institute of Technology Warangal (corresponding author)

papers.title: Archaeal cell envelopes selectively activate innate immunity through TLR2 in contrasts with multi-receptor bacterial sensing
papers.abstract: The cell envelope of bacteria and fungi is a major source of microbial-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs), which are recognised by multiple host pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) such as TLRs and NODs. The key role of this recognition in protecting against infection and regulating diverse physiological processes has been studied for decades. In contrast, although the archaea are growingly recognised as an important component of the animal and human microbiome, their interaction with the innate immune system has been largely understudied. Here, we asked whether the archaeal cell envelope acts as MAMP. We selected 15 archaeal species from different environments, including the human microbiome, and harbouring diverse envelope characteristics, and we tested their ability to activate innate immune responses in human and murine immune cells. We first show that archaeal cells activate the innate immune transcription factor NF-kB and induce IL-6 secretion. Using whole archaeal cells, supernatants, and purified envelope components, we then find that none of the main PRR receptors which recognise the bacterial envelope (TLR4, TLR5, NOD1 and NOD2) are involved in this activation. We only detected activation of TLR2, regardless of the environmental origins of the archaea tested, although with overall lower activity compared to bacteria. We further demonstrate that different TLR2 heterodimers are involved, depending on the species, although the archaeal agonist remains unknown. Altogether, our results highlight a surprising paucity of interaction of archaeal cell envelope components with host PPRs, in contrast to bacteria, and open new avenues of research toward further investigation of archaea/host interplay.
affiliations: Institut Pasteur (corresponding author)

papers.title: Chronic stress remodels gut bacterial ecology and polysaccharide metabolism with neuroendocrine consequences despite unchanged behavior
papers.abstract: The gut-microbiome-brain axis (GMBA) links the gut and brain through metabolic, immunological, and neuroendocrine pathways, and can become dysregulated during psychological stress (PS). While previous studies primarily infer microbial function and use physical stressors that incompletely model human PS, here, functional multi-omics was applied to a chronic social-isolation mouse model. Although isolation caused no measurable behavioral changes, brain proteomics revealed stress-associated molecular responses. Taxonomic and short-chain fatty acid analyses suggested limited microbiome changes; however, metaproteomics uncovered sex-specific restructuring of bacterial ecology and carbohydrate-active enzymes. In females, isolation increased Petralouisia muris proteins involved in bacterial microcompartment metabolism and {beta}-glucuronidases across Lachnospiraceae taxa. Enriched {beta}-glucuronidase abundance coincided with reduced circulating glucuronides and altered brain estrogen-receptor activity, suggesting a microbial deconjugation-host estrogen-signaling interaction. These findings demonstrate that functional GMBA alterations may precede or occur independently of overt behavioral phenotypes and highlight the value of direct functional profiling in PS.
affiliations: Baylor University (corresponding author)

papers.title: MnSOD Diversifies, while FeSOD Dominates Superoxide Defense in Cyanobacteria
papers.abstract: Cyanobacteria are unique among prokaryotes in possessing photosynthetic thylakoid membranes enclosing an internal lumen, where superoxide production is expected to be substantial. Thylakoid-associated superoxide dismutases (SODs) would seem the obvious first line of defense, yet many cyanobacteria rely instead on a single soluble cytoplasmic enzyme, raising the question of what role thylakoid-associated SOD isoforms actually play. Using Cyanothece sp. PCC 7425, which encodes both a cytoplasmic FeSOD and a thylakoid-associated MnSOD, we combined sequence analysis, structural, genetics, and biochemical approaches to characterise FeSOD and MnSOD cellular localisation and assess each enzyme's contribution to superoxide defense. Cyanobacterial MnSODs display diverse N-terminal architectures, consistent with soluble, transmembrane, or lipid-anchored forms, yet contribute only modestly to superoxide defense in Cyanothece PCC 7425 and, very likely, across cyanobacteria broadly. Soluble FeSOD instead provides the major line of defense, showing that thylakoid association does not guarantee physiological importance. This predominance of a cytoplasmic enzyme highlights the central role of cytoplasmic superoxide detoxification, consistent with superoxide being generated mainly at the PSI acceptor side, and extends to the chloroplast stroma of plants. Our findings support a model in which SOD distribution reflects metal availability, enzyme properties, and subcellular organisation : FeSOD protects the compartment harbouring the main targets of PSI-associated superoxide, whereas MnSOD is retained where thylakoid association offers additional local protection, but becomes dispensable when the local ROS burden is limited. Spatial matching between superoxide production, antioxidant localisation, and target vulnerability may thus shape the diversification and maintenance of antioxidant systems across cyanobacteria and chloroplasts.
affiliations: Paris-Saclay University, CEA, CNRS, Institute for Integrative Biology of the Cell (I2BC), Gif-sur-Yvette, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: Shedding light on the virome of Caliothrips phaseoli, an emergent pest in peanut
papers.abstract: The bean thrips, Caliothrips phaseoli, is an emergent pest affecting peanut production. Thus, gaining a deeper understanding of the naturally occurring viral populations associated with this insect is of major importance, as such knowledge could support the design of novel pest management strategies that are both ecologically responsible and sustainable over the long term. In this study, we performed the first RNA high-throughput sequencing (HTS) analysis of C. phaseoli to unravel its virome, discovering a wide number of novel RNA viruses. Our HTS analysis revealed the presence of 31 viral segments, corresponding to 18 viruses, including double-stranded RNA viruses as well as positive- and negative-sense single-stranded RNA viruses. All these are novel viruses and cover multiple viral lineages belonging to diverse families. Overall, these results indicates that C. phaseoli hides a complex virome. The findings presented here provide an important framework for subsequent studies aimed at understanding the ecological significance, evolutionary patterns, and possible use of these viruses as components of biologically based management programs for this emerging peanut pest.
affiliations: CONICET (corresponding author)

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Heterogeneity of HPV Integration Architectures Drive Oncogenic Features of Oropharyngeal Cancer
papers.abstract: Viral integration is common in human papillomavirus-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (HPV+ OPSCC), but its structural and clinical significance remains unclear. We integrated targeted capture sequencing of 197 HPV+ OPSCCs with long-read nanopore sequencing of 17 tumors and models to characterize HPV-host rearrangements. We developed a novel quantitative informatics framework that classifies integration structures as Type1 (simple, single/low-copy) or Type2 (clustered, high-copy, rearranged). HPV integration occurred in 83% of tumors, with recurrent hotspots including TP63, MYC, CD274, TRAF2, and KMT2C. Type2 events were enriched for HPV E2 disruption, focal human amplifications, preferential transcription, and noncanonical HPV-host RNA fusion isoforms. Type2 tumors showed increased HPV oncogene expression and activation of MYC, NF-{kappa}B/TNF, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, Hippo/YAP-TAZ, and epithelial stemness programs. Multi-region and longitudinal analyses revealed intratumoral heterogeneity and clonal selection of Type2 architectures during progression, supporting integration structure as a potential marker of aggressive behavior and risk stratification.
affiliations: University of Michigan (corresponding author)

papers.title: Buried Ion-Pairs Reshape Folding Pathways of Artificial Proteins
papers.abstract: Ion-pairs are central charged motifs that control the biological function of several proteins. Yet, the physical principles linked to the formation of ion-pairs during protein folding remain poorly understood. Here, we show that buried ion-pairs of de novo-designed helical bundle proteins reshape the folding pathways by introducing kinetic barriers that are overcome by a hydrophobic collapse linked to packing of the protein core. By combining protein design with co-translational folding studies, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, and molecular dynamics simulations, we show that introduction of a buried ion-pair leads to a shifted folding transition that balances desolvation and electrostatic interactions within the protein and the bulk solvent. Moreover, we find that the folding pathway is sensitive to modifications in non-polar interactions and motifs that electrostatically shield the ion-pair from its surroundings. Our combined findings provide a blueprint for understanding how functional motifs affect protein folding and how mutation of charged networks alter the stability of proteins.
affiliations: Stockholm University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Bovine serum albumin interaction modulates the cellular potency of the BUB1 inhibitor BAY-1816032: fluorescence, molecular docking, and mesothelioma cell evidence
papers.abstract: Albumin binding can substantially alter the unbound concentration and apparent cellular potency of small-molecule anticancer agents. BAY-1816032 is a selective BUB1 kinase inhibitor with activity in malignant pleural mesothelioma, but its interaction with serum albumin has not been defined. This study combined intrinsic bovine serum albumin (BSA) fluorescence measurements, molecular docking, and cell-viability assays to examine whether albumin association influences BAY-1816032 activity. BAY-1816032 produced pronounced quenching of BSA fluorescence at low drug-to-protein molar ratios, and the quenching response was greater at mildly acidic pH than at mildly basic pH. Docking to BSA (PDB 4F5S) placed the top-ranked pose in Sudlow site I (subdomain IIA), with a Vina score of -7.8 kcal/mol and predicted hydrogen-bond contacts with Tyr149, Arg256, and Asp450. In NCI-H28, NCI-H2052, NCI-H2452, and AB12 mesothelioma cells, supplementation of 10% fetal bovine serum medium with 2% (w/v; 20 mg/mL) BSA shifted BAY-1816032 concentration-response curves to the right. Relative to 10% serum alone, IC50 values increased from 2.4 to 11.1 uM in H28, 3.6 to 22.0 uM in H2052, 2.0 to 4.9 uM in H2452, and 2.4 to 11.1 uM in AB12. These data support an albumin-dependent reduction in the freely available drug fraction and identify site I as the leading computational binding-site hypothesis. Because fluorescence-intensity and docking data do not independently establish a dissociation constant or quenching mechanism, direct unbound-fraction measurements and competitive displacement experiments are required for quantitative confirmation.
affiliations: Izmir Biomedicine and Genome Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: The Mitochondria-Modulating Small Molecule TEM1657 Suppresses NFKBIZ Pathway and Resolves Th17-Driven Psoriatic Inflammation
papers.abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic skin disease characterized by red, scaly plaques mainly driven by dysregulated T cells that induce keratinocytes (KCs) proliferation and inflammation. Despite significant advancements in disease management through biologics and topical therapies, these treatments offer only temporary relief and fail to prevent disease recurrence. Considering the current therapeutic needs, we described herein a novel small molecule TEM1657, derived from 3,5-dicaffeoylquinic acid with anti-inflammatory potency in imiquimod-induced psoriasis mouse model as well as in Th17-stimulated KCs. Mechanistically, its action is mediated through modulation of mitochondrial dynamics, specifically via OPA1, an inner mitochondrial membrane protein that alters mitochondrial calcium influx, and further impacts cellular bioenergetics. Moreover, TEM1657 rapidly suppresses transcription of NFKBIZ and various other psoriasis-associated genes. These observations highlighted a pathway that represents an innovative target in psoriasis and other NFKBIZ-related disorders.
affiliations: Universite de Lorraine, CNRS, IMoPA, F-54000 Nancy, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: A tetracycline-inducible promoter for gene expression in Gram-negative bacteria including Acinetobacter baumannii
papers.abstract: Carbohydrate inducible promoters on expression plasmids are widely used for biotechnology and basic science research. However, using carbohydrates for inducers has drawbacks including influencing bacterial metabolism, the inducer being used as a carbon source by the bacteria, high background expression, and only a subset of cells experiencing promoter activation. Furthermore, some bacteria including the pathogen Acinetobacter baumannii currently lack good carbohydrate-inducible promoters. To address this issue, a tetracycline-inducible promoter, PtetB, isolated from A. baumannii was cloned and evaluated in a number of important bacteria: Acinetobacter baumannii, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Pseudomonas fluorescens, and Serratia marcescens. A highly sensitive luxCDABE reporter was used to evaluate promoter activity. S. marcescens strains with elevated and reduced cyclic-AMP levels were used to evaluate the impact of cAMP on PtetB function. The PtetB promoter was induced over 800-fold in A. baumannii and 10-750-fold inducible in the other tested species. Background expression was lower from PtetB in the pseudomonads than previously described carbohydrate inducible promoters. Data indicated that the PtetB promoter system may be a useful tool for future basic science research with the tested bacteria.
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh (corresponding author)

papers.title: Twisted superconducting quantum diodes for high fidelity anharmonic qubits
papers.abstract: In superconducting circuits, bidirectional signal propagation can cause back-reflections and back-action that couple environmental noise back to coherent elements, degrading fidelity. Nonreciprocal superconducting diodes provide an intrinsic route to suppress such back-scattering at the circuit level. However, their diode efficiency and quantum integration remain limited. Here, we realize a quantum diode in twisted NbSe2 under in-plane and out-of-plane magnetic fields. A mere 1∘ twist yields an efficiency enhancement over pristine devices, reaching 27.6%. Quantum simulations reveal that this intermediate efficiency, well below 100% ideal, is both experimentally practical and optimal for preserving qubit anharmonicity and stabilizing two-level systems. These findings show that maximal rectification is not always beneficial for quantum information, establishing a new principle for designing the fundamental properties of twisted superconductors towards low-power, high-fidelity quantum circuits. Superconducting diodes can provide nonreciprocal elements for superconducting and quantum circuits, but the role of diode efficiency in quantum-device performance remains unclear. Here, the authors demonstrate an enhanced superconducting diode effect in twisted NbSe2 and show that even a moderate degree of nonreciprocity is sufficient to stabilize anharmonic qubit circuits.

Department of Physics and Center for Quantum Frontiers of Research and Technology (QFort), National Cheng Kung University, Tainan, Taiwan, ROC
