Department of Physics, State University of New York at Buffalo, Buffalo, USA

papers.title: Dopamine-induced mitochondrial dysfunction activates cGAS-sTING to drive IL-6 secretion in macrophages
papers.abstract: Daniali et al. demonstrate that dopamine exposure disrupts mitochondrial function in human macrophages, mediating the release of the inflammatory cytokine IL-6. Rapid mitochondrial dysregulation shifts cellular respiration toward glycolysis and induces the release of mitochondrial DNA into the cytoplasm, activating a biased cGAS-STING- NF-κB pathway.

papers.title: The ENL-USP7 complex regulates HIV latency through BRD4 protein stabilization
papers.abstract: Ahmed et al. identify ENL-USP7-BRD4 as a host pathway that maintains HIV latency. Targeted degradation of ENL or USP7 reactivates latent HIV in resting CD4+ T cells and brain microglia from individuals receiving antiretroviral therapy. Mechanistically, ENL recruits USP7 to stabilize BRD4 and maintain viral latency.

papers.title: Genomic insights into millennia of genetic continuity and trans-regional admixture in the middle-lower Yellow River basin
papers.abstract: Qin et al. reveal long-term genetic continuity in the middle-lower Yellow River basin over four millennia, punctuated by limited Silk Road-related admixture during the Tang-Song period and declining archaic hominin ancestry, highlighting the interplay of agricultural expansion, state-level transformations, and transcontinental connectivity in East Asia.

papers.title: Bovine H5N1 influenza viruses have adapted to more efficiently use receptors abundant in cattle
papers.abstract: Sustained mammal-to-mammal transmission of high pathogenicity H5N1 avian influenza viruses is reshaping the host range of these pathogens. One of the longest-running mammalian transmission chains involves the B3.13 genotype circulating in U.S. dairy cattle which was detected in early 2024. Genomic analyses revealed selection and rapid fixation of haemagglutinin mutations D104G and V147M. We demonstrate, via glycomic profiling, that bovine tissues, including the mammary gland, are enriched in N- and O-linked glycans capped with N-glycolylneuraminic acid (NeuGc), a sialic acid which is not synthesised by humans and birds, which instead express only N-acetylneuraminic acid (NeuAc). Early cattle H5 viruses poorly recognised NeuGc, but D104G and V147M enabled efficient engagement of both NeuAc- and NeuGc-containing receptors. These mutations enhanced replication in bovine mammary tissue without major attenuation of replication in human lung and primary nasal epithelial cells. NeuGc-driven receptor adaptation therefore promotes viral fitness in cattle without majorly changing zoonotic risk. Deep mutational scanning was able to identify alternative haemagglutinin substitutions that confer NeuGc usage and represent surveillance markers for emerging cattle H5 lineages. Finally, structural analyses suggest a potential molecular mechanism for the dual binding of the cattle-adapted viruses.
affiliations: The Pirbright Institute, Woking, Surrey, UK, GU24 0NF; Department of Infectious Disease, Imperial College London, UK, W2 1PG (corresponding author)

papers.title: Gene-level evolutionary conservation and human constraint decline at comparable rates across the age of onset of Mendelian disease
papers.abstract: Background Gene-level constraint and conservation scores are widely used to prioritise disease genes and to benchmark genomic language models. Purifying selection acts weakly on phenotypes manifesting after reproduction, so these scores are expected to carry less information about late-onset disease. An onset-dependent gradient has been demonstrated for human allele frequencies but not for the gene-level scores used in practice. Results We built an age-of-onset axis for 2,885 Mendelian diseases from Orphanet and fitted cross-species conservation (241-way phyloP) and human-population constraint (shet) on the same 5,322 gene-disease pairs against matched controls, to test whether one decays faster with onset. Their onset slopes differed by 0.23 logit units (97.5% confidence interval -0.10 to 0.56), equivalent to 0.024 units of area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) in a design resolving 0.049; the interval excludes constraint losing discriminative power faster than conservation by more than 0.011 AUROC units, widening to 0.033 when somatic associations are dropped. The usual explanation, that early-onset disease genes are developmental, pleiotropic and haploinsufficient by construction, did not account for the contrast; conditioning barely moved it. The answer did, however, depend on the constraint metric: three alternatives yielded larger contrasts excluding zero, though paired comparison could not distinguish the estimates. The metrics also diverged on recessive disease genes, with shet ranked below the gene pool (AUROC 0.487) and loss-of-function depletion above it (0.533), though, against matched controls, both ranked them below (0.457 and 0.450). Evolutionary scores improved a non-evolutionary baseline by 17 to 23%, with no onset gradient. Conclusions Conservation and constraint do not lose their value at measurably different rates as disease onset rises, and with only 283 late-onset Mendelian diseases annotated genome-wide, the question cannot be settled more finely. The gene-class explanation does not account for the contrast. Metrics that rank genes near-identically can still yield opposite onset-stratified answers, so a result reported by one metric carries a sensitivity that its confidence interval does not show. No constraint metric identifies recessive disease genes against matched controls, so a pipeline with recessive disease in scope needs a correction that switching metric does not supply.
affiliations: School of Bio Sciences and Technology, Vellore Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: A chromosome-level genome assembly of the chilli thrips Scirtothrips dorsalis Hood (Thysanoptera: Thripidae)
papers.abstract: Thrips are known for being pests of many agricultural crops, as well as vectors of plant viruses. Yet despite their economic importance, genomic resources for this group remain limited, and no chromosome-level genome has been available for the genus Scirtothrips. One such species is the chilli thrips, Scirtothrips dorsalis Hood (Thysanoptera: Thripidae). This invasive and highly polyphagous pest is established across much of the world and transmits several tospoviruses. Genomic resources would provide a new means to understand the traits that make thrips difficult to manage. Here, we present a chromosome-level genome assembly for S. dorsalis. The assembly is 266.5 Mb, with 96.9% of the sequence anchored in 16 chromosome-scale scaffolds. It contains 20,557 genes, and repetitive elements account for 28.8% of the sequence, which is comparable to those of other sequenced Thripidae. A species tree based on 3,019 single copy orthologs placed S. dorsalis as sister to Scirtothrips hansoni, with Scirtothrips most closely related to Frankliniella, Megalurothrips, and Odontothrips. The mitochondrial genome is a single circular molecule of 15,207 bp in which the sequence of the published mini circle is integrated, in contrast to the bipartite mitogenome previously reported for the same cryptic species.
affiliations: University of Florida (corresponding author)

papers.title: PRMT5 inhibition induces a histone methylation switch that drives chromatin plasticity, drug resistance, and metastatic progression
papers.abstract: PRMT5 is the major type II protein arginine methyltransferase, regulating fundamental processes including transcription, splicing, and translation. Its expression is restricted to stem and progenitor cells but reactivated in many tumors. Numerous PRMT5 inhibitors (PRMT5i) have been developed, and several are currently in clinical trials. Their efficacy is largely attributed to disruption of PRMT5's role in splicing. Here we show that PRMT5i produce dichotomous effects in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD): they induce lethal splicing defects but also trigger epigenetic changes that actively enable acquisition of drug resistance. Of concern, the resulting stably resistant populations have undergone accelerated dedifferentiation, gaining molecular and phenotypic hallmarks of metastatic disease. Moreover, even brief PRMT5i treatment of drug-naive tumors is sufficient to drive disease progression in vivo. This epigenetic rewiring reflects a previously unappreciated dominance of PRMT5 over PRMT1, arising from differential subcellular localization. Our data indicate that cytoplasmic PRMT5 likely dimethylates histones symmetrically before nuclear import. PRMT5i block this, allowing unmodified histones to reach nuclear PRMT1 and undergo asymmetric dimethylation instead. This symmetric-to-asymmetric switch flips histones from repressive to activating states, yielding rapid chromatin opening and derepression of lineage programs, a subset of which are selected for and retained in resistant cells. Accordingly, inhibition of asymmetric dimethylation suppresses PRMT5i-induced chromatin derepression and synergizes strongly with PRMT5 inhibition. Finally, endogenous PRMT5 suppression in MTAP-deficient human cells partially engages this switch, and CDKN2A/MTAP-deficient tumors are correspondingly more dedifferentiated. Thus, PRMT5i create a splicing vulnerability while simultaneously licensing epigenetic escape toward a more dedifferentiated and aggressive cell state.
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cooperative cis-interactions between ectodomains of TCRαβ CD3 subunits enable mechanotransduction
papers.abstract: TCR signaling poses a mechanical problem: pMHC binding occurs at the TCR{beta} ectodomain (ECD) head, whereas ITAM phosphorylation occurs on CD3 cytoplasmic tails. Chemistry cannot bridge this >10 nm gap, so the two events must be coupled through the TCR-CD3 interface, involving conformational allostery allowing force-based regulation. Although weak ECD cis-interactions between TCR{beta} and CD3 have been proposed to contribute to this coupling, their kinetics and mechanical competence remain elusive. Here, we quantify TCR{beta}-CD3 ECD cis-interactions in a pseudo-cis configuration by two-dimensional affinity and single-bond force spectroscopy, finding that TCR{beta}-CD3{gamma}{epsilon} and TCR{beta}-CD3{delta}{epsilon} bimolecular interactions have low affinity and rapid kinetics, yet form catch bonds. Critically, concurrent engagement of CD3{gamma}{epsilon} and CD3{delta}{epsilon} generates cis-cooperativity, yielding a stronger and longer-lasting CD3{gamma}{epsilon}-TCR{beta}-CD3{delta}{epsilon} trimolecular catch bond than the sum of the two dimeric bonds, with force-stabilized lifetimes matching those of agonist TCR-pMHC trans-interaction. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal an expanded, cooperative, and asymmetric contact network, making CD3{delta}{epsilon} more force-responsive and susceptible to conformational change than CD3{gamma}{epsilon}. Interface mutations do not alter force-free affinities but remodel force-dependent cis-bond profiles, leading to an inverse correlation with trans-bond profiles and T cell signaling. These results define cooperative ECD cis-interaction as a mechanically regulatable allosteric coupling element at the TCR-CD3 junction important to antigen recognition and signal initiation.
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: A surviving beta cell subpopulation enriched in patients with T1D
papers.abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is characterized by the autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells. While most beta cells are lost, a subset of beta cells persists years and even decades after disease onset. Studying these surviving cells is challenging, and thus how they escape immune killing remains poorly understood. Here, we applied a gene regulatory network inference-based clustering approach on existing islet scRNAseq data from cadaveric donors with T1D, autoantibody positive donors at risk for T1D, and non-diabetic donors to analyze beta cells from patients with established T1D. This approach identified a novel beta cell subtype enriched in T1D donors defined by the activity of several transcription factors which have well-characterized roles in beta cell survival, most notably IRF1. We found increased expression of immunomodulatory genes (e.g. SOCS1/3, HLA-E) as well as decreased expression of autoantigens and secretory genes, suggesting loss of cellular identity. We identified inflammatory cytokines as a driver of this phenotype by reanalyzing public data from primary human beta cells stimulated with inflammatory cytokines in vitro. We find a similar transcriptional program active in a subset of alpha cells, consistent with cell-extrinsic inflammatory cytokine signaling in vivo. We additionally use immunofluorescence to validate these findings. Overall, this study defines the features of surviving beta cells in patients with T1D, revealing several genes and pathways active in these cells as potential targets for T1D prevention and reversal.
affiliations: Yale University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Relatedness of Gardnerella prophages and their endolysins
papers.abstract: The Gardnerella genus includes a complex sub-taxonomy of bacterial species and subgroups which have been implicated in bacterial vaginosis. We analyzed G. leopoldii, G. swidsinski, G. piotii, and G. vaginalis genomes available in public databases and predicted proviral sequences using Cenote-Taker3. We clustered 266 prophage sequences into 140 viral genera level groupings that encode four distinct gene clusters and 19 different lysin proteins. Analysis of the bacterial and prophage sequence phylogenies reveals that while there were no specific prophage sequence lineages that infected each bacterial host, there is clustering of the prophage sequences by bacterial species within the Gardnerella genus.
affiliations: University of Washington (corresponding author)

papers.title: The staphylococcal type VII secretion system delays inflammatory cell death during macrophage infection
papers.abstract: The human pathogen Staphylococcus aureus is a facultatively intracellular bacterium that can replicate and survive within macrophages. While macrophage-mediated immune modulation is pivotal in S. aureus pathogenesis, bacterial manipulation of macrophage pathways remains poorly understood. The specialised type VII secretion system (T7SSb) is an important virulence-associated factor during staphylococcal infection, although, unlike its mycobacterial counterparts, its role in controlling staphylococcal-macrophage interactions remains unclear. Employing high-resolution time-lapse imaging, we demonstrated an induction of pore-induced cellular traps (PITs) during S. aureus infection of macrophages in vitro, with a higher number of PITs forming in macrophages infected with S. aureus lacking EssC ({Delta}essC), a central T7SS transporter. Interestingly, {Delta}essC-infected macrophages displayed increased bacterial escape compared to wild type (WT)-infected cells, implicating a role for T7SS in delaying macrophage cell death. Changes in cell death were accompanied by a reduction in efferocytosis of {Delta}essC-infected cells in vitro. Investigation of cell death signalling markers in WT and {Delta}essC-infected macrophages demonstrated that the T7SS delayed induction of key cell death pathways, necroptosis and pyroptosis, and a dual RNAseq analysis of WT- and {Delta}essC-infected macrophages indicated a T7SS-dependent modulation of bacterial oxidative stress and selected host chemokines. We also demonstrated that T7SS effectors, EsxA and EsxC individually delayed macrophage cell death. Interestingly, {Delta}esxC mutants demonstrated accelerated calcium fluxes, indicating that the T7SS-mediated suppression of cellular calcium signalling may cause the delay in cell death. Furthermore, in a murine skin infection model, we showed that effector and transporter mutants have distinct S. aureus infection outcomes. Our findings suggest for the first time a key role for T7SSb proteins in controlling macrophage cell death, which impacts staphylococcal survival within the host during infection.
affiliations: University of Warwick (corresponding author)

papers.title: Targeted Depletion of rRNAs and Tobamoviruses Enhances Viral Discovery in Wastewater Metatranscriptomes
papers.abstract: Wastewater contains a complex mixture of nucleic acids derived from human cells, microorganisms, diets, and agricultural or industrial inputs. Metatranscriptomics has the potential to broaden the understanding of wastewater viromes, but its utility is constrained by high-abundance RNA molecules that prevent the detection of lower-abundance signals, including human pathogens. Two major sources of this interfering background signal are ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) from various organisms, and plant-infecting tobamoviruses from human diets, which are often the most abundant RNA viruses in wastewater. These rRNA molecules and RNA genomes can account for upwards of 95% of total RNA sequences, thereby obscuring the detection of lower-abundance viruses of public health importance. This study evaluated whether combined depletion of ribosomal RNAs and genomic RNA from abundant plant tobamoviruses can improve the recovery of underrepresented viral sequences from wastewater. RNA extracts from a large municipal wastewater treatment plant in Calgary, Canada, were processed with or without probe-based depletion of rRNAs and eight abundant tobamoviruses. Metatranscriptomes revealed that depletion reduced rRNA reads by 90%. Reads assigned to tobamoviruses, which accounted for up to 25% of viral reads in untreated samples, were reduced to <2% of viral reads after depletion. This decrease in undesired RNA signal led to an order of magnitude increase in viral read signals and improved assembled viral genome quality. Furthermore, the number of reads assigned to human and animal pathogens increased 42-fold after depletion, enabling the detection of important pathogens like influenza, RSV, and hepatitis A, which were undecteable in untreated samples. Together, these findings demonstrate that targeted depletion of abundant background RNAs improves the detection of low abundance viruses, and enhances the utility of metatranscriptomic approaches for wastewater viral surveillance.
affiliations: University of Calgary (corresponding author)

papers.title: Sequence-Dependent DNA Base Selection Fidelity: A Kinetics-Based Model and its Validation
papers.abstract: DNA replication achieves error rates as low as 10-9-10-11 per base pair through the combined contribution of base selection, exonuclease proofreading, and mismatch repair. Among those processes, base selection determines the initial level of accuracy and is strongly modulated by local sequence context. Existing models address this dependence either by fitting individual rate constants for each sequence context or by invoking the global template properties, neither of which derives sequence dependence from the underlying thermodynamics and kinetics of base pair formation. Here we present a mechanism for sequence-dependent base selection fidelity, built from two physical properties: nearest-neighbor stacking thermodynamics and directional kinetic asymmetry. The model fits the experimentally observed mutation spectra from three mismatch repair-deficient organisms well (r=0.74, 0.70, and 0.63), and predicts that base-selection accuracy varies non-monotonically with temperature in a sequence-dependent manner. Our model, therefore, provides a framework that connects sequence-dependent thermodynamic and kinetic effects during nucleotide incorporation to experimentally observed mutation rates.
affiliations: National Institute of Technology Durgapur (corresponding author)

papers.title: EventHorizon: A Foundation Model for Clinical Flow Cytometry
papers.abstract: Clinical flow cytometry is central to diagnosing hematologic malignancies, but its reliance on manual expert interpretation and fixed panel designs limits scalability and adaptability. To address this, we developed EventHorizon, a self-supervised foundation model that combines a hierarchical, marker-aware transformer with self-distillation pre-training. EventHorizon integrates heterogeneous, multi-tube panels into a unified, specimen-level embedding. Pre-trained without labels on 100,937 routine clinical specimens, comprising over 50 billion cells, the model yields frozen embeddings that enable lightweight classifiers to accurately identify recurrent genetic abnormalities in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), including t(15;17) (AUROC 0.991) and an unexpected signal for DDX41 mutations (AUROC 0.970). EventHorizon maintained strong performance on a temporally separated 2026 cohort (macro AUROC 0.970 across 28 diagnoses) and demonstrated zero-shot transferability across a five-site B-cell lymphoma cohort (CLL vs. normal AUROC 0.988), the FlowCAP-II AML challenge (AUROC 0.973), and B-ALL measurable residual disease detection (AUROC 0.920 at [≥]1% disease burden). Although class ranking transferred reliably across sites, decision thresholds shifted; however, these were rapidly recalibrated using as few as four labeled AML cases. Sensitivity decreased at disease burdens below 0.1%, yet embeddings remained robust to simulated assay perturbations. Overall, EventHorizon offers a reusable, panel-agnostic representation for diagnostic flow cytometry.
affiliations: University of Utah (corresponding author)

papers.title: The CAHRA Challenge: A Community-Wide Assessment of Cryo-EM Heterogeneous Reconstruction Algorithms
papers.abstract: The ability of cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to interrogate the atomic structure and motion of biomolecules has motivated the development of a wide range of algorithms for heterogeneity analysis. However, evaluating and comparing these methods remains challenging because ground-truth structures are generally unknown for experimental samples. Here, we introduce the 2026 Community-Wide Assessment of Heterogeneous Reconstruction Algorithms (CAHRA), a community-wide challenge centered on three benchmark datasets that probe distinct tasks in heterogeneity analysis. These include (1) compositional heterogeneity arising from mixtures of distinct protein complexes, (2) continuous conformational variability and atomic modeling, and (3) entanglement between molecular conformation and particle pose. We describe the design, construction, and validation of these datasets, as well as their use in the recently completed CAHRA Challenge.
affiliations: Princeton University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cell cycle exit is required for differentiation and cell fate diversification but not neoblast specialisation in planarians
papers.abstract: In planarians, adult stem cells constantly proliferate and differentiate into dozens of different cell types to maintain tissue homeostasis. However, how cell fate acquisition is coordinated with cell cycle progression remains poorly understood. To address this, we generated single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets from cells enriched for 2C or 4C DNA content and from animals subjected to RNAi against the cell cycle regulators cdh1 and h2b. We found that progenitor populations from multiple lineages contain actively cycling cells enriched in the 4C state. Cell fate acquisition to most cell types is acquired progressively during neoblast differentiation. Comparative analysis of cell cycle regulators confirmed a simplified regulatory repertoire in Schmidtea, supporting a central role for cdh1 in controlling cell cycle exit. RNAi-mediated knockdown of cdh1 caused homeostasis defects, impaired regeneration, accumulation of neoblasts and depletion of progenitors. Together, our findings demonstrate that cell cycle exit is required for terminal differentiation but not for neoblast specialisation. Instead, lineage commitment is initiated in actively cycling neoblasts, whereas terminal differentiation depends on cdh1-mediated cell cycle exit.
affiliations: Living Systems Institute, University of Exeter, Exeter, UK (corresponding author)

papers.title: Human Th17 state classification reveals a selective vulnerability in acylcarnitine metabolism in type 2 diabetes
papers.abstract: Th17 cells are categorized as non-pathogenic (Th17np) and pathogenic (Th17p), states defined primarily in murine autoimmune models. In contrast, studying these states in humans remains difficult because these subsets lack validated identifiers. We developed a nanovial-based single-cell ELISA to isolate cytokine-secreting human Th17 cells and define Th17np vs Th17p cell transcriptional states. These signatures enabled predictive classification and flow-cytometric identification across tissues and diseases. Application of these strategies with single-cell metabolic modeling and functional profiling revealed that Th17np cells predominate in type 2 diabetes yet exhibit impaired fatty acid oxidation capacity despite elevated carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A). CRISPR perturbation and pharmacologic inhibition identified acylcarnitine metabolism as a regulator of Th17 state balance and exposed a selective metabolic vulnerability in type 2 diabetes. This framework links human Th17 cell pathogenicity to lipid metabolism.
affiliations: University of California, Irvine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Brain-Resident CD8+ T Cells Regulate Neuronal Activity and Behavior via Interferon-Gamma
papers.abstract: Maintaining brain homeostasis is crucial for proper function of the central nervous system and has traditionally been attributed to neuronal and glial interactions. However, recent research highlights the essential role of brain-resident immune cells in this process. Our study characterizes brain-specific CD8+ T cells and elucidates their significant contribution to brain homeostasis and behavior. We identified a distinct population of CD8+ T cells that infiltrates the brain during early development, undergoes clonal expansion, and acquires effector memory-like characteristics through interactions with microglia. Notably, the absence of these cells results in hyperactivation of neuronal activity and abnormal behaviors, due to loss of regulation of interferon-gamma (IFN-{gamma}) secreted by CD8+ T cells. Our findings demonstrate that IFN-{gamma} secreting brain-specific CD8+ T cells are crucial for maintaining the physiological level of neuronal excitability and normal behavioral patterns. This study provides novel insights into neuroimmune interactions, emphasizing the critical role of CD8+ T cells in sustaining brain function and behavior.
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania (corresponding author)

papers.title: The transition to postpartum lactation establishes a state of maternal antiviral resilience
papers.abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) causes severe disease during late pregnancy, yet how maternal adaptations in host defense shape susceptibility following childbirth remains unknown. Here, we show that the postpartum period represents a state of enhanced maternal antiviral immunity. Across postpartum stages, dams infected before weaning exhibited increased survival and reduced disease following lethal IAV challenge compared with nonpregnant females. Postpartum protection was associated with enhanced viral clearance and increased pulmonary antigen-specific CD8+ T cells and IL-17A-producing gamma-delta T cells. We identify the transition into lactation as a critical determinant of this protection. Protection extended to highly pathogenic avian influenza. Together, these findings reveal that maternal antiviral immunity remains actively shaped after childbirth, establishing the postpartum lactational period as a distinct state of maternal antiviral resilience.
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania (corresponding author)

papers.title: A mast cell receptor is associated with fibrosis and itch in systemic sclerosis
papers.abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is an autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by symmetric fibrosis of the skin and multiple internal organs. The mechanisms that trigger early fibrotic changes remain unclear. Mast cells are known to infiltrate human SSc lesional skin in early disease stages, yet the role of mast cells in initiating fibrosis and pruritus in SSc remains debated, in part due to unclear pathways of mast cell activation. Here, we show that mast cells, via the receptor Mrgprb2, contribute to fibrosis in the bleomycin (BLM)-induced skin fibrosis mouse model. Mast cells accumulate in the skin of BLM-treated wild-type (WT) but not Mrgprb2-knockout (Mrgprb2-/-) mice. Mrgprb2-/- mice show attenuated disease severity, with reduced collagen deposition and lower expression of matrix metalloproteinases and inflammatory markers associated with fibrosis. BLM treatment also increases pruritus in WT mice in the early stages of the model; an effect reduced in Mrgprb2-/- mice. This is the first report of itch in this model of skin fibrosis, further linking it to clinical SSc, where pruritus is an early and prevalent symptom affecting nearly half of patients. In a parallel human cohort, lesional SSc skin harbors significantly more mast cells than paired non-lesional skin from the same patients, demonstrating that mast cell accumulation is specific to affected tissue. Lesional mast cell counts also track with skin disease severity, correlating with modified Rodnan skin score and patient-reported skin tightness. Together, these findings implicate Mrgprb2-mediated mast cell activity in both fibrosis and pruritus in SSc, highlighting mast cells as a candidate therapeutic target in this understudied disease process.
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Restoration of deficient IL-15 signaling enhances innate lymphoid cell immunity in brain metastasis
papers.abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells and type 1 innate lymphoid cells (ILC1s), collectively known as group 1 innate lymphoid cells (ILCs), are critical mediators of anti-tumor immunity, yet their role in brain metastasis remains poorly defined. Using single-cell RNA sequencing and functional depletion models, we show that group 1 ILCs fail to provide adequate tumor control in breast cancer brain metastasis (BCBM). In contrast to the liver, where diverse, functionally competent group 1 ILC populations facilitate excellent metastatic control, group 1 ILCs in BCBM show limited diversity and profound tissue-specific dysfunction such that their depletion had no effect on tumor burden despite modest parenchymal infiltration. We attribute this group 1 ILC dysfunction to severely restricted IL-15 availability, with IL-15R protein detected at 500-fold lower concentration in the brain than in the liver. Local IL-15 complex administration restored group 1 ILC accumulation, cytotoxicity, and tissue residency, significantly reducing brain metastatic burden independent of T cells. Intracranial delivery of IL-15-secreting induced pluripotent stem-cell-derived (iPSC)-NK cells, already in clinical testing for non-small cell lung cancer, significantly reduced tumor burden. Collectively, these findings reveal how tissue-specific differences in cytokine availability shape group 1 ILC population diversity and disease response, establishing localized IL-15 signaling as a compelling strategy to unlock innate immunity against intracranial malignancies.
affiliations: University of California, Irvine (corresponding author)

papers.title: A semi-automated tool for improving Assessments and Lab Tests data annotation in ImmPort
papers.abstract: Public data sharing in immunological and clinical research is essential for transparency, reproducibility, and secondary analysis. However, many datasets in repositories such as ImmPort lack sufficient structured data to enable reuse. ImmPort's Assessments and Lab Tests templates -- which capture critical clinical information -- are often incomplete or omitted due to their complexity and the manual effort required. To address this challenge, an application with a graphical user interface requiring no programming was developed to facilitate population of these templates. The tool streamlines the submission process by reducing time and complexity for data contributors while ensuring template formatting. It integrates ImmPort files, study-specific data files, and a curated data dictionary to automate the mapping of study variables to the required fields within each template. The tool was evaluated on seven ImmPort studies with diverse designs. It successfully generated submission-ready templates that passed ImmPort's internal validation and will be incorporated into the repository. By improving the feasibility and completeness of templates, this approach enhances the quality, findability, and reusability of data within ImmPort.
affiliations: Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center/University of Cincinnati (corresponding author)

papers.title: Discoidins are cytosolic lectins that recognize methylated L-rhamnose epitopes on mycobacterial glycolipids and glycopeptidolipids upon vacuole damage
papers.abstract: Mycobacteria are surrounded by a dynamic, glycolipid-rich envelope that governs virulence and immune recognition, yet how cytosolic lectins sense its organization during intracellular infection remains unclear. Here, we show that Dictyostelium discoideum discoidins act as cytosolic sensors of mycobacterial envelope exposure. During infection, Mycobacterium marinum damages the limiting vacuolar membrane, triggering recruitment of all canonical isoforms (DscA, DscC, DscD, and DscE) to distinct foci around bacilli. Discoidins are not recruited after sterile endolysosomal damage, indicating that, unlike galectins, they recognize non-self surface-associated bacterial glycans rather than exposed host glycans. DscA and DscE display distinct glycan specificities. Combining transposon mutagenesis, synthetic glycan arrays, biochemical fractionation, and envelope mutants, we identify a restricted set of lipid-associated determinants enriched in methylated L-rhamnose motifs within LOS-, PGL-, and GPL-related structures. Recognition requires the conserved beta-galactoside-binding pocket of the H-type lectin domain, and isoform-specific synthetic disaccharides inhibit binding to intact bacteria. Analyses exclude AG-PG, AM/LAM, alpha-glucan, and TDM as major ligands and identify LOS and GPL-like glycolipids as dominant targets. PDIM/PGL or LOS disruption reduces discoidin binding to intact bacteria, although some ligands remain detectable in envelope extracts, underscoring the importance of accessibility. LOS deficiency also reduces DscA recruitment to intracellular bacilli. Therefore, binding of discoidins to glycan epitopes depends on ligand presence and accessibility, as well as on envelope perturbations and unmasking of specific glycolipids and glycopeptidolipids. These findings reveal pathogen envelope glycans as direct targets of cytosolic lectin surveillance and establish discoidins as probes of mycobacterial envelope remodeling during infection.
affiliations: University of Geneva (corresponding author)

papers.title: Type 6 secretion systems of adherent-invasive Escherichia coli isolated from Crohn's disease patients shape intestinal microbiota.
papers.abstract: Adherent Invasive Escherichia coli (AIEC) colonize the ileal mucosa of Crohn's disease patients. Among bacterial virulence factors potentially implicated, type 6 secretion systems (T6SS) are molecular machineries sending effectors in prokaryotic or eukaryotic target cells. Two T6SS have been reported in AIEC LF82 reference strain. Here, we show that T6SS genes are more prevalent in Crohn's disease patients' microbiota compared to healthy controls, and that T6SS are more frequent in AIEC pathovar compared to E. coli in general and associated with FimH pathoadaptive polymorphism. The use of an in vitro gastrointestinal system coupled with T6SS promoter reporter assay highlighted expression of LF82 T6SS under gastrointestinal conditions, with a major role for bile salts. In mice infected with AIEC LF82 versus T6SS-deleted mutants, T6SS showed a functional impact in modulating the composition of mucosa-associated gut microbiota. Thus, AIEC may use their T6SS to compete with endogenous microbiota to colonize host mucosa.
affiliations: UMR 1071 M2iSH (Microbes, Intestine, Inflammation and Susceptibility of the Host), Clermont Auvergne University, Inserm, INRAe USC 1382, Clermont-Ferrand, Franc (corresponding author)

papers.title: HIV remodels germinal centers through T follicular helper cell loss
papers.abstract: T follicular helper cells (Tfh) within germinal centers are among the most permissive cells for HIV infection and serve as a critical part of the viral reservoir. Given the key role of Tfh in affinity maturation and the production of plasma cells and memory B cells, an understanding of this critical viral reservoir is fundamental not only for cure strategies but also for understanding immunodeficiency in people living with HIV (PLWH). Using rare clinical specimens from PLWH, we demonstrate that HIV causes both a change in the cellular composition of germinal centers and changes in their overall architecture in ways that are consistent with the immunodeficiency seen in PLWH, independent of their CD4 count. We note a significant decrease in the number of GC Tfh cells and an increase in the number of follicular CD8 T cells in lymphoid tissues obtained from PLWH. Our data further show that GC size is decreased both by HIV and with increased age. Single-cell RNA sequencing data demonstrate that HIV acutely decreases the expression of Tfh B-cell support pathways and disrupts Tfh expression of cell trafficking receptors. Additionally, in a lymphoid organoid model of acute infection that forms GC-like structures, these findings are recapitulated, suggesting that New Approach Methodologies could be germane to understanding the impact of HIV on the reservoir and immunodeficiency. This study describes previously undocumented remodeling of the germinal center niche in PLWH, providing insight into the immune microenvironment of a key HIV reservoir that may help inform future cure strategies.
affiliations: University of South Florida Morsani College of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Label-free identification of bacterial species using adapted vision transformers
papers.abstract: Antibiotic resistance is an increasingly serious problem worldwide. Identifying the bacterial species can help guide antibiotic selection and improve patient outcomes. In sepsis, where every minute counts, rapid identification is particularly important, and new approaches are needed. In this study, deep learning models were trained to identify bacterial species from phase-contrast time-lapse images of cells growing in microfluidic traps, without fluorescent labels. We demonstrated this approach in two previous studies using laboratory strains. Here, the previous work is extended to clinical bacterial isolates, evaluating performance on isolates not seen during training. Furthermore, it was tested whether autofluorescence could aid species identification. Two validation sets were acquired in separate experiments from the training data, the first containing clinical-isolate traps with five species (Escherichia coli, Enterococcus faecalis, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus and Enterobacter cloacae), imaged every two minutes, and the second containing clinical isolates of two species (E. coli and K. pneumoniae) recovered from spiked donor blood, imaged every minute. Training with the best previous CNN method achieved unsatisfactory results. Therefore, vision transformers were explored, and a self-supervised adaptation procedure was developed for pretrained DINOv3 using a frozen teacher, followed by supervised classification using time-lapse montages. Mean macro-F1 was 93.6 {+/-} 1.3% for isolates precultured in Mueller-Hinton medium using 60 frames (118 minutes) and 87.2 {+/-} 2.7% for isolates precultured in blood using 55 frames (54 minutes) (mean {+/-} sample standard deviation across training seeds). Performance was evaluated over time by increasing the number of frames available to the model during testing, and Fourier-domain filtering approximated reduced numerical aperture. The results are promising and suggest that the aperture can be decreased while retaining good results. However, further evaluation on independent isolates, experiments and patient samples is needed to establish generalization. Together with previous findings, these results bring us closer to rapid image-based diagnostics that could transform the initial treatment of acute bacterial infections by enabling better-informed antibiotic selection.
affiliations: Department of Information Technology, Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden (corresponding author)

papers.title: A niche-specific role for ArlRS enables Staphylococcus aureus growth within Kupffer cells
papers.abstract: Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infections cause severe morbidity and mortality despite antibiotic therapy. We previously identified Kupffer cells (KCs) as the primary hepatic macrophages that rapidly clear circulating S. aureus, yet a subset of bacteria survives intracellularly and seeds systemic infection. Here, using spinning-disk intravital and super-resolution microscopy, we show that bacterial two-component system (TCS) signaling is required for intracellular replication within KCs in vivo. A global mutant lacking all non-essential TCSs failed to form intracellular microcolonies, and targeted analysis identified the ArlRS system as specifically required for KC replication. {Delta}arlRS bacteria remained as single non-replicating organisms within KCs, exhibited reduced dissemination and kidney abscess formation, and showed attenuated virulence with improved host survival. Complementation with arlRS restored the wildtype phenotype. Notably, the intracellular replication defect was not observed in primary or cultured macrophages, indicating that ArlRS-dependent replication is highly niche-specific and not reproduced by conventional in vitro models. Furthermore, restricting the KC reservoir with vancomycin treatment after infection further reduced renal infection by {Delta}arlRS bacteria. These findings identify ArlRS as a critical regulator of intracellular replication within KCs and establish the KC intracellular reservoir as a key driver of S. aureus pathogenesis and a potential therapeutic target during bloodstream infection.
affiliations: University of Calgary Cumming School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: A domesticated prophage enzyme links bacterial metabolism, episymbiosis and phage fitness
papers.abstract: Prophages are increasingly recognized as drivers of bacterial adaptation, yet how domesticated prophage genes shape microbial symbiosis remains poorly understood. Here, we identify GDPDXhp1, a glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase encoded by prophage Xhp1 of Schaalia odontolytica XH001, as a metabolic regulator linking bacterial physiology, episymbiosis and phage fitness. Association with the epibiotic bacterium Nanosynbacter lyticus TM7x strongly induced gdpdXhp1 expression and triggered GDPDXhp1-dependent lipid droplet accumulation in XH001. GDPDXhp1 orchestrated glycerophospholipid remodeling, membrane biophysical properties, respiration and cell-surface glycan composition in XH001, thereby promoting TM7x episymbiosis. Remarkably, GDPDXhp1 was also required for productive Xhp1 infection by remodeling susceptible bacterial host envelope structures to facilitate phage-host interactions. Together, our findings reveal a domesticated prophage enzyme that contributes to bacterial metabolism, interspecies symbiosis and viral reproduction, highlighting prophage as an overlooked source of metabolic innovation in microbial symbiosis.
affiliations: ADA Forsyth Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: AMMPER-2: A spatially explicit agent-based model of microbial radiobiology with redox dye simulation
papers.abstract: To reduce health risks for human space exploration, it is important to model the effects of deep-space radiation on biological systems. The budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a common model organism in space radiobiology, but little is known about how radiation damage to individual cells translates into the population-level effects that experiments measure. The Agent-Based Model for Microbial Populations Exposed to Radiation (AMMPER) is a spatially explicit agent-based model that simulates the effects of ionizing radiation on S. cerevisiae cells and produces population-level results. Its goal is to improve experiment design and data interpretation. AMMPER-1 demonstrated that agent-based simulations can qualitatively reproduce the effects of proton radiation on the growth rate of wild-type and DNA-repair mutant yeast. Here, we present AMMPER-2, which addresses limitations of the first model and expands its capabilities. AMMPER-2 incorporates the dynamics of the redox dye alamarBlue, a data type commonly generated in spaceflight microbiology experiments, and models the fate of reactive oxygen species in more detail. It also adds an improved graphical interface and runs faster. AMMPER-2 remains easy to execute in Python on a standard personal laptop, providing space biologists a tool to explore experimental conditions, generate hypotheses, and interpret data from microbial space radiation experiments.
affiliations: NASA Ames Research Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Complete ammonia-oxidizing Nitrospira and ammonia-oxidizing archaea as biological supplements for freshwater aquaria
papers.abstract: Biological filtration in newly established aquaria depends on the establishment of nitrifying microorganisms that prevent accumulation of toxic ammonia and nitrite. Many aquarists use commercial nitrifying supplements to accelerate biofilter establishment and reduce ammonia and nitrite accumulation. However, the microbial composition and in situ efficacy of these products remain poorly characterized. We evaluated the ability of enrichment cultures containing comammox Nitrospira (CX) and the ammonia-oxidizing archaeon Ca. Nitrosotenuis aquarius (AQ) to serve as aquarium nitrifying supplements, tested alongside a conventional supplement (CS) containing ammonia-oxidizing bacteria. Inoculation of new aquaria containing zebrafish (Danio rerio) with nitrifying supplements resulted in distinct nitrifier profiles within biofilters of each treatment group corresponding with significant reductions in peak ammonia and nitrite concentrations, which were most evident when applied at the maximum tested supplement dose. Treating aquaria with CX, AQ, or CS maintained ammonia and nitrite at low concentrations, and CX effectively prevented ammonia and nitrite accumulation through all stages of aquarium operation and biofilter establishment. After removing all fish from the aquaria, ammonia "spike-in" experiments demonstrated biofilters treated with CX and AQ conferred long-term protection against nitrite accumulation following acute ammonia loading events. Whereas 16S rRNA gene sequences associated with CS were rarely detected within biofilter profiles, those associated with CX and AQ established early and persisted temporally. Overall, results demonstrate how nitrifiers might be differentially adapted to home aquarium conditions and the potential of AOA and comammox Nitrospira to improve biofilter establishment and maintaining safe water quality in newly established freshwater aquaria.
affiliations: University of Waterloo (corresponding author)

papers.title: Widespread attraction of marine bacteria to the macroalgae-derived polysaccharide fucoidan
papers.abstract: Fucoidan is the second most abundant polysaccharide in brown macroalgae, contributing up to 50% of the dissolved organic matter released daily from these algae into the ocean, substantially influencing the marine carbon cycle. Due to its complex chemical structure, fucoidan is highly resistant to microbial degradation and accumulates on the surface of macroalgae, where it contributes to regulating their microbiome. Here, we used a range of microfluidic assays to quantify the chemotactic and physiological responses of marine bacteria to fucoidan. Our results reveal that all the strains tested (14 out of 14) are attracted to fucoidan produced by two different species of brown macroalgae. Attraction occurred only at high fucoidan concentrations (0.1 to 1 mg/mL), such as those expected in the immediate vicinity of algal surfaces, whereas low concentrations elicited no response or modest chemorepulsion. Although fucoidan did not support bacterial growth under our experimental conditions, it did not impair the utilization of other carbon sources. Together, these findings suggest that fucoidan gradients can act as chemical cues guiding marine bacteria toward the nutrient-rich microenvironment of macroalgal surfaces, pointing to a potential ecological role of fucoidan in shaping macroalgal microbiota, bacterial behavior, and ultimately carbon cycling in the ocean.
affiliations: Institute for Environmental Engineering, ETH Zurich, Switzerland (corresponding author)

papers.title: Urban Vietnam at the microbiome transition: Co-existing enterotypes reflect the global industrialization patterns
papers.abstract: Vietnam's rapid socioeconomic and dietary transition offers a rare window into how industrialization is reflected in the gut microbiome, yet Vietnamese populations remain underrepresented in global reference datasets. We investigated whether healthy Vietnamese adults in Hanoi harbor microbial community configurations associated with different stages of industrialization. Metagenomic data from stool samples of 183 clinically screened participants in Hanoi were analyzed alongside 629 publicly available metagenomic datasets from populations in low to middle income (LMI) and high income (HI) countries. Species-level taxonomic composition and gene-content-based metabolic pathways were characterized using community clustering and multivariable association analyses. Rather than forming a single population profile, the Vietnamese cohort separated into two enterotypes that mirrored the global industrialization gradient. Enterotype 1 more closely resembled populations from LMICs and showed greater microbial richness and diversity, whereas Enterotype 2 aligned with taxonomic and functional profiles observed in HICs. Both taxonomic and functional potential shows similar trajectories. Diet and lifestyle patterns describe some of the variance between enterotypes, supporting an association between contemporary exposures and microbiome structure without establishing causation. Antibiotic resistance profiles also varied between enterotypes, suggesting that the transition may encompass functions relevant to antimicrobial exposure. Together, these findings position urban Vietnam at a microbiome transition, where community states associated with different levels of industrialization coexist within a single population. This Vietnamese reference cohort expands representation in global metagenomic research and provides a baseline for tracking how rapid socioeconomic change may reshape microbial ecology, metabolic capacity, and antimicrobial resistance.
affiliations: Vinmec-VinUni Institute of Immunology, College of Health Sciences, VinUniversity, Hanoi, Vietnam (corresponding author)

papers.title: Staphylococcus aureus GpsB, Stk, and VraSR form a cell wall surveillance network to maintain cell envelope integrity and mediate antibiotic resistance
papers.abstract: Antibiotic resistance is an alarming threat to public health worldwide. Specifically, drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus remains a major contributor to global mortality. Therefore, in-depth understanding of antibiotic resistance mechanisms is urgently needed to inform alternative therapeutic strategies. We previously showed that GpsB is a critical regulator of cell wall synthesis in S. aureus. GpsB executes its regulatory role via protein-protein interactions. Yet, how GpsB function is modulated in this organism has remained unclear. Intriguingly, a prior proteomics report indicated that GpsB is phosphorylated at six different residues by the sole serine/threonine kinase Stk. Hence, we explored the physiological significance of GpsB phosphorylation. We identify three phosphosites that are each independently sufficient to drive GpsB phosphoregulation, which likely alters its partner preference. We find that cells lacking gpsB exhibit heightened fosfomycin sensitivity, and that this is exacerbated by stk deletion. Our findings reveal that GpsB collaborates with Stk and the VraSR cell wall stress response system to coordinate the demand-driven availability of cell wall precursors. Collectively, this report establishes GpsB as a pivotal peptidoglycan supply chain sentinel that together with Stk and VraSR forms an integrated cell wall stress monitoring network that maintains cell envelope homeostasis and aids in antibiotic resistance.
affiliations: Department of Molecular Biosciences, University of South Florida, Tampa, Florida, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Water Kefir as a Model for Aggregative Development of Microbial Multicellularity within a Multispecies Biofilm
papers.abstract: Water kefir is a traditional fermented beverage and a non-dairy alternative to milk kefir. Water kefir grains are cauliflower-like aggregates, ranging in size from 1-20 mm. They are composed of an exopolysaccharide matrix derived from the fermentation substrate sucrose. The microbial community on and within the grains is a complex, highly stable multicellular aggregate typically consisting of 10-15 core species that primarily belong to three major groups: lactic acid bacteria, acetic acid bacteria, and yeasts. Remarkably, the structural organisation, stability, and growth of kefir grains cannot be readily explained by their constituent species alone, and attempts to reconstitute them from the isolated species have so far been unsuccessful. Here, we combined a comprehensive structural investigation of the macro- and micromorphology of water kefir grains with culture-dependent and -independent analyses of its microbial biodiversity. The dynamics and interactions within this complex microbial community were studied by combining flow cytometry, fluorescence-activated cell sorting, and amplicon sequencing of selected subpopulations. Furthermore, the growth of water kefir grains was spatiotemporally resolved and quantitatively characterised, thereby unravelling an emergent multicellular growth function, documented for the first time. Our combined evidence provides an unprecedented understanding of a highly structured and metabolically synergistic multicellular microbial aggregate and lets us propose water kefir as a model system for the aggregative development of microbial multicellularity from multiple species. It should lay the foundation for future mechanistic studies aimed at understanding how multispecies microbial communities self-organise into stable, spatially structured multicellular aggregates.
affiliations: TUD Dresden University of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Transcriptomics uncovers outer membrane remodeling as conserved strategy for Burkholderia cenocepacia survival in protozoan and macrophage phagosomes
papers.abstract: Bacterivorous protists expose bacteria to hostile stress conditions that resemble those encountered within macrophage phagosomes and may therefore act as training grounds for bacterial pathogens. However, the mechanisms enabling bacterial survival within protozoan phagosomes remain poorly understood. Here we characterized the transcriptome of the opportunistic pathogen Burkholderia cenocepacia during transit through phagosomes and expelled food vacuoles of the ubiquitous protozoan ciliate Tetrahymena elliotti. Our data revealed a coordinated response involving bacterial metabolic reprogramming, with the upregulation of NADPH-generating pathways and host nutrient uptake systems, alongside the activation of several stress responses and envelope remodeling to maintain outer membrane barrier function and repair phagosomal damage. Disruption of antioxidant defenses, the RpoE-dependent envelope stress response, the Mla pathway and other proteins required for outer membrane integrity severely impaired intracellular survival in both protozoa and macrophages, revealing conserved mechanisms required for persistence within evolutionarily distant phagocytes. This adaptive response not only contributed to survival but it also primed B. cenocepacia for increased chlorhexidine resistance and adhesion to collagen and human lung epithelial cells. Collectively, our findings reveal that protozoan phagosomes drive physiological adaptations with consequences extending beyond grazing resistance. Protozoa may therefore disseminate stress-adapted bacteria with enhanced resistance and colonization potential, providing a mechanistic link between adaptation to environmental predators and survival in the human host.
affiliations: Complutense University of Madrid (corresponding author)

papers.title: TonB-dependent Transporters of Fe-petrobactin in Marinobacter nauticus and Southern Ocean bacteria
papers.abstract: TonB-dependent transporters (TBDTs) play a central role in siderophore-mediated iron acquisition in the marine environment. However, assigning substrate specificity to TBDTs remains a major bottleneck in understanding the ecological and mechanistic roles of siderophore production and uptake. Here, we identify in Marinobacter nauticus two TBDTs, OptA and OptB, that share low sequence identity yet both mediate Fe-petrobactin uptake. Despite this functional overlap, they underlie distinct regulatory mechanisms, suggesting differential utilization under specific environmental conditions. Phylogenetic analyses indicate that OptA likely co-evolved with the petrobactin biosynthetic gene cluster, whereas OptB appears to have followed a distinct evolutionary trajectory, acquiring the capacity to import petrobactin as a xenosiderophore. Using resuscitated communities from the Southern Ocean, we further show that Fe-petrobactin stimulated prokaryotic growth. Based on amino acid similarity, we identified OptB-like transporters encoded in metagenomes and MAGs and show that taxa harbouring these transporters, such as Pseudoaltermonas, respond specifically to Fe-petrobactin addition. OptB-like transporters were also detected in environmental metagenomes from the Southern Ocean, whereas the petrobactin biosynthetic gene clusters were not, indicating that petrobactin primarily functions as a xenosiderophore in natural communities.
affiliations: IPREM: Institut des Sciences Analytiques et de Physico-chimie pour l'Environnement et les Materiaux (corresponding author)

papers.title: Non-canonical alternate interactors of SARS CoV-2 Spike protein implicated in placental susceptibilty
papers.abstract: Vertical transmission of SARS-CoV-2 is controversial. Owing to the low expression of ACE2 along with TMPRSS2 in placenta, role of secondary receptors becomes significant. In our study we predicted twelve interactors of spike protein expressed in placenta through interactome analysis followed by docking and molecular dynamic simulation. Three interactors of SARS-CoV-2 spike protein were found to be CD147, EGFR and LDLR. Expression at transcriptomic and translational level by real-time PCR and immunohistochemistry respectively was observed in placenta samples obtained from women with COVID exposure risk and compared to control. Elevated protein levels of CD147 (OR=14.667), ACE2 (OR=8.25) and LDLR (OR=1.9) was associated with higher exposure risk. However, the variation in mRNA expression was not statistically significant. Computational study showed that CD147/basigin, EGFR and LDLR stably interact with spike protein outside its primary receptor binding domain. In-vitro binding assay confirmed the physical interaction between spike protein and the placental receptors. In-silico site-directed mutagenesis further identified key potential binding hotspots of spike protein- Tyr28 and Trp64 for CD147, Phe643, Val642, Thr632 for LDLR and Leu8, Phe59, Phe32, Tyr28, Trp64, Trwp152, His245, and Val213 for EGFR. Finally, concluded that CD147, EGFR and LDLR might act as secondary non-canonical cofactors for SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in placenta, thereby increasing its susceptibility and tissue tropism. The study overall gives a better insight into potential placental suscpetibility providing targeted therapeutic opportunities.
affiliations: Presidency University (corresponding author)

papers.title: The porin MspA is a phage-specific determinant of mycobacteriophage infection
papers.abstract: Mycobacteriophages are being developed as therapeutics for mycobacterial infections, but their highly variable host ranges limit this application and the bacterial factors that determine whether infection succeeds remain poorly defined. The determinants characterized so far are dominated by cell envelope lipids and glycolipids. Here, we performed a genome-wide CRISPRi screen in Mycobacterium smegmatis to identify host functions associated with susceptibility to BPs{Delta}33HTH HRM10. After prolonged phage challenge, the outer membrane porin genes mspA and mspC were among the most strongly enriched hits, whereas the closely related paralogs mspB and mspD were not enriched despite sharing high amino-acid identity across the family. Deletion of mspA or mspC reduced BPs{Delta}33HTH HRM10 plaque formation and produced smaller, more turbid plaques, with the stronger phenotype following loss of mspA, the major outer membrane porin of M. smegmatis. Across a panel of 25 mycobacteriophages, 11 showed either a more than tenfold reduction in titer or loss of discrete plaque formation on {Delta}mspA, while the remainder were largely unaffected. These findings identify outer membrane porins as phage-dependent determinants of mycobacterial susceptibility, revealing an additional layer of specificity in phage infection beyond previously characterized cell envelope lipids and glycolipids.
affiliations: Department of Microbiology, Tumor and Cell Biology (MTC), Karolinska Institutet, Solna, Sweden; Science for Life Laboratory, Karolinska Institutet, Solna, Swede (corresponding author)

papers.title: Insights Into an Antibacterial Type VI Membrane-Disrupting Effector Of Adherent Invasive Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Adherent Invasive Escherichia coli (AIEC) strains are associated with ileal Crohn's disease and may contribute to intestinal dysbiosis through antibacterial competition. The AIEC reference strain LF82 encodes two type VI secretion systems (T6SSs), a contractile machine that injects an effector-loaded needle made of Hcp, VgrG and PAAR into neighbouring rivals, favoring niche colonization. LF82 T6SSs harbour several putative antibacterial toxin-immunity modules. Here we characterize the T6SS-1 encoded TmeAIEC, a PAAR-fused T6SS effector carrying a C-terminal Tme domain, hallmark of Tme (Type VI membrane disrupting effector) toxins, and its DUF1240-like immunity protein TmiAIEC. When heterologously produced in E. coli K-12 as well as in E. coli and Citrobacter clinical isolates, TmeAIEC is toxic only upon periplasmic targeting, and its toxicity is neutralized by TmiAIEC. Periplasmically-targeted TmeAIEC inserts into the inner membrane, collapses the proton motive force and increases cell permeability, consistent with a membrane-disrupting activity. Mutational analyses coupled to functional assays identified a predicted hydrophobic transmembrane segment and a conserved aspartate residue within the Tme domain as key determinants for TmeAIEC toxicity. These findings establish TmeAIEC/TmiAIEC as a functional T6SS toxin-immunity pair and reveal conserved determinants underlying the activity of Tme-family membrane-disrupting effectors.

papers.title: Exchange of metabolic pathway intermediates as the origin for metabolite cross-feeding interactions in E. coli auxotrophic co-cultures
papers.abstract: A large fraction of microbes in natural environments are auxotrophs that rely on metabolite exchange for growth. The Black Queen hypothesis and related frameworks explain gene loss and reliance on shared metabolites. Yet it is not fully understood how metabolite cross-feeding emerges and gives rise to experimentally observable community performance. Here, we propose that exchange of biosynthetic pathway intermediates provides a mechanistic route for the emergence of metabolite cross-feeding. Building on prior work demonstrating intermediate exchange in E. coli auxotrophs, we investigated co-cultures between a methionine auxotroph ({Delta}metA) and a panel of histidine auxotrophs. Among these, only {Delta}hisD exhibited efficient co-culture growth with {Delta}metA, suggesting a unique role for the final step of histidine biosynthesis, which converts histidinol to histidine. We found that {Delta}metA-{Delta}hisD co-cultures accumulated high levels of extracellular histidinol (>200 M), suggesting a mechanism for metabolite exchange. Spent media from these co-cultures supported growth of all histidine auxotrophs except {Delta}hisD, confirming that histidinol, rather than histidine, was the dominant exchanged metabolite. Furthermore, we observed that {Delta}metA efficiently converted histidinol to histidine only under methionine-limited conditions, suggesting that nutrient limitation promoted overflow of converted histidine to the extracellular environment. To quantitatively assess whether histidinol exchange could account for the observed co-culture behavior, we constructed a mechanistic model that links extracellular histidinol dynamics to co-culture growth through independently measured conversion capacity of the {Delta}metA strain. Rather than fitting growth empirically, we used experimentally derived parameters to predict co-culture growth from the measured histidinol-to-histidine conversion flux. The model accurately recapitulated the timing and magnitude of growth and population dynamics, supporting the idea that accumulation of histidinol enabled the conversion-driven supply of histidine that sustained {Delta}hisD, while coupling growth between the two strains. Taken together, these results suggest that metabolite cross-feeding in syntrophic co-cultures can emerge from the accumulation of pathway intermediates and their conditional conversion under nutrient limitation, providing a plausible mechanism for the rapid establishment of mutualistic interactions.
affiliations: University of Michigan (corresponding author)

papers.title: Predicted structure of the 89-kDa invasion-tip protein of Holospora obtusa, an endonuclear symbiont of Paramecium caudatum, suggests a pH-dependent conformational change
papers.abstract: The endonuclear symbiont Holospora obtusa invades the macronucleus of Paramecium caudatum using an infectious-form invasion-tip containing a major 89-kDa periplasmic protein implicated in escape from the host digestive vacuole and macronuclear invasion. Sequence-based analyses placed this protein within a Holospora-specific family and predicted an N-terminal membrane-anchoring module and a long alpha-helical C-terminal region. AlphaFold2 modeling followed by molecular dynamics indicated that the C-terminal region forms an antiparallel, spectrin-repeat-like helical solenoid containing a localized three-helix coiled-coil. The protein exhibits a large pH-dependent charge difference, becoming 55 units more positive at pH 4 than at pH 7. Independent simulations at these pH values differed mainly in the relative orientation of the N-terminal core and C-terminal rod, described by DynDom as an approximately 35 degrees rigid-body rotation about a hinge centered on Gly291. However, none of the nearby glutamates (Glu273, Glu275, and Glu302) formed a pH-dependent salt bridge, and no specific protonation-dependent interaction responsible for the conformational difference was identified. We nonetheless propose, as a testable hypothesis, that acidification of the digestive vacuole may promote this reorientation, thereby repositioning the N-terminal membrane-anchoring module at the bacterial surface as an early step toward escape from the vacuole.
affiliations: Yamaguchi University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Immunomodulatory RIG-I Agonist SLR14 Confers Protection Against a Range of Highly Pathogenic Negative Sense RNA viruses
papers.abstract: Emerging and re-emerging zoonotic RNA viruses, including filoviruses, henipaviruses and Rift Valley Fever virus (RVFV), pose a significant threat to human health. Due to their epidemic potential and high pathogenicity, these viruses are categorized as WHO priority pathogens, yet we still lack effective medical countermeasures (MCMs) against most of these dangerous pathogens, supporting that host-directed antivirals will be advantageous for broadly acting MCMs. Here we assessed the antiviral efficacy of SLR14, an immunomodulatory stem-loop RNA that activates RIG-I, for its activity against a panel of highly pathogenic viruses. SLR14 treatment provided broad-spectrum protection, markedly reducing infection with Ebola virus (EBOV), Marburg virus, and Sudan virus in human primary monocyte-derived macrophages, and Nipah virus replication in iPSC-derived endothelial cells, whether administered prophylactically or therapeutically. In vivo, a single dose of SLR14 protected mice against lethal RVFV infection when administered prophylactically, and, notably, retained significant efficacy when administered up to two days post-infection. Therapeutic SLR14 administration also improved survival rates of EBOV-infected mice. Although EBOV infection and SLR14 treatment activated overlapping innate immune pathways in human macrophages, viral infection induced a nonprotective response, whereas SLR14 elicited a well-regulated, markedly stronger and protective interferon-stimulated and inflammatory gene signature while avoiding prolonged IFN gene upregulation. Our data identify SLR14 as a potent host-directed therapeutic with broad antiviral efficacy against some of the most lethal viral pathogens.
affiliations: Boston University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Loss of KMT2D accelerates hypertrophic chondrocyte differentiation and senescence by increasing mitochondrial ROS production
papers.abstract: Longitudinal bone growth occurs through endochondral ossification, which is accompanied by the differentiation of chondrocytes in the growth plate. Disruption in chondrocyte maturation can lead to skeletal growth abnormalities, such as those observed in Kabuki syndrome type 1 (KS1), a genetic disorder caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the KMT2D gene. KS1 patients exhibit postnatal growth deficiency, craniofacial hypoplasia, and skeletal deformities, yet the mechanisms underlying these phenotypic manifestations remain poorly understood. Our study investigated the effects of KMT2D deficiency on chondrocyte maturation and identified premature chondrocyte hypertrophy as a key driver of skeletal abnormalities in KS1. We previously observed reduced femur and tibia length in a KS1 mouse model, along with altered growth plate architecture, particularly affecting the heights of the proliferative and hypertrophic zones. Here, we show that KMT2D-deficient chondrocytes exhibit accelerated differentiation and early senescence upon exposure to supraphysiological oxygen levels (20% O2). These pathological changes were linked to increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production likely caused by deficiencies in electron transport chain function, leading to oxidative stress and premature hypertrophy. Pharmacological ROS neutralization or hypoxic conditions mitigated these effects, restoring normal chondrocyte differentiation and preventing premature ossification. These findings demonstrate that KMT2D loss induces oxidative stress-driven chondrocyte hypertrophy, disrupting the balance of cartilage growth and ossification. Our study provides crucial mechanistic insights into KS1-associated skeletal abnormalities and suggests mitochondrial ROS regulation as a potential therapeutic avenue.
affiliations: University of Iceland, National University Hospital of Iceland, Johns Hopkins University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Queuosine glycosylation occurs after anticodon loop methylations and protects against stress-induced tRNA fragmentation
authors: Schwarzer, A. C. d. A. P.
papers.abstract: Queuosine, present at position 34 (Q34) of vertebrate tRNAAsp and tRNATyr, is mannosylated and galactosylated by QTMAN and QTGAL, respectively. However, the interplay between these glycosylations and other anticodon loop modifications, and their impact on tRNA fragmentation, have remained unknown. Here, we define hierarchical modification pathways for the anticodon loop modifications of the two human glycoQ34-containing tRNAs. Our data reveal bidirectional interdependence of Q34 and m5C38 in tRNAAsp with subsequent Q34 mannosylation occurring in an m5C38-independent manner. Anticodon loop modifications of tRNATyr are installed independently, but sequentially in a pathway in which TRMT5-mediated m1G37 formation precedes queuosinylation and galactosylation. Q34 glycosylation enhances protein synthesis but alongside their canonical function in translation, tRNAs are precursors of tRNA-derived fragments that can regulate diverse aspects of gene expression. Our data reveal that Q34 mannosylation protects tRNAAsp from stress-induced cleavage and modulates cleavage site selection, thus expanding the relevance of Q glycosylation beyond translation.
affiliations: University Medical Center Goettingen (corresponding author)

papers.title: A developmental resource mapping tubulin isotype deployment during corneal morphogenesis
papers.abstract: Microtubules are core cytoskeletal polymers that support epithelial organization, polarity, and tissue morphogenesis. They are composed of - and {beta}-tubulin heterodimers encoded by multigene families that generate closely related but distinct isotypes. Although several tubulin isotypes have been implicated in ocular development and disease, their spatial organization during corneal morphogenesis remains poorly defined. Here we establish a resource visualizing and quantifying tubulin isotype localization during corneal development using the chick embryo. Comparative amino acid sequence analysis demonstrates that chick and human - and {beta}-tubulin isotypes are highly conserved within structural and catalytic domains, with divergence concentrated in C-terminal regions normally associated with post-translational modification sites. Relating sequence features to tissue organization, we performed longitudinal immunohistochemical analysis of five tubulin isotypes across corneal development. These analyses reveal distinct and dynamic patterns of isotype enrichment along apicobasal axes, as well as stage-dependent redistribution during epithelial maturation and endothelial differentiation. TUBA5/TUBA4A displays particularly restricted localization, including enrichment in migratory corneal stromal progenitors and the developing corneal epithelium and endothelium . Together, these data provide a conserved spatial framework for tubulin isotype organization during corneal morphogenesis and establish the chick embryo as a tractable model for investigating isotype-specific microtubule organization during epithelial development.
affiliations: University of California, Davis (corresponding author)

papers.title: Single-cell exploration of ovarian aging across mammalian models
papers.abstract: Female reproductive lifespan is limited by a finite ovarian reserve, and its depletion leads to menopause and chronic disease risk. However, the molecular drivers of ovarian aging remain poorly understood, and preclinical models are not well benchmarked against human ovarian biology. We harmonized public single-cell and single-nucleus ovarian RNA-seq datasets from human, macaque, mouse, and goat for cross-species analysis of ovarian aging. Granulosa cell loss was the most consistent compositional change, and granulosa and theca cells showed the largest age-associated transcriptional shifts. Aging granulosa cells downregulated DNA repair genes and induced cell-cycle inhibitor genes across species, and shifted along an age-associated pseudotime trajectory in human and mouse. Using ASGARD, we nominated drug repurposing candidates with cross-species support that could reverse age-related transcriptional changes. Together, our meta-analysis identifies conserved and species-specific features of ovarian aging, which provides a framework to nominate potential interventions prolonging fertility or protecting against its systemic impacts.
affiliations: University of Southern California (corresponding author)

papers.title: Expanding the DNA Motif Lexicon of the Transcriptional Regulatory Code
papers.abstract: Cis-regulatory sequences in metazoan genomes contain elaborate combinations of transcription factor (TF) motifs. Stereospecific arrangements of simple motifs constitute composite elements (CEs) that enhance DNA-protein interaction specificity and enable combinatorial regulatory logic. Despite their importance, CEs remain underexplored. We integrate genome-scale computational discovery (CEseek) with customized massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs) to uncover cell type-specific and shared CEs, corroborated by coincident and/or cooperative TF binding in vivo and in vitro. A deep learning model, GRACE, trained on MPRA data at single-nucleotide resolution, learns the CE lexicon and predicts activities of variants and alternative stereospecific CE configurations not included in the experimental design. Comparative analysis with models trained on orthogonal features such as chromatin accessibility, demonstrates convergence within the CE lexicon while resolving how individual motifs contribute to transcription versus chromatin accessibility. The expanded lexicon enables CE-aware predictions and interpretation of the impact of disease-associated non-coding variants in. the human genome.
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genomic insights into bacterial isolates dominating honeypot ant crop microbiomes reveal metabolically distinct Fructilactobacillus sp.
papers.abstract: Honeypot ants engage in a convergently-evolved phenotype called repletism, where specialized workers expand their crops and gasters to store vast amounts of food internally. They then store that food for months to support colonies during times of food scarcity. This fascinating phenotype is not well-understood and only recently have the microbial interactions been studied within the fructose-rich replete crops of these ants. Previous research using amplicon sequencing showed that Fructilactobacillus dominates the crop microbiomes of Myrmecocystus mexicanus repletes. This striking result and successful isolation of those strains led to the present investigation into the phylogenetic diversity of these strains and any clues to the nature of the symbiotic relationship between them and the ant host.
