Using a dataset of 83 RNA-Seq samples from five time points during adult mouse lifespan, we show that colon aging is characterized by multiple gene-expression trajectories unfolding in parallel, with a major shift occurring during a mid- to late-life transition marked by a collapse of the unfolded protein response (UPR). Moreover, we report widespread non-monotonic trajectories, including genes that peak or dip in midlife and would be missed by comparisons limited to young versus old ages. We further describe age-dependent dynamics of transposable element-containing transcripts and a nonlinear course of transcriptomic entropy across the lifespan. Importantly, we identify a small set of genes that track chronological age and use only three of them to construct a compact transcriptomic clock, which we validate using an independent RNA-seq dataset and qPCR data. Together, our results indicate that nonlinear patterns dominate the aging colon transcriptome and underscore the value of high temporal resolution for identifying key transitions during aging.
affiliations: Leibniz Institute on Aging - Fritz Lipmann Institute (FLI) (corresponding author)

papers.title: CCT2 expression marks a translation-activated state in sporadic ALS motor neurons and is associated with functional decline
papers.abstract: Sporadic disease accounts for about 90% of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases, and its biological heterogeneity is a major contributor to the failure of trials that enroll patients under a single diagnosis. Because sporadic ALS lacks a shared genetic anchor, identifying biological signals is critical for effective patient stratification. We analyzed induced pluripotent stem cell derived motor neurons from 619 AnswerALS participants using transcriptomics, proteomics, and whole-genome sequencing and identified CCT2 as the first single-gene marker of a molecular state within sporadic ALS, providing a measurable basis for trial enrollment according to biology. We first anchored the analysis in known ALS genotypes. C9orf72 and SOD1 motor neurons did not converge on a common signature but retained genotype-specific differences that bulk postmortem tissue compresses. Scoring 391 sporadic patients along three transcriptomic axes (bioenergetic stress, cell cycle, and inflammation) resolved three states. One state was marked by CCT2, a TRiC chaperonin subunit, which distinguished it from the quiescent state with an area under the curve of 0.892. CCT2 was also elevated at the protein level and associated with the rate of ALSFRS-R decline, although this association weakened after adjustment for culture composition. Upstream regulator analysis placed this state downstream of MYC and mTORC1 activation. No germline test across 360 whole genomes explained these states. Validation using Target ALS data showed that the relationship between CCT2 and the cell cycle program was also present in postmortem cortex enriched for layer 5b projection neurons.
affiliations: Department of Computational Biomedicine, Cedars Sinai Medical Center, CA, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Interchain base-stacking and spermine bridges govern ssDNA condensation and reentrant transitions
papers.abstract: Polyvalent-cation-induced condensation and reentrant transition in double-stranded DNA are classically described by backbone electrostatics. Whether the same principles govern single-stranded DNA, whose solvent-exposed bases can interact within and between chains to form complex phases, is unknown. Here, we employ simulations and experiments to show that the tetravalent cation spermine (Spm4+) drives two equilibrium transitions in poly(dT) and poly(dA). The onset of phase separation, resulting in thermodynamic equilibrium between the dispersed low-density phase and high density coacervate, occurs at a low sequence independent Spm4+ concentration and is primarily driven by charge balance between phosphate groups and Spm4+. Strikingly, the condensed phases are stabilized by at most 1.5 (poly dT) and 2.5 (poly dA) bridging Spm4+ per chain. The ssDNA chains condense to form fluid-like networks without chain collapse. The fluidity of chains in the dense phases is confirmed by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching experiments. Both simulations and experiments show that the range of spermine concentration over which phase coexistence persists is sequence dependent and nearly threefold wider in poly(dA). At higher sequence dependent spermine concentrations, a reentrant phase, characterized by dissolution of the coacervates, emerges. The transition to the reentrant phase occurs when the number of bridging Spm4+ molecules vanishes at high sequence dependent spermine concentration. The combination of experiments and simulations show that the two phase transitions in ssDNA are driven by an interplay of stacking and electrostatic interactions.
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin (corresponding author)

papers.title: Efficient detection of cryptic pockets on challenging drug targets using MD-free co-vibrational modes
papers.abstract: Allosteric and cryptic binding sites provide unique opportunities in drug discovery for achieving selectivity, reducing toxicity and unlocking challenging therapeutical targets. Yet, cryptic pockets are particularly elusive in that they are difficult to capture with experimental methodologies, and therefore often remain undetected. Computational approaches for flexible cryptic site detection traditionally involve extensive unbiased molecular dynamics simulations, or more efficient but computationally still highly demanding biased MD alternatives that make use of enhanced sampling along low-frequency motions of the protein structure. Here we utilize a new variant of the recently introduced and orders of magnitude faster, MD-free COVIB algorithm to identify cryptic pockets efficiently in two challenging targets, the KRAS oncoprotein and the N-terminal domain of the STAT5B transcription factor. Using experimental and AI-modelled structures, respectively, we identify numerous cryptic sites, some of which have not yet been reported. The sites are prioritized and validated with our pharmacophore optimized photoaffinity-tagged fragment library via MS-based peptide mapping and NMR spectroscopy. Besides identifying new, targetable regions on the surface of these important oncotargets, we have established a protocol combining COVIB-based cryptic pocket detection and photoaffinity-based experimental peptide mapping as a robust approach for exploring unique and tractable cryptic pockets.
affiliations: Flagship Pioneering, Pioneering Intelligence, 55 Cambridge Pkwy, Cambridge, MA 02142, U. S. A. (corresponding author)

papers.title: The Dilated Cardiomyopathy E525K Mutation Stabilizes the Cardiac Myosin Interacting-Heads Motif While Activating the Isolated Motor Domain
papers.abstract: Mutations in {beta}-cardiac myosin are a common cause of inherited cardiomyopathies. The dilated cardiomyopathy E525K mutation alters both thick filament regulation and motor activity, yet the structural basis for these effects has remained unclear. Here, we combined cryo-EM and MD simulations to determine how E525K affects the conformational landscape of cardiac myosin in both its autoinhibited interacting-heads motif (IHM) and isolated myosin head states. E525K-mutated myosin exclusively adopted a single S2 conformation in IHM, in contrast to the conformational heterogeneity observed in wild-type myosin. Structural and electrostatic analyses revealed that the mutation increased positive charge density at the blocked-head (BH) - S2 (subfragment-2) interface, strengthening interactions with negatively charged residues within S2. 3D variability analysis and MD simulations of the E525K IHM demonstrated reduced S2 mobility, consistent with strengthened BH - S2 interactions, and decreased conformational flexibility, providing a structural mechanism for stabilization of the IHM state. To investigate the isolated myosin head, we determined cryo-EM structures of wild-type and E525K subfragment-1 (S1). The mutation induced local conformational rearrangements in the activation-loop and Loop 3 region, the SH3-like domain, and the essential light chain of S1, revealing structural changes that support the enhanced motor activity previously reported for isolated E525K myosin motors. These findings show that E525K stabilizes the autoinhibited IHM through electrostatic stabilization of the BH - S2 interface while inducing structural changes consistent with activation of the isolated motor domain, providing structural insights into how a single DCM mutation differentially regulates cardiac myosin S1 and IHM structure and function.
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School, Worcester, MA, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Minimal Model of Functional Redundancy as a Route to Enzyme Specialisation
papers.abstract: Functional overlap among enzymes could permit individual proteins to specialise while maintaining organismal reaction performance. We examine this possibility in a minimal origin--fixation model in which weak generalists jointly supply 120 reactions and fitness depends on aggregate catalytic capacity. Pleiotropic mutations act on loop-local activity profiles subject to a tunable structural incompatibility constraint. No gene duplication occurs during evolution. A factorial sweep combines five initial redundancies, two mutation kernels, and four incompatibility values, with five replicates per combination and 250 fixed substitutions per simulation. Across all 40 parameter combinations, effective protein breadth decreases and the strongest function accounts for a larger share of activity. Mean breadth reductions range from 1.59 to 3.97 under the loss-biased kernel and from 6.32 to 8.16 under the symmetric kernel. Specialisation therefore does not require a mutational bias towards biochemical loss. Higher redundancy generally buffers weakest-reaction performance under loss-biased mutation, while structural incompatibility has a non-monotonic effect on specialisation. Total activity increases, but is not conserved by the model and does not measure a conservation-based efficiency gain. These results establish that duplication is not a logical prerequisite for specialisation in this class of model: distributed catalytic contributions can reorganise while aggregate reaction performance remains comparatively buffered.
affiliations: UCL Department of Chemistry, Christopher Ingold Building, 20 Gordon Street, London, UK (corresponding author)

papers.title: A signaling-optimized TIGIT chimeric switch receptor promotes metabolic fitness and antitumor efficacy of TCR/CAR T cells
papers.abstract: Adoptive T cell therapies have revolutionized the treatment of hematological malignancies, however, their efficacy against solid tumors often remains limited. Lack of activation and overabundance of immune checkpoint-mediated inhibitory signals from cancer cells drive T cell dysfunction and limit persistence. To circumvent this imbalance towards inhibitory factors, we engineered a chimeric switch receptor (CSR) that repurposes the immunosuppressive TIGIT extracellular domain by fusing it to a CD28-derived stimulatory signaling tail. Here we show that while the prototype CSR design enhances immediate cytolytic activity, it also induces premature proliferative arrest and terminal differentiation due to excessive tonic signaling. By introducing a strategic point mutation within the CD28 cytoplasmic domain, we "fine-tuned" the activation threshold of the CSR for optimal functional properties. Engineered T cells with 'fine-tuned' CSR exhibit superior mitochondrial bioenergetics and sustained metabolic flux in an in vitro system of chronic antigen exposure. In preclinical xenograft models, fine-tuned CSR-expressing T cells demonstrated robust expansion and durable persistence, leading to complete tumor eradication. These findings provide a scalable strategy to rewire inhibitory checkpoints into tailored costimulatory signals, offering a potent approach to enhance the metabolic fitness and persistence of therapeutic T cells, in suppressive tumor microenvironments, in particular.
affiliations: Department of Hematology and Medical Oncology, University Medical Center Mainz (UMC), Mainz, Germany; German Cancer Consortium (DKTK), Partner Site Frankfurt/Ma (corresponding author)

papers.title: PPARγ brakes cytosolic DNA-induced macrophage inflammation by super-enhancer metabolic reprogramming
papers.abstract: Cytoplasmic DNA sensing triggers intense innate immune responses that require tight regulation. PPAR{gamma} is a master metabolic regulator in macrophages, but its role in cytoplasmic DNA immunity remains unclear. Using poly(dA:dT) to mimic cytoplasmic DNA stimulation, we combined transcriptomics, epigenomics (PPAR{gamma}/H3K27ac ChIP-seq), and functional assays. Poly(dA:dT) induced a cytokine storm with MAPK activation and apoptosis/necrosis. PPAR{gamma} activation by rosiglitazone (RGZ) antagonized this response, reducing cell death and transcriptionally inhibiting MAPK genes (e.g., DUSP4/10). Mechanistically, PPAR{gamma} bound promoters/enhancers via PPRE motifs and distal intergenic regions, remodeling H3K27ac (reduced at inflammatory loci, increased at metabolic genes). RGZ induced de novo super-enhancers coupling PPAR metabolic programs (e.g., CPT2) with immune suppression by targeting TLR4, CEBPB, and PIM3. Thus, PPAR{gamma} acts as a brake in cytoplasmic DNA immunity, integrating metabolic reprogramming and inflammation suppression through a multi-level genomic/epigenetic program. This study highlights PPAR{gamma} as a key immune-metabolic integrator and therapeutic target for diseases driven by excessive cytoplasmic DNA sensing.
affiliations: Northwest A&F University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Phage phenotyping by measuring plaque expansion dynamics
papers.abstract: Bacteriophages exhibit staggering genomic diversity, yet phenotypic characterization remains bottlenecked by assays that generally yield simple binary infection outcomes. Quantitative traits can be extracted from standard liquid cultures, but many phages fail to produce a measurable effect in these settings, necessitating an improved quantitative approach on semi-solid media. While end-point plaque size is commonly used for quantitative phenotyping, it only provides a static snapshot that fails to disentangle phage performance across changing bacterial growth phases. Here, we report a cost-effective, scalable method to quantify the bacterial killing rates of diverse phages by continuously tracking plaque development using a consumer-grade flatbed scanner and custom open-source computer vision software. By fitting a minimal, five-parameter phenomenological model to the diverse BASEL collection of Escherichia coli phages, we accurately captured plaque expansion dynamics across all bacterial growth phases. We discovered that plaque expansion parameters vary significantly across individual phages and taxonomic families, with the initial expansion rate demonstrating an inverse correlation with viral genome size. Notably, these plaque expansion dynamics did not correlate with bacterial collapse times in liquid culture, indicating that they represent distinct physiological and kinetic processes. Finally, we demonstrated that phage taxonomic family can be predicted with 72.1% accuracy solely from dynamic plaque parameters using a random forest classifier, whereas conventional endpoint plaque sizes held no predictive power. This time-lapse phenotyping approach yields robust kinetic data superior to end-point measurements, establishing a scalable platform to accelerate phage discovery and genotype-phenotype mapping.
affiliations: Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam (corresponding author)

papers.title: An endolysin-expressing probiotic attenuates Clostridioides difficile infection in germ-free and dysbiotic microbiota-associated mice
papers.abstract: Disruption of the intestinal microbiota increases susceptibility to Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI), creating an opportunity for prophylactic interventions before symptomatic disease develops. We investigated whether Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) engineered to express the bacteriophage-derived endolysin CD27L could enhance pathogen inhibition and attenuate CDI. Using a plasmid-cured EcN chassis and pMUT2-derived vectors, we generated strains expressing CD27L under constitutive or anaerobically regulated promoter control. The constitutive strain, BioEcN1, reduced viable C. difficile recovery relative to parental EcN and was selected for animal studies. BioEcN1 remained recoverable from monoassociated mice without in vivo antibiotic selection, with similar recovery on selective and nonselective media supporting construct retention. Prophylactic administration reduced clinical disease, body-weight loss, and intestinal histopathological injury in germ-free mice. Observed survival was 100% in BioEcN1-treated challenged mice versus 50% in untreated challenged mice during the monitored period. Protection was accompanied by lower fecal and cecal pathogen burdens. In mice harboring a human-derived dysbiotic microbiota, prophylactic BioEcN1 also reduced clinical and stool-consistency scores, with lower early fecal pathogen recovery and less colon shortening. These findings establish preclinical proof of concept for prophylactic administration of an endolysin-expressing probiotic to attenuate CDI.
affiliations: Oklahoma State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Complex I Inhibition Redirects Autophagy from Bulk Turnover to Mitochondrial Clearance
papers.abstract: Mitochondria are both a major autophagic substrate and a principal source of signals that control autophagy, yet it is unknown whether a mitochondrial signal can specify which substrate the pathway degrades. Using metformin to inhibit Complex I in human cells, we find that autophagy is redirected rather than induced or suppressed. Inhibition shifts the NAD+/NADH ratio before perturbing the adenylate pool, separating the redox arm of the lesion from the bioenergetic arm. Single-molecule tracking of endogenous ATG13 and WIPI2 shows that initiation is preserved while WIPI2 tethering fails, generating short-lived, abortive autophagosomes; the ULK1 interactome concurrently disengages from cytoskeletal scaffolds, and Parkin-independent mitolysosomes accumulate. This response differs from mTORC1 inhibition and does not require PEN2, and AMPK is engaged non-canonically: 1/2 restrain ATG13 at initiation, while AMPK activation alone does not reproduce the WIPI2 phenotype. Occurring at therapeutic concentrations, these results identify the ULK1 complex as the step at which Complex I inhibition reassigns autophagic substrate.
affiliations: University of Kansas - Lawrence (corresponding author)

papers.title: Seascape genomics reveals shared spatial genetic structure in three co-occurring sea snakes
papers.abstract: Marine species with broad distributions often exhibit complex patterns of genetic connectivity, shaped by historical and contemporary processes. Understanding these patterns is critical for conserving taxa threatened by ongoing and future environmental change. Here, we use reduced-representation and whole-genome sequencing to investigate population genetic patterns in three co-occurring sea snake species (Hydrophis stokesii, Hydrophis major, and Aipysurus laevis) across northern Australia and New Caledonia. Broadscale analyses revealed major genetic breaks across all species between: (1) Australia and New Caledonia, (2) northwestern and northeastern Australia, and (3) the offshore Timor Sea reefs and adjacent northwestern continental shelf of Australia. More subtle genetic differentiation was observed between Shark Bay in Western Australia and northern localities. All species showed relatively large effective population sizes and broadscale connectivity across ~1,300 km of Australia's northwestern continental shelf. This likely reflects substantial historical range expansion over late Quaternary timescales, which may have contributed to the observed genetic connectivity across the region. However, subtle patterns of isolation by distance emphasised the contribution of species-specific traits in shaping connectivity. The isolated offshore reef populations are genetically distinct and potentially threatened by environmental change. Disjunct populations in Shark Bay and the Timor Sea maintain similar levels of genetic diversity to the extensive continental shelf populations, while New Caledonian populations exhibit reduced diversity. Our results support the delineation of spatial units for sea snake conservation based on shared phylogeographic structure, while also finding important population- and species-specific differences in connectivity at finer spatial and temporal scales.
affiliations: Adelaide University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Exploring noise in TCR specificity data through supervised learning
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of T cell receptor (TCR) specificity can potentially accelerate development of novel immunotherapies, yet public databases used to train these models contain substantial label noise. This uncertainty complicates model evaluation and limits the reliability of predicted TCR-pMHC interactions. In this work, we present a simple supervised machine learning denoising scheme to identify low-quality labels in TCR specificity data. We evaluated the framework using the TCRvdb validation dataset and further corroborated it via structural modeling with AlphaFold 3. Here, our denoising approach successfully identified non-validated TCRs, achieving an average MCC of 0.47 for filtering non-validated examples while retaining high sensitivity for validated examples. Applying our denoising approach to the complete NetTCR training dataset, we observed that data associated with known noisy attributes were significantly enriched in the filtered subset. Furthermore, TCR-pMHC complexes identified as noise consistently produced lower AlphaFold 3 confidence scores, providing independent evidence of misannotation. Experimental validation of 30 selected TCRs further supported the approach, with 80% of TCRs predicted as noise failing to demonstrate functional reactivity. Our findings demonstrate that current performance metrics may be obscured by dataset inaccuracies and provide a method for refining training data in the absence of gold-standard benchmarks.
affiliations: Technical University of Denmark (corresponding author)

papers.title: Division-resolved inference of flow and trajectories in proliferating cell populations
papers.abstract: Interpreting cellular responses requires understanding how cellular states change over time, yet many scalable assays provide only population snapshots. In proliferating populations, changes in population distributions reflect both state progression within cells and redistribution caused by division. We introduce division-resolved inference of flow and trajectories (DRIFT), a computational framework that infers the dynamics of a measured cellular state from population distributions collected over time, without synchronizing or tracking individual cells. DRIFT solves a population-balance equation to separate state progression from the redistribution caused by cell division. In simulations of growth and division perturbations, DRIFT recovered the ground-truth mean volume trajectories across simulated single-cell lineages. Applied to live L1210 leukemia cells, DRIFT inferred perturbation-specific volume trajectories consistent with longitudinal single-cell measurements. Beyond volume, the framework captured cell area dynamics in live HeLa cells, with validation by continuous imaging. Its application to an endpoint molecular assay further yielded DNA-content dynamics from fixed-cell flow cytometry in L1210 cells, consistent with complementary analyses of DNA synthesis. Overall, DRIFT converts population measurements into division-resolved cellular dynamics, extending the utility of routine population assays to kinetic studies of cellular progression when longitudinal tracking is impractical.
affiliations: Seoul National University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Reductive carboxylation via isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 supports cardiac metabolic adaptation during oncometabolic stress.
papers.abstract: Background: Cardiovascular disease and cancer are the two leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Metabolic dysregulation of cancer cells extends beyond the tumor microenvironment and increases the risk for cardiovascular diseases. One common somatic mutation in cancer cells affects isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) 1 and 2, which catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate in the cytosol and mitochondria, respectively. IDH1 and 2 mutations cause the production of the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D2-HG), which allosterically inhibits alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (alpha-KGDH) and is associated with reduced cardiac contractile function. Methods: We combined stable isotope tracer studies with computational modeling to investigate the fundamental role of IDH isoforms in cardiac adaptation under oncometabolic stress. Results: We uncovered an unexpected cardiac phenotype that expands the role of IDH1 in the heart beyond oxidative metabolism. We quantified the stable isotopomer distributions from glucose and glutamine in perfused working rat hearts and isolated adult ventricular cardiomyocytes using mass spectrometry-based metabolomics. Our analysis revealed that defective mitochondrial metabolism causes the redirection of carbon flux from oxidative towards reductive pathways. Reductive carboxylation of alpha-KGDH increases glutamine uptake and glutamine-derived citrate formation in working rat heart perfusions and cultured adult mouse ventricular cardiomyocytes. To identify which IDH isoform is responsible for redirecting carbon flux, we developed knockout models of IDH1, IDH2, and IDH3 in adult mouse ventricular cardiomyocytes. Loss of IDH1 expression impaired the reductive formation of citrate and caused functional defects in cardiomyocytes. Lastly, epigenetic analyses of histone marks revealed that IDH1 induces widespread alterations in histone acetylation and tri-methylation. Conclusion: Our results highlight a novel role for IDH1 in cardiac metabolism and transcriptional control of metabolic adaptation to tumor-mediated stress, and provide evidence that reductive citrate formation may induce epigenetic modifications in the heart.
affiliations: Cedars-Sinai Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: The MRTFs are required for thymocyte trafficking and Treg-mediated immune tolerance
papers.abstract: The MRTFs (myocardin-related transcription factors) are essential for effective cytoskeletal function during differentiation and development. To investigate the role played by the MRTFs in T cell development and function we inactivated Mrtfb in Mrtfa-null mice at the DN2 stage (MrtfabKOT animals). Positive selection, and development of MrtfabKOT regulatory (Treg), {gamma}{delta}, and NK T cells proceeded normally. Thymic egress was impaired, however, with mature T cells accumulating at the cortico-medullary junction, and in vitro MrtfabKOT thymocytes exhibited impaired cytoskeletal responses to S1P and migratory cytokines. MrtfabKOT mice were lymphopenic, with defective homeostatic proliferation and T cell homing to peripheral lymphoid organs. Although thymocyte negative selection was unaffected, MrtfabKOT animals develop autoimmune phenotypes in lacrimal gland and intestinal mucosa. Using the experimental colitis model, we show that these phenotypes reflect functional deficits in MrtfabKOT Treg cells. Our findings show that MRTF-SRF signalling plays an unanticipated role in thymocyte egress and immune tolerance, and reveal a role of the MRTFs in Treg function.
affiliations: The Francis Crick Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by immunoglobulin A
papers.abstract: Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody isotype produced by mammals, playing a specialised role in mucosal homeostasis. IgA is constantly secreted into the intestinal lumen and binds commensal microbiota to regulate their colonisation and function, with unclear implications for health. IgA deficiency is common in humans but is difficult to study due to its complex aetiology and comorbidities. Using genetically and environmentally controlled mice, here we show that multiple animal models of IgA deficiency result in increased susceptibility to multiple models of endogenous colorectal tumours. Cellular and molecular analyses revealed that, in the absence of IgA, colonic epithelial cells induce antibacterial factors and accelerate cell cycling in response to the microbiota. Oral treatment with IgA was sufficient to reduce steady-state proliferation and protect mice from tumours; however, this function was due to the antibody structure rather than binding specificity. In a reductionist culture system, IgA directly suppresses epithelial growth. Co-immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and targeted CRISPR screening identified DMBT1 as an IgA-binding epithelial surface protein required for IgA-mediated suppression of proliferation. Together, IgA and DMBT1 tune the normal cycling of absorptive colonocyte progenitors. In mice, deletion of the transmembrane and cytoplasmic signalling portions of DMBT1 was sufficient to reverse both the increased proliferation and tumour susceptibility of IgA knockouts. These experiments establish a homeostatic function for IgA in tempering physiological epithelial responses to microbiota to maintain mucosal health.
affiliations: The Rockefeller University (corresponding author)

papers.title: An integration-free CRISPR platform for genetic dissection of respiratory virus host dependencies in human nasal epithelium
papers.abstract: Respiratory viruses, including coronaviruses, generally initiate infection in the upper respiratory tract, where mechanistic studies of host-virus interactions require models amenable to genetic manipulation. Human nasal air-liquid interface (ALI) cultures are realistic models of the nasal epithelium, but robust CRISPR/Cas9 engineering workflows for this primary cell system have been lacking. Here, we established an integration-free CRISPR/Cas9 workflow for genetic engineering of human nasal basal cells, which are subsequently differentiated into gene-edited ALI cultures. GFP-based sorting of RNP-transfected nasal basal cells substantially increases editing, achieving knockout efficiencies of 70-90% across gene targets (B2M, SLC35A1, ACE2, and TMPRSS2). Genetic disruption of ACE2 markedly reduces infection by SARS-CoV-2 and hCoV-NL63, confirming its important role for both viruses in the human nasal epithelium. TMPRSS2 knockout substantially reduces replication of both viruses, demonstrating SARS-CoV-2 depending on TMPRSS2 in the human nasal epithelium and providing genetic evidence in primary human cell cultures that hCoV-NL63 relies on TMPRSS2. This platform enables systematic genetic perturbation in a physiologically relevant model of the primary site of respiratory virus infection, validates ACE2 and TMPRSS2 as targets for medical countermeasures against SARS-CoV-2 and hCoV-NL63, and provides a versatile approach to identify host dependency factors for both circulating and emerging respiratory viruses.
affiliations: Duke-NUS Medical School (corresponding author)

papers.title: A growth-inhibitory dUTPase from Mosigvirus AV110 disrupts cell division and host physiology in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: dUTPases are essential enzymes for nucleotide metabolism as they catalyze the hydrolysis of dUTP to dUMP, thus preventing the toxic incorporation of uracil into DNA. dUTPases are found in all domains of life, including bacteriophages, where they serve multiple functions to support phage propagation. Phage-encoded dUTPases reduce cellular dUTP levels and provide precursors for de novo dTTP synthesis and the synthesis of modified nucleotides, which are important to avoid DNA-based phage defense systems. In this study, we focused on the dimeric dUTPase Gp135, encoded by the Mosigvirus phage AV110, and examined its effect on growth, cell morphology, DNA replication and cell division of AV110s host, extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing E. coli. We observed that Gp135 significantly inhibited growth by disrupting DNA replication and cell division. This resulted in cytoplasmic voids, cell elongation, and ultimately cell death. We further demonstrated the diversity of phage-encoded dUTP/dCTPases through phylogenetic analysis, identifying four distinct clusters: one comprising the most common dUTPases, which form trimers; two more divergent clusters comprising dimeric dUTP/dCTPases; and one new cluster of more diverse, uncharacterized dUTPases and dNTPases. Overall, our results highlight the evolutionary and functional diversity of phage-encoded dUTP/dCTPases, with the Mosigvirus AV110 dUTP/dCTPase illustrating their role in supporting phage propagation.
affiliations: University of Copenhagen (corresponding author)

papers.title: MXRA8-dependent chikungunya virus infection in PDGFRα+ mesenchymal cells increases vascular permeability and facilitates hematogenous spread
papers.abstract: Alphaviruses are mosquito-transmitted pathogens in the Togaviridae family that cause severe arthritogenic or encephalitic disease in humans. Swelling of peripheral joints and soft tissues is a hallmark of arthritogenic alphavirus infection, although the mechanism by which tissue edema occurs is not well understood. The cell surface protein, matrix remodeling-associated protein 8 (MXRA8), is a cell entry receptor for several arthritogenic alphaviruses. Global loss of MXRA8 expression in mice abrogates foot swelling and reduces virus dissemination. Here, we demonstrate that specific ablation of MXRA8 from platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha (PDGFR) cells, including fibroblasts, phenocopies the foot swelling and dissemination deficits observed in chikungunya virus (CHIKV)-infected global MXRA8 knock-out mice. Edema in the foot requires CHIKV infection of PDGFR+ cells, which enhances both infection efficiency and permeability of endothelial cells. CHIKV-induced vascular leakage requires both MXRA8 expression and vascular endothelial growth factor signaling and contributes to dissemination by enabling virus access to the bloodstream. Collectively, our study establishes the role of MXRA8-dependent cell tropism in CHIKV dissemination and pathogenesis.
affiliations: Washington University School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genetic accessibility, not superior fitness, determines which anti-HBs antibody escape variants are selected in patients
papers.abstract: Background and Aims: Genetic diversity within the hepatitis B virus (HBV) surface antigen (HBsAg) drives the emergence of immune escape variants, but studying this diversity in vivo has been limited by the difficulty of establishing infection from patient isolates. We aimed to perform unbiased in vivo screening of variants in the HBs antigenic loop for antibody escape and fitness, using synthetic DNA launch of HBV in human hepatocyte chimeric mice. Approach and Results: Direct intrahepatic injection (IHI) of barcoded, recombinant cccDNA established infection from up to 32,000 independent launch events of a genotype A strain and successfully launched clinical consensus sequences across the major genotypes. Using IHI, we performed deep mutational scanning of 4,608 codon variants across the HBs antigenic loop. Under control antibody treatment, diverse variants expanded, revealing differences in variant fitness in the absence of adaptive immune pressure. Anti-HBs monoclonal antibody treatment suppressed wild-type viremia while permitting breakthrough of resistant variants from the library. Sequencing identified strong enrichment for substitutions at G145 (G145Q, G145H, G145R). Notably, G145Q, rather than the clinically dominant G145R, showed the greatest fitness advantage, indicating that G145R's clinical prevalence does not reflect superior intrinsic fitness. Conclusions: Unbiased in vivo screening reveals that clinically observed HBV escape mutations reflect which substitutions are genetically accessible by single nucleotide change and compatible with the overlapping polymerase reading frame, rather than which confer optimal fitness. This approach establishes a platform for high-resolution mapping of viral variant fitness under antiviral selection pressure.
affiliations: Weill Cornell Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: A bacterial endosymbiont with a highly reduced genome forms extensive membrane contact sites with host organelles
papers.abstract: Bacterial endosymbionts that establish long-term associations inside of host cells often lose a huge number of genes and become dependent on their hosts for essential cellular functions. One such example is the mealybug endosymbiont Tremblaya princeps: its ~139-kb genome encodes only ~120 protein coding genes and lacks all recognizable genes for lipid and fatty acid synthesis, cell wall components, membrane transport, protein translocation, and transmembrane proteins, raising fundamental questions of how Tremblaya's cellular envelope is formed and maintained. Here, using a combination of transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) of an entire endosymbiont-containing insect cell, we identified extensive and specific contacts between host cell mitochondria and Tremblaya. These contacts occurred at close membrane appositions and contained electron-dense bridge-like structures closely resembling classical eukaryotic membrane contact sites. Whole-cell segmentation showed that approximately 53% of host mitochondria were in contact with Tremblaya, with some mitochondria extensively wrapped by Tremblaya-associated membranes. Mitochondria in contact with Tremblaya were larger and contained proportionally greater cristae volume and surface density compared to non-contact mitochondria, exhibiting differences in both external and internal mitochondrial architecture. As membrane contact sites are well known to mediate lipid and metabolite exchange between membranes, these findings suggest that direct interactions with host organelles may be a source of vital membrane and cellular components for endosymbionts that have lost the autonomous ability to produce and transport these molecules.
affiliations: Arizona State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Nation-scale recovery of complete environmental plasmids pushes the boundaries of plasmid diversity through long-read sequencing
papers.abstract: Plasmids are important agents of prokaryotic evolution and yet existing reference databases remain biased towards cultivable species, limiting our knowledge of their function and ecology in the environment. Here we present a major expansion of known plasmid diversity, through curation and annotation of 8,744 topologically complete plasmids from 9,972 short- and 154 long-read metagenomes as part of the Microflora Danica project. These were found to increase plasmid taxonomic unit diversity by 15% and 99% relative to all and environmental plasmids, respectively, from public sources. In particular, we identify a novel lineage of plasmids in the genus Methanosarcina, encoding genes associated with methanogenesis and cell surface properties, expanding our understanding of chromosome-plasmid complementarity and its potential contribution to host biology. Combining our plasmids with public sources, we curated a set of 17 replication-associated proteins that could be found in 82% of known plasmids and can serve as hallmarks for future detection of plasmids. We present this resource, and a tool for confirming topological completeness of plasmid assemblies, as a toolkit for future plasmid discovery.
affiliations: Center for Microbial Communities, University of Aalborg, Denmark (corresponding author)

papers.title: Comparative genomics and structure-informed analysis identify a putative tandem receptor-binding module in Pseudomonas phage UF_RH1
papers.abstract: Abstract Bacteriophage receptor-binding proteins (RBPs) determine host recognition and host range but are frequently missed by conventional annotation because they evolve rapidly and often lack recognizable sequence domains. Pseudomonas phage UF_RH1 is a lytic Septimatrevirus with a 42,567 bp double-stranded DNA genome encoding 57 predicted open reading frames, several of which remain annotated as hypothetical proteins. Here, we reanalyzed the UF_RH1 distal-tail region using comparative synteny, phage RBP specific prediction tools, structure-informed domain analysis, oligomeric-symmetry prediction, and independent physicochemical calculations. Two adjacent proteins, WCF59042.1 (317 aa) and WCF59043.1 (320 aa), emerged as the strongest candidates for functional reannotation. WCF59042.1 was classified by DepoScope as a tail-spike protein with probability 1.00 and contains a high confidence C terminal tail-spike-associated segment spanning residues 210 to 317. WCF59043.1 was independently classified as a tail-spike candidate by RBPdetect2 (probability 0.51) and showed a strong Seq2Symm prediction for C3 homo-trimeric symmetry (0.990). Comparative genomic analysis places these proteins at positions corresponding to DLP2 gp22 and gp23, two similarly sized hypothetical virion proteins immediately downstream of the tape measure gene in a conserved distal-tail morphogenesis cassette. Because the closely related phages DLP1 and DLP2 use type IV pili for adsorption, we propose a testable model in which WCF59042.1 functions as a proximal connector/adaptor and WCF59043.1 contributes a distal trimeric receptor binding element. The model is computational and does not establish direct binding to PilA or assembled pili. Together, the convergent sequence, structural, oligomeric, and syntenic evidence supports a previously unrecognized tandem distal tail receptor-binding module in UF_RH1 and provides experimentally tractable targets for defining Septimatrevirus adsorption and host range.

papers.title: gRely: Relyability for genome trained sequence-to-expression models
papers.abstract: Sequence-to-function (S2F) models predict molecular phenotypes from DNA sequence and are increasingly applied to variant effect prediction (VEP), where the goal is to quantify how genetic variants alter gene expression. However, S2F model predictions are not uniformly reliable: accuracy varies substantially across variants, genes, and tissues, and current practice relies on crude magnitude thresholding to enrich for trustworthy predictions, which discards the majority of variants where S2F models could still provide signal. We developed gRely, a meta-modeling framework that estimates the probability that a given Borzoi VEP correctly predicts eQTL direction, using 1,121 features derived from the target variant, gene, and model outputs. On held-out tissues, gRely achieves a mean average precision of 0.885 (random baseline 0.744). Critically, within the low-magnitude regime where thresholding fails entirely, gRely identifies a high-confidence subset with 76% accuracy compared to a 58% baseline, recovering reliable predictions that magnitude filtering would discard. Interpretation via SHAP reveals that in this low-magnitude regime, gene expression level and cross-replicate signal concentration replace VEP magnitude as the primary discriminators of reliability. gRely is the first framework to provide per-prediction confidence scores for S2F model VEPs, and generalizes across architectures, producing consistent improvements on AlphaGenome predictions. By making reliability quantifiable, gRely enables principled filtering rather than blanket thresholding, and marks a step toward trustworthy deployment of S2F models in genomic research and clinical applications.
affiliations: Genentech (corresponding author)

papers.title: Asymmetric DNA targeting by RNA-guided TIGR-Tas systems
papers.abstract: Tandem interspaced guide RNA (TIGR)-TIGR-associated (Tas) are RNA-guided defense systems, which use a dual-repeat or stem-loop tigRNA to direct a Tas dimer to DNA targets through RNA-DNA heteroduplex formation between both DNA strands. While previous work has shown the basic principles of DNA targeting, how the guide architecture influences target recognition and whether recognition and cleavage are coordinated across the two RNA-DNA heteroduplexes at a target site remain poorly understood. Here, we combine cryo-electron microscopy, biochemistry, and cell-based assays to investigate two TIGR-Tas effectors: the nuclease-lacking Peromyscus leucopus TasA (PlTasA), associated with a stem-loop tigRNA, and the nuclease-active Salicola phage TasH (SpTasH). Cryo-EM structures of PlTasA binary and ternary complexes reveal a dimeric scaffold similar to SpTasH and TaTasR with a distinct stem-loop tigRNA architecture and additional peripheral structural elements. Binding assays using DNA substrates containing local bubbles across the spacer-matching region show equivalent bubbles produced position- and spacer-dependent effects, indicating that target engagement is asymmetric in both PlTasA and SpTasH. Kinetic and cryo-EM analyses of SpTasH further reveal stepwise heteroduplex formation, with a partially engaged intermediate that undergoes substantial conformational rearrangements of the second protomer, preceding a fully paired state poised for catalytic activation. Cleavage of the two DNA strands occurs through a coordinated, slow process and productive cleavage requires stringent surveillance of both heteroduplexes. Together, these findings define a conserved, ordered mechanism of bipartite target recognition and activation shared by TIGR-Tas effectors, expanding our understanding of the molecular principles underlying programmable DNA targeting by TIGR-Tas systems.
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Weighted Estimation Approach to Correct for Imperfect Mutation Detection Due to Intra-tumor Heterogeneity in Tumor Sequencing
papers.abstract: Somatic mutations in sequenced tumors are often detected with imperfect sensitivity. They can be missed because tumor heterogeneity results in some mutations being absent in a sample at hand or present at very low frequencies which, combined with technical limitations like insufficient sequencing depth, reduces their detectability. It becomes apparent with multi-regional sequencing that some mutations confined to specific areas can be overlooked in single-region analyses. Adjusting for such sensitivity becomes critical when mutation frequencies between groups of subjects are compared, such as responders and non-responders to a given therapy. Otherwise, the estimate of the mutation prevalence, or of the difference in prevalences between the groups, can be biased, leading to inflated type I error. Here, we propose a weighted approach to adjust for imperfect sensitivity of the mutation detection and compared it to the unweighted approach. We assume that a surrogate of mutation sensitivity is observed only among patients with called mutation, and we derive its unconditional mean. Such adjustment leads to less biased estimates of mutational frequencies and better control of the type 1 error.
affiliations: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Partner determination from protein sequences using class information
papers.abstract: Mapping protein interaction networks and understanding how duplicated proteins acquire distinct functions require determining which paralogs from interacting protein families bind to each other. Paralogs often fall into functional or architectural classes whose interactions can be conserved across organisms. Here, we introduce CLAPP (CLAss Pooling for Paralog matching), which pools interaction scores across organisms by class to infer one class-to-class map that constrains matching within each organism. It accepts any pairwise score assessing the likelihood of interaction of two proteins. On nine bacterial family pairs, with test sets restricted so that the class map determines every pairing, CLAPP recovered the correct map, and hence every reference pair. Recovering the map required little information: in the two systems tested, one training epoch of a coevolution-based model sufficed, whereas an untrained model performed no better than chance; and in eight of nine systems, a conservation-only score lacking inter-protein couplings also gave perfect matching. On unrestricted test sets, where the class map no longer uniquely determines every pairing, accuracy depended on the quality of the class labels: on 320 chaperone pairs, CLAPP performed below chance with unsupervised labels but reached 94\% with phylogeny-informed ones; remaining errors involved paralogs which can interact promiscuously. Paralog matching therefore need not rely on strong coevolutionary signals within individual pairs: when interactions between classes are conserved and labels are reliable, CLAPP can use even weak or noisy scores to accurately assign interaction partners.
affiliations: EPFL (corresponding author)

papers.title: SpatialOmicsLab: an integrated research environment for AI co-scientists in spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Spatial profiling is moving from method development into a central platform for biological discovery and clinical translation, but analyzing such complex data has become the bottleneck of scientific discovery. Translating spatial transcriptomic measurements into biological insight requires reproducible workflows that integrate diverse analytical methods. Although language-model agents can plan and execute multistep analyses, fragmented data and software ecosystems hinder their use as reliable research assistants. In this study, we introduce SpatialOmicsLab, an integrated research environment for spatial transcriptomics comprising 113 curated computational tools, 63 reference datasets and 4,614 task specifications. We also introduce ST-Coscientist, an AI co-scientist that uses this environment to assemble, execute and refine spatial transcriptomic analyses. Within SpatialOmicsLab, ST-Coscientist outperformed expert-led workflows and other scientific agents across six benchmark settings spanning spatial clustering, cell-type deconvolution and spatially variable gene detection. It constructed alignment-aware workflows for three-dimensional MERFISH data and addressed biological questions by selecting and analysing relevant reference datasets. Procedural memory increased the success rate of integrating and validating additional analytical tools from 48% to 95%. Together, SpatialOmicsLab and ST-Coscientist establish an extensible ecosystem for reproducible spatial transcriptomic research, enabling AI co-scientists to address evolving biological questions with an expanding analytical repertoire.
affiliations: Department of Genetics, Washington University in St. Louis, St. Louis, Missouri, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: drugMR: A multi-omics pipeline for genetically anchored drug-target discovery
papers.abstract: Motivation: Genetically supported drug targets are an estimated 2.6 times more likely to succeed clinically, yet a disease association alone does not show which protein to target, in which direction, or what other effects may follow. This currently requires chaining separate tools. Results: drugMR is a Nextflow pipeline that, from GWAS and pQTL summary statistics, runs cis-Mendelian randomisation, colocalisation, SMR-HEIDI with bulk and/or single-cell QTLs, three-trait colocalisation and a phenome-wide screen for adverse effects and repurposing. Datasets are added through a manifest, every step runs in containers on a laptop, cluster or cloud, and results are explored in a dashboard. Applied to schizophrenia with brain pQTLs, drugMR tested 2,019 proteins in 4 h 19 min and prioritised 58 proteogenomic targets, 22 with multi-omic support; 4 had potential adverse effects. Availability and implementation: drugMR: https://github.com/guillermocomesanacimadevila/drugMR; documentation: https://guillermocomesanacimadevila.github.io/drugMR/. Demo data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22917384.
affiliations: Cardiff University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Approximate local alignment via chained MEM divergence estimation for detecting horizontal gene transfer
papers.abstract: Local alignment tools struggle at querying against thousands of bacterial genomes, because the reference indexes are memory-intensive and base-level dynamic programming is slow. We present alamem (https://github.com/yunwilliamyu/alamem), an approximate local aligner that streams unprocessed reference databases and estimates average nucleotide identity (ANI) from Maximal-Exact-Match (MEM) chaining statistics. Alamem can query a bacterial genome against >85,000 prokaryotic genomes in under 30 seconds (with multithreading) using 4 GB of memory, making it over 16x faster and 21x more memory-efficient than existing local aligners using their default running modes. On top of alamem, we built alasight (https://github.com/graceoualline/alasight) for detecting signatures of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) by finding pairs of alamem hits to divergent genomes. Alasight achieves over an order of magnitude better sensitivity on data from real bovid microbiomes than existing mobile genetic element-detection software and provides depth and sparsity information supporting each putative HGT region.
affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Evo2HiC: a multimodal foundation model for integrative analysis of genome sequence and architecture
papers.abstract: Understanding how genome sequences shape three-dimensional (3D) genome architecture is fundamental to interpreting diverse biological processes. Although previous studies have shown that sequence information can predict 3D genome architecture, these models fall short in capturing cell type-specific structures because they are trained solely on sequence inputs. The widely available Hi-C data, which contains rich structural information across biosamples, can provide complementary features to sequence data for studying cell type-specific architectures. Recently, DNA foundation models have demonstrated encouraging performance in capturing long-range genomic dependencies, holding promise for modeling chromatin interactions. However, the extremely high computational cost of running these models limits their applicability to Hi-C analysis, which requires genome-wide sequence embeddings. Here, we present Evo2HiC, a multimodal foundation model that jointly models genome sequences and structures to study cell type-specific chromatin structure. The key idea of Evo2HiC is to distill a large-scale DNA foundation model, Evo 2 (7B), into a compact encoder, while guiding the distillation with Hi-C data to preserve genomic features critical for 3D genome analysis. The model supports two types of encoders, one that operates directly on DNA sequences, and a second that additionally takes as input corresponding Hi-C data. Using the DNA-only encoder and predicting raw Hi-C contact matrices, Evo2HiC improved distance-stratified Spearman correlation by 10.9% over Orca. Moreover, by jointly embedding Hi-C and sequence information Evo2HiC achieved the best overall Pearson correlation when predicting five representative epigenomic assays. Interpretation analysis of Evo2HiC revealed its ability to identify cell type-specific sequence motifs that explain changes in epigenomic signals. Finally, we demonstrated the cross-species generalizability of Evo2HiC on 177 species from the DNA Zoo dataset for Hi-C resolution enhancement. In summary, Evo2HiC is a foundation model that integrates genome sequences and 3D chromatin structure information, substantially reduces computational cost while maintaining state-of-the-art accuracy on predicting various epigenomic signals and genome architecture, enables the identification of cell type-specific motifs, and demonstrates robust generalizability across species.
affiliations: University of Washington (corresponding author)

papers.title: mCranberry: A rationally engineered monomeric red fluorescent protein with 85% quantum yield
papers.abstract: Fluorescent proteins (FPs) are the workhorse of modern-day cellular imaging and biosensing. However, rationally predicting and engineering the photophysical properties of FPs remain challenging, as these are governed by complex three-dimensional microenvironments and post-translational modifications. Here, we present a novel surface-mutation-guided engineering strategy combined with iterative rounds of rational mutagenesis to improve key photophysical properties of red fluorescent proteins (RFPs). This approach generated two bright, monomeric RFP variants from the mFruits lineage, mCranberry and mCranberry2, with quantum yields of 85% and 80%, respectively. Strategic incorporation of charged amino acid residues on the protein surface enhanced fluorescence quantum yield without compromising photostability. Comprehensive photophysical characterization and live-cell microscopy demonstrate enhanced performance of these variants and establish their utility as robust probes for fluorescence imaging. However, the exact mechanism of such improvements is subject to further investigation. Collectively, this work introduces a strategy for optimizing fluorescence properties and provides a framework that may be broadly applicable to other pigment-protein systems such as genetically encoded metal-ion indicators and photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes.
affiliations: The Ohio State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Islet size and spatial organization govern endocrine cell composition throughout the human pancreas
papers.abstract: Stem cell-derived (SC) islets hold promise as a transformative therapy for type 1 diabetes (T1D). To enhance graft uniformity, SC-islet organoids are often dissociated and reaggregated into standardized sizes. However, how endocrine cell composition varies with islet size in native human islets remains largely unknown. Defining this relationship is essential for establishing physiological benchmarks for islet engineering for transplantation. In this study, we examined the relationships among islet size, endocrine cell composition, and spatial distribution throughout whole pancreata from 10 age-matched, non-diabetic male subjects. Insulin-, glucagon-, and somatostatin-positive endocrine cells were identified as single-, double-, and triple-hormone populations ranging from non-islet single endocrine cells and small clusters (niSSCs) to large islets. Approximately 80% of the total endocrine area was contained in islets positive for all three hormones. Islet size strongly correlated with endocrine composition. Specifically, larger islets had increased alpha-cell fractions and reduced beta-cell fractions, while delta-cell fractions were consistent across sizes. Spatial analysis revealed that niSSCs, mono-, and tri-hormone islets frequently exhibit a clustered distribution. Additionally, tri-hormone islets were positioned near the core of the pancreas, whereas mono-somatostatin islets were often localized in the periphery. These findings were consistent across all three pancreatic regions (head, body and tail).
affiliations: University of Chicago (corresponding author)

papers.title: Angiotensin II Promotes Mitral Valve and Left Atrial Pathology in Fibrillin-1C1041G/+ Mice
papers.abstract: Background: Activation of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS) contributes to aortic diseases caused by fibrillin-1 haploinsufficiency (Fbn1C1041G/+). However, whether RAS activation influences mitral valve disease associated with FBN1 variants remains undefined. This study determined whether inhibition or augmentation of the RAS affects mitral valve pathology in Fbn1C1041G/+ mice. Methods: Angiotensinogen (AGT) antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) were administered for 12 weeks to inhibit the RAS in male and female Fbn1C1041G/+ mice. To augment the RAS, mice were infused with angiotensin II (AngII; 1,000 ng/kg/min) for 28 days. Mitral valve and heart function were monitored by ultrasound. At termination, hearts were dissected free and tissue sectioned to assess mitral valve leaflet thickness and pathology. Results: Mitral valve leaflet thickness was significantly increased in Fbn1C1041G/+ mice compared to Fbn1+/+ littermates of both sexes. ASO-mediated AGT inhibition did not alter this phenotype despite markedly reduced plasma AGT concentrations. AngII infusion increased mitral valve leaflet thickness in Fbn1C1041G/+ mice with increased proteoglycan and collagen content, while exerting minimal effects in Fbn1+/+ mice. Twenty-five percent of AngII-infused Fbn1C1041G/+ mice died of non-vascular causes. Ultrasound showed mitral valve dysfunction in AngII-infused Fbn1C1041G/+ mice. Grossly expanded left atria were common in AngII-infused Fbn1C1041G/+ mice. These markedly enlarged left atria contained increased fibrosis, macrophage accumulation, and platelet-rich masses. Conclusions: Mitral valves of Fbn1C1041G/+ mice did not respond to AGT inhibition but were markedly more susceptible to AngII infusion, with greater increases in thickness and compositional changes than mitral valves of Fbn1+/+ mice. In addition, AngII promoted mitral valve dysfunction that were associated with pronounced left atrial pathology.
affiliations: University of Kentucky (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structural engineering of dual-targeting antisense oligonucleotides enhances exon 44 skipping for treating Duchenne muscular dystrophy
papers.abstract: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) inducing exon-skipping during pre-mRNA splicing offer promising treatment for diseases such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Recently, dual-targeting ASOs that simultaneously bind two splicing regulatory sequences have been shown to improve exon-skipping efficiency. Current ASOs are designed to interact with target RNAs solely based on Watson-Crick base pairing. Here we report the development of dual-targeting three-dimensional bridge (3D-bridge) ASOs in which tertiary interactions are engineered to increase target-binding affinity and the number of target residues occupied. We designed a 3D-bridge ASO for skipping exon 44 of dystrophin mRNA and biochemically validated its enhanced binding affinity for the target RNA over a similar ASO with the tertiary interactions disrupted. We subsequently optimized the 3D-bridge ASO by varying its ends and ribose chemical modifications using patient-derived induced directly reprogrammed myotubes and identified an LNA/DNA mixmer as the most potent. We further demonstrate enhanced exon-skipping efficacy and potency of the 3D-bridge ASO compared to previously reported ASOs in myotubes differentiated from patient-derived primary myoblasts and MyoD-reprogrammed fibroblasts harboring mutations amenable to reframing through exon 44 skipping. In conclusion, the 3D-bridge ASO technology improves the current dual-targeting design, demonstrating the utility and power of structure-based ASO design methods.
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (corresponding author)

papers.title: Hybrid Mechanistic-Neural Modeling of Concentration-Time Dynamics Generalizes Human Pharmacokinetics Prediction Across Unseen Chemical Space
papers.abstract: The pharmacokinetics concentration-time profile encodes ADME dynamics. Its optimization in drug discovery curbs late-stage attrition, yet forecasting human pharmacokinetics from chemical structure remains difficult. Machine learning models ignore continuous ADME dynamics, whereas physiologically based pharmacokinetics (PBPK) models demand unavailable parameters and impose rigid, misspecified compartmental structures. We present PK-MUSE (PharmacoKinetic hybrid Mechanistic Universal System Equation), augmenting a two-compartment model with bounded, state- and time-dependent neural corrections to elimination and intercompartmental distribution. Molecular structure parameterizes compound-specific behavior, while learned corrections refine dynamic equations. Across scaffold and temporal out-of-distribution evaluations, PK-MUSE achieved the lowest mean exposure-endpoint MdFE, reducing MdFE by 7.2%, 45.2%, and 26.2% versus state-of-the-art machine learning (HML- RF), deep learning compartmental (DeepCt), and PBPK (PK-Sim) models. Interrogating the corrections localized misspecification to distribution rather than elimination. By extending mechanistic simulators with data-driven constrained neural dynamics that preserve interpretability and generalize to unseen chemotypes, PK-MUSE advances digital twins for drug discovery.
affiliations: Northeastern University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Lead Exposure During Differentiation Perturbs Electrophysiological Function in iPSC Derived Cardiomyocytes in a Cell Line-Dependent Manner
papers.abstract: Lead (Pb) exposure is strongly associated with cardiovascular diseases, but the effects of developmental Pb exposure on the electrophysiological properties of human cardiomyocytes have not yet been investigated. Using human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cardiomyocytes, we investigated the effects of human-relevant Pb exposure during ventricular cardiomyocyte differentiation on action potential properties and calcium dynamics in differentiated myocytes. We exposed 2 iPSC lines, from 1 male and 1 female donor, to Pb (0.5 or 5 micromolar) or control during only the first 8 days of differentiation, prior to functional maturation. Differentiation was carried out using an established protocol involving temporal modulation of Wnt signaling, followed by purification and maturation of contractile myocytes. We measured action potential properties and calcium dynamics using fluorescent dyes and optical mapping. We hypothesized that Pb exposure would adversely affect cardiomyocyte function, with effects persisting after cessation of exposure. In keeping with this hypothesis, we found significant Pb-induced changes in calcium (Ca) transients and action potential dynamics that were concentration and cell line specific and persisted well after exposure had ended. In the female cell line, beat frequency significantly increased with Pb exposure for both action potentials and Ca transients, while in the male cell line, beat frequency significantly decreased with Pb exposure for action potentials and increased for Ca transients. For voltage measurements, we observed significantly increased arrythmias with Pb exposure in both cell lines. Significant changes in repolarization and recovery time (for voltage and Ca, respectively) were present with Pb exposure in both cell lines. Gene expression of Ca transporters/channels and K channels were not affected, suggesting that persistent effects of Pb exposure on cardiomyocyte electrophysiology may occur through post-translational mechanisms. Overall, this study paves the way for future work to examine how exposure to Pb impacts long-term cardiac function through developmental programming.
affiliations: University of Michigan (corresponding author)

papers.title: A strategy for genome-wide seamless tagging of human protein-coding genes
papers.abstract: Comprehensive and systematic proteome-wide experiments require financial and technical resources unavailable to most researchers. Here we describe a universal and scalable method based on CRISPR/Cas9-non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) for Pooled Recombinant Integration of Seamless Markers (PRISM) into protein coding genes. We created two genome-wide gRNA libraries for 5'- and 3'-tagging of 18,489 human protein-coding genes. Selection for in-frame integration of the donor cassette can be favored by fusing it to an antibiotic resistance enzyme (ARE) and P2A self-cleaving peptide, resulting in tagged proteins and free ARE to select for clones with inserted donor cassettes. We achieved a library integration rate of ~20% and tagging of at least 36% of genes expressed in HEK 293T cells including, at least 28% of essential genes, with donor DNA. Our strategy is universal, scalable, specific, and selective, paving the way for genome-scale construction of human cell lines tagged with different types of reporter genes for protein functional characterization.
affiliations: University of Montreal (corresponding author)

papers.title: Age-associated transcriptional programs in tumor-associated macrophages are associated with tumor progression in HPV-negative oral cancer
papers.abstract: Aging and tobacco exposure are major determinants of risk and outcome in HPV-negative oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), yet the cellular programs linking host factors to tumor immunity remain poorly defined. We reprocessed and reanalyzed previously published single-cell RNA-seq data from 19 HPV-negative OSCC tumors and we identified a robust age- and smoking-associated expansion of SPP1high tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), accompanied by a shift toward a myeloid-dominant and lymphocyte-reduced tumor microenvironment. SPP1high TAMs exhibit a distinct transcriptional state enriched for extracellular-matrix remodeling and metabolic programs and reduced antigen-presentation pathways. They also express inflammatory chemokines such as CXCL2 and CXCL3 and down-regulate the cytotoxic mediator TNFSF10, suggesting a broadly protumor TAM phenotype. Ligand-receptor modeling suggests that SPP1high TAMs act as key communication hubs, with dominant SPP1-CD44 signaling to T-cell subsets. Transcription-factor analysis further implicates a POU2F1/POU2F2/SP1 module in maintaining this state. In the TCGA HNSCC cohort, the association between SPP1 expression and overall survival did not reach statistical significance after adjustment for age and tumor purity. These findings demonstrate that aging and tobacco exposure converge to expand an SPP1high TAM population that remodels the extracellular matrix and suppresses antitumor immunity, highlighting the SPP1-CD44 axis and its upstream regulators as potential therapeutic targets in high-risk OSCC.

papers.title: Lactation Remodels the Maternal Lung to Promote Preemptive Innate Defense
papers.abstract: Lactation is a hallmark of mammalian evolution, imposing extraordinary physiological demands on mothers to nourish their offspring. Yet how mothers maintain their own health while meeting these demands remains poorly understood. Here, we discover that lactation establishes a preemptive innate defense program in the maternal lung through enhanced epithelial production of surfactant proteins and mucin, vascular remodeling that supports granulocyte recruitment and accumulation of activated intravascular neutrophils. These tissue-wide adaptations safeguard lactating dams against diverse respiratory pathogens. We further identify prolactin and CGRP as neuroendocrine signals contributing to pulmonary remodeling and uncover parallel lactation-associated granulocyte adaptations in marsupial and non-human primate models. Together, our findings expand the framework of reproductive immunology, revealing that reproduction couples systemic fetal tolerance with tissue-specific immune adaptations that safeguard maternal health during lactation.
affiliations: Princeton University (corresponding author)

papers.title: A PATHOGENIC NFKB2 VARIANT CAUSES COMBINED IMMUNODEFICIENCY WITH THYMIC AND PERIPHERAL LYMPHOID DEFECTS IN RATS
papers.abstract: The non-canonical NF-kappa B pathway, in which NFKB2 plays a central role, is critical for lymphoid organ development and immune homeostasis. Pathogenic NFKB2 variants have been strongly associated with a broad spectrum of human pathologies, notably immunodysregulation syndromes, characterized by recurrent infections, autoantibody production and endocrine abnormalities. The mechanisms underlying the resulting immune defects remain incompletely understood. In the present study, we characterized the immune phenotype of a novel rat model harboring a Nfkb2 non-sense mutation located in the c-terminal region of the gene (c.2602T>A; p.Tyr867*, Nfkb2p.Tyr867*). This variant has been identified in patients with a familial form of common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) presenting with autoimmunity manifestations. Using this model, we demonstrate that mutated NFKB2 resulted in profound alterations of the thymic microenvironment, including reduced K5+ medullary thymic epithelial cells and decreased AIRE expression, accompanied by altered thymocyte development and impaired thymic regulatory T populations. Peripheral lymphoid organization was also profoundly affected, with absence of lymph nodes, defects in the splenic marginal zone, and alterations of CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell homeostasis, including impaired Treg populations and reduced ICOS expression on CD4+ T cells. The B-cell compartment was markedly altered, with impaired B-cell maturation, characterized by accumulation of IgM+IgD- transitional cells and a marked reduction of IgD+ mature B cells. These abnormalities were associated with impaired humoral immunity and complete absence of circulating immunoglobulins. Collectively, our findings define a systemic combined immunodeficiency phenotype in the Nfkb2-mutated rat, highlighting its utility for studying the role of non-canonical NF-kB signaling in immune system organization and adaptative immunity.
