papers.title: ESX-1 remodels the Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen storage compartment in macrophages
papers.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) secretes antigenic proteins that drive protective T cell responses, yet how Mtb intracellular localization affects the trafficking and spatiotemporal distribution of mycobacterial antigens in macrophages remains elusive. Here, we developed a split fluorescent protein reporter to monitor the dynamics of the TB vaccine lead antigen Ag85B in infected human macrophages. We discovered that Mtb triggers the formation and remodeling of two distinct types of Mtb Antigen Storage Compartment (MASC) that retains Ag85 within macrophage membranes. Using subcellular spatial proteomics, we profiled the composition of the MASC, identifying both the Mtb and macrophage proteins that constitute these compartments. Unexpectedly, MASCs are defined by metabolic compartmentalization and rewiring to lipid metabolism in both the macrophage and Mtb. Thus, Mtb builds via the ESX-1 system a metabolically distinct antigen storage compartment in immune cells, with potential implications for antigen selection and delivery in TB vaccine development.
affiliations: The Francis Crick Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: Disentangling maternal pregnancy and fetal-specific plasma signatures through integrated proteomics and site-specific N-glycoproteomics
papers.abstract: During pregnancy, mother and fetus co-exist albeit as two physiologically distinct individuals, connected through the placenta and the umbilical cord. This connection allows for the exchange of vital substances, while individual blood homeostasis remains intact. We hypothesized that comparing maternal and cord plasma (N-glyco)proteomes would provide insights into the biological communication and unique physiological state of each individual. As comparing only matched maternal and umbilical cord blood plasma misses a crucial identifier in determining whether observed changes are related to infancy, pregnancy or both, we designed a triad study by adding a non-pregnant women control group. This allowed us to distinguish pregnancy-specific proteins and their potentially altered N-glycosylation from those in infancy. We found that the fetus and mother have distinct proteomes, N-glycoproteoforms and alternative complement regulation. Moreover, we observed that pregnancy in women led to specific N-glycosylation changes on a select set of primarily HDL-associated and acute-phase proteins. Lastly, our data provide evidence for an early fetal development of the humoral immune system as especially fetal IgM displayed distinctive N-glycosylation signatures.
affiliations: Utrecht University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Ambient-Condition Visualization of Metalloenzyme Reactive Intermediates Enabled by the SHINERS Paradigm
papers.abstract: Reactive metal-oxygen intermediates are central to metalloenzyme catalysis, yet their low populations and short lifetimes make vibrational characterization under aqueous reaction conditions challenging. Here, we establish shell-isolated nanoparticle-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SHINERS) as a powerful vibrational approach for visualizing reaction-associated metal-ligand signatures of reactive metalloenzyme states. Across the heme and non-heme iron enzymes TauD, VioC, CYP119, and TqaLNc, isotope-sensitive features provide vibrational information on reactive coordination states. In TauD and VioC, isotope-sensitive features provide vibrational characterization of Fe(IV)=O intermediates. In CYP119, an isotope-sensitive Fe(IV)=O vibration is assigned to P450 Compound I generated by m-CPBA, including under lauric-acid turnover conditions. Most notably, in TqaLNc, combined 18O- and 15N-sensitive vibrational responses support formation of the proposed (R)HN-Fe(IV)=O coordination state and the dynamic-coordination mechanism underlying selective C-N bond formation. These results demonstrate that SHINERS can serve as a powerful technique for the in situ vibrational visualization of reactive intermediates and their coordination states in metalloenzyme catalysis.
affiliations: Xiamen University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Pathogenic DRP1 variants reveal a role for biomolecular condensation in mitochondrial fission
papers.abstract: Fission is essential for proper mitochondrial function and for cellular homeostasis. Dysfunction in mitochondrial fission is associated with several neurological disorders, including the rare and lethal encephalopathy EMPF1, which is caused by de novo heterozygous DNM1L variants. DNM1L encodes the mitochondrial fission mechanoenzyme DRP1, which can intrinsically self-assemble and induce membrane scission. Wild-type DRP1 puncta that appear throughout the cytoplasm are thought to be pre-scission complexes of well-ordered oligomeric assemblies. Immunofluorescence imaging of patient-derived EMPF1 fibroblasts carrying assembly-deficient DNM1L variants reveals elongated mitochondrial networks consistent with impaired fission. Despite this loss-of-function phenotype, these cells retain essentially wild-type numbers of DRP1 puncta. We confirmed the previously reported inability of purified pathogenic DRP1 variants p.Gly363Asp and p.Gly401Ser to assemble under conditions in which WT DRP1 forms helical polymers. Under macromolecular crowding conditions, however, both wild-type and mutant DRP1 access condensed states whose formation depends on protein concentration and solution conditions. Acute treatment of EMPF1 fibroblasts with 1,6-hexanediol preferentially alters DRP1 puncta fluorescence intensity and distribution in mutant cells relative to wild type, indicating genotype-dependent differences in puncta material properties. Together, these findings support a model in which DRP1 puncta occupy a continuum of condensed states, only a subset of which mature into fission-competent assemblies, revealing biomolecular condensation as a previously unrecognized layer of DRP1 regulation. Biasing DRP1 along this continuum may provide a mechanistic basis for impaired fission in EMPF1 and suggest opportunities to restore productive assembly in select pathogenic contexts.
affiliations: Skaggs School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, Aurora, CO, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Discovering Latent Scientific Concepts through Discrete Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Scientific imaging is undergoing a fundamental transformation. Advances in multiplex immunofluorescence, computational pathology, and electron microscopy now enable observation of biological and physical systems at unprecedented spatial resolution. Rather than simply classifying known objects, these data offer the opportunity to discover previously unknown organizational principles. However, scientific image datasets are typically highly curated, information-rich, and limited in size, making reliable representation learning particularly challenging. We show that standard continuous self-supervised adaptation can become unstable in this regime, allowing teacher representations to drift and degrading downstream transfer. We introduce Kodiak, a discrete representation learning architecture that discovers latent scientific concepts through Sinkhorn-balanced codebook assignments. Instead of learning unconstrained continuous embeddings, Kodiak constructs a reusable vocabulary of discrete concepts that provides stable supervision for both masked-patch prediction and cross-view representation learning within a single-stage framework. Across five scientific imaging domains, including multiplex immunofluorescence for pancreatic cancer pathology and scanning electron microscopy, Kodiak consistently improves representation quality under both continued foundation-model adaptation and training from scratch. Beyond improved classification and transfer,the learned concepts are interpretable, reusable, and produce spatially coherent concept maps that support applications such as cell phenotyping, segmentation-free patch phenotyping, spatial niche discovery, tissue organization, and materials characterization. We view Kodiak as the representation-learning engine of our foundation model for spatial biology. More broadly, our results suggest that discrete representation learning provides a principled foundation for discovering reusable latent scientific concepts that can accelerate scientific interpretation across imaging domains.
affiliations: MSKCC (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genetic dissection of DNA damage response pathways reveals divergent modulation of PD-1 blockade response in colorectal cancer
papers.abstract: Although MSI-H/dMMR colorectal cancers and the rarer subset with pathogenic POLE exonuclease domain mutations can benefit from immune checkpoint blockade, MSS colorectal cancer remains largely refractory, raising the question of whether other DNA damage response defects may also confer sensitivity to immunotherapy. Here, we performed a systematic in vivo screen of recurrently altered DNA damage response (DDR) genes to determine whether distinct repair defects modulate response to PD-1 blockade in MSS colorectal cancer. Using a genome-edited murine model in immunocompetent mice, we found that DDR perturbations produced heterogeneous outcomes, indicating that the immunologic consequences of DNA repair deficiency may be pathway-specific. Loss of Brca1, Brca2, Atm, and Fanca enhanced response to anti-PD-1 therapy, whereas Atr and Msh6 deficiency were associated with poor benefit. Brca1/2-deficient tumors showed the strongest regressions, supporting a link between core homologous recombination deficiency and increased immune sensitivity. In an independent cohort of colorectal cancer patients treated with ICB from the MSK-IMPACT Clinical Sequencing Cohort, BRCA1 alterations were associated with improved survival status, while FANCA alterations showed a similar trend. Because ATM is therapeutically targetable, we evaluated pharmacologic ATM inhibition in MSS colorectal cancer. Sustained ATM inhibition induced immune-related transcriptional programs in vitro and, when administered as a pre-treatment in vivo, enhanced the antitumor activity of PD-1 blockade. Together, these findings suggest that selected DDR alterations may represent candidate biomarkers of immunotherapy sensitivity, while ATM inhibition may provide a rational combination strategy to enhance PD-1 blockade in MSS colorectal cancer.
affiliations: Massachusetts General Hospital Cancer Center and Department of Medicine, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: CRISPR-Cas9 Editing of Myeloid Lectins Reveals Target-Dependent Transcriptional Remodeling in Tumor-Associated Macrophages
papers.abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) integrate multiple microenvironmental signals, including lectin-mediated recognition of tumor-associated glycans. Although several myeloid lectins have been implicated in tumor-macrophage interactions, their contributions to immunosuppressive TAM phenotypes remain poorly defined. We implemented a CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) workflow in primary human monocytes to enable comparative loss-of-function interrogation of five potentially immunosuppressive lectins we previously reported. CRISPR-Cas9 RNP delivery conditions were benchmarked in freshly isolated monocytes using CD14 as a technical target, followed by sgRNA editing efficiency screening for CLEC4E, CLEC6A, CD209, SELL, and SIGLEC9 in HeLa S3 cells. Selected guides were applied to primary monocytes before co-culture in a 3D model with BT474 breast cancer cells. Editing was quantified by Sanger-sequencing deconvolution, while co-culture-derived CD45+ macrophages were isolated by fluorescence-activated cell sorting and characterized by bulk RNA sequencing. All five lectins were successfully perturbed, although gene editing efficiency remained target- and donor-dependent. Transcriptomic analysis revealed target-specific reprogramming and recurrent immunometabolic responses. mTORC1 signaling was consistently enriched, together with the remodeling of cholesterol homeostasis, fatty acid metabolism, and oxidative phosphorylation. CLEC6A deletion achieved attenuation of hypoxia-, angiogenesis-, and TNF/NF-kB-associated programs. CD209 and SIGLEC9 deletion similarly reduced hypoxia- and angiogenesis-associated signatures while promoting lipid and oxidative metabolism. CLEC4E perturbation induced broad remodeling of lipid and oxidative metabolism and stress-response, despite comparatively limited editing efficiency. Comparative lectin perturbation thus identified CLEC6A as the strongest candidate for further mechanistic investigation, while CLEC4E showed broad transcriptional remodeling despite lower editing efficiency, supporting its prioritization for improved genetic interrogation. Responses to CD209 and SIGLEC9 targeting further support tumor glycan-myeloid signaling as a regulator of TAM state. Overall, lectin perturbation redirected TAM transcriptional states through distinct immunometabolic programs rather than a uniform pro-inflammatory polarization, highlighting lectin-dependent immunometabolic regulation as a promising axis for further investigation.
affiliations: Instituto de Biologia Experimental e Tecnologica (corresponding author)

papers.title: RBFOX2 restrains oncogenic cell plasticity in Group 3 medulloblastoma
papers.abstract: Cancer cell plasticity underlies tumor progression, metastasis and therapeutic resistance, yet how RNA-binding proteins regulate malignant state transitions remains poorly defined. Here, we identify the splicing regulator RBFOX2 as a suppressor of oncogenic cell plasticity in Group 3 medulloblastoma (MB). OTX2 antagonizes RBFOX2 by directing an opposing alternative splicing program that mirrors developmental origins and controls cytoskeletal dynamics and cell state transitions. Mechanistically, OTX2 alters the RBFOX2 RNA-binding landscape, limiting RBFOX2 engagement at cytoskeletal loci and suppressing exon inclusion. RBFOX2 loss rewires splicing and transcriptional outputs to promote highly plastic proliferative, mesenchymal-like and undifferentiated cellular states associated with enhanced oncogenic properties. Consistent with these findings, RBFOX2low states mark highly plastic cell populations in patient tumors and xenografts, positioning RBFOX2 as a determinant of malignant cell stability. Together, these findings establish RBFOX2 as a developmental gatekeeper that restrains malignant cell plasticity through coordinated control of cytoskeletal gene programs.
affiliations: Baylor College of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: The p53-Mdm2 interaction through the lens of antithetic feedback
papers.abstract: We show that the p53-Mdm2 gene interaction can be understood as a form of antithetic feedback, but with mixed feedback loops. In particular, we show that this viewpoint sheds light on the emergence and robustness properties of p53's oscillatory behaviour, as observed experimentally.
affiliations: KTH Royal Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: RI-SINDy: Regulation-Informed Sparse Model Discovery in Biological Gene Networks
papers.abstract: Oscillatory and saturating dynamics in regulatory gene networks govern processes such as cell cycle timing, circadian rhythms, and inflammatory signaling, and sparse regression methods such as SINDy offer an interpretable method for recovering their governing equations from time-series data. However, these networks are typically governed by Hill-type nonlinearities that become nearly collinear with polynomial candidates over most bounds of an oscillating curve, and placing them in a shared library produces ill-conditioned regressions and unreliable coefficient estimates. Standard approaches such as ridge regularization, library normalization, and orthogonalization can marginally improve conditioning but cannot remove the structural multicollinearity of these systems, in turn limiting our ability to produce accurate parameter estimates. To address this issue, we propose the Regulation-Informed Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (RI-SINDy) method, which removes known regulatory terms from the regression and recovers their coefficients directly from an asymptotic drift-balance condition. Because the time averaged derivative of a bounded trajectory approaches zero, the coefficients of regulatory nonlinearities can be computed independently by constraining them to offset the mean contribution of the remaining terms. We demonstrate that this method effectively reduces library collinearity and improves conditioning numbers by 3-45x, substantially improving coefficient recovery and regression accuracy. We test the RI-SINDy method on experimental Hes1 data and on synthetic Goodwin and NF-{kappa}B models. On Hes1, it achieves the lowest trajectory error among the compared methods (Traditional SINDy, SR3, and Nullcline Reconstruction). On the synthetic systems, it recovers the correct sparse structure with lower trajectory error than SR3 and Nullcline Reconstruction, and in a Goodwin noise sweep it recovers all active terms at noise levels up to 15%, where Traditional SINDy and E-SINDy fail to. In conclusion, the RI-SINDy method provides a robust framework to overcome the issue of multicollinearity for system identification in biological systems.
affiliations: University of Missouri-Kansas City (corresponding author)

papers.title: Ultrasensitive response in bacterial replication initiation
papers.abstract: In bacteria, the time at which genome replication initiates is carefully regulated, as precision in this timing is crucial for cell cycle stability. Theoretical and experimental studies have shown that the probability of replication initiation sharply depends on cell volume as the cell grows. Such sharp response is usually termed "ultrasensitive" in biology, and has been subject of extensive theoretical study. Nevertheless, the source of ultrasensitivity in this system remains unclear. In this work, we show how ultrasensitivity in replication initiation emerges from the dynamics of DnaA, the central protein regulating initiation in all bacterial species. To do so, we propose a mechanistic, thermodynamically consistent model of the dynamics of DnaA, and study the conditions under which an ultrasensitive response arises. We find that ultrasensitivity results from a combination of regulatory processes, that varies with growth conditions. In slow growth, we find an interplay between sequestration of DnaA on chromosomal binding sites and DnaA binding at the origin of replication. This mechanism requires a "sweet spot" of origin binding affinities, whose values are consistent with available experimental measurements. In fast growth, ultrasensitivity instead arises from rapid transition between an inactive and an active form of DnaA, and requires cooperative binding at the origin of replication to be effective. Our results point to ultrasensitivity as the organizing principle underlying regulation of bacterial replication initiation.
affiliations: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology School Corp and Graduate University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Intracellular genomic variability driven by cellular compartmentalization in the giant bacterium Achromatium spp.
papers.abstract: Bacteria of the genus Achromatium harbor hundreds of chromosomes that were previously suggested to be genetically diverse. By sequencing multiple regions from individual cells, we demonstrate that chromosomes within a single cell differ in nucleotide and amino acid sequence, reaching levels of divergence well below accepted bacterial species boundaries and below the range associated with homologous recombination. Sequencing of dividing cells further revealed that daughter cells inherit distinct chromosome populations, a mode of inheritance previously associated with sexual reproduction in eukaryotes. Combining subcellular sequencing with high-resolution microscopy, we reconstruct the three-dimensional cellular architecture of Achromatium and show that extensive intracellular heterogeneity arises from the spatial segregation of chromosome populations by the cell's internal structure, which limits genome-wide recombination. Our findings establish cellular architecture as a determinant of genome evolution in giant polyploid bacteria and identify spatial genome segregation as a mechanism enabling the maintenance and inheritance of divergent chromosome populations in bacteria.
affiliations: Department of Environmental Microbiomics, Technische Universitaet Berlin, Berlin, Germany (corresponding author)

papers.title: RBM25 exhibits distinct RNA- and chromatin-associated target programs in human embryonic stem cells
papers.abstract: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) are increasingly recognized to perform chromatin-associated functions in addition to their canonical roles in RNA regulation, yet how these activities are coordinated in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) remain poorly understood. Here, we characterize distinct RNA- and chromatin-associated activities for RBM25 in hESCs. Transcriptome-wide profiling showed that RBM25 preferentially associates with transcripts involved in RNA processing and splicing, consistent with its canonical role as an RBP involved in post-transcriptional regulation. Genome-wide chromatin profiling further uncovered a distinct chromatin-associated program, with RBM25 occupying accessible promoters of actively expressed cell-cycle genes and introns predominantly associated with transcriptionally inactive neuronal genes. Interestingly, RBM25 chromatin-binding sites showed substantial co-occupancy with regions bound by the transcription factor CEBPZ in hESCs. We further show that RBM25 and CEBPZ physically interact and exhibit shared chromatin-binding patterns at both promoter and intronic regions. Importantly, reciprocal depletion experiments revealed that RBM25 is required for CEBPZ occupancy at CCAAT-containing promoters of highly expressed cell-cycle genes, whereas CEBPZ is not similarly required for RBM25 chromatin occupancy. Together, our findings establish RBM25 as a multifunctional factor with distinct roles in RNA processing and chromatin-associated regulation and reveal a context-dependent RBP-TF interaction that contributes to transcriptional regulation in hESCs.
affiliations: Technion - Israel Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: HIV-1 Assembly is Assisted by IRSp53 Through an Interaction that Extends Gag Conformation
papers.abstract: Budding of the immature virion is an essential part of the HIV-1 life cycle. However, understanding and inhibiting this process has been challenging, as both simulations and theoretical studies suggest that the energy required to bend the membrane is too high for the complete assembly of a spherical viral particle at the plasma membrane without the assistance of cellular host factors. Recent results suggest that the I-BAR protein IRSp53 may be one such host factor, but the molecular mechanism by which the Gag-IRSp53 interaction promotes HIV-1 assembly and budding remains poorly understood. We employ molecular dynamics simulations, starting from AlphaFold models, to show that the SH3 domain of IRSp53 interacts directly with the MACANTD domain of Gag and we experimentally validate this interaction. Our simulations show that the specificity of the interaction with IRSp53 arises from its ability to extend the MACANTD Gag conformation in a manner similar to RNA binding, which is known to activate Gag assembly. We then computationally design HIV-1 Gag mutants that, as confirmed by simulations, do not undergo conformational changes upon interaction with theIRSp53 SH3 domain. Experimentally, these Gag mutants are tested and shown to accumulate in cells. In addition, for these mutants we observe large quantities of Gag assembling at the plasma membrane but exhibiting large budding defects. These results validate the proposed mechanism by which the Gag-IRSp53 interaction promotes completion of HIV-1 budding and suggest new routes for inhibiting viral assembly or budding.
affiliations: University of Chicago (corresponding author)

papers.title: Interferon-induced OASL restricts ADAR1 p150 RNA binding and A-to-I RNA editing
papers.abstract: The interferon (IFN)-inducible RNA editor ADAR1 p150 catalyzes adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing of host and viral double-stranded RNAs, limiting aberrant innate immune sensing and regulating gene expression. How ADAR1 p150 activity is regulated during host-virus interactions remains poorly understood. Here, we identify the IFN-stimulated gene OASL as an inhibitor of ADAR1 p150. OASL engages p150 through two distinct interactions: its N-terminal OAS domain associates with the RNA-binding domains in an RNA-dependent manner, whereas its C-terminal ubiquitin-like domains bind the Z domain independently of RNA. Despite their distinct canonical functions, the OAS and ubiquitin-like domains converge to limit ADAR1 p150 RNA binding and suppress A-to-I editing across the transcriptome. OASL also reverses p150-mediated suppression of antiviral and innate immune gene expression and counteracts p150-mediated enhancement of measles virus and vesicular stomatitis virus replication. Thus, OASL restrains ADAR1 p150, linking interferon signaling to the control of RNA editing and antiviral immunity.
affiliations: Cleveland Clinic Research (corresponding author)

papers.title: The RNA-binding protein TRIM71 Promotes Supporting Cell Reprogramming and Hair Cell Regeneration by Activating Sall4
papers.abstract: Hair cell (HC) loss in the auditory organ (cochlea) is irreversible and represents the leading cause of deafness in humans. The absence of HC regeneration is primarily due to the limited plasticity of cochlear supporting cells (SCs). Using a novel doxycycline-inducible TRIM71 transgenic mouse model, this study demonstrates that overexpression of the RNA-binding protein TRIM71 promotes spontaneous cochlear HC regeneration in neonatal mice. Experiments in cochlear organoids indicate that TRIM71 reprograms SCs into progenitor-like cells and that this reprogramming is further enhanced by coactivation of follistatin (FST). FST augments TRIM71-induced increases in chromatin accessibility at progenitor and HC-specific gene loci, facilitating their transcriptional activation in SCs. Notably, FST also enhances TRIM71-induced reactivation of Sall4, which, like Trim71, is highly expressed in early otic progenitors. Using cochlear organoids and explants, we show that the early otic transcription factor SALL4 is required for TRIM71-induced HC formation. By contrast, SALL4 overexpression inhibits HC formation by maintaining reprogrammed SCs in an undifferentiated, proliferative state. These findings establish TRIM71 as an activator of HC regeneration in vivo, provide mechanistic insights into TRIM71's role in SC reprogramming, and identify SALL4 as its essential effector.
affiliations: Xi'an Jiaotong University (corresponding author)

papers.title: A reversible GNAS-PKA-RUNX2 checkpoint governs skeletal stem cell fate in fibrous dysplasia
papers.abstract: Fibrous dysplasia (FD) arises from activating GNAS mutations that increase cAMP signaling in skeletal stem/progenitor cells (SSPCs), but the underlying mechanisms and whether the resulting fate imbalance can be reversed remain unclear. Using controlled GNAS induction with transcriptomic, pharmacologic, and cell-fate analyses, we identify a PKA-dependent checkpoint governing SSPC lineage commitment. GNASR201C redirects SSPCs toward osteoclastogenesis while suppressing osteoblast maturation; genetic or pharmacologic PKA inhibition reverses both effects, revealing this fate decision is dynamically reversible. Mechanistically, PKA phosphorylates RUNX2, the master regulator of osteogenesis, enforcing its cytoplasmic retention and blocking osteogenic transcription; a non-phosphorylatable RUNX2 mutant restores nuclear localization and osteoblast differentiation, defining RUNX2 phosphorylation as a disease-initiating molecular switch. Critically, PKA inhibition in vivo reduces fibrosis and osteoclast burden in established bone lesions, demonstrating reversibility even in advanced FD. These findings define a druggable GNAS-PKA-RUNX2 checkpoint and identify PKA inhibition as a strategy to reverse existing disease in FD.
affiliations: Moores Cancer Center, University of California San Diego. Department of Pharmacology, School of Medicine, University of California San Diego (corresponding author)

papers.title: NucLogic: Logic-based geometric 3D nuclear segmentation for fast and robust analysis of challenging biological imaging data
papers.abstract: Nuclear segmentation in 3D microscopy remains challenging, particularly for low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) data from timelapse imaging, in vivo experiments, or dense tissue samples. Yet accurate 3D nuclear segmentation is a prerequisite for quantitative single-cell analysis, making this a key bottleneck for high-throughput study of challenging datasets. We present NucLogic, a fast and robust 3D nuclear segmentation algorithm that combines the maturity of 2D segmentation with geometric stitching rules based on nuclear shape, orientation, and intensity, to reconstruct accurate 3D volumes. NucLogic reliably segments challenging datasets including long-term timelapse imaging of organoids, and large dense structures such as the zebrafish brain. Benchmarked against other state-of-the-art segmentation tools, NucLogic matches F1 scores at high SNR, with increasing outperformance as SNR decreases. Importantly, segmentation completes at 20-50% of the computation time, with greater speed gains on larger images. Beyond segmentation, NucLogic includes an intuitive graphical user interface allowing non-experts to segment, quantify, and visualize 3D and 4D data. This enables easy quantification of cell numbers and integration of a variety of both cell-intrinsic properties, such as phenotype, morphology, and local environment metrics, including density and spatial interactions. Together, NucLogic makes quantitative 3D nuclear analysis of previously unmanageable datasets accessible to a broad research community.
affiliations: Utrecht University (corresponding author)

papers.title: TriPort tangential flow filtration: a lab-assembled system for EV isolation across diverse cell-culture sources
papers.abstract: Tangential flow filtration (TFF) is an effective method for scalable EV isolation. Here, we describe and validate a reference protocol for TriPort-TFF, a laboratory-assembled TFF system featuring a three- port reservoir design enabling sample circulation, retentate return, and diafiltration. Constructed from individually sourced, commercially available components with detailed assembly and operating parameters, TriPort-TFF can be built at a lower cost than commercially integrated TFF platforms. We evaluated the system using conditioned media (CM) from human MDM cultured with EV-depleted human serum, human cerebral organoids in serum-free medium, and mouse BMDM cultured with EV-depleted foetal bovine serum (FBS) unstimulated or LPS-stimulated. The system reproducibly isolated EVs from all three sources, and biological replicates of BMDM showed distinct proteomic clusters between LPS-stimulated and unstimulated conditions. The requirement for subsequent size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) after TFF depended on the sample serum-presence. In serum-containing CM, TFF alone co-concentrated serum proteins alongside EVs, subsequent SEC improved the particle-to- protein ratio, reduced inter-replicate variability and improved proteomic depth. TFF alone in serum- free organoid CM already yielded higher particle-to-protein ratios than TFF-only preparations from serum-containing CM, with SEC further improving this ratio. TriPort-TFF offers an accessible system for EV-isolation that can be combined with SEC for diverse sample types.
affiliations: School of Medical Sciences, University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW, Australia (corresponding author)

papers.title: Capture of Post-Pluripotency Human Neuromesodermal and Neural Tube Axial Stem Cell States
papers.abstract: The capture of pluripotent and adult tissue stem cells has transformed biomedicine, yet stable stem cell states between these developmental extremes have remained elusive. Here, we capture two human axial stem cell (AxSC) states corresponding to neuromesodermal and derivative neural tube progenitors. These states maintain telomere length without teratoma formation, and neuromesodermal AxSCs were recaptured from human embryonic tail buds. Mechanistically, genome-wide knockout screening and multiomics analyses revealed capture-associated acquisition of a stemness regulatory network with Trithorax-Polycomb dual functionality. Integration with genome-wide DNA methylation analysis identified a novel HOX timer driven by time-grouped DNA demethylation of target genes. Additionally, stage-specific glycolytic/OXPHOS remodeling in AxSCs was linked to bioenergetic pathways and histone acetylation dynamics. Finally, we captured mouse AxSCs that contribute to chimeras and exhibit an evolutionary divergent neuromesodermal-neural combined state. AxSCs are authentic post pluripotent stem cells for upscalable interrogation of development, with potential for regenerative medicine and drug discovery.
affiliations: Division of Drug Discovery and Safety, Leiden Academic Centre for Drug Research (LACDR), Leiden University, The Netherlands Department of Cell and Chemical Biol (corresponding author)

papers.title: Adenosine refines the balance of spermatogonial proliferation and differentiation
papers.abstract: The balance between spermatogonial proliferation and differentiation is essential for sustaining male fertility, yet the contribution of cellular metabolism remains poorly understood. Here, we showed that adenosine levels increased significantly during spermatogonial differentiation and promoted the formation of differentiating spermatogonia. Using a conditional knockout mouse model in which Ahcy, a gene encoding an enzyme in adenosine synthesis, is deleted from spermatogonia, we found that disruption of adenosine generation blocked spermatogonial differentiation, resulting in a transient delay in spermatogenesis. We further demonstrated that adenosine exerted its effects partially through ADORA2A- and ADORA2B-mediated signaling. Downregulating these receptor activities by specific inhibitors in spermatogonial culture or by genetic ablation in mice led to increased spermatogonial proliferation. Taken together, our study identified adenosine as a metabolic signal in refining the balance between spermatogonial proliferation and differentiation, linking cellular metabolism to critical developmental timing and stem cell fate decisions.
affiliations: MIchigan State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Integrin α3β1 is required for alveolar-capillary barrier formation through regulation of epithelial differentiation
papers.abstract: Laminin-binding integrins regulate critical morphogenic processes, but their specific roles in lung development are unknown. In this study, we combined an in vivo model of epithelial 3 subunit deletion in the murine lung with a multiomics approach to investigate the role of the epithelial 3{beta}1 integrin during murine lung development. We demonstrate that 3{beta}1 integrin is dispensable for airway branching morphogenesis due to delayed epithelial expression. Instead, in vivo deletion of 3{beta}1 integrin impaired alveolar epithelial cell differentiation and disrupted alveolar-capillary barrier formation, functionally limiting gas exchange. A discontinuous alveolar BM contained abnormal collagen IV and laminin networks and widened the gap between epithelial and endothelial cells in the alveolar-capillary barrier niche. Mechanistically, mice deficient in epithelial 3{beta}1 integrin possessed an intracellular trafficking and secretion defect for BM components. Thus, integrin 3{beta}1 orchestrates the temporal maturation of alveolar epithelial cells required for organization of the alveolar-capillary barrier.
affiliations: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (corresponding author)

papers.title: Nuclear RNA cap-chaperones eIF4E and NCBP2 influence distinct mRNA fates
papers.abstract: Gene expression is considered to converge on a single nuclear checkpoint: NCBP2 which binds the methyl-7-guanosine (m7G) cap on the 5' end of mRNAs and chaperones these transcripts through all downstream processing steps as a constitutive, housekeeping activity. We show instead that a second cap-binding protein, the translation initiation factor eIF4E, also acts in the nucleus, where it and NCBP2 influence largely separate mRNA populations toward divergent outcomes rather than performing redundant, interchangeable roles. Supporting this, eIF4E and NCBP2 overexpression or genetic reduction produced distinct transcriptomic and splicing signatures affecting thousands of transcripts but only a few shared splicing events. We propose a model, mRNA Specification by Cap Chaperones (SOCCs), in which selective association of transcripts with specific cap-chaperones influences their processing. We show that altering cap-chaperone levels changes the association of specific transcripts in the nucleus with eIF4E or NCBP2 and is accompanied by altered processing outcomes that can affect the structure and function of the resulting mRNAs. Multiple properties underpin SOCCs, including spatial segregation of eIF4E and NCBP2 within the nucleus and non-overlapping cap-chaperone protein-partner networks as well as differential influence of eIF4E and NCBP2 on production of the processing machinery itself. Together, these findings suggest cap-chaperone selection as a previously unrecognized regulatory layer in gene expression, positioned to influence all nuclear mRNA processing steps as well as nuclear mRNA export.
affiliations: Department of Pharmacology and Robert H. Lurie Cancer Centre, Northwestern University, Chicago, Illinois, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Conservation of gene co-expression networks and neuropsychiatric-neurological disease gene programs between mouse and human frontal cortex at single-cell resolution
papers.abstract: Mouse models are widely used in translational neuroscience, but whether a gene has the same partners in mouse and human prefrontal cortex (PFC) is unknown. The genes whose expression rises and falls with a given gene across samples (its co-expression partners) indicate the molecular program to which it belongs. We compared the co-expression of 13,214 genes between mouse medial PFC and human dorsolateral PFC in 246,211 single-nucleus RNA-sequencing profiles. These two regions are not homologous, so part of any measured difference may reflect region and not species. The study has five main findings. First, the similarity of partners for single genes was modest (median 0.169; 0, unrelated; 1, identical). This median was below that of every comparison among human datasets but within the range of comparisons among mouse datasets, and correction for measurement noise raised it to 0.349 at most. Second, groups of co-expressed genes (modules) were strongly preserved. Third, neuropsychiatric disease genes were modestly more conserved than other genes, but no more than control genes matched for mutational constraint and expression, consistent with general gene properties and with how these genes are discovered. Fourth, no disease gene was shown to have different partners in the two species. Fifth, four of five human modules recurred in an independent human dataset. We also identified two sources of error: analyzing only the most variable genes excludes most disease genes, and networks built from few samples, as for glial cells, underestimate the similarity between species. Scores and code are released for cross-species studies.
affiliations: University of Wyoming (corresponding author)

papers.title: Metatranscriptomics reveals diverse microbial communities in PCR-negative severe acute respiratory infections
papers.abstract: Severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) are a major cause of hospitalisation and mortality globally, yet a proportion of cases remain without an identified aetiology following routine diagnostic testing. Here, we used metatranscriptomic sequencing to characterise microbial communities in 300 PCR-negative SARI nasopharyngeal samples collected through sentinel hospital-based surveillance in Aotearoa New Zealand between 2014 and 2021. Transcripts from microbial species with recognised or potential associations with respiratory infection were detected in 43% of samples, comprising 10 RNA viruses, three DNA viruses, nine bacterial species and four fungal species. Multiple microbial species were detected in 26% of positive samples, highlighting the polymicrobial composition of a subset of PCR-negative SARI cases. Human rhinoviruses were the most frequently detected viruses despite being included in the original PCR screening, while seasonal human coronaviruses, human parechovirus A1 and parainfluenza virus type 4 were also identified, including viruses not included in the diagnostic panel. Bacterial and fungal taxa associated with respiratory infection were also detected, alongside transcripts corresponding to characterised virulence factors and antimicrobial resistance genes. Infectome composition showed statistically significant but modest associations with patient age and year of sample collection. As healthy comparative samples were unavailable, detection of microbial RNA cannot establish causality or distinguish infection from colonisation or incidental detection. Nevertheless, these findings demonstrate the additional microbial and genomic information obtainable through unbiased sequencing of diagnostically unresolved respiratory samples and support further evaluation of metatranscriptomics as a complementary approach to targeted PCR for respiratory disease surveillance and investigation.
affiliations: University of Otago - Dunedin Campus: University of Otago (corresponding author)

papers.title: Tertiary structure of a Nif11-like leader peptide mediates protein-protein interactions with a RiPP biosynthetic enzyme
papers.abstract: Ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) are produced from precursor peptides that typically contain a short, unstructured N-terminal leader region that engages RiPP biosynthetic enzymes through peptide-protein contacts. A distinct subclass of leader peptides, the nitrogen-fixing protein 11-like leader peptides (Nif11-LPs), are unusually long and conspicuously enriched in cyanobacteria. No atomic structures of Nif11-LPs have been reported. Here, we report the solution structure of MppEleader, a Nif11-LP from the marine cyanobacterium Moorena producens PAL. MppEleader adopts a bipartite architecture with a rigid N-terminal tetrahelical bundle stabilized around a hydrophobic nucleus, followed by a dynamic, largely disordered C-terminal region containing a conserved L(X)L motif. We show that the -ketoglutarate/non-heme iron enzyme MppG dihydroxylates the macrocyclized MppEcore peptide in a strictly leader-dependent manner. NMR titrations and structure-guided mutagenesis demonstrate that both the tetrahelical hydrophobic nucleus and the L(X)L motif of MppE make direct, functionally required contacts with MppG, including its RiPP recognition element (RRE) domain. An AlphaFold3-guided structural model rationalizes these contacts. Together, these findings establish a tertiary structure-dependent protein-protein interaction paradigm for RiPP core peptide modification, distinguishing Nif11-LP recognition from canonical short-leader mechanisms and expanding the understanding of substrate recognition in RiPP biosynthesis.
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: β-Hairpin Fold Peptide Brush Polymers
papers.abstract: Peptide-brush polymers prepared via graft-through polymerization of peptide-based olefinic monomers form Protein-Like Polymers (PLPs) with demonstrated utility as chemical biology tools for modulating intracellular protein--protein interactions and are in development as a emerging class of therapeutic. This favorable bioactivity has been achieved in part by mimicking some of the structural and functional features of proteins, such as their dynamic, globular solution-phase structures, ability to insert into lipid membranes and enter cells, and tendency to enforce -helicity in peptide side chains. However, because structure leads to function, insight into the structure of these proteomimetic polymers, particularly their overall tertiary structure and the extent to which this influences the brush peptide structure, is incomplete. To further this understanding, we prepared a set of brush polymers incorporating the trpzip2 peptide sequence, commonly used as a model system for protein folding. We examine these polymers via circular dichroism spectroscopy, infrared spectroscopy, and small-angle X-ray scattering, coupled with insights from molecular dynamics simulations. Here, a loss of the {beta}-hairpin structure of the monomer is observed regardless of polymer composition, and simulations corroborate that the polymer backbone destabilizes local secondary structure, restricting peptide motion and altering the accessible free-energy landscape. This study provides insight into design rules governing these synthetic polymer-based proteomimetics.
affiliations: Northwestern University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structural basis of eIF4E recognition of synthetic mRNA 5' cap analogues links cap architecture to affinity and biological activity
papers.abstract: Eukaryotic mRNAs carry a 5'-terminal 7-methylguanosine (m7G) cap that is recognized by multiple cellular proteins and is essential for mRNA self-discrimination, stability, and translation. The eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E (eIF4E) binds the 5' cap and promotes recruitment of mRNAs to the ribosomal translation initiation complex, a critical step in cap-dependent translation. Beyond naturally occurring cap modifications that modulate mRNA interactions and fate, non-natural 5' cap modifications can be used to finely tune diverse aspects of mRNA biology. This has gained particular relevance with the emergence of in vitro transcribed mRNAs as a powerful therapeutic modality for protein replacement therapies and vaccines. Here, we report binding data for a series of synthetic 5' cap analogues interacting with eIF4E, together with X-ray crystal structures of eIF4E-cap complexes, providing detailed insights into the structural determinants of cap recognition by eIF4E. Furthermore, analysis of gene expression from mRNAs carrying different synthetic cap analogues in human cell lines and mice revealed a relationship between cap architecture and protein expression. Taken together, our structural, biochemical, and functional data establish structure-activity relationships for synthetic cap analogues and identify structural features associated with enhanced translational performance.
affiliations: University of Munich (LMU) (corresponding author)

papers.title: Differential Adaptation of Osteocyte Lacunar Morphology at Bone (Re)modeling Sites under Mechanical Loading and Pharmacological Therapies in a Mouse Model of Osteoporosis
papers.abstract: Postmenopausal osteoporosis is a highly prevalent disease characterized by low bone mass and structural deterioration of bone tissue leading to increased bone fragility and fracture risk. Osteocytes orchestrate local bone (re)modeling and therefore, characterizing their 3D morphological and spatial distribution across distinct (re)modeling microenvironments is essential for understanding the cellular mechanisms underlying divergent tissue-level responses. To address this, we used a 3D-3D multiscale registration framework mapping endpoint osteocyte lacunae onto dynamic, time-lapsed in vivo (re)modeling sites. Ovariectomized 15-week-old mice were subjected to 4 weeks of anabolic parathyroid hormone (PTH) or anti-catabolic bisphosphonate (BIS) treatment as monotreatment or combined with cyclic mechanical loading (ML). Biweekly in vivo micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) to identify (re)modeling sites and endpoint ultra-high resolution (ultra-HR) micro-CT to characterize osteocyte lacunae was performed. Osteocyte lacunae were characterized by lacunar density, volume and sphericity. Our findings showed that physical and pharmacological therapies differentially regulate the osteocyte lacunar network through distinct perilacunar adaptations across functional microenvironments. While BIS stabilizes local lacunar architecture, PTH drives asymmetrical lacunar expansion (increased volume with reduced sphericity) through perilacunar remodeling that supersedes any added ML effects. Crucially, estrogen loss disrupts the natural spatial maturation gradient by inducing rounding of lacunae in newly formed bone. Therapies counteract this disruption, restoring the healthy gradients in lacunar morphometry between spatially distinct microenvironments. Additionally, despite restoring tissue-level bone volume, physical and pharmacological osteoporosis therapies do not fully recover persistent lacunar density deficits. The overall lacunar morphological spatial signatures confirm active osteocytic tuning to endocrine, physical and matrix cues.
affiliations: ETH Zurich (corresponding author)

papers.title: Slice, Subtract, Segment: Efficient 2D and Physiologically Informed 3D Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.abstract: Background. Automated segmentation of glioma subregions on multiparametric MRI can be improved by changing either the network architecture or the information presented to the network. These two design levers are usually studied together, which makes their individual contributions difficult to see. We present an integrated analysis of two completed, independent studies, each of which isolates one lever. Methods. In the architecture-level study (Slice), SIBA-UNet - a 2D U-Net combining depthwise separable convolution, inverted-bottleneck blocks and attention-guided skip fusion - was trained on 128 x 128 multimodal slices from BraTS 2020 with a patient-level split, and a sigmoid decision threshold was selected on validation data. In the representation-level study (Subtract), CMSR-3D augmented the four standard MRI sequences with four voxel-wise cross-modal subtraction maps (T1-T1CE, T2-FLAIR, FLAIR-T1CE, T2-T1CE) and evaluated 4-, 6- and 8-channel inputs with an identical 3D U-Net on 1,251 BraTS-GLI 2023 cases (1,001/125/125 split). Results. SIBA-UNet reached an overall validation Dice of 0.8601 at a validation-selected threshold of 0.51, with reported subregion Dice of 0.8795 (necrotic core), 0.8501 (edema) and 0.9125 (enhancing tumor); the source ablation was only partially reported. With the architecture held fixed, the 8-channel CMSR-3D configuration gave the highest mean Dice among the evaluated inputs (0.8699 vs. 0.8534 for the 4-channel baseline) and the lowest mean HD95 (5.9859 vs. 8.2308), whereas either two-map subset alone changed mean Dice by at most 0.0037. Conclusions. Architecture design and input-representation design are separable levers for brain tumor segmentation. The controlled representation ablation indicates that the complete set of subtraction maps was more informative than either subset under a fixed 3D U-Net. Both studies were evaluated internally on their respective datasets, and their numerical results are not directly compared because the datasets, dimensionality and evaluation protocols differ.
affiliations: Sikkim Manipal Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Benchmarking cartilage regeneration across ten chondrogenic cell sources using native tissue references
papers.abstract: A persistent challenge in cartilage tissue engineering is identifying cell sources capable of regenerating cartilage with native-like properties. Variability in chondrogenic potential among human- and animal-derived cells complicates graft development and disease modeling. Here we benchmarked ten chondrogenic cell sources under standardized culture conditions using hyaluronan-alginate biomaterials and implementing a functionality index combining histological and mechanical metrics referenced to native tissue. Mesenchymal stem cells and fetal chondroprogenitors demonstrated superior regenerative capacity, achieving 103% and 95% of native cartilage functionality, respectively. In contrast, adult articular chondrocytes from healthy and osteoarthritic donors produced fibrocartilaginous tissue with functionality scores below 50%. These findings provide a quantitative framework to guide cell source selection and optimize cartilage graft standardization for clinical applications and physiologically relevant disease models, addressing regulatory demands for product characterization.
affiliations: Tissue Engineering and Biofabrication, Department of Health Science and Technology, ETH Zurich; Otto-Stern-Weg 7, Zurich, CH-8093, Switzerland; Manufacturing 4 (corresponding author)

papers.title: Complex enzyme active site scaffolding by iteratively detuned catalytic guidance
papers.abstract: De novo enzyme design requires sequences whose structures reproduce prescribed catalytic geometries. This remains challenging for active sites that couple multiple catalytic residues, cofactors and substrates. Here we introduce the Catalytic Guidance Engine (CaGE), which optimizes designed sequences to satisfy complex sets of functional constraints by alternating constraint guided structure prediction trajectories with sequence design, gradually fading the strength of the constraint information over cycles to nudge the designed sequence towards satisfying all the constraints. We train RF3 to accept atom-pair distances and other design conditions, and use classifier-free guidance to fade their influence over multiple design cycles. We also develop training-free motif guidance protocols which operate at inference time by directly adjusting selected atoms towards the design target geometry during diffusion sampling. CaGE improves catalytic-motif geometry across a diverse enzyme benchmark and yields sequences that recover complex target active sites in independent AF3 predictions. We experimentally demonstrate the power of CaGE by designing active enzymes with complex catalytic sites: a nonheme-iron design positions four active-site residues around an iron centre and a transition-state ligand, and a PLP-dependent design positions four catalytic residues around a PLP cofactor with multiple functional groups. Active site substitutions and a 2.7[A] crystal structure support the designed mechanisms and structures. Thus, CaGE provides a route to functional de novo enzymes with complex active sites.
affiliations: Institute for Protein Design, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98105, USA; Howard Hughes Medical Institute, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98105, US (corresponding author)

papers.title: Dynamic RhoA-Mediated Remodeling of Ordered Membrane Domains
papers.abstract: The formation of ordered proteolipid membrane domains (OMDs) within the plasma membrane has emerged as a fundamental process that modifies membrane function, particularly in response to cell stresses that promote pathological states. Here, we identify a previously unrecognized role for the small GTPase RhoA to rapidly modulate OMDs, thereby linking cytoskeletal remodeling and membrane mechanics to OMD formation. Pharmacological and optogenetic manipulation of RhoA rapidly altered OMD dimensions in both human cell lines and dorsal root ganglion (DRG) nociceptors. The RhoA-dependent OMD expansion required actin remodeling, changes in membrane mechanical state, and protein palmitoylation. Furthermore, in a spared nerve injury (SNI) model of neuropathic pain associated with altered membrane mechanics, disrupted OMD organization, and neuronal hyperexcitability, RhoA activation promoted OMD remodeling and was accompanied by reduced HCN channel activity and action potential firing. These findings highlight alterations in plasma membrane physical properties, including changes in OMD organization, as key features of neuropathic stress. RhoA-driven OMD remodeling, mediated by diaphanous-related formin and Rho-associated kinase, may serve as a compensatory membrane adaptation that counteracts neuropathic hyperexcitability.
affiliations: Saint Louis University (corresponding author)

papers.title: RNA and protein are not interchangeable in single-cell spatial multi-omics
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics is increasingly used to infer cellular phenotypes, molecular interactions, and functional tissue organization from RNA, although most of these biological processes are ultimately mediated by proteins. Here, we directly tested the interchangeability of spatial RNA and protein measurements using paired Xenium profiling of 21 matched targets across ~1.8 million cells from primary lung adenocarcinoma and metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. After accounting for marker- and dataset-specific protein background, we quantified concordance at multiple levels, including single-cell detection, expression magnitude, cell-type distribution, patient-level abundance, and spatial organization. Agreement at single-cell level was strongly marker-dependent. Canonical lineage markers generally showed concordant RNA and protein patterns, whereas several molecules, including in our study PD-1, PD-L1, and LAG-3, showed little concordance across modalities. Importantly, spatial organization remained substantially more discordant between modalities than overall abundance, indicating that spatial biomarkers are not directly transferable across modalities. Together, our results show that spatial RNA and protein measurements provide largely overlapping information for lineage markers and overall abundance, but can diverse for specific molecules and for higher-order spatial features, where the two layers provide complementary rather than equivalent readouts. These findings provide practical guidance on when spatial transcriptomic readouts can be interpreted as proxies for protein and when orthogonal protein validation is advisable.
affiliations: Josep Carreras Research Institute, Spain; Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC), Spain (corresponding author)

papers.title: HMGA2 Expression in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Controls Tumor Microenvironment and Immunosuppression via IL1α
papers.abstract: The basal-like subtype of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is associated with poor outcomes and increased chemoresistance. Expression of high mobility group AT-hook 2 (HMGA2), a chromatin architectural protein, marks basal PDAC cells and associates with specific features of the tumor microenvironment (TME), including more immunosuppressive cancer associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and fewer cytotoxic CD8+ T cells. Expression of HMGA2 by tumor cells leads to upregulation of the immunosuppressive markers interleukin 6 (IL6) and leucine-rich repeat containing protein 15 (LRRC15) in associated fibroblasts. Mechanistically, HMGA2 in the tumor cell binds the interleukin 1 alpha (IL1) promoter and upregulates transcription, increasing IL1 in the TME, in turn inducing immunosuppressive fibroblast polarization, increasing regulatory T cells, and decreasing CD8+ T cells. Blockade of the IL1 signaling axis disrupts this tumor-driven microenvironment phenotype and combines with inhibitors of oncogenic KRAS to improve tumor control.
affiliations: Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Targeted tumor desialylation by engineered probiotic reprograms the tumor microenvironment to potentiate immunotherapy
papers.abstract: Tumor hypersialylation drives immunosuppression and limits immunotherapy efficacy by shielding tumor cells and engaging inhibitory immune receptors. Here, we engineered Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN{Delta}pgi-SAS) as a metabolically confined "desialylation catalyst" to remodel the tumor microenvironment. This strain combines HER2-directed adhesion, hypoxia-inducible surface sialidase display for targeted glycan cleavage, and sialic acid catabolism to prevent glycolytic recycling. Critically, disrupting glucose metabolism ({Delta}pgi) restricts bacterial proliferation to sialic acid-rich tumor microenvironment, significantly enhancing biosafety. In mice, EcN{Delta}pgi-SAS colonized tumors and effectively desialylated tumor cells, synergizing with anti-PD-L1 to suppress growth of immunologically "cold" tumors. Mechanistically, desialylation reversed immunosuppression by broadly enhancing antitumor immunity. Orally administered EcN{Delta}pgi-SAS substantially inhibited colorectal carcinogenesis, repaired epithelial barrier integrity by restoring tight junctions, and prevented adenoma formation. This integrated strategy establishes a clinically translatable platform for reversing immunosuppression in solid tumors.
affiliations: Sun Yat-sen University (corresponding author)

papers.title: PepRePs: Peptide-Retargeted Phosphatases Designed with Generative Language Models
papers.abstract: Phosphorylation is a fast, reversible layer of post-translational control that directly governs protein activity, signaling flux, and cell state. Kinases and phosphatases collectively establish these phosphorylation states, but their dysregulation drives cancer, neurodegenerative diseases, and developmental disorders. Selectively manipulating the phosphorylation of individual proteins in cells remains challenging, particularly for disordered substrates. Here, we introduce Peptide-Retargeted Phosphatases (PepRePs), a genetically encoded system that fuses a peptide binder to a serine/threonine phosphatase subunit to localize phosphatase activity to a target protein. We first establish the PepReP architecture using characterized tau-binding peptides, then apply protein language model-guided peptide design to target Rab8A, PTEN, and STAT3. Across endogenous and exogenous targets, PepRePs reduce phosphorylation, with downstream effects on tau aggregation, Rab8A-associated protein interactions, and cellular proliferation following PTEN and STAT3 targeting. Sequence-based peptide design enables targeting without structural inputs, supporting application to substrates with disordered regions that challenge conventional structure-based binder design. By coupling programmable peptide binders with modular phosphatase subunits, PepRePs enable targeted control of protein phosphorylation to probe cellular signaling and develop strategies for correcting disease-associated protein dysfunction.
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania (corresponding author)

papers.title: Diet-conditioned microbiota enhances fecal microbiota transplantation efficacy in alcoholic liver disease through caproic acid-PPARα signaling
papers.abstract: Background and Aim: Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) in Alcohol-related liver disease (ALD) has shown therapeutic potential, with variable efficacy and unclear mechanism. Because dietary protein influences gut microbiota composition, we hypothesized that donor dietary preconditioning could enhance FMT efficacy. We therefore examined in a murine ALD model if high-protein donor diet improves FMT outcome. Methods: ALD was induced in C57BL/6N mice using a Lieber-DeCarli ethanol diet combined with thioacetamide administration for 12 weeks. FMT was performed using stool from diet-modulated donors, and recovery was assessed on day7 post-FMT. Multi-omics analysis using 16s rRNA and mass spectroscopy was performed for Gut microbiota composition, plasma- and stool-metabolome, and hepatic proteomes. Multi-omics outcomes were validated in ALD animal and Huh7 hepatocytes. Results: Both protein-based FMTs improved ALD recovery; Veg-FMT indicated superior efficacy, significantly reducing hepatic injury (AST 1.2FC, p=0.002; bilirubin 1.2FC, p=0.03; steatosis 1.7FC,p=0.01) and restoring gut barrier integrity (occludin 1.5FC,p=0.04; mucin 2 2.2FC, p=002; and plasma endotoxin 1.7FC, p=0.02). A significant 2FC increase was observed in Lachnospiraceae NK4A136, Coriobacteriaceae UCG-002, and short-chain fatty acids, particularly caproic acid. Functional validation confirmed that caproic acid promoted hepatic fatty acid {beta}-oxidation through PPAR-dependent mechanisms, reducing triglyceride accumulation and lipogenesis in both cellular and animal models. Conclusion: Donor preconditioning with a plant-protein enriched diet enhances FMT efficacy in ALD by gut microbiota modulation with increased metabolites like caproic acid. These findings highlight a microbiota-metabolite-host axis through which diet-modulated FMT improves hepatic lipid metabolism and injury, and identifies a pathway via which FMT imparts its effect.
affiliations: Institute of Liver and Biliary Sciences (corresponding author)

papers.title: Metabolic commitment to human motor neurons is characterized by mitochondrial depletion and pyruvate rewiring
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial remodelling is a key feature of neurogenesis in cortical and hippocampal neuronal lineages, yet the temporal control of organellar homeostasis in developing human motor neurons remains poorly understood. Here, we generated a high-resolution temporal resource integrating proteomics, metabolomics, and mitochondrial characterization across human iPSC-to-motor neuron differentiation. This analysis revealed prolonged mitochondrial depletion during early neurogenesis, characterized by reduced mitochondrial content, mitochondrial fragmentation, and lysosome-dependent turnover. This state persisted throughout the neural progenitor stage and was followed by recovery of mitochondrial content during neuronal maturation. During this transition, pyruvate utilization shifted from pyruvate carboxylation towards pyruvate dehydrogenase-dependent oxidation. Pharmacological manipulation of pyruvate partitioning demonstrated that this metabolic switch is required for human neuronal differentiation. Our findings establish a temporal framework for the metabolic control of human motor neuron differentiation and reveal a progenitor-specific state linking mitochondrial depletion to pyruvate metabolism.
affiliations: University of Helsinki (corresponding author)

papers.title: Glutathione Protects Hematopoietic Stem Cells from Proteotoxic Stress
papers.abstract: Glutathione is a redox buffer, best known for preventing oxidative stress and ferroptosis, but rarely studied in stem cells. We studied glutathione function in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) by deleting the glutamate-cysteine ligase catalytic subunit (GCLC), which synthesizes glutathione, or glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), which employs glutathione to prevent ferroptosis. GCLC deficiency eliminated glutathione from hematopoietic cells, severely impairing HSC function and hematopoiesis. In contrast, GPX4 deficiency did not affect HSC function and had little effect on hematopoiesis, even after vitamin E depletion, suggesting glutathione has ferroptosis-independent functions in HSCs. Consistent with this, GCLC deficiency increased reactive oxygen species levels in hematopoietic cells. But treatment with antioxidants or ferroptosis inhibitors gave little or no rescue of HSC function despite reducing ROS levels. Rather, GCLC-deficient, but not GPX4-deficient, HSCs exhibited unfolded protein accumulation, proteostatic stress, and cell death marked by elevated p53 levels and Annexin V staining. Deficiency for p53 prolonged the function of GCLC-deficient HSCs after transplantation. Glutathione is thus necessary in HSCs for proteostasis but may be dispensable for ferroptosis inhibition in vivo.
affiliations: Howard Hughes Medical Institute, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: A tonic PDGFA-dependent niche organizer maintains alveolar homeostasis
papers.abstract: Tissue homeostasis requires mechanisms that preserve quiescence while allowing rapid activation after injury, but how tissues actively restrain injury responses during homeostasis remains poorly understood. Here we identify alveolar type 1 (AT1) cells as organizers of the distal lung niche through tonic expression of PDGFA, which maintains alveolar fibroblast identity and restrains myofibroblast activation. Cell type-specific ablation revealed that loss of AT1s, but not other major alveolar cell populations, was sufficient to evoke spontaneous fibroblast activation and tissue-wide responses that recapitulate injury. In silico ligand-receptor analysis, ex vivo screening, and conditional genetic models identified AT1-derived PDGFA as a key homeostatic signal. Loss of AT1-derived PDGFA caused spontaneous myofibroblast induction and tissue remodeling, whereas increasing PDGFA promoted fibroblast proliferation while suppressing myofibroblast differentiation. Integrated phosphoproteomic, transcriptomic, and chromatin accessibility analyses showed that PDGFA engages SHP2-ERK signaling, suppresses MRTFA-associated SRF programs, and promotes E2F-associated cell-cycle programs, thereby opposing the pro-fibrotic effects of TGF{beta}-driven fibroblast activation. Restoring PDGFA signaling abrogates myofibroblast features from human idiopathic pulmonary fibrotic lungs and attenuated fibrotic remodeling in vivo. These findings define a tonic AT1-derived PDGFA signal that maintains alveolar homeostasis and offers a therapeutic target to prevent or revert lung fibrosis.
affiliations: Department of Cell Biology, Duke University School of Medicine, Durham, NC 27710, USA; Duke Regeneration Center, Duke University, Durham, NC 27710, USA; Divisio (corresponding author)

papers.title: Evolution and remodeling of acceptor specificity in the NodZ α-1,6-fucosyltransferase
papers.abstract: Glycosyltransferases have broad diversity in their acceptor substrates, yet the molecular and evolutionary basis of this diversity remains poorly understood. NodZ is an -1,6-fucosyltransferase that fucosylates Nod factors, lipochitooligosaccharide molecules involved in the establishment of rhizobium-legume symbioses. While NodZ is the only known bacterial member of the GT23 family of -1,6-fucosyltransferases, the determinants of its acceptor selectivity and the evolutionary origins thereof are unclear. Here, a phylogenetic analysis of 332 NodZ-like proteins revealed a distinct rhizobial clade and significantly greater structural diversity in the N-terminus than in the C-terminus. Kinetic analysis of a Mesorhizobium japonicum NodZ demonstrated selectivity for longer chitooligosaccharide acceptors (comprised of four to five GlcNAc units), while alanine scanning revealed W139 as a primary determinant of this chain length preference. We propose that W139 forms an aromatic platform that engages distal GlcNAc units present only in longer acceptors, coupling productive binding to acceptor chain length. We then used the NodZ phylogeny to reconstruct ancestral NodZ homolog sequences, which indicated that W139 emerged at the base of the rhizobial clade, and thus may represent a key evolutionary step towards canonical NodZ function. Additionally, the most recent resurrected ancestor was capable of fucosylating chitooligosaccharides with lower efficiency than the extant NodZ, suggesting that efficiency towards chitooligosaccharides was improved during the evolution of this family. Results described here demonstrate that evolutionary diversification of the N-terminal region can remodel acceptor specificity while preserving the conserved catalytic architecture of GT23 fucosyltransferases, providing a framework for understanding and engineering fucosyltransferase specificity.
affiliations: Queen's University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Prime editing enables high-throughput identification and characterization of selective MutSβ inhibitors
papers.abstract: DNA mismatch repair (MMR) maintains genome stability but paradoxically drives expansion of pathogenic repeats responsible for trinucleotide repeat disorders. Attenuating repeat instability through targeted inhibition of MMR is therefore a therapeutic strategy of interest; however, progress is constrained by a lack of robust methods for defining and isolating MMR subpathways. We exploited features of prime editing to profile the effects of core MMR genes on thousands of programmed DNA mispairs in cells and resolved distinct MMR processes, including a noncanonical, loop-directed mechanism. Guided by these results, we built a set of scalable reporters that detect loss of separable MMR processes and screened ~72,000 small molecules for activity against MutS{beta}-directed MMR. This effort identified a novel series of MutS{beta} inhibitors that reduced (CAG)n expansion in a cell model. Altogether, this study establishes several methods for systematically interrogating MMR, with demonstrated capacity to identify inhibitors of therapeutic value.
affiliations: Princeton University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Blood-brain barrier-traversing multivalent TGFβ trap for anti-cancer immunomodulation of gliomas
papers.abstract: Clinical studies have revealed that glioblastoma (GBM) is refractory to immunotherapy, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), due to the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) primarily intensified by intratumoral upregulation of transforming growth factor-{beta} (TGF{beta}). Primary GBM tumor bulks are surgically removed in clinic, but invasive tumor cells infiltrated into surrounding normal brain tissue cannot be eradicated by systemic therapy due to the integral blood-brain barrier (BBB), leading to near-inevitable tumor recurrence. To address these translational challenges, we have engineered a TGF{beta}-inhibiting protein nanocage comprising human heavy-chain ferritin protein and TGF{beta} receptor II ectodomain that enables BBB penetration and multivalent TGF{beta} entrapment, respectively. We demonstrate that the nanocage platform, denoted T{beta}R2-HFt, following systemic administration, traverses the BBB, and extensively modulates immunosuppressive TME, both stromal and immune components, thereby potentiating the therapeutic efficacy of a clinically used ICI in multiple mouse glioma models. Notably, a majority of the glioma-bearing animals that received surgical tumor resection, followed by treatment with T{beta}R2-HFt and the ICI, survived the tumor and resisted tumor rechallenge, providing a potential means to control GBM in a durable manner.
affiliations: Department of Neurosurgery, University of Maryland School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD 21201, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: digestome: a licence-clean marker-gene panel for functional profiling of anaerobic digestion microbiomes
papers.abstract: Functional profiling of anaerobic digestion microbiomes is routinely performed against KEGG or MetaCyc, whose paid commercial licences block fee-for-service analysis for biogas operators, the setting where the results have the most immediate operational value. We present digestome, a curated marker-gene panel for anaerobic digestion built exclusively on sources that are free for commercial use (NCBIfam, public domain; Pfam, CC0; Rhea, CC BY), together with a scorer that reports pathway completeness, branch capability and, for hydrolysis, whether the enzyme is built for export. Benchmarked against 1,401 metagenome-assembled genomes from 134 anaerobic digesters, the panel assigned no methanogenesis route to any of 1,361 non-methanogens, and every acetoclastic call fell within Methanosarcina or Methanothrix. The result held for 3,043 species representatives from the Genome Taxonomy Database, spanning 203 phyla, which are built differently from binned metagenomes: the only background genomes given a route were two archaea carrying mcrA, and none of the 90 anaerobic methane and alkane oxidisers was given one. Specificity against non-methanogens does not show that a methanogen gets the right route: with a family-level check, 59 of 156 acetoclastic calls in that sample fell on methylotrophic genera that do not use acetate, and a lineage policy removed them, with 14 more left unconfirmed in unnamed genera. Testing whether a catalytic domain shares a polypeptide with an export module reduced the genomes credited with cellulolytic capacity from 597 to 50. A causal graph of the measurement shows that a profile reports the community together with three measurement choices (sampling, DNA extraction and sequencing depth, and reference genomes), which fixes what one profile can attribute and what a prospective validation would have to record.
